item.content:encoded:
一句话：支撑轨迹连同它的控制一起当奖励，冻结 Yume-5B 主干只更新 LoRA，把任意一段场景视频变成可交互世界。

要点：

  • 奖励来自「支撑轨迹上的后续采样」：用同一段视频里的画面与控制做对照，统一奖励涵盖场景外观、视觉连续性和运动
  • GRPO 组内相对优化只更新紧凑 LoRA，并用 base-policy anchoring 约束对预训练生成先验的改动；另给 DiffusionNFT 版本作为替代
  • 自建 PWM-Bench 150 个定制任务（室内 / 室外 / 游戏），GRPO 版在 71.3% 的场景优于原生 Yume，DiffusionNFT 版 65.3%；与同等 SFT 相比各域平均增益和画质都更高

为什么值得看：世界模型要落地做内容，缺的就是「用自己的一小段素材定制」。这里的关键设计是奖励不依赖额外标注——支撑轨迹本身就是监督，工程上比再训一个奖励模型便宜得多。

中文摘要：预训练世界模型能生成多样环境，但用户往往只想探索自己视频里的那个场景。PWM 用在线强化学习从短场景视频定制交互式世界模型：支撑轨迹及其控制为当前策略采样的后续提供奖励反馈。在 GRPO 实现里，组内相对优化只更新一个紧凑的 LoRA 适配器，统一奖励同时约束场景外观、视觉连续性与运动，base-policy anchoring 则防止偏离冻结的 Yume-5B 主干先验。同一套适配流程在真实与渲染环境中都适用，另提供 DiffusionNFT 版本。配套的 PWM-Bench 含室内、室外、游戏三类共 150 个定制任务，GRPO 版本在 71.3% 的评测场景中优于原生 Yume。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·AI原生（English）

原文发布：2026-10-04

本期推送：2026-10-24

PWM: Personalized World Models with
Online Reinforcement Learning

Abstract

Pretrained world models can generate diverse environments, yet users often want to explore a particular scene specified by their own video. This requires learning the scene’s visual identity while retaining the quality of action-conditioned generation. We introduce Personalized World Models (PWM), a framework for customizing interactive world models from short scene videos through online reinforcement learning. In PWM, the support trajectory and its associated controls provide reward feedback on continuations sampled from the current policy. In the GRPO instantiation, group-relative optimization updates a compact LoRA adapter using a unified reward for scene appearance, visual continuity, and motion, while base-policy anchoring regularizes changes to the pretrained generation prior of a frozen Yume-5B backbone. The same adaptation procedure is applied across real and rendered environments. We also instantiate PWM with DiffusionNFT as an alternative reward-guided optimization method for learning the scene-specific adapter. We also introduce PWM-Bench, comprising 150 customization tasks across Indoor, Outdoor, and Gaming, with paired evaluation on held-out continuations. The GRPO and DiffusionNFT instantiations of PWM improve customization over native Yume in 71.3% and 65.3% of the evaluated scenes, respectively, with positive mean gains across all three domains. For the GRPO instantiation, matched SFT comparisons further demonstrate higher mean customization gains and better mean image-quality scores in every domain, while retaining frame-level visual quality close to the pretrained model. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/PWM. Website: https://aigeeksgroup.github.io/PWM.

1 Introduction

Interactive world models enable users to explore environments through action-conditioned video generation. Recent systems combine pretrained visual generation priors with user controls and autoregressive rollout, supporting interactive exploration across diverse environments [(Yu et al., 2025; Mao et al., 2026)]. Personalizing this experience introduces a concrete requirement: the generated world should retain the identity of the environment provided by the user. For a particular interior, outdoor location, or game scene, its characteristic appearance and content should remain recognizable as the generated trajectory progresses.

Personalization methods have demonstrated that pretrained generators can acquire visual identity from limited reference observations [(Ruiz et al., 2023)]. Interactive world generation extends this objective to action-conditioned continuations. A short support video provides observations of a scene’s materials, lighting, visual style, and characteristic content. Successful customization should therefore strengthen fidelity to the target environment while retaining the visual quality of the underlying generator.

Reward-based optimization provides a way to express preferences directly on generated images and videos [(Xue et al., 2025)]. For scene customization, the support trajectory can supply the reference needed to evaluate those outputs: whether they match the environment’s appearance and whether their visual evolution is consistent with the observed trajectory.

We introduce Personalized World Models (PWM), a framework for per-scene customization through online reinforcement learning. Given a short support trajectory and its controls, PWM learns a compact LoRA adapter on a frozen Yume-5B backbone. The current policy samples groups of candidate continuations, and reward feedback derived from the support trajectory guides updates to the scene-specific adapter. We instantiate this framework with GRPO and DiffusionNFT as alternative reward-guided optimization methods. Online learning here refers to collecting fresh rollouts from the current policy during adaptation.

Both instantiations use native generation windows, the same adapter capacity, and a shared reward for scene appearance, visual continuity, and motion. The GRPO instantiation additionally uses a base-policy anchor. Optimization and checkpoint-averaging settings are fixed across scenes within each instantiation.

To evaluate this capability, we introduce PWM-Bench, a suite of 150 per-scene customization tasks spanning Indoor, Outdoor, and Gaming. Each task provides an 80-frame support segment and a temporally later, non-overlapping 145-frame test continuation. The benchmark evaluates scene fidelity through appearance agreement and an entity-based hallucination penalty, complemented by frame-level image-quality measurements. Comparisons use three paired random seeds per scene under shared initial context, controls, and generation settings.

Across PWM-Bench, the GRPO instantiation of PWM improves customization over native Yume in 107 of 150 scenes, with a mean relative gain of 6.39%. The DiffusionNFT instantiation improves 98 of 150 scenes, with a mean relative gain of 5.22%. Both instantiations achieve positive mean gains in every domain. Compared with matched SFT, the GRPO instantiation increases the fraction of scenes improved over Native from 57.3% to 71.3% and achieves higher mean customization gains across all three domains. It also obtains better domain-level means than SFT on MUSIQ, NIQE, and BRISQUE, while remaining close to native Yume in these frame-level quality measures.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We introduce PWM, a per-scene customization framework that learns a compact adapter from a short support trajectory through online reinforcement learning on a frozen interactive world model, instantiated with GRPO and DiffusionNFT.

  • •

    We introduce PWM-Bench, comprising 150 customization tasks across three first-person domains, with held-out continuations and a shared protocol for evaluating scene fidelity and visual quality.

  • •

    We demonstrate positive average customization gains over native Yume across all three domains with both optimization methods. Matched SFT comparisons show that the GRPO instantiation benefits more scenes and achieves better mean image-quality scores.

    • 2 Related Work

    Interactive world models.

    Interactive world generation combines visual synthesis with action control to produce trajectories that respond to user inputs. GameFactory [(Yu et al., 2025)] learns action control from game videos and uses a domain adapter with multi-phase training to transfer this capability to open-domain scenes. Yume [(Mao et al., 2025)] combines camera control with autoregressive video generation, while Yume-1.5 [(Mao et al., 2026)] develops context compression and text-controlled interaction for continuous world exploration. These advances establish a foundation for generating and navigating diverse environments. PWM studies how to specialize such a pretrained model to a particular observed scene. Given a short support trajectory, it learns a compact scene adapter for subsequent action-conditioned generation in the same environment.

    Personalization of generative models.

    Personalization adapts a generative prior to visual content specified by limited reference observations. DreamBooth [(Ruiz et al., 2023)] learns a subject from a few images and synthesizes that subject in new contexts. Tune-A-Video [(Wu et al., 2023)] extends adaptation from limited observations to video generation by tuning an image diffusion model on a single text–video pair. Parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA [(Hu et al., 2022)] support this adaptation through trainable low-rank updates to frozen pretrained weights. PWM applies scene-level personalization to an interactive world model: the support video provides observations of the target environment, and the learned adapter is evaluated on a temporally held-out continuation under action controls.

    Reinforcement learning for visual generation.

    Reward-based fine-tuning adapts visual generators to objectives defined on their outputs. DDPO [(Black et al., 2024)] treats iterative denoising as a sequential decision process and applies policy gradients to optimize sample-level rewards. VADER [(Prabhudesai et al., 2024)] optimizes video generation by propagating gradients from differentiable reward models. DanceGRPO [(Xue et al., 2025)] applies group-relative policy optimization to diffusion and rectified-flow models across image and video generation. DiffusionNFT [(Zheng et al., 2026)] performs online reward-guided optimization through the forward noising process, incorporating positive and negative learning signals into a flow-matching objective without requiring likelihood estimation. Building on this line of work, PWM obtains reward feedback from the target scene’s support trajectory and updates a scene-specific adapter using online rollouts. We instantiate PWM with GRPO and DiffusionNFT, using the same scene-level task, adapter capacity, and reward definition. The reward combines visual agreement with initial-frame consistency and motion magnitude matching, connecting reward-based optimization to the scene customization objective.

    Weight averaging.

    Weight averaging combines parameter states into a single model. Stochastic Weight Averaging [(Izmailov et al., 2018)] averages weights along a training trajectory, while Model Soups [(Wortsman et al., 2022)] averages models fine-tuned from a shared pretrained initialization. PWM uses this idea within each scene’s adaptation run, averaging adapter checkpoints to retain a single compact adapter for inference. Each optimization instantiation uses a checkpoint-averaging rule that is fixed across scenes and does not use held-out test frames.

    3 Method

    We propose PWM, a per-scene personalization approach for interactive world models. Given a short preceding trajectory, PWM trains a scene-specific LoRA on frozen Yume-5B to transfer scene knowledge to a subsequent trajectory. The core objectives are visual identity tailored to the target scene, persistent spatial layout, and action responsiveness, while retaining the general action and control priors of the pretrained world model. For this reason, PWM combines scene-specific low-rank parameterization, online reward-guided optimization with GRPO or DiffusionNFT based on native generation windows, a unified reward that balances scene fidelity and motion, and a weight averaging strategy that does not require selecting a single checkpoint.

    Figure 2 summarizes the shared adaptation pipeline and the two online optimization instantiations.

    3.1 Preliminaries: Yume, GRPO, and DiffusionNFT

    Yume interactive world model.

    Yume-1.5 [(Mao et al., 2026)] extends a pretrained video generator into an action-command-controllable interactive world model. Given a compressed visual history hₜ and a sequence uₜ containing action commands for generation window t, the frozen Yume-5B model, parameterized by θ₀, generates the next video segment according to

    Xₜ∼p_θ₀(Xₜ|hₜ,uₜ).

    		(1)

    The control sequence combines discrete translation and camera commands with continuous motion magnitudes. Each generated segment is incorporated into the visual history to condition the subsequent window, resulting in a segment-level autoregressive interaction trajectory. PWM keeps θ₀ frozen and learns only a scene-specific low-rank adapter.

    Group Relative Policy Optimization.

    Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) estimates advantages by comparing a group of samples generated under the same condition, thereby eliminating the need for a learned critic [(Shao et al., 2024)]. Given a condition c, GRPO samples G trajectories from an old-policy snapshot and normalizes their outcome rewards within the group:

    τᵢ∼π_θ_old(·|c), Âᵢ=(rᵢ-r̄)/(sᵣ), i=1,…,G,

    		(2)

    where r̄ and sᵣ denote the mean and standard deviation of {rⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^G. Under outcome-level supervision, the same Âᵢ is assigned to every decision step along trajectory τᵢ.

    Let Kᵢ be the number of decision steps in τᵢ. GRPO optimizes the empirical clipped surrogate

    \beginsplitĴ_clip(θ)&=1/G∑ᵢ₌₁^G1/Kᵢ∑ₖ₌₁^Kᵢ\min(ρ_i,k(θ)Âᵢ, & clip(ρ_i,k(θ),1-ε_clip,1+ε_clip)Âᵢ), ρ_i,k(θ)&=(π_θ(a_i,k|s_i,k))/(π_θ_old(a_i,k|s_i,k)).\endsplit

    		(3)

    GRPO therefore replaces a learned critic with a group-reward baseline rather than removing the baseline altogether. Its original formulation additionally regularizes the policy toward a separate reference policy π_ref. The GRPO instantiation of PWM instead employs the base-policy anchor introduced in Section 3.2.

    Policy interpretation of diffusion and flow sampling.

    Following DDPO and DanceGRPO [(Black et al., 2024; Xue et al., 2025)], iterative diffusion and rectified-flow sampling can be formulated as a finite-horizon Markov decision process. Let cₜ=(hₜ,uₜ) denote the visual history and control condition for video window t. After stochasticizing the reverse-time transition, the state, action, and policy at denoising step k are defined as

    \begingathereds_t,k=(cₜ,k,z_t,k), a_t,k=z_t,k-1, π_θ(a_t,k|s_t,k)=p_θ(z_t,k-1|z_t,k,cₜ).\endgathered

    		(4)

    A complete latent trajectory τₜ=(z_t,K,…,z_t,0) produces one video segment and receives a terminal reward. Under group-relative optimization, the resulting trajectory advantage is assigned to each denoising transition. Here, k indexes the internal denoising process, whereas t indexes the external sequence of autoregressive video windows.

    We use online to mean that each data-collection round collects fresh trajectories from the latest behavior-policy snapshot. It does not refer to continual adaptation after deployment.

    DiffusionNFT.

    DiffusionNFT [(Zheng et al., 2026)] performs online reward-guided optimization through a forward-process flow-matching objective. Generated samples are assigned reward-dependent weights, which determine their contributions to positive and negative learning branches. These branches are constructed from the current model’s velocity prediction and a fixed behavior-policy prediction, allowing reward-guided updates without estimating sampling-trajectory likelihoods. PWM instantiates this objective for scene-specific LoRA adaptation, as described in Section 3.3.

    Problem Formulation: Per-scene Customization

    Let a scene s be a temporally ordered controlled trajectory Dₛ={(xₜ,uₜ)}ₜ₌₁ᵀ, where xₜ is a video frame and uₜ contains translation, camera, and continuous motion controls. A support prefix Dₛˢᵘᵖ is available for adaptation. The goal is to specialize the model to the persistent identity of s and transfer that knowledge to a later, unseen portion of the same scene. No frame from the future evaluation portion is used for optimization or checkpoint construction.

    We start from a frozen Yume-5B world model with parameters θ₀. For each scene, PWM learns an independent rank-8 LoRA adapter Δθₛ (20.2M trainable parameters), while all backbone parameters remain fixed. The resulting policy is π_θ₀+Δθₛ. This factorization assigns complementary roles to the two parameter sets: the frozen backbone supplies the general action-conditioned generation prior, whereas the adapter stores knowledge specific to the target scene. The current paper uses the same adapter capacity for both optimization methods, every scene, and every first-person domain.

    3.2 Per-scene Customization via Online GRPO

    Learning in the deployment geometry.

    PWM trains directly with Yume’s native 29-frame generation window. We cover the support trajectory with six overlapping windows whose start indices are [0,9,18,27,36,45]. Each window is initialized by its real first frame and is conditioned on the controls measured for that window. Training and deployment therefore share the same temporal geometry; no auxiliary short-window policy is introduced.

    On-policy group-relative optimization.

    PWM instantiates the GRPO update in Eq. 3 with a group of G=4 diffusion trajectories for each support window. The trajectories share the initial latent noise to control nuisance variation while retaining independent stochastic SDE transitions. Because the unified reward contains components with different numerical scales, we normalize each component separately before combining their advantages. For reward component m and rollout i, we compute

    Aᵢ=∑ₘαₘ(R_i,m-μₘ)/(σₘ+ε), (μₘ,σₘ)=MeanStdⱼ₌₁^G [R_j,m],

    		(5)

    where αₘ is the weight of component m in Eq. (12). The resulting Aᵢ replaces the scalar-reward advantage Âᵢ in Eq. (3). This component-wise normalization prevents a reward term from dominating the policy update merely because of its numerical scale.

    We use ε=10⁻⁶ and set a component’s contribution to zero when its within-group standard deviation is below 10⁻³ (Appendix A.3).

    In the PWM implementation, the clipped surrogate uses ρ̃_i,k=ρ_i,k^1/d, computed from Gaussian log densities averaged over the d scalar latent elements in the generated region (Appendix A.3).

    Noise-robust score-on-mean.

    In few-step diffusion sampling, the final stochastic transition can inject visible noise into the decoded rollout. Scoring that sample directly can make the relative advantage reflect the last noise draw rather than scene content. PWM therefore separates the trajectory used for policy learning from the video used for reward measurement. For the final transition

    zᵢ^′=μ_θ(zᵢ,cₛ)+σεᵢ,

    		(6)

    the policy likelihood is evaluated at the sampled state zᵢ^′, but the reward is evaluated on the decoded conditional mean x̃ᵢ=Dec(μ_θ(zᵢ,cₛ)). Thus, exploration remains stochastic and on-policy, while rollout ranking is based on a noise-reduced estimate of scene content.

    Finally, the GRPO instantiation of PWM anchors every updated transition to the frozen base model. Let μ_θ(s_i,k) and μ_θ₀(s_i,k) denote the transition means predicted with the adapter enabled and disabled, respectively, at the same denoising state. The GRPO objective used in PWM is

    L_PWM=-Ĵ_clip(θ₀+Δθₛ)(7)
    +λ/G∑ᵢ₌₁^G1/Kᵢ∑ₖ₌₁^Kᵢ1/d∥μ_θ₀+Δθₛ(s_i,k)-μ_θ₀(s_i,k)∥₂².

    This mean-matching anchor preserves the pretrained transition dynamics while the group-relative advantage moves the adapter toward better continuations for the target scene. We use four Euler denoising steps, four PPO passes per rollout group, λ=0.1, a learning rate of 10⁻⁴, and SDE temperature β=0.5. For the GRPO instantiation, every scene is trained for eight epochs with the same configuration.

    3.3 Per-scene Customization via DiffusionNFT

    We also instantiate PWM with DiffusionNFT [(Zheng et al., 2026)], which incorporates reward feedback through a forward-process flow-matching objective. This instantiation uses the same frozen Yume-5B backbone, LoRA capacity, six native support windows, and unified reward as the GRPO instantiation.

    Online sampling and reward normalization.

    For each support window, we sample G=4 continuations with independent initial latent noise and compute their rewards using the same score-on-mean procedure. Let Rᵢ be the scalar reward from Eq. (12), and let R̄ be its mean within the current window’s rollout group. We convert each reward into a bounded weight

    qᵢ=1/2+1/2clip((Rᵢ-R̄)/(Zₛ),-1,1),

    		(8)

    where Zₛ is the running standard deviation of rollout rewards collected during adaptation of scene s, with a lower bound of 10⁻³.

    Reward-guided flow matching.

    Let zᵢ⁰ denote the generated latent segment used for reward measurement. We sample a noise level σ from the four levels of the generation schedule and draw fresh Gaussian noise:

    \begingatheredzᵢ^σ=(1-σ)zᵢ⁰+σε, ε∼ℕ(0,I), vᵢ^⋆=ε-zᵢ⁰.\endgathered

    		(9)

    The visual history and action condition are kept fixed. Let v_θ be the current velocity prediction at (zᵢ^σ,σ,cₜ) and v_old the prediction cached before the update. DiffusionNFT defines

    vᵢ⁺=(1-β_NFT)v_old+β_NFTv_θ,(10)
    vᵢ⁻=(1+β_NFT)v_old-β_NFTv_θ,

    and minimizes

    L_NFT=𝔼_i,σ,ε[qᵢ MSE(vᵢ⁺,vᵢ^⋆)(11)
    +(1-qᵢ) MSE(vᵢ⁻,vᵢ^⋆)].

    Here, MSE averages over latent elements, and gradients are taken only through v_θ. The reward weights determine the contribution of the positive and negative branches to the adapter update.

    We collect 24 rollouts across the six support windows and draw two noise-level/noise pairs per rollout. We perform four optimization passes over this collected batch, accumulating gradients across windows. The cached behavior predictions remain fixed during these passes. We use β_NFT=0.5, a learning rate of 5×10⁻⁵, and eight training epochs. This instantiation uses the current behavior-policy snapshot without an EMA teacher or an additional base-policy anchor.

    3.4 A Unified Reward Across Domains

    Both the GRPO and DiffusionNFT instantiations of PWM use one reward for all scenes and first-person domains:

    R=0.50 R_gt+0.30 Rₗₚᵢₚₛ+0.10 R_cross+0.10 R_dyn.

    		(12)

    The four terms give the optimizer distinct responsibilities. R_gt measures spatially aligned DINO feature agreement between the generated segment and the real continuation of the support window. Rₗₚᵢₚₛ is one minus their LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)] distance and therefore preserves perceptual appearance. Both terms are computed per frame and aggregated as 0.7 times the temporal mean plus 0.3 times the minimum, so a short failure cannot be hidden by otherwise strong frames. R_cross measures DINO feature agreement between the first generated frame and the window’s ground-truth first frame. Finally, R_dyn rewards agreement between generated and real optical-flow magnitudes, so appearance fidelity cannot be obtained by suppressing motion. Together, the first two terms specify what the scene should look like, while the latter two constrain how a valid continuation should evolve.

    All reward references are drawn exclusively from the support trajectory. We do not tune reward weights per scene or per domain, and the evaluation metric is separate from this training reward (Section 4). This separation makes PWM a single customization procedure rather than a collection of scene-specific reward recipes.

    GRPO combines component-wise normalized advantages through Eq. (5), while DiffusionNFT uses the combined scalar reward through Eq. (8).

    3.5 Checkpoint Soup

    Small-data policy optimization can visit useful but different adapter states across epochs. Selecting one of them per scene would introduce an additional selection rule and could couple the delivered model to a noisy validation estimate. For both GRPO and DiffusionNFT, PWM instead saves the adapter at every epoch and averages all eight checkpoints element-wise:

    Δθ̄ₛ=1/8∑ₑ₌₁⁸Δθₛ⁽ᵉ⁾.

    		(13)

    Here, averaging is applied to the corresponding stored LoRA factor tensors. This checkpoint soup [(Wortsman et al., 2022)] is the final scene model. Because factor-wise averaging preserves the adapter’s rank and architecture, PWM still deploys one compact adapter and incurs no additional inference cost. The delivery rule is fixed across scenes and does not inspect the future test trajectory.

    4 PWM-Bench

    Customization promises that the model reproduces the persistent identity of this scene — its layout, materials, and sense of place — on a continuation it has never observed. Our benchmark evaluates this promise directly: each generated rollout is scored against the held-out ground-truth continuation of its own scene.

    Figure 3 shows representative training-support frames from the three domains of PWM-Bench.

    4.1 Customization-Fidelity Score

    For a generated rollout g_1:T and the ground-truth test segment x_1:T (T=145 frames), the score is

    S=Dₚₐᵢᵣ+0.5 Dₕₐₗₗ,(14)
    Dₚₐᵢᵣ=1/T∑ₜ₌₁ᵀ(1-\cos(φ(gₜ),φ(xₜ))),(15)
    Dₕₐₗₗ=1/T∑ₜ₌₁ᵀ1[gₜcontains an entity class absent fromx₁],(16)

    where φ(·) is the DINOv2 class-token embedding [(Oquab et al., 2024)]. Lower S indicates higher fidelity to the scene’s true continuation.

    Dₚₐᵢᵣ measures appearance fidelity as the average feature distance between generated and ground-truth frames at the same timestep, in the DINO feature space commonly used to measure fidelity in personalized generation [(Ruiz et al., 2023)]. We use a time-aligned comparison over the full horizon, rather than a distributional one, because distributional metrics can reward plausible but generic continuations; matching the specific scene as it unfolds is precisely what customization is expected to deliver.

    Dₕₐₗₗ measures the fraction of generated frames containing an entity class (person, vehicle, or animal, detected by zero-shot CLIP [(Radford et al., 2021)]) that is absent from the first frame of the ground-truth test segment. It serves as a proxy for unexpected entity introduction relative to the initial scene. The detection rules and thresholds are specified in Appendix C.4.

    Both PWM instantiations and Yume are scored by the same pipeline, with identical captions, initial context, and generation horizon. For each instantiation m, we report the paired difference

    Δₘ=S(m)-S(Yume),

    		(17)

    where m denotes PWM (GRPO) or PWM (DiffusionNFT). A negative Δₘ indicates improved customization over Yume.

    4.2 Scoring Protocol

    Each scene is evaluated with three random seeds, shared across Yume and both PWM instantiations, under deterministic inference. For each instantiation, a scene counts as improved if its mean paired difference against Yume over the three seeds is negative. We report improvement rates and mean and maximum scene-level relative gains by domain.

    Adaptation uses only the support windows, and evaluation uses only the held-out test segment, so no evaluated frame is seen during training. Both PWM instantiations are evaluated on the same fixed set of scenes.

    5 Experimental Setup

    5.1 Cross-domain Evaluation Suite

    We evaluate 150 independent customization tasks across three first-person domains: 50 outdoor walking scenes, 50 indoor walking scenes, and 50 Minecraft scenes (Table 1). Each task has its own support trajectory, scene adapter, and held-out test trajectory.

    Real-world videos come from the visual–inertial odometry (VIO) annotated subset of EgoVid-5M [(Wang et al., 2025)], YouTube, and, for Indoor, InCrowd-VI [(Bamdad et al., 2024)]. YouTube camera motion is estimated from video and mapped to the shared control representation.

    Following GameFactory’s [(Yu et al., 2025)] automated collection paradigm, our scripted agents record Minecraft videos and synchronized locomotion and camera controls in MineDojo [(Fan et al., 2022)].

    5.2 Per-scene Task Construction

    Each task contains an 80-frame support segment and a temporally later, non-overlapping 145-frame test segment from the same scene. PWM adapts independently on each support segment and evaluates the resulting adapter on its held-out continuation.

    We use a shared control interface across all three domains. Each video window is conditioned on translation commands (W/A/S/D), a camera-direction token, and three continuous motion magnitudes. For EgoVid-5M, these annotations are obtained from the associated VIO trajectory. For YouTube videos, they are derived from estimated camera motion. For Minecraft, they are recorded directly from the scripted agents.

    The same source-side quality criteria are applied across domains. The retained tasks provide continuous and non-degenerate camera motion, consistent scene identity across the support and test segments, and agreement between the control annotations and observed visual motion.

    5.3 Controlled Comparisons

    We compare PWM with native Yume-5B using the same 29-frame autoregressive generation process, initial visual context, controls, decoding configuration, and rollout horizon. Native Yume uses the same inference pipeline with the scene adapter disabled, isolating the effect of per-scene adaptation.

    We additionally compare PWM with a matched SFT-LoRA baseline in the reinforcement-learning ablation. SFT-LoRA uses the same frozen Yume-5B backbone, LoRA capacity, support data, control annotations, optimization budget, and evaluation protocol as PWM. This comparison isolates the contribution of online GRPO beyond scene-specific parameter updates alone.

    5.4 Shared Training and Evaluation Configuration

    All videos are processed at a resolution of 832×480. Each scene is adapted independently with a rank-8 LoRA using α=16, corresponding to 20.2M trainable parameters. We instantiate PWM with GRPO and DiffusionNFT, as described in Sections 3.2 and 3.3. Both instantiations use the same adapter capacity and unified reward in Eq. (12), with checkpoint averaging described in Section 3.5. Within each instantiation, the optimization configuration and checkpoint-averaging rule are fixed across all 150 tasks.

    Evaluation follows Section 4.2. Each scene is evaluated with three paired random seeds, {42,123,777}, shared between PWM and native Yume under deterministic inference. Both methods generate the full 145-frame test trajectory. Seed-level paired differences are first averaged within each scene, and every scene contributes once to its domain and to the overall benchmark.

    6 Experiments

    We evaluate PWM along three dimensions: customization gains over native Yume, the contribution of reinforcement learning beyond supervised adaptation, and visual quality after customization. The evaluation covers 150 scenes across Indoor, Outdoor, and Gaming, with three paired generation seeds per scene. All customization scores are computed over the complete 145-frame held-out continuation, following Section 5.

    6.1 Scene Customization across Domains

    Scene appearance and content retention.

    Figure 4 illustrates scene customization in a shopping-mall continuation. Both PWM instantiations retain shop displays, while Yume replaces them with window-like structures in later frames.

    Measuring customization benefit.

    We quantify customization benefit as the relative reduction in the score S defined in Eq. (14). For scene s and method m, let S̄ₛᵐ denote the score averaged over the three generation seeds. The scene-level gain, expressed as a percentage, is

    gₛ(m)=100 (S̄ₛ^Native-S̄ₛᵐ)/(S̄ₛ^Native).

    		(18)

    Positive values indicate improved customization over Native. We report the mean gain across all evaluated scenes, the maximum scene-level gain, and the fraction of scenes with gₛ(m)>0. Every scene receives equal weight, and negative gains are included in the average. Both the mean and maximum are computed after averaging the three seeds within each scene.

    Positive gains across real and rendered environments.

    The GRPO and DiffusionNFT instantiations of PWM improve customization in 107 and 98 of the 150 evaluated scenes, respectively, achieving mean relative gains of 6.39% and 5.22% over native Yume (Table 2). The corresponding improvement rates are 71.3% and 65.3%. Both instantiations achieve positive mean gains across Indoor, Outdoor, and Gaming. These results support the effectiveness of per-scene customization across real and rendered environments using either online reward-guided optimization method.

    Benefits beyond the strongest examples.

    For the GRPO instantiation, the largest scene-level gains reach 49.00% in Indoor, 75.11% in Outdoor, and 28.66% in Gaming. The median gains are also positive in all three domains: 5.18%, 5.82%, and 8.18%, respectively. Together, the average gain, median gain, and improvement frequency show that the observed customization benefit extends beyond a few highly successful examples.

    Snow-cover retention in Gaming.

    Figure 6 complements the indoor example with a rendered environment: both PWM instantiations retain snow-covered ground in the selected continuations.

    Object hallucination.

    Figure 5 shows a local object hallucination: a human face appears on the blue equipment in Yume, while both PWM instantiations retain its equipment appearance.

    6.2 The Benefit of Reinforcement Learning

    Comparison with matched supervised adaptation.

    We assess online RL against matched SFT-LoRA under the settings in Section 5.3. Customization gains and improved-scene counts are measured against the same native Yume baseline.

    Figure 7 provides a qualitative comparison of Native Yume, SFT, and both PWM instantiations. In this outdoor example, both PWM instantiations retain visible passage space as generation progresses.

    Higher average customization benefit.

    Both the DanceGRPO and DiffusionNFT instantiations of PWM achieve higher mean gains than SFT in every domain (Table 3). In Indoor and Outdoor, both instantiations achieve positive mean gains, compared with negative mean gains for SFT. In Gaming, the mean gain increases from 6.08% with SFT to 7.91% with DanceGRPO and 6.35% with DiffusionNFT. Across all 150 scenes, the mean gain rises from -8.39% with SFT to +6.39% with DanceGRPO and +5.22% with DiffusionNFT.

    Scene-level improvement coverage.

    Across all 150 scenes, the DanceGRPO and DiffusionNFT instantiations of PWM improve over Native in 107 and 98 scenes, respectively, compared with 86 scenes for SFT. The corresponding improvement rates are 71.3%, 65.3%, and 57.3%. Together with the higher mean gains across all three domains, these results show that both PWM instantiations deliver stronger average customization and benefit a larger fraction of the overall evaluation suite than SFT.

    The matched SFT comparison examines how support observations are converted into a scene-specific generation policy. SFT optimizes a supervised diffusion objective on the observed support windows. PWM instead samples continuations from the current policy and uses their relative rewards to guide adaptation. The learning signal therefore depends on what the adapted model actually generates under the support conditions.

    6.3 Preserving Visual Quality

    Figure 8 illustrates this contrast: SFT exhibits visible blur and repetitive texture artifacts, while PWM (DanceGRPO) retains natural-looking scene appearance in the selected examples.

    Quality assessment alongside customization.

    We complement the customization score with three no-reference image-quality metrics: MUSIQ-SPAQ [(Ke et al., 2021)], NIQE [(Mittal et al., 2013)], and BRISQUE [(Mittal et al., 2012)]. These metrics characterize frame-level visual quality, while S evaluates scene-specific customization. MUSIQ uses all frames; NIQE and BRISQUE use 19 uniformly sampled frames, including the first and last. Scores are averaged over frames, seeds, and scenes, in that order. Native Yume provides a reference for the pretrained model’s visual quality.

    Quality close to Native after customization.

    PWM outperforms SFT on the domain means of all three reported image-quality metrics (Table 4). In Indoor, MUSIQ increases from 47.26 with SFT to 59.06 with PWM, compared with 58.93 for Native. In Outdoor, BRISQUE improves from 33.58 to 23.24, close to Native’s 22.66. In Gaming, NIQE improves from 5.90 to 3.82, compared with 3.81 for Native. Across individual scenes, MUSIQ favors PWM over SFT in 123 of 150 cases, and NIQE does so in 132 cases.

    Scene identity and image quality provide complementary evidence. The customization score evaluates agreement with the target scene, while the image-quality metrics characterize frame-level appearance. Together, Tables 2 and 4 support the intended benefit of PWM: stronger fidelity to the target scene with frame-level quality close to native Yume.

    6.4 Training Dynamics

    Figure 9 summarizes the training reward trajectories of PWM with DanceGRPO and DiffusionNFT across Indoor, Outdoor, and Gaming. The curves report rewards collected under each method’s training sampling procedure, complementing the held-out customization results in Table 2.

    7 Conclusion and Future Work

    We introduced PWM, a framework for customizing a pretrained interactive world model to an individual scene through online reinforcement learning. PWM turns a short support trajectory into a compact LoRA adapter using native-window generation, a shared reward, and a fixed checkpoint-averaging rule. We also introduced PWM-Bench to evaluate per-scene customization across Indoor, Outdoor, and Gaming. Across the evaluated suite, PWM improves customization over native Yume in 107 of 150 scenes. The matched SFT comparison further demonstrates higher mean customization gains and broader scene-level benefits, alongside visual quality close to the pretrained model.

    Future work will extend this approach to longer interaction horizons and richer support trajectories, enabling scene customization over more extensive exploration.

    Reproducibility Statement

    Section 5 specifies task construction and the shared experimental protocol. Appendices A–C provide optimization settings, reward definitions, and scoring details. Evaluation uses three paired seeds on held-out continuations, with no test frames used for adaptation or checkpoint construction.

    AI Use Declaration

    OpenAI ChatGPT was used to assist with language polishing and improving the clarity of the manuscript. The authors take full responsibility for the final content.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Implementation Details

    This appendix describes the DanceGRPO implementation. DiffusionNFT follows Section 3.3. The checkpoint averaging procedure described below applies to both instantiations. The four reward components are specified in Appendix B.

    A.1 Adaptation Configuration

    For each scene, we train one LoRA adapter on the frozen Yume-5B backbone. The adapter is shared across six overlapping support windows of 29 frames, starting at zero-based indices [0,9,18,27,36,45]. Each window is conditioned on its own ground-truth first frame and corresponding control caption. Windows are processed in this order, with adapter updates carried forward within the scene.

    For each window, the current policy generates a group of G=4 trajectories using K=4 stochastic denoising steps. We compute the trajectory advantages and perform four optimization passes on the collected group. Each pass accumulates gradients over all GK transitions before taking one optimizer step. We train for eight epochs and save the adapter after each complete pass through the six windows. This gives 48 rollout groups and 192 optimizer updates per scene.

    Table 5 lists the shared configuration. Backbone forward passes use bfloat16, and trainable LoRA parameters are stored in float32. Reward networks are frozen and evaluated without gradient propagation through them.

    A.2 Trajectory Sampling and Reward Measurement

    Let zₖ denote the generated latent variables at denoising step k, c the conditioning information, and σₖ the noise schedule. The stochastic Euler transition is

    μ_θ(zₖ,c)=zₖ+(σₖ₋₁-σₖ)v_θ(zₖ,c,σₖ),(19)
    ηₖ=β√|σₖ₋₁-σₖ|\max(σₖ,10⁻⁴)+10⁻⁴,(20)
    zₖ₋₁=μ_θ(zₖ,c)+ηₖεₖ, εₖ∼ℕ(0,I).(21)

    Trajectories within a group share their initial latent noise and use independent transition noise. We record the sampled transitions and their behavior-policy log densities for subsequent optimization.

    For reward measurement, we decode the conditional mean of the final transition. This excludes the final noise injection from the scored video while retaining the effects of earlier stochastic transitions. Policy optimization uses the recorded stochastic transitions.

    A.3 Advantage Computation and Policy Updates

    Each reward component is normalized within the rollout group before the component advantages are combined. For component m, let

    μₘ=1/G∑ᵢ₌₁^GR_i,m, σₘ=√1/G∑ᵢ₌₁^G(R_i,m-μₘ)².

    		(22)

    Using the fixed component weights αₘ, we compute

    Aᵢ=∑ₘαₘ 1[σₘ≥10⁻³](R_i,m-μₘ)/(σₘ+10⁻⁶).

    		(23)

    Components with standard deviation below 10⁻³ contribute zero to that group’s advantage. The same Aᵢ is assigned to all denoising steps of trajectory i.

    For a generation region containing d scalar latent variables, we use the mean Gaussian log density

    ℓ_θ(zₖ₋₁|zₖ,c)=-1/2d∑ⱼ₌₁ᵈ[((z_k-1,j-μ_θ,j)²)/(ηₖ²)+\log(2πηₖ²)].

    		(24)

    The ratio used in the clipped surrogate is

    ρ̃_i,k=\exp (ℓ_θ-ℓ_θ_old),

    		(25)

    with both densities evaluated at the same recorded transition. This is the 1/d power of the corresponding joint density ratio. Behavior-policy log densities remain fixed during all four optimization passes on a group.

    The resulting loss is

    L_PWM=-1/GK∑ᵢ₌₁^G∑ₖ₌₁^K\min (ρ̃_i,kAᵢ,clip(ρ̃_i,k,1-ε_clip,1+ε_clip)Aᵢ)
    +λ/GK∑ᵢ₌₁^G∑ₖ₌₁^K(∥μ_θ(s_i,k)-μ_θ₀(s_i,k)∥₂²)/(d).(26)

    The anchor compares transition means at the same denoising state. The frozen-base mean is obtained with the adapter disabled.

    A.4 Adapter Checkpoint Averaging

    We uniformly average the corresponding LoRA parameter tensors from the eight epoch checkpoints of each scene’s adaptation run. For a linear layer with pretrained weight W₀, write its adapted weight as W₀+(α/r)BA. The delivered layer uses

    Ā=1/8∑ₑ₌₁⁸A⁽ᵉ⁾, B̄=1/8∑ₑ₌₁⁸B⁽ᵉ⁾, W_PWM=W₀+α/rB̄ Ā.

    		(27)

    Thus, averaging operates on the trainable adapter tensors; the resulting update is the product of their averages. The final model retains one rank-8 adapter. All eight checkpoints receive equal weight, and checkpoint construction uses no held-out test frames.

    Appendix B Reward Definitions

    Let x_1:L be the reference support window and y_1:L the generated video used for reward measurement, with L=29. We specify the four components of the shared reward below. All reference quantities are computed from the current support window.

    B.1 Feature Extraction and Temporal Aggregation

    We use DINOv2-small for visual features, AlexNet-based LPIPS for perceptual distance, and RAFT-small [(Teed and Deng, 2020)] for optical flow. Images are resized to 224×224 using bilinear interpolation with align_corners=False. DINOv2 inputs use ImageNet normalization with channel means (0.485,0.456,0.406) and standard deviations (0.229,0.224,0.225). LPIPS and RAFT inputs are mapped to [-1,1].

    Frame-wise appearance scores are aggregated as

    A(a_1:L)=0.7/L∑ₜ₌₁^Laₜ+0.3\min_1≤t≤Laₜ.

    		(28)

    The minimum term gives additional weight to the lowest-scoring frame within the window.

    B.2 Reward Components

    Scene feature fidelity.

    Let f_cls(u) and fₚ(u) denote the DINOv2 CLS feature and the feature at patch position p, respectively. With P patches, we compute

    qₜ=0.3\cos (f_cls(yₜ),f_cls(xₜ))
    +0.7/P∑ₚ₌₁^P\cos (fₚ(yₜ),fₚ(xₜ)),(29)
    R_gt=

item.title: 2 亿次 Unity CLI 调用里 98% 是 agent 在跑：引擎的接口正在为 agent 重做 ｜ Meeting you where you work: Inside 200M+ Unity CLI events
item.description:
一句话：Unity 首次公开全量遥测：调引擎的主力已经不是人——终端里手敲命令的只占 0.2%，CI 占 0.3%。

要点：

  • 2026-07-20 到 10-13 期间约 22.6 万名登录用户产生 2 亿次以上 CLI 事件，约 98% 来自编码 agent 与其它自动化，人类在终端手敲 0.2%、CI 0.3%
  • 命令排行说明工作发生在跑着的编辑器里：unity run 约 1.24 亿次，unity status 约 670 万，unity pipeline list 约 140 万
  • Unity 为 Claude Code、Codex、Grok 发布官方插件，插件内含 Unity 团队自己写的 agent skill（含驱动 CLI 的那个）；实际使用中 Claude Code 最多，其次 Codex，再次是 Cursor、Grok

为什么值得看：这是引擎厂商公布的「agent 如何使用引擎」的实测数据：可发现的状态查询、可脚本化的管线命令、官方写给 agent 的 skill，比面向人类的 UI 更决定接入效率。日后设计引擎 API，要把 agent 当成第一等调用者。

中文摘要：Unity 公布了 CLI 的使用遥测：自 7 月以来，超过 22.6 万名登录用户通过命令行管理 Unity，并记录了 2 亿次以上的事件。数据揭示的规律是：人先把环境准备好（装管线包、打开工程、登录、把 agent 指向 Unity、装 CLI 技能），然后就把活交出去。2026-07-20 至 10-13 期间约 98% 的 CLI 运行来自编码 agent 与其它自动化，人在终端输入只占 0.2%，CI 管道占 0.3%。跑得最多的命令是在已连接编辑器上执行命令（约 1.24 亿次）、查看编辑器状态（约 670 万次）、列出管线实例（约 140 万次）。Unity 同时为 Claude Code、Codex 与 Grok 发布了带官方技能的插件。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：Unity Blog（English）

原文发布：2026-10-22

本期推送：2026-10-24

Developers start in the agent they already use, in the editor they already like, with the terminal they already have open. The Unity CLI meets you there. It’s a single binary that installs and manages Unity from the terminal and, with the Pipeline package, drives a running Editor, so scripts, CI, and coding agents all reach Unity the same way.

Since July, more than 226,000logged-in users have used the Unity CLI, and it has logged more than 200 million events(and growing). Almost all of them are commands being run. What those commands show is a simple habit: people set Unity up, then their agent does the work.

People set it up, then hand it off

From July 20 to October 13, 2026, about 98% of CLI runs come from coding agents and other automation. People typing at a terminal account for 0.2%, and CI pipelines for 0.3%. A small share of runs falls outside those three groups.
When people do type, they are getting ready. They install the Pipeline package, open a project on the right Editor version, sign in, point their agent at Unity, and install the CLI skill. Then they hand the work over. That is what meeting developers where they work looks like in practice: Unity shows up inside the agent they already chose, and the agent takes it from there.

Most of the work happens inside a live Editor

The three commands run most:

  • unity command
     about 124 million runs: runs a command on a connected Editor, either a built-in one or one you defined yourself.
  • unity status
    about 6.7 million: shows the live state of every connected Editor, including its project and version.
  • unity pipeline list
    about 1.4 million: lists Editor instances and whether each one has the Pipeline package.

    • Unity’s plugins bring official skills to agents

    Most of the CLI's usage came after Unity released official plugins for Claude Code and Codex, and most recently, Grok. Each plugin gives the agent skills written by Unity's own teams, including one that drives the CLI, so the agent works in Unity the way Unity intends. 

    unity setup claude
    installs the Claude Code plugin for you, and the plugin also works in the Claude Code extension for VS Code. Agents that are not integrated with Unity’s official plugin can still work in Unity through the CLI, so you keep the agent you already use.

    Claude Code is the agent used most with the CLI, followed by Codex, then other agents such as Cursor and Grok. The rest come from scripts and tools that do not identify an agent.

    Where it is being used

    By signed-in users, the CLI's largest audiences are in the United States, Japan, South Korea, followed by Germanyand Turkey.

    What’s next

    We will keep adding agents, and keep publishing what we learn. To get started, see the Unity CLI documentation and the Unity plugin documentation.

    How we measured this

    All CLI figures come from aggregated Unity CLI telemetry, July 20 to October 13, 2026. Agent usage by user covers September 1 to October 13, 2026, with each user counted once. Unity employees are excluded, and users who opt out of telemetry are not counted. Each event is counted once, so retries do not inflate totals. Country is based on the location attached to each event, and some events have no location. A run counts as CI when a CI environment variable is set, and as a person when both input and output are a terminal. Runs in MCP mode, runs from a known AI tool, and other piped or scripted runs count as agents and automation. Command counts are based on the command name recorded with each event.

item.title: AI 生成关卡之后要查什么：Unity 里按连通、长度、捷径的顺序过三遍 ｜ AI 关卡生成之后要查什么？Unity 里要过的三道检查
item.description:
一句话：先钉住四个数字、要字符网格而不是概念图，再按连通→最短路径→捷径的顺序验收，最后用灰盒跑一遍对表。

要点：

  • 先写表再出手：一格几米、整张多少格、几个房间、一局目标秒数四个数字先钉住；角色能力也要写成数字（最远横向几格半、最高落差一格二），写「能跳」没有用
  • 要字符网格不要概念图：点号表示空地、井号表示墙、字母标出起点终点与必经点，附上坐标；改一个字符等于挪一堵墙，比在引擎里拖模型快得多，定稿前一张美术图都不要出
  • 三道检查顺序固定：连通性（终点与必经点是否都走得到）→ 最短路径对照目标时长（差得多先调房间数，别急着加障碍）→ 列最短三条路径看第二条差多少格（差两三格说明有贴边近道）；节奏用主路切六段、每段 1–5 强度值的强度线回测，峰值一般放在关卡三分之二处

为什么值得看：这是把「AI 生成关卡」接进 Unity 工作流最朴素也最有效的一层中间产物：用可编辑的字符网格承载 AI 输出，用可量化的三道检查代替主观判断，减少的是返工次数。

中文摘要：把一张手画方格纸拍照丢进对话框，两分钟就能拿回一张关卡平面图，能走通、起点到终点四十秒——问题出在格子之间的路和节奏上。作者的做法是先把要求写成一张表：一格几米、整张多少格、打算放几个房间、一局目标多少秒，再把角色能力写成数字（一次跳跃最远铺开几格、最高落差多少），否则生成出来的地形摆错，角色会卡在原地。然后只让它画平面、并且要字符网格而不是概念图（点空地、井号墙、字母标起点终点与必经点），改一个字符就是挪一堵墙。定稿前依次过三道检查：连通性、最短路径是否贴近目标时长、最短三条路径里第二条差多少格（有没有贴边近道）。最后把主路切六段标强度值做节奏回测，再用灰色方块跑一遍对表。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：公众号·AI游戏工坊（中文）

原文发布：2026-10-12

本期推送：2026-10-24

AI游戏方法论

2026.10.12　·　AI游戏工坊　·　阅读约 7 分钟

有人把一张手画的方格纸拍照丢进对话框，两分钟拿回一张关卡平面图。
放进去能走，从起点到终点只用四十秒。
问题出在格子之间的那条路，也出在节奏。
我把做过的三张关卡拆开看，真正省时间的只有一件事：先把要求写成一张表。

关卡交给 AI 生成之后，你从哪一步开始查？

01

先写表，再出手

这一步不能跳。

顺序反过来做，你会在改第三遍的时候发现，所有别扭都来自最开始没写清的那两行。

●　第 1 步　四个数字先钉住

一格代表几米，整张关卡多少格乘多少格，打算放几个房间，一局目标时长多少秒。四个数字，写在你自己的文档里。

举个例子：一格两米，整张 96 格乘 64 格，十二到十五个房间，一局目标三分钟。有了这四个数，AI 给出的东西才有参照系，你也才有得挑。

●　第 2 步　写清角色能做什么

这一行最容易被漏掉。把你角色的能力写成数字：能跨过多高的落差，一次跳跃最远铺开几格，需要钥匙的门一共有几扇。

写「能跳」没用。写「最远横向三格半、最高一格二」才有用，因为生成出来的地形要照这个数字摆，摆错了你的角色就卡在原地。

02

只让它画平面

先别急着要美术。

一张画得很好的关卡概念图，改起来比一张丑的平面图慢十倍。

●　第 3 步　要字符网格，不要图

让 AI 按你的尺寸吐一张字符网格出来：点号代表空地，井号代表墙，字母标出起点、终点和必经点。九十六乘六十四行字符，粘进文档里就能改。

这一层的好处是你不用打开引擎。改一个字符就是挪一口墙，比拖一次模型快得多。等网格定稿了，再把它转成 Unity 里的地块预制体。

就像先用铅笔在方格纸上排家具，再进屋搬沙发。纸上挪一次不花力气，屋里挪一次要两个人。

顺便让它在旁边标上坐标。这三个坐标是下一步查连通性的起点。

“

字符网格定稿之前，一张美术图都不要出。

03

三道检查，顺序不能换

三道检查有先后。跳着做，你会反复返工。

●　第 4 步　连通性

先问一句：从起点出发，终点和三个必经点是不是都走得到。这一项不用写代码，把字符网格贴回对话框，让它自己走一遍也行。

走不到的位置通常集中在两处：必经点被墙整个围住，或者两块区域之间只留了一个宽度不够的豁口。

●　第 5 步　最短路径

连通之后再量长度。让 AI 把起点到终点的最短路径标出来，数一格两米，算出一局要跑多少米、大概多少秒。

这一步的靶子是你第 1 步写下的目标时长。差得远，就去调房间数量，别急着加障碍物。

●　第 6 步　有没有一条捷径

最后一条最值钱。让 AI 列出从起点到终点的所有路径里最短的三条，看第二条比第一条多了多少格。

两条只差两三格，说明这张图上有一条贴着边走的近道，玩家十有八九会找到它，然后绕过你精心摆的那一段。补一堵墙，或者干脆把那一段的价值挪到近道上来。

04

节奏用一条线回测

前面三步保证能走通，这一步管好不好玩。

做法很土，但有效。把主路切成六段，每段给一个一到五的强度值，再把六个点连成一条线。

线走到顶再回落，就是要的那个形状。连续三段都贴在下面，玩家会觉得这一段在散步。最高那个点，一般放在整张关卡三分之二的位置。

最后一个动作：用一堆灰色方块把主路先摆出来，自己从头跑一遍，记下花了多少秒。数字对得上第 1 步那张表，这张关卡就可以进美术了。

“

表写得越细，后面改的次数越少。

整套动作收成一句话：先写四个数字，再要一张字符网格，然后按连通、长度、捷径的顺序过三遍，最后用灰色方块自己跑一次。今天就能动的一步，把你手上那张关卡的主路切成六段，标上强度值。

◆ ◆ ◆

ABOUT · 关于我

面向想用 AI 做游戏的普通开发者与爱好者，写的是能当天动手的小方法，也盯 AI 游戏这条线上刚发生的事。

数据说明

本篇所有数字都是可以按自己项目改的经验区间：一格两米、96 乘 64 格、十二到十五个房间、一局三分钟、跳跃最远三格半、最高落差一格二、把主路切成六段、强度值一到五、最高点放在三分之二处。这些值来自常见平面关卡的手感区间，你的角色跑得更快或者跳得更高时，可以按同一套比例整体放大或缩小。字符网格的做法只是把平面的排布变成可编辑的文字，任何支持文本输出的模型都能做。三道检查的顺序建议固定下来，先连通、再长度、后捷径，前一项没过就改图，不必往下走。

NEXT · 下一篇

这是「关卡清单」第 1 篇，下一篇写怎么用同一张表把一条关卡改出三档强度：只动哪几个数字，节奏线要往上抬多少。你的项目现在卡在哪一段，留言说一声，下一篇可以先写它。关注一下，下一篇出来就能看到。

AI游戏工坊

每日 AI 游戏方法论

●　第 4 步　连通性

先问一句：从起点出发，终点和三个必经点是不是都走得到。这一项不用写代码，把字符网格贴回对话框，让它自己走一遍也行。

走不到的位置通常集中在两处：必经点被墙整个围住，或者两块区域之间只留了一个宽度不够的豁口。

●　第 5 步　最短路径

连通之后再量长度。让 AI 把起点到终点的最短路径标出来，数一格两米，算出一局要跑多少米、大概多少秒。

这一步的靶子是你第 1 步写下的目标时长。差得远，就去调房间数量，别急着加障碍物。

●　第 6 步　有没有一条捷径

最后一条最值钱。让 AI 列出从起点到终点的所有路径里最短的三条，看第二条比第一条多了多少格。

两条只差两三格，说明这张图上有一条贴着边走的近道，玩家十有八九会找到它，然后绕过你精心摆的那一段。补一堵墙，或者干脆把那一段的价值挪到近道上来。

04

节奏用一条线回测

前面三步保证能走通，这一步管好不好玩。

做法很土，但有效。把主路切成六段，每段给一个一到五的强度值，再把六个点连成一条线。

线走到顶再回落，就是要的那个形状。连续三段都贴在下面，玩家会觉得这一段在散步。最高那个点，一般放在整张关卡三分之二的位置。

最后一个动作：用一堆灰色方块把主路先摆出来，自己从头跑一遍，记下花了多少秒。数字对得上第 1 步那张表，这张关卡就可以进美术了。

“

表写得越细，后面改的次数越少。

整套动作收成一句话：先写四个数字，再要一张字符网格，然后按连通、长度、捷径的顺序过三遍，最后用灰色方块自己跑一次。今天就能动的一步，把你手上那张关卡的主路切成六段，标上强度值。

◆ ◆ ◆

ABOUT · 关于我

面向想用 AI 做游戏的普通开发者与爱好者，写的是能当天动手的小方法，也盯 AI 游戏这条线上刚发生的事。

数据说明

本篇所有数字都是可以按自己项目改的经验区间：一格两米、96 乘 64 格、十二到十五个房间、一局三分钟、跳跃最远三格半、最高落差一格二、把主路切成六段、强度值一到五、最高点放在三分之二处。这些值来自常见平面关卡的手感区间，你的角色跑得更快或者跳得更高时，可以按同一套比例整体放大或缩小。字符网格的做法只是把平面的排布变成可编辑的文字，任何支持文本输出的模型都能做。三道检查的顺序建议固定下来，先连通、再长度、后捷径，前一项没过就改图，不必往下走。

NEXT · 下一篇

这是「关卡清单」第 1 篇，下一篇写怎么用同一张表把一条关卡改出三档强度：只动哪几个数字，节奏线要往上抬多少。你的项目现在卡在哪一段，留言说一声，下一篇可以先写它。关注一下，下一篇出来就能看到。

item.title: LoCoSplat：高斯本来就是局部的东西，别再用重型 3D 网络去推它 ｜ LoCoSplat: Real-Time Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting with Minimal 3D Reasoning
item.description:
一句话：预测完深度，剩下的尺度、旋转、不透明度取邻域的固定局部平均就够，整个编码器是一张 fp16 CUDA graph。

要点：

  • 把 16 维点特征的线性投影 splat 进一细一粗两层网格，再在每个锚点上读回，用一个 0.14M 参数的点式 MLP 出剩余属性——没有可学习的 3D 网络，也没有动态稀疏计算
  • RealEstate10K 上 6/12/24 视图的 PSNR、SSIM、LPIPS 全面超过此前所有前馈方法，视图越密领先越多（24 视图比 VolSplat 高 3.3 PSNR）
  • 单张 RTX PRO 6000 上 6 视图重建 33ms，比此前 SOTA 快 4.2 倍，推理显存少 6.7 倍，训练快 2.7 倍（24 视图时 5.9 倍）

为什么值得看：前馈 3DGS 的算力一直砸在「用网络推理 3D」上，这篇给出了相反的证据：把 3D 推理压到最简、把局部性用足，速度和画质可以同时赢。做移动端或批量重建的团队值得先抄这个结构。

中文摘要：前馈式 3D 高斯泼溅近年靠越来越重的可学习 3D 网络来聚合多视图证据。LoCoSplat 的出发点是：高斯是局部基元，一旦深度预测出来，3D 阶段要补的尺度、旋转、不透明度其实只取决于每个锚点周围的点云，用该邻域的一个固定局部平均就能提供。它把这个平均做成两次 splat：16 维点特征投影进细网格和粗网格，再在每个锚点处读回，经 0.14M 参数的点式 MLP 输出属性；没有可学习 3D 网络与动态稀疏计算，整个编码器可跑成一张 fp16 CUDA graph。RealEstate10K 上各视图数全指标领先，24 视图较 VolSplat 高 3.3 PSNR。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-03

本期推送：2026-10-24

LoCoSplat: Real-Time Feed-Forward
3D Gaussian Splatting
with Minimal 3D Reasoning

Abstract

Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) increasingly aggregates multi-view evidence with heavy learned 3D networks. We propose LoCoSplat (Local-Context Splatting), motivated by the observation that a Gaussian is a local primitive: once depth is predicted, what the 3D stage must add (scale, rotation, opacity) depends on the point cloud around each anchor, and a fixed local average of that neighbourhood is enough to supply it, no heavy network required. LoCoSplat realises exactly this average: it splats a 16-d linear projection of the point features into a fine and a coarse grid and reads both back at each anchor with a 0.14M-parameter pointwise MLP; with no learned 3D network and no dynamic sparse computation, its whole encoder runs as one fp16 CUDA graph. On RealEstate10K, LoCoSplat outperforms every prior feed-forward method on PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS at 6, 12, and 24 views, with a margin that widens as views densify (+3.3 PSNR over VolSplat, the prior voxel-aligned state of the art, at 24 views) and grows further under zero-shot transfer to ACID and fine-tuning on ScanNet. It reconstructs a 6-view scene in 33 ms on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU, the fastest of seven feed-forward methods and 4.2× faster than the previous state of the art, trains 2.7× faster (5.9× at 24 views), and uses 6.7× less inference memory.

11footnotetext: Equal contribution.

1 Introduction

Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting [(Charatan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025)] predicts the Gaussian primitives of 3DGS [(Kerbl et al., 2023)] from a handful of posed images in a single forward pass, replacing the per-scene optimization of NeRF and 3DGS [(Mildenhall et al., 2020; Kerbl et al., 2023)] with a learned prior. Pixel-aligned prediction, the dominant approach, suffers from multi-view misalignment and resolution-bound Gaussian budgets, and the field’s answer has been to reason with ever-heavier learned modules, mostly by moving prediction into 3D: sparse 3D U-Nets and CNNs [(Wang et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2022)], 3D cost-volume networks, or long-sequence Mamba/transformer models over image tokens [(Ziwen et al., 2025)]. VolSplat [(Wang et al., 2026a)], the state of the art of the depth-guided voxel-aligned family, predicts depth, voxelizes the unprojected pixels into anchors, and then refines the sparse volume with a 17M-parameter sparse 3D U-Net before decoding Gaussians. That U-Net is its largest inference cost (∼7 scenes per second): a dynamic-shape sparse computation [(Choy et al., 2019)] that cannot be captured in a CUDA graph and barely benefits from mixed precision, and the dominant training memory as views grow (24-view training takes 159 hours). Behind this trajectory lies an implicit assumption: that aggregating multi-view evidence in 3D requires substantial learned 3D capacity.

Our motivation is a local view of the 3D stage: what a Gaussian needs from its neighbours is the kind of low-order local information that a grid computes for free, not a learned 3D network. LoCoSplat (Local-Context Splatting, Fig.1) keeps the depth-guided voxel-aligned pipeline (Section2.1) up to the anchors: a hybrid monocular–multi-view depth branch and a DPT feature head place one anchor per occupied voxel. Its 3D stage is a fixed grid average: each anchor’s feature, linearly projected to 16 dimensions, is averaged into a fine and a coarse grid, and both grids are read back at the anchor by a 0.14M-parameter pointwise MLP and a pointwise head. With no learned 3D network and no dynamic sparse computation, the whole encoder runs as one fp16 CUDA graph.

The motivation is structural: a 3D Gaussian is a local primitive. Once depth is predicted, each anchor’s colour and position are determined by its own pixel. The 3D stage must add scale, rotation, and opacity, the layout of the surface around the anchor; no single pixel observes this layout, but it is determined by the neighbouring points, which a fixed average over a coarser neighbourhood, computed for free by a grid, can summarize. The anchors are also so sparse at the working voxel size (99.6% have no occupied neighbour at 6 views) that a 3³ sparse convolution over them is already pointwise (Section2.4), so any context must come from a coarser scale, which the coarse grid supplies. This intuition led to the design.

We then measure what the 3D stage of this pipeline actually needs (Section3): very little. A fixed grid average read by a pointwise MLP of under 0.2M parameters beats the 17M-parameter U-Net by +0.70 PSNR (Table9). LoCoSplat has the best PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS of all feed-forward methods on RealEstate10K at 6, 12, and 24 views, with a margin that grows on ACID and ScanNet, and reconstructs a 6-view scene in 33.0 ms (30.3 FPS) on one GPU, 4.2× faster than VolSplat (2.4× at equal fp32 precision) with 85% less peak inference memory, and trains 2.7× faster (5.9× at 24 views; Table2).

Our contributions are:

  • •

    A 3D stage with no learned 3D network, motivated by the locality of a Gaussian, with controlled experiments showing that the 3D stage of this pipeline needs very little: a fixed grid average read by a pointwise MLP of under 0.2M parameters beats a 17M-parameter sparse 3D U-Net, and the minimal coarse context it keeps needs neither learning nor appearance content (Section3.5).

  • •

    LoCoSplat, a state-of-the-art real-time feed-forward 3DGS method, leading at 6, 12, and 24 views, in and out of domain, whose fp16 CUDA-graph encoder reconstructs at 30 FPS on one GPU, 4.2× faster than VolSplat with 6.7× less inference memory and 2.7× faster training (Section3.3).

  • •

    A predictive account of the dense-view collapse of depth-guided reconstruction: an optimization failure of the depth branch governed by the per-candidate plane-sweep disparity; LoCoSplat does not collapse and leads VolSplat by +3.3 PSNR at 24 views (Section3.5).

    • 2 Method

    LoCoSplat reconstructs a set of 3D Gaussians from V posed images in one forward pass (Fig.1). Its 2D stage (Section2.1) is a depth-guided pipeline in the VolSplat/DepthSplat family [(Wang et al., 2026a; Xu et al., 2025)]: per-view depth and per-pixel features, unprojected and voxelized into anchors (Section2.2). Its 3D stage (Section2.3) has no learned 3D network: a fixed local average of the point features is read by a pointwise MLP, and a pointwise head decodes each anchor’s Gaussian (Section2.4); Section2.5 gives the training objective.

    2.1 Depth and Feature Prediction

    The input is V images Iᵢ∈ℝ^H×W×3 with intrinsics Kᵢ and camera-to-world poses (Rᵢ,tᵢ). A frozen DepthAnythingV2 ViT-B backbone [(Yang et al., 2024)] provides monocular features, mapped by a trainable linear interface from 768 to 384 channels (ViT-S width); a CNN with a local-window cross-view transformer over the two nearest views [(Xu et al., 2023)] provides matching features, from which a plane-sweep cost volume over D=64 inverse-depth candidates {dₖ} is built. A depthwise-separable, half-width UniMatch-style regressor turns it into matching probabilities pᵢ[k,p] and the coarse inverse depth d̃ᵢ(p)=∑ₖpᵢ[k,p] dₖ; one DPT head [(Yang et al., 2024)] refines it with the monocular features into the full-resolution depth Dᵢ, and a second DPT head yields the per-pixel feature f_i,p∈ℝ¹³² (image, depth, and peak matching probability appended) that enters the 3D stage.

    2.2 Anchors

    Every pixel is unprojected along its depth and voxelized at the fine voxel size v=0.001:

    x_i,p=Rᵢ Dᵢ(p) Kᵢ⁻¹\beginbmatrixp 1\endbmatrix+tᵢ, cᵥ(x)=rnd(x/v)∈ℤ³.

    		(1)

    This gives the point cloud P={(xᵢ,fᵢ)}_i≤n, n=V·H·W, and the anchor set A={cᵥ(xᵢ)} of occupied voxels, one Gaussian per anchor; anchor a carries the mean position xₐ and mean feature fₐ of its points. At v=0.001 almost every occupied voxel holds a single point (Table7) and at 6 views only 0.42% of anchors have an occupied 3³ neighbour, so anchors are points and the fine lattice carries no neighbourhood structure: any context the 3D stage uses must come from a coarser scale.

    2.3 Local-Context Aggregation

    The role of the 3D stage.

    Write Yₐ=(μₐ,Σₐ,αₐ,cₐ) for the Gaussian of anchor a. Its colour and position are functions of the anchor’s own pixel, (fₐ,xₐ). Scale, rotation, and opacity describe the surface arounda, which no single pixel observes; they are what the 3D stage has to supply, and they depend on the layout of P around a. Since anchors are isolated at the fine voxel size (Section2.2), this information has to be gathered at a coarser scale H, and the simplest fixed operator that does so is a local average. With wᵢ(a)=K_H(xₐ,xᵢ) for a kernel of bandwidth H and a linear projection W of the point features, splatting Wfᵢ into a grid of cell size H and reading the cell at a computes the Nadaraya–Watson estimate [(Nadaraya, 1964; Watson, 1964)] in its binned form,111 Binning here is a computational device, the same grid accumulation used by binned kernel estimators [(Hall and Wand, 1996)]. That analysis concerns density estimation, and we do not rely on it for a guarantee on the regression estimate in Eq.2; what the average is worth is measured empirically in Section3.5.

    u_H(a)=(∑ᵢwᵢ(a) Wfᵢ)/(∑ᵢwᵢ(a)).

    		(2)

    Because fᵢ carries each point’s depth and peak matching probability alongside its image features, W can route geometric information about the neighbourhood (such as its mean depth) into u_H as well as appearance. The motivation for LoCoSplat is that this fixed average, together with the anchor’s own feature, gives a pointwise map enough context to predict the Gaussian without a learned 3D network (Fig.2). Section3.5 measures what this context is worth, whether it needs to be learned or to carry appearance (by replacing u_H with an untrained low-pass or with geometric statistics of the cell), and how well a learned 3D refiner trains in this pipeline.

    Two grids and a pointwise map.

    LoCoSplat instantiates Eq.2 with the box kernel at two scales, with a learned 16-d projection per scale, W₀fᵢ and W₁fᵢ. The fine level is the base voxelization of Section2.2 itself: its grid is the anchor lattice cᵥ, and u₀(a)=W₀fₐ is the projection of the anchor’s own mean feature. The coarse level is a grid of cell size H=0.128 with its own cell index c_H(x)=rnd(x/H)∈ℤ³, the same rounding rule as cᵥ so that cell centres sit at integer multiples of H; writing n_H(c) for the number of points in coarse cell c,

    project & splat:fᵢ↦W₁fᵢ, u₁(c)=(1)/(n_H(c))∑_i: c_H(xᵢ)=cW₁fᵢ,(3)
    query & fuse:u₁(a)=u₁(c_H(xₐ)), f^′ₐ=fₐ+g([u₀(a);u₁(a);fₐ]),(4)

    with W₀,W₁∈ℝ^16×132, g:ℝ¹⁶⁴→ℝ²⁵⁶→ℝ²⁵⁶→ℝ¹³², and u₁(c)=0 for empty cells. The splat in Eq.3 is u_H of Eq.2 with wᵢ(a)=1[c_H(xᵢ)=c_H(xₐ)]. The fine level needs no splat: a nearest-cell splat of W₀fᵢ at cell size v under the same rounding rule, read back at the anchor, returns exactly the per-voxel mean W₀fₐ (a linear map commutes with the mean, and each voxel’s mean point lies inside its voxel), so u₀ is taken from the base voxelization directly and only the coarse level is splatted. The aggregation has no parameters and no data-dependent shape; the 3D stage’s only learned parameters are (W₀,W₁) (4.3k) and g (0.14M).

    2.4 Gaussian Prediction

    A two-layer pointwise MLP h:ℝ¹³²→ℝ³⁸→ℝ³⁸ (6.5k parameters) maps f^′ₐ to raw parameters (ᾱₐ,ōₐ,s̄ₐ,q̄ₐ,c̄ₐ)∈ℝ¹⁺³⁺³⁺⁴⁺²⁷, decoded as

    μₐ=xₐ+3v (σ(ōₐ)-\tfrac12),αₐ=σ(ᾱₐ),(5)
    sₐ=clip(softplus(s̄ₐ-4), s_\min, s_\max),Σₐ=R(q̄ₐ/∥q̄ₐ∥) diag(sₐ)² R(q̄ₐ/∥q̄ₐ∥)^⊤,

    where σ is the sigmoid, R(·) the rotation matrix of a unit quaternion, and the offset is confined to ±1.5 fine voxels around the anchor. The colour cₐ is a degree-2 spherical-harmonics vector whose DC term is set from the mean RGB of the anchor’s pixels; h predicts the higher orders. A pointwise head suffices because 99.6% of anchors have no occupied 3³ neighbour (Section2.2), so a sparse convolution would reduce to its centre tap at almost every anchor (Remark1); it also keeps the pipeline free of sparse-tensor operations.

    2.5 Training Objective

    Following DepthSplat and VolSplat [(Xu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026a)], the network is trained end to end from RGB supervision alone. Writing Î⁽ᵐ⁾_G for the m-th of M target views rendered from a Gaussian set G with a differentiable rasterizer [(Kerbl et al., 2023)],

    L=∑ₘ₌₁^M[ℓ(Î⁽ᵐ⁾_G(D),I⁽ᵐ⁾)+β ℓ(Î⁽ᵐ⁾_G(D̃),I⁽ᵐ⁾)], ℓ(Î,I)=∥Î-I∥₂²+λ LPIPS(Î,I),

    		(6)

    with λ=0.05 and β=0.9. G(D) is the Gaussian set built from the final depth and G(D̃) the one built from the coarse depth of Section2.1 through the same anchors, 3D stage, and head (shared weights); no depth ground truth is used. All models train for 150k steps with AdamW under VolSplat’s training protocol (SectionsB.1 and B.2). Nothing in Sections2.2, 2.3 and 2.4 has a data-dependent shape, so at inference the entire encoder runs as one fp16 CUDA graph (Section3.3).

    3 Experiments

    3.1 Experimental Setup

    Datasets and protocol.

    We train on RealEstate10K [(Zhou et al., 2018)] (256×256) and evaluate on VolSplat’s official indices (∼700 test scenes, 8 target views each) at 6, 12, and 24 context views; zero-shot generalization uses ACID [(Liu et al., 2021)] (173 scenes), and indoor transfer follows the FreeSplat protocol [(Wang et al., 2024b)] on ScanNet [(Dai et al., 2017)], fine-tuning every RealEstate10K checkpoint for 150k steps and evaluating on VolSplat’s official 72-sequence index. All our models and our retrained VolSplat follow VolSplat’s official training protocol (Sections2.5 and B.2; 4× NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000).

    Baselines and metrics.

    We compare against pixel-aligned (pixelSplat, MVSplat, TranSplat, DepthSplat), post-processed (GGN), and pose-free (AnySplat, WorldMirror; released checkpoints) methods, FreeSplat on ScanNet, and VolSplat as published and retrained, the anchor for all paired analyses (SectionB.2). We report PSNR, SSIM [(Wang et al., 2004)], and LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)]; all methods are timed with their released code on the same GPU under the same protocol (AppendixA).

    3.2 Main Results on RealEstate10K

    Table1 reports quality across view counts. LoCoSplat has the best PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS at every view count: +0.58 PSNR over our retrained VolSplat at 6 views and +0.61 at 12 (paired, 68% of scenes). Our retrained VolSplat is the stronger 12-view baseline (30.86 vs. the published 29.40) and anchors every paired comparison (SectionB.2). At 24 views every RealEstate10K-trained method degrades as the context densifies, VolSplat most; LoCoSplat does not share the drop: 30.57 PSNR, +3.3 paired over VolSplat (98% of scenes) and +1.2 over WorldMirror, which is pretrained on a large multi-dataset corpus and essentially flat in the view count; Section3.5 traces the difference to one hyper-parameter of the depth branch. Qualitatively, pixel-aligned methods blur and duplicate thin structures at 6 views (Fig.3); at 24 views VolSplat streaks and the pose-free baselines blur branches and text (Fig.8; 12 views in Fig.7).

    3.3 Real-Time Reconstruction

    Table2 summarizes efficiency at 6 views. The 3D stage has no data-dependent shape (a sort-based voxel group-by padded to a static V·H·W row count, fixed-table gathers and scatters, pointwise g and h), so the whole encoder is captured as one fp16 CUDA graph (SectionB.1). LoCoSplat reconstructs 4.2× faster than VolSplat on this path and 2.4× faster at equal fp32 precision (56.9 vs. 137.0 ms), trains 2.7× faster (13.2 vs. 35.4 h; 27 vs. 159 h at 24 views), and uses 85% less peak inference memory with 76% fewer trainable parameters; VolSplat gains only 1.4% from the same optimizations, as its sparse U-Net resists mixed precision, static shapes, and graph capture. Most of the speedup is architectural: removing the U-Net takes the fp32 eager encoder from 137.0 to 94.4 ms while improving quality (Tables9 and 8). Against the released baselines, LoCoSplat is the fastest at every view count, at the lowest memory and the highest PSNR (2.5× faster than DepthSplat, the next fastest; 2.9 vs. 27.3 GB for VolSplat at 24 views; Tables6 and 7); MVSplat and GGN match its trainable-parameter count but run 2.8–5.4× slower and lose 2.4 and 4.8 PSNR.

    3.4 Generalization: Zero-Shot ACID and ScanNet Fine-Tuning

    Table4 evaluates RealEstate10K-trained models on ACID without fine-tuning. The margin over VolSplat does not shrink out of domain: it grows to +0.87 PSNR paired (77% of scenes) against +0.58 in domain, and LoCoSplat also exceeds the PSNR and LPIPS VolSplat reports for its own checkpoint. In Fig.4, VolSplat’s refinement smears thin structures such as a radio tower and the pixel-aligned baselines ghost or dissolve them, which LoCoSplat preserves. Table4 fine-tunes LoCoSplat and VolSplat from their RealEstate10K checkpoints under VolSplat’s ScanNet fine-tuning protocol; the ordering carries over with a wider margin: LoCoSplat gains +0.92 PSNR over the fine-tuned VolSplat (on all 8 scenes) and lies above every published entry (Fig.5, SectionE.3).

  • 单张 RTX PRO 6000 上 6 视图重建 33ms，比此前 SOTA 快 4.2 倍，推理显存少 6.7 倍，训练快 2.7 倍（24 视图时 5.9 倍）

为什么值得看：前馈 3DGS 的算力一直砸在「用网络推理 3D」上，这篇给出了相反的证据：把 3D 推理压到最简、把局部性用足，速度和画质可以同时赢。做移动端或批量重建的团队值得先抄这个结构。

中文摘要：前馈式 3D 高斯泼溅近年靠越来越重的可学习 3D 网络来聚合多视图证据。LoCoSplat 的出发点是：高斯是局部基元，一旦深度预测出来，3D 阶段要补的尺度、旋转、不透明度其实只取决于每个锚点周围的点云，用该邻域的一个固定局部平均就能提供。它把这个平均做成两次 splat：16 维点特征投影进细网格和粗网格，再在每个锚点处读回，经 0.14M 参数的点式 MLP 输出属性；没有可学习 3D 网络与动态稀疏计算，整个编码器可跑成一张 fp16 CUDA graph。RealEstate10K 上各视图数全指标领先，24 视图较 VolSplat 高 3.3 PSNR。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-03

本期推送：2026-10-24

LoCoSplat: Real-Time Feed-Forward
3D Gaussian Splatting
with Minimal 3D Reasoning

Abstract

Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) increasingly aggregates multi-view evidence with heavy learned 3D networks. We propose LoCoSplat (Local-Context Splatting), motivated by the observation that a Gaussian is a local primitive: once depth is predicted, what the 3D stage must add (scale, rotation, opacity) depends on the point cloud around each anchor, and a fixed local average of that neighbourhood is enough to supply it, no heavy network required. LoCoSplat realises exactly this average: it splats a 16-d linear projection of the point features into a fine and a coarse grid and reads both back at each anchor with a 0.14M-parameter pointwise MLP; with no learned 3D network and no dynamic sparse computation, its whole encoder runs as one fp16 CUDA graph. On RealEstate10K, LoCoSplat outperforms every prior feed-forward method on PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS at 6, 12, and 24 views, with a margin that widens as views densify (+3.3 PSNR over VolSplat, the prior voxel-aligned state of the art, at 24 views) and grows further under zero-shot transfer to ACID and fine-tuning on ScanNet. It reconstructs a 6-view scene in 33 ms on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU, the fastest of seven feed-forward methods and 4.2× faster than the previous state of the art, trains 2.7× faster (5.9× at 24 views), and uses 6.7× less inference memory.

11footnotetext: Equal contribution.

1 Introduction

Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting [(Charatan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025)] predicts the Gaussian primitives of 3DGS [(Kerbl et al., 2023)] from a handful of posed images in a single forward pass, replacing the per-scene optimization of NeRF and 3DGS [(Mildenhall et al., 2020; Kerbl et al., 2023)] with a learned prior. Pixel-aligned prediction, the dominant approach, suffers from multi-view misalignment and resolution-bound Gaussian budgets, and the field’s answer has been to reason with ever-heavier learned modules, mostly by moving prediction into 3D: sparse 3D U-Nets and CNNs [(Wang et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2022)], 3D cost-volume networks, or long-sequence Mamba/transformer models over image tokens [(Ziwen et al., 2025)]. VolSplat [(Wang et al., 2026a)], the state of the art of the depth-guided voxel-aligned family, predicts depth, voxelizes the unprojected pixels into anchors, and then refines the sparse volume with a 17M-parameter sparse 3D U-Net before decoding Gaussians. That U-Net is its largest inference cost (∼7 scenes per second): a dynamic-shape sparse computation [(Choy et al., 2019)] that cannot be captured in a CUDA graph and barely benefits from mixed precision, and the dominant training memory as views grow (24-view training takes 159 hours). Behind this trajectory lies an implicit assumption: that aggregating multi-view evidence in 3D requires substantial learned 3D capacity.

Our motivation is a local view of the 3D stage: what a Gaussian needs from its neighbours is the kind of low-order local information that a grid computes for free, not a learned 3D network. LoCoSplat (Local-Context Splatting, Fig.1) keeps the depth-guided voxel-aligned pipeline (Section2.1) up to the anchors: a hybrid monocular–multi-view depth branch and a DPT feature head place one anchor per occupied voxel. Its 3D stage is a fixed grid average: each anchor’s feature, linearly projected to 16 dimensions, is averaged into a fine and a coarse grid, and both grids are read back at the anchor by a 0.14M-parameter pointwise MLP and a pointwise head. With no learned 3D network and no dynamic sparse computation, the whole encoder runs as one fp16 CUDA graph.

The motivation is structural: a 3D Gaussian is a local primitive. Once depth is predicted, each anchor’s colour and position are determined by its own pixel. The 3D stage must add scale, rotation, and opacity, the layout of the surface around the anchor; no single pixel observes this layout, but it is determined by the neighbouring points, which a fixed average over a coarser neighbourhood, computed for free by a grid, can summarize. The anchors are also so sparse at the working voxel size (99.6% have no occupied neighbour at 6 views) that a 3³ sparse convolution over them is already pointwise (Section2.4), so any context must come from a coarser scale, which the coarse grid supplies. This intuition led to the design.

We then measure what the 3D stage of this pipeline actually needs (Section3): very little. A fixed grid average read by a pointwise MLP of under 0.2M parameters beats the 17M-parameter U-Net by +0.70 PSNR (Table9). LoCoSplat has the best PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS of all feed-forward methods on RealEstate10K at 6, 12, and 24 views, with a margin that grows on ACID and ScanNet, and reconstructs a 6-view scene in 33.0 ms (30.3 FPS) on one GPU, 4.2× faster than VolSplat (2.4× at equal fp32 precision) with 85% less peak inference memory, and trains 2.7× faster (5.9× at 24 views; Table2).

Our contributions are:

  • •

    A 3D stage with no learned 3D network, motivated by the locality of a Gaussian, with controlled experiments showing that the 3D stage of this pipeline needs very little: a fixed grid average read by a pointwise MLP of under 0.2M parameters beats a 17M-parameter sparse 3D U-Net, and the minimal coarse context it keeps needs neither learning nor appearance content (Section3.5).

  • •

    LoCoSplat, a state-of-the-art real-time feed-forward 3DGS method, leading at 6, 12, and 24 views, in and out of domain, whose fp16 CUDA-graph encoder reconstructs at 30 FPS on one GPU, 4.2× faster than VolSplat with 6.7× less inference memory and 2.7× faster training (Section3.3).

  • •

    A predictive account of the dense-view collapse of depth-guided reconstruction: an optimization failure of the depth branch governed by the per-candidate plane-sweep disparity; LoCoSplat does not collapse and leads VolSplat by +3.3 PSNR at 24 views (Section3.5).

    • 2 Method

    LoCoSplat reconstructs a set of 3D Gaussians from V posed images in one forward pass (Fig.1). Its 2D stage (Section2.1) is a depth-guided pipeline in the VolSplat/DepthSplat family [(Wang et al., 2026a; Xu et al., 2025)]: per-view depth and per-pixel features, unprojected and voxelized into anchors (Section2.2). Its 3D stage (Section2.3) has no learned 3D network: a fixed local average of the point features is read by a pointwise MLP, and a pointwise head decodes each anchor’s Gaussian (Section2.4); Section2.5 gives the training objective.

    2.1 Depth and Feature Prediction

    The input is V images Iᵢ∈ℝ^H×W×3 with intrinsics Kᵢ and camera-to-world poses (Rᵢ,tᵢ). A frozen DepthAnythingV2 ViT-B backbone [(Yang et al., 2024)] provides monocular features, mapped by a trainable linear interface from 768 to 384 channels (ViT-S width); a CNN with a local-window cross-view transformer over the two nearest views [(Xu et al., 2023)] provides matching features, from which a plane-sweep cost volume over D=64 inverse-depth candidates {dₖ} is built. A depthwise-separable, half-width UniMatch-style regressor turns it into matching probabilities pᵢ[k,p] and the coarse inverse depth d̃ᵢ(p)=∑ₖpᵢ[k,p] dₖ; one DPT head [(Yang et al., 2024)] refines it with the monocular features into the full-resolution depth Dᵢ, and a second DPT head yields the per-pixel feature f_i,p∈ℝ¹³² (image, depth, and peak matching probability appended) that enters the 3D stage.

    2.2 Anchors

    Every pixel is unprojected along its depth and voxelized at the fine voxel size v=0.001:

    x_i,p=Rᵢ Dᵢ(p) Kᵢ⁻¹\beginbmatrixp 1\endbmatrix+tᵢ, cᵥ(x)=rnd(x/v)∈ℤ³.

    		(1)

    This gives the point cloud P={(xᵢ,fᵢ)}_i≤n, n=V·H·W, and the anchor set A={cᵥ(xᵢ)} of occupied voxels, one Gaussian per anchor; anchor a carries the mean position xₐ and mean feature fₐ of its points. At v=0.001 almost every occupied voxel holds a single point (Table7) and at 6 views only 0.42% of anchors have an occupied 3³ neighbour, so anchors are points and the fine lattice carries no neighbourhood structure: any context the 3D stage uses must come from a coarser scale.

    2.3 Local-Context Aggregation

    The role of the 3D stage.

    Write Yₐ=(μₐ,Σₐ,αₐ,cₐ) for the Gaussian of anchor a. Its colour and position are functions of the anchor’s own pixel, (fₐ,xₐ). Scale, rotation, and opacity describe the surface arounda, which no single pixel observes; they are what the 3D stage has to supply, and they depend on the layout of P around a. Since anchors are isolated at the fine voxel size (Section2.2), this information has to be gathered at a coarser scale H, and the simplest fixed operator that does so is a local average.
