Novel view synthesis has significantly advanced the reconstruction and interactive exploration of real-world environments. Recent progress in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [KKLD23] combines the visual fidelity of neural radiance field approaches [MST∗20] with the efficiency of point-based rendering, enabling high-quality real-time rendering even on resource-constrained platforms. Despite these advances, reconstructed scenes remain predominantly static and often fail to capture dynamic phenomena that are essential for visual realism. This limitation is particularly evident in fluid regions, where 3D Gaussian primitives frequently produce temporally inconsistent or structurally unstable reconstructions. As a result, phenomena such as flowing water often appear unnaturally frozen. In this work, we show that introducing plausible motion specifically in these regions can substantially enhance the perceived realism and liveliness of reconstructed scenes.

Recent dynamic Gaussian Splatting methods have made substantial progress toward extending static reconstruction frameworks to dynamic scenes, but primarily focus on explicitly moving foreground objects [LKLR24, WYF∗24, YYPZ24]. In contrast, subtle continuous background phenomena such as rivers or waterfalls remain largely underexplored. Moreover, many dynamic reconstruction approaches rely on multi-view synchronized capture setups, limiting their applicability to casually captured or in-the-wild data. An alternative direction augments static 3DGS reconstructions with synthesized dynamics. While physics-based methods [XZQ∗24] can produce convincing simulations across materials including fluids, they incur substantial computational cost and are difficult to apply in real-time or casual capture settings. Instead of targeting physically accurate simulation, which is often unnecessary for visual realism, we aim to generate visually plausible motion that improves scene perception while remaining efficient.

To this end, we draw inspiration from cinemagraphs, which introduce temporally looping motion into otherwise static imagery and are particularly effective for fluid phenomena in 2D [HCSS21]. Prior work extending cinemagraphs to 3D either combines layered depth representations with neural networks [LCS∗23], resulting in slow rendering and limited free-viewpoint capability, or relies on self-similarity in Gaussian point clouds [LCW∗24], which provides insufficient structure to recover realistic fluid motion. These limitations motivate a more efficient approach for visually plausible water animation in static 3DGS scenes.

Given a 3DGS model and its training views (or alternatively model renderings), we estimate per-view fluid flow with an existing pretrained network [MK22]. Our first contribution is lifting these multi-view estimates into a grid-based 3D Eulerian motion field via depth-based reprojection, refined via static/dynamic voxel hit ratios and view-hit thresholding. Second, we adopt the concept of symmetric warping from 2D cinemagraphs [HCSS21], which is defined for pixels, and reformulate it for 3D Gaussians treated as Lagrangian particles: volume-aware covariance propagation, density-preserving opacity blending, and randomized per-Gaussian temporal offsets replace the feature warping and inpainting used in 2D. The resulting method integrates directly into the 3DGS rendering pipeline, enabling real-time animation of static scenes with low overhead and allowing interactive exploration of dynamically enhanced environments (cf. ).

For evaluation, we introduce a new dataset of seven casually captured 3DGS scenes containing fluid phenomena such as waterfalls. We compare against dynamic Gaussian Splatting [YYPZ24] and recent 3D cinemagraph methods [LCS∗23, LCW∗24] qualitatively and in terms of efficiency. As evident in our video, our method produces more realistic and temporally coherent novel view renderings while remaining computationally efficient.

In summary, we make the following contributions:

  • •

    The first method to animate fluid regions in a static 3DGS scene, without dynamic capture, retraining, or simulation.

  • •

    An efficient, 3DGS-based approach for lifting multi-view optical flow into a 3D Eulerian motion field.

  • •

    A deformation framework for temporally looping, visually plausible fluid animation, integrated into a real-time 3DGS rendering system for interactive exploration of animated scenes.

  • •

    A curated dataset of seven casual scenes with fluid motion.

    • We will release our full implementation, including preprocessing scripts, interactive GUI, and dataset.

    2 Related Work

    Our work extends novel view synthesis by integrating cinemagraph-inspired motion into static 3D scene representations, with a focus on efficient and perceptually plausible fluid animation.

    2.1 Novel View Synthesis

    Early image-based rendering and light field methods [DTM96, GGSC96, LH96] are limited by sparse viewpoint coverage. Neural radiance fields (NeRF) [MST∗20] significantly advanced novel view synthesis, but are expensive to train and render, which motivated more efficient scene parameterizations [FKYT∗22, SSC22, MESK22, CXG∗22]. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [KKLD23] models scenes as anisotropic Gaussians optimized for real-time rasterization and forms the basis of our approach.

    Extensions of both NeRF and 3DGS to dynamic scenes introduce temporal variation either through explicit time-conditioned representations or learned deformation fields [PCPMMN21, PSB∗21, CJ23, FKMW∗23, FYW∗22, LDZY24, YYPZ24, WYF∗24]. These methods achieve compelling results for structured and well-observed motion such as humans or rigid objects, but typically assume controlled multi-view capture setups or availability of strong data-driven priors. Such assumptions restrict their applicability to casually captured or in-the-wild scenes. Moreover, they are less suitable for subtle, continuous background phenomena such as water, where motion is locally smooth, temporally repetitive, and driven more by perceptual consistency than strict geometric reconstruction.

    2.2 Cinemagraphs and Motion Synthesis

    Cinemagraphs and the closely related video textures [SSSE00] introduce looping motion into static imagery while preserving spatial consistency. Early work focused on manual or semi-automatic creation, followed by numerous methods for automatic loop synthesis and fluid animation in videos [LJH13, LFH15, TPSK11]. These techniques have demonstrated that fluid regions such as waterfalls are particularly well-suited for perceptually convincing motion synthesis.

    Recent learning-based approaches extend cinemagraph generation to single-image or sparse-input settings using generative models or optical flow prediction [HHB18, GXG18, EKK19]. More recently, diffusion-based image-to-video models have enabled controllable cinemagraph synthesis with localized motion editing and user-guided spatial constraints [LIM∗26]. While visually compelling, these approaches remain computationally expensive and typically require repeated inference for long-duration or seamlessly looping animations, limiting interactivity and real-time applicability.

    To address this, recent works learn static or quasi-static motion fields that enable efficient looping animations [HCSS21, MK22, HHV∗21]. These approaches are effective for synthesizing fluid motion and form the foundation of our motion generation framework.

    Recent work has further explored lifting cinemagraph synthesis into 3D scene representations. Approaches based on layered depth images or multi-view video synthesis project 2D motion into 3D representations, but remain limited in viewpoint flexibility or reconstruction quality [LCS∗23, MLLS23]. More recent methods leverage neural or Gaussian-based scene representations to synthesize motion directly in 3D [LCW∗24, JMG∗25]. However, these methods often rely on appearance-based similarity, specialized motion priors, or computationally expensive learned pipelines, which work well for their specific application but limit their ability to model coherent directional fluid motion in unconstrained scenes.

    Related approaches also augment static Gaussian scenes with specialized scene dynamics such as snowfall using physics-guided diffusion models [FAEB26], or fluids using physics-based simulation with artificially added fluid particles rather than animating reconstructed water [FFS∗25]. Physics-based methods incur substantial computational cost, require careful per-scene setup, or noticeably alter scene appearance. Recent methods targeting oscillatory scene dynamics, such as swaying vegetation, employ specifically tailored motion models [SHK∗24, LGB∗26, THM∗26]. While effective for such structured oscillatory motion, these assumptions do not readily generalize to fluid phenomena.

    In contrast to dynamic reconstruction, learned 3D cinemagraph approaches and physics-based simulation, we augment static 3DGS scenes using motion derived from 2D flow priors, enabling efficient and controllable fluid animation without reconstructing a fully dynamic scene.

    3 Method

    We propose an end-to-end pipeline for animating fluid regions in a static 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [KKLD23] reconstruction (cf. Fig.1). In contrast to previous methods [LCS∗23, MLLS23], our objective is a complete animated 3D scene observable from arbitrary viewing directions. Besides its real-time rendering capabilities, 3DGS offers an explicit scene representation based on a set of points G with anisotropic Gaussian extent that are straightforward to animate. Specifically, each Gaussian is described by its mean μ∈ℝ³, 3D covariance Σ∈ℝ^3×3, opacity o∈[0,1], and view-dependent color c∈ℝ³ computed from Spherical Harmonics coefficients ∈ℝ⁴⁸. This representation is then optimized from multi-view RGB images I_1,⋯,N with known camera poses. To render an image, 3DGS linearly approximates the perspective projection onto the image plane at a point x (usually μ) [ZPvBG01]:

    J_n, x=\beginpmatrix(f)/(x̂₃)&0&-(fx̂₁)/((x̂₃)²) 0&(f)/(x̂₃)&-(fx̂₂)/((x̂₃)²)\endpmatrixRₙ, with x̂=Rₙx+tₙ

    		(1)

    where x̂ᵢ denotes the i-th component of x̂, (Rₙ,tₙ) the world-to-camera transformation of the n-th view, and f the focal length. Optionally, I_1,⋯,N can be extended by renderings from user defined camera poses. For each pixel p in a rendered image Iₙ, color is accumulated by alpha blending Gaussian contributions:

    Iₙ(p)=∑ᵢ₌₁^McᵢTᵢoᵢgᵢ(p) with Tᵢ=∏ⱼ₌₁ⁱ⁻¹(1-oⱼgⱼ(p)),

    		(2)

    where gᵢ(p) is the i-th Gaussian value at the pixel p. Since our method assumes G and I_1,⋯,N are provided as input, no training modifications and minimal renderer changes (see Sec.3.3.3) are required. In the following subsections, we describe each step in our pipeline for animating fluids in such 3DGS models.

    3.1 Optical Flow Estimation

    To construct a 3D motion field, we first estimate 2D optical flow F_1,⋯,N for each input view. Since the input images are static and non-time-consecutive, conventional optical flow methods [TD20] are not applicable. Instead, following prior cinemagraph approaches [HCSS21, MK22], we employ a specialized neural network trained on fluid motion. For improved controllability and cross-view consistency, the network is guided by user-defined motion hints and segmentation masks.

    We define a set of global 3D motion hints H={(pₗ,dₗ)}ₗ₌₁^L interactively within the 3DGS scene using our GUI. Each hint consists of a 3D position pₗ∈ℝ³ and a motion direction dₗ∈ℝ³, where \lVertdₗ\rVert₂ controls motion strength. Defining hints directly in 3D ensures consistent motion guidance across views. The hints are projected into each camera view using the projection operator πₙ, resulting in sparse 2D flow hints Hₙ={(πₙ(p),πₙ(p+d)-πₙ(p))|(p,d)∈H} that are converted to sparse flow maps:

    Fˢᵖᵃʳˢᵉₙ(x)=\begincasesd/r^H,&if∃ dwith(x,d)∈Hₙ 0,&otherwise\endcases ,

    		(3)

    with a regulation factor r^H=median{\lVertd\rVert₂|(p,d)∈Hₙ} to limit the extent of projected motion hints in screen space.

    To restrict motion to fluid regions, we additionally compute binary segmentation masks S_1,⋯,N for all input images using the promptable segmentation model SAM3 [CGH∗26]. These masks are used both to guide the motion synthesis network and to constrain subsequent 3D motion field fusion. In practice, simple prompts such as “water” or “waterfall” are sufficient for robust segmentation in most scenes. For cases requiring additional user control, we use an interactive segmentation tool [COP∗24].

    Following Mahapatra and Kulkarni [MK22], the sparse flow maps are converted into dense flow maps Fᵈᵉⁿˢᵉ_1,⋯,N via distance-weighted interpolation within the segmented regions (see AppendixA). Finally, a learned flow refinement network takes RGB images I_1,⋯,N, segmentation masks S_1,⋯,N, and dense flow maps Fᵈᵉⁿˢᵉ_1,⋯,N as input to generate high-quality fluid flow maps F_1,⋯,N. We adopt the SPADE-based U-Net architecture of Mahapatra and Kulkarni [MK22] using the implementation and pretrained weights provided by Li et al. [LCS∗23].

    3.2 3D Motion Field

    In contrast to motion estimated from Gaussian self-similarity [LCW∗24], which suits subtle motion such as swaying vegetation but not dense directional fluid flow, or to flow projected onto a single-view layered depth image [LCS∗23], we project multi-view optical flow into the 3DGS scene to obtain a coherent 3D motion field M.

    Depth Rendering.

    In order to reproject 2D optical flow into the scene, depth information is required. To this end, we render depth maps D_1,⋯,N from the 3DGS model for all input views. We compute the depth of each pixel via alpha blending as defined in Eq.2, where the color of each Gaussian is replaced by its depth μ̂₃ (cf. Eq.1). Note that we divide by the final alpha value of the pixel to obtain meaningful depth for semi-transparent pixels. We further highlight that using depth renderings of the underlying 3DGS model aligns the motion field with Gaussians that can be animated.

    Multi-View Reprojection.

    Our setup for the motion field fusion can be thought of as a multi-view reprojection problem [HZ03, TIF24], with n known projections vₙ=Fₙ(xₙ)∈ℝ² of an unknown vector v∈ℝ³. This vector is anchored at x=π⁻¹ₙ(xₙ,Dₙ(xₙ)), which is the common point when unprojecting each xₙ into world space using depth information. The goal is minimizing the geometric non-linear reprojection error:

    \minᵥ∑ₙ\lVertπₙ(x+v)-(xₙ+vₙ)\rVert₂² .

    		(4)

    As vₙ, i.e., the optical flow is usually small, it is reasonable to linearly approximate the perspective projection by first-order Taylor expansion πₙ(x+v)≈πₙ(x)+J_n, xv, with J_n, x as defined in Eq.1. Since πₙ(x)=xₙ is known, we can solve a simplified linear system of equations for v with the iterative Gauss-Newton algorithm:

    \underbrace(∑ₙJ_n,x^⊤J_n,x)_Av=\underbrace∑ₙJ_n,x^⊤vₙ_b.

    		(5)

    3.2.1 Voxel Grid Fusion

    We implement the motion field M:ℝ³→ℝ³ as a regular voxel grid with fixed voxel size and store motion at voxel centers c∈C. To enable querying for motion v at an arbitrary scene point x, we apply trilinear interpolation of the neighboring voxel centers of x. The trilinear interpolation weights wᵗʳⁱ define the motion contribution of each involved c, based on distance of c and x. Every query for an x outside the bounding box of the grid results in v=0⃗. The bounding box is initialized by the dimensions of the point cloud containing all reprojected dynamic pixels.

    For fusion, we apply the concepts of multi-view reprojection and accumulate A and b (Eq.5), per voxel over all views and solve for v afterward. We leverage GPU-accelerated linear algebra to efficiently solve the Gauss–Newton system in parallel across voxels. After fusion, M is converted into a sparse voxel grid, for memory efficient storage on disk. Note that fusion is only performed once, since we use M as a static velocity field for all animation frames similar to Holynski et al. [HCSS21].

    In a first pass through the input data we approximate v at c∈C for all voxels based on Fₙ and Dₙ of the projected views n. Pixels within dynamic regions x∈Sₙ are reprojected with x=π⁻¹ₙ(x, Dₙ(x)), and grouped to the corresponding voxels. Grouping uses either hard indexing within the voxel bounds (each pixel has weight 1) or trilinear splatting to neighboring voxels (weight wᵗʳⁱ). Per view and voxel, the weighted flow values are averaged to obtain vₙ, and wₙ denotes the sum of weights. With the Jacobian J_n, c evaluated at the voxel center, A_c and b_c are accumulated over all views, each view contributing once per voxel. After accumulating all views, the per-voxel 3×3 linear systems A_cv=b_c are solved and motion is stored such that M(c)=v. For refinement, we also accumulate dynamic pixel hits wᵈʸⁿ_c=∑ₙwₙ and view hits wᵛⁱᵉʷ_c, i.e., how many views contributed motion to a voxel.

    3.2.2 Refinement

    Wrong depth information from misplaced Gaussians causing wrong pixel reprojection, or voxels intersecting the boundary of static and dynamic regions, can lead to motion within static regions. To this end, we refine M by deleting these incorrect voxels by performing a second pass through the input data. Pixels outside the masked region Sₙ(x)=0 are projected and grouped by voxels as before, but rather than performing reprojection, now only static hits are tracked as wˢᵗᵃᵗ_c weighted by wᵗʳⁱ if necessary. Intuitively, a voxel observed more often as static than as dynamic most likely lies in a static region, and its motion is reduced accordingly:

    M(c)=(1-min(1, (wˢᵗᵃᵗ_c)/(wᵈʸⁿ_c)))·v .

    		(6)

    We also find that the multi-view reprojection problem becomes ill-posed when there are limited observations, especially if the associated viewing directions are mostly collinear. In practice, we therefore assume that a number of observations below a threshold is insufficient to reconstruct a plausible v. Consequently, we set the motion of voxels with view hits wᵛⁱᵉʷ_c below this threshold rᵛⁱᵉʷ to zero, further reducing the size of M.

    We show pseudocode for our 3D motion field fusion approach and refinement techniques in AppendixB.

    3.3 Gaussian Animation and Rendering

    We treat 3D Gaussians as Lagrangian particles that undergo deformation within Eulerian grids. The majority of Gaussians reside in static scene regions and will therefore not be deformed by M. This enables us to efficiently segment the scene into static Gˢᵗᵃᵗ=G∖Gᵈʸⁿ and dynamic Gaussians Gᵈʸⁿ={g∈G|\lVertM(μ)\rVert₂>0} by querying motion at their means.

    3.3.1 Transforming Gaussians

    To achieve volume-aware transformation of 3D Gaussians, we iteratively apply Unscented Transform[JU97] with velocities queried from M to transform mean and covariance of each g∈Gᵈʸⁿ. The volume of a 3D Gaussian is approximated by seven sigma points:

    σᵢ(μ,Σ)=\begincasesμ&i=0 μ+(-1)ⁱ√(3+λ)√Σ_⌈i/2⌉&i=1,…,6\endcases ,

    		(7)

    with √Σᵢ being the i-th column of the Cholesky-decomposed covariance and λ = 3α² - 3 and α a parameter to control the spread around μ. The sigma points have corresponding weights for mean and covariance defined as

    w^μᵢ=\begincasesλ/3+λ&i=0 1/2(3+λ)&i=1,…,6\endcases, w^Σᵢ=w^μᵢ+\begincases3-α²&i=0 0&i=1,…,6\endcases.(8)

    The Unscented Transform can be applied iteratively via Euler integration to acquire updated mean μₖ₊₁ and covariance Σₖ₊₁ for any Gaussian g and iteration k. The sigma points are displaced by the motion queried from M as

    σ̃ᵢ=σᵢ(μₖ,Σₖ)+r^MM(σᵢ(μₖ,Σₖ)) .

    		(9)

    The recursion is initialized with the original Gaussian parameters μ₀=μ, Σ₀=Σ. We also apply a regulation factor r^M to manually control the motion extent in cases where M does not contain physically meaningful velocities. The displaced sigma points σ̃ᵢ are used to update mean and covariance as

    μₖ₊₁=∑⁶ᵢ₌₀w^μᵢσ̃ᵢ , Σₖ₊₁=∑⁶ᵢ₌₀w^Σᵢ(σ̃ᵢ-μₖ₊₁)(σ̃ᵢ-μₖ₊₁)^⊤.

    		(10)

    3.3.2 Symmetric Animation

    Naturally, M contains motion sources, i.e., regions from which particles move away without new particles moving in, such as the top of a waterfall. For a looping animation, we extend the symmetric warping technique of Holynski et al. [HCSS21] to 3D Gaussians by applying forward and backward transformations. Each g∈Gᵈʸⁿ is forward transformed through K iterations of Eq.10 into a keyframe-sequence A^fw=((μₖ,Σₖ))^Kₖ₌₀. Analogously, a backward keyframe-sequence Aᵇʷ=((μ_K-k,Σ_K-k))^Kₖ₌₀ is calculated using the negated motion field -M. Although mean and covariance are calculated by forward propagating the transformation update from 0→K, the order of keyframes in Aᵇʷ is reversed, such that A^fw₀=Aᵇʷ_K. Due to -M, g moves backward within the motion field, which is reversed into forward flow direction. Phenomenologically, this means motion sources from A^fw act as motion drains for Aᵇʷ. Note that a general inverse motion field M⁻¹ is not available but -M offers a reasonable approximation and ensures the required symmetry [HCSS21]. We visualize this in AppendixD.

    Opacity Blending.

    While A^fw and Aᵇʷ internally offer a smooth animation, looping both will result in a visible cut when Gaussians snap back to their initial state at the end of the sequence. Furthermore, two instances of each dynamic Gaussian double the local scene density. To mitigate these effects, we multiply opacity o of each g∈Gᵈʸⁿ by wₖᵒ=\sin²(πk/2K). Opacity for the forward and backward sequence is defined as O^fw=((1-wₖᵒ)o)^Kₖ₌₀ and Oᵇʷ=(wₖᵒo)^Kₖ₌₀. As O^fw decreases from o to 0 and Oᵇʷ increases from 0 to o, the backward instance fades in while the forward instance fades out. This results in Gaussians being most visible in their original state while becoming less visible as they diverge due to applied transformations. Note that O^fwₖ+Oᵇʷₖ=o for all k ensures consistent local scene density and O^fw_K=Oᵇʷ₀=0 in combination with A^fw₀=Aᵇʷ_K ensures a seamless transition between looping sequences (cf. AppendixD).

    Randomized Animation States.

    Loops can still be perceivable due to large repeating patterns, which 2D cinemagraphy mitigates by warping deep features and inpainting. For 3D Gaussians, we instead randomly offset the global animation state t∈[0,1) of each g by an individual offset t^off∈[0,1). The offset differs between Gaussians, but corresponding forward and backward instances are offset by the same t^off to maintain the symmetric transformation of each individual g. Note that the looping dynamic is not disrupted; only the starting point of each g along its transformation trajectory is shifted. It may be infeasible to completely disrupt patterns in specific fluid regions, so a maximum allowed random offset can be used to restrict t^off.

    3.3.3 Rendering

    We implement our CUDA renderer on top of an optimized 3DGS implementation [HFEM26]. Our symmetric animation technique requires rendering multiple instances of each g∈Gᵈʸⁿ, each transformed by the keyframe of its own animation state. For VRAM efficiency, these instances are virtual, i.e., share all animation-independent parameter buffers. With the local animation state τ=(t+t^off)\bmod1, the keyframe of a virtual Gaussian instance is k=⌊τK⌋. For smoother animation, means, covariances, and opacities of neighboring keyframes can be linearly interpolated with weight τK-k. While linearly interpolating covariances is not exact with respect to rotation, the covariance difference between keyframes is typically small. Consequently, it is a visually smooth and efficient alternative to proper rotation interpolation.

    4 Evaluation

    We evaluate our method and compare it to recent approaches with similar goals in a series of experiments. We conduct all experiments on the same system using an RTX 4090 GPU. Quantitatively evaluating synthesized fluid motion is inherently difficult: casually captured scenes provide no ground-truth motion, and static 3DGS represents moving water as a temporally averaged, blurred region whose high-frequency detail no method operating on a static reconstruction can recover without hallucination. As our goal is visual plausibility rather than physical accuracy, and no suitable no-reference metrics for fluid motion exist, we assess motion quality qualitatively, primarily through our video, and evaluate efficiency quantitatively.

    4.1 Dataset

    As public benchmark datasets rarely feature fluid elements, we captured seven scenes containing waterfalls of different scales and shapes as well as a cascading creek and a weir. All scenes were captured either by taking photographs with a DSLR camera or by recording multiple video clips with a drone. We preprocess the raw data using COLMAP[SF16] for camera parameter estimation, image undistortion, and scene alignment. Next, we train a standard 3DGS model on 4× downsampled images using default hyperparameter settings [KKLD23, HFEM26]. In addition to this data, our dataset release will include several auxiliaries, such as pre-defined 3D motion hints, motion fields, and dynamic Gaussian segmentation masks (cf. Tab.1). Per-scene motion field properties are provided in AppendixC.

    4.2 Baselines

    We compare our method with 4DGS[YYPZ24], LoopGaussian[LCW∗24], and 3D-Cinemagraphy[LCS∗23]. We train 4DGS models at the same resolution as our 3DGS models and limit the maximum number of Gaussians to 6.5M to prevent VRAM issues. For fair comparison and precise evaluation, we integrate the LoopGaussian method, i.e., their trained 3D motion field MLP and their symmetric animation technique into our framework and GUI. LoopGaussian also relies on Gaussian segmentation to determine dynamic scene regions, which we generate based on our motion field similar to how we separate static and dynamic Gaussians in our method. For 3D-Cinemagraphy, we render novel views by performing their layered depth image (LDI) reconstruction on the downsampled RGB image of the closest dataset view. As an additional required input, we project our 3D motion hints based on the input pose to obtain sparse flow hints. We note that achieving identical camera poses within our 3DGS model and the LDI of 3D-Cinemagraphy is challenging since depth information is acquired by monocular depth estimation, resulting in significantly different scene scales. This effect grows with the distance between novel and input pose and thus complicates free-viewpoint exploration, our target application.

    For all comparisons, we render a single 4-second animation loop of 240 frames in total. We limit 3D-Cinemagraphy to 60 frames, since we find that using more tends to degrade the quality of their animation. For each scene, we render from a novel viewpoint diverging from the closest input pose both in camera translation and rotation.

    4.3 Qualitative Comparisons

    Fig.2 presents qualitative comparisons of rendered animation frames for all methods. 3D-Cinemagraphy produces visually compelling animations for viewpoints close to the input image, as it largely relies on high-detail 2D cinemagraph synthesis. However, as the viewpoint deviates further from the reference pose, limitations of the underlying layered depth image representation become increasingly apparent, leading to geometric inconsistencies, animation artifacts, and missing content not observed in the reference view. In contrast, Gaussian splatting-based approaches maintain viewpoint-consistent scene geometry, making visual quality primarily dependent on the reconstruction and animation of fluid regions. Under casual capture conditions, 4DGS struggles to reconstruct high-frequency water dynamics, resulting in unstable and visually implausible motion. As 4DGS models the entire scene as dynamic, it also fails to converge to the static solution in some regions (e.g., the darker rocks in Fig.2). LoopGaussian preserves a temporally stable appearance, but its motion does not follow coherent fluid flow and instead exhibits locally inconsistent warping behavior (best seen in our video). To further analyze this effect, Fig.3 visualizes the time-dependent motion of individual Gaussians by encoding projected motion direction as color. LoopGaussian produces motion that varies both spatially and temporally within similar fluid regions, leading to incoherent flow patterns. This behavior stems from its symmetric interpolation scheme, which blends forward- and backward-transformed Gaussian positions instead of rendering them separately. In contrast, our method generates temporally consistent directional motion that more closely resembles plausible fluid flow. Fig.4 shows the corresponding closest input views together with intermediate results of our pipeline: sparse hints are refined into detailed flow maps that follow the water, and the fused motion field reproduces this flow when rendered. Our video further compares our animation side by side with the drone-captured footage used for reconstructing the 3DGS model of the “Weir” scene.

    4.4 Quantitative Comparisons

    In Tab.2, we compare rendering performance and VRAM consumption across methods. All Gaussian Splatting-based methods render interactively at over 300 FPS on average. Between these, 4DGS exhibits the lowest average memory consumption at 2.7 GiB, followed by our method at 3.8 GiB. LoopGaussian requires considerably more memory in several scenes, reaching 8.7 GiB for “Frogfall” compared to 5.5 GiB for our approach. This overhead is primarily caused by the per-Gaussian MLP evaluations required for motion prediction. 3D-Cinemagraphy is neither real-time capable nor memory efficient. We also show static 3DGS for reference.

    Tab.3 further evaluates the one-time cost for constructing the 3D motion field. Our method requires approximately one minute on average, with runtime scaling primarily with the number of processed input views. The dominant cost stems from image segmentation. LoopGaussian exhibits substantially higher preprocessing times, averaging around six minutes and reaching roughly thirteen minutes for the “Waterfall” scene. Notably, we provide the required static/dynamic Gaussian segmentation for LoopGaussian directly from our motion field pipeline; obtaining such a segmentation independently, e.g., using SAGA [CFY∗25], would introduce additional preprocessing overhead. The peak memory usage of our fusion stage is 13.4 GiB, which can easily be bounded by limiting the initial voxel grid resolution. Despite relying on a dense voxel grid during fusion, the resulting sparse motion field requires only 2 MB on average.

    4.5 Ablation Study

    In Fig.5 (top row), we render our animation without opacity blending and find that start and end frames of one animation sequence differ visually. Looping such sequences results in a visible cut due to the backward instance snapping back to its starting position. We also show the benefit of our proposed random state offset in Fig.5 (middle row), where the top of the waterfall creates a recurring pattern in the sequence when such state offset is disabled. In Fig.6, we analyze our motion field refinement techniques. The left column clearly shows the effectiveness of motion reduction within static scene regions to prevent visual artifacts of unwanted movement caused by incorrectly reprojected flow pixels. The middle column shows that our view hit thresholding reduces incoherent motion of dynamic scene regions due to an ill-posed reprojection problem (bottom image). It also further reduces voxels within empty scene regions to better fit the shape of the dynamic Gaussian region (top-middle compared to the top-right image). We also evaluate the use of many 3D motion hints compared to a single directional hint in Fig.7. In the top row, we show that for some scenes a single motion hint offers enough guidance for the flow estimation network to produce motion of similar quality to using multiple hints. Other scenes require additional hints to capture the transition from water falling down the waterfall to flowing along the river. In practice, hints can be added where the animation deviates from the expected flow, as demonstrated for “Smallfall” in our video.

    5 Discussion, Limitations, and Future Work

    Our method demonstrates that visually plausible fluid animation can be efficiently integrated into static 3DGS scenes without requiring a fully dynamic reconstruction. While we primarily focus on water, the proposed approach also generalizes to other fluids such as lava (Fig.8).

    Since the 3D motion field is precomputed only once and stored compactly, it could be distributed alongside static 3DGS scenes and rendered efficiently even on resource-constrained devices. Furthermore, the optical flow estimation process is flexible with respect to the input views. The RGB inputs I_1,⋯,N may consist of original training images, renderings from user-defined viewpoints, or a combination of both, enabling targeted refinement of motion in challenging scene regions through our interactive GUI.

    Despite these advantages, our approach is not without limitations. First, the quality of the generated motion field strongly depends on the underlying 3DGS reconstruction. Depth inconsistencies or reconstruction artifacts can lead to inaccurate motion fusion and visible animation artifacts (Fig.9).

    Similarly, the method assumes that the fluid surface itself is reconstructed reasonably well. This assumption may fail for highly reflective or visually ambiguous water surfaces, where the 3DGS reconstruction does not create enough Gaussians. Our method also cannot recover fluid detail that is absent from the reconstructed 3DGS representation and, as depth stems from Gaussians at the visible water surface, motion is largely confined to this surface.

    Future work could explore dynamic updates of the motion field to enable interactive or physically responsive fluid behavior. This could allow animated fluids to react to user interaction or external scene events while maintaining real-time performance.

    6 Conclusion

    We presented a method for animating water in static 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes using cinemagraph-inspired motion synthesis. Our approach lifts 2D fluid motion into a coherent 3D Eulerian motion field and applies it to Gaussian primitives to generate seamless looping animations that preserve real-time rendering and free-viewpoint navigation. In contrast to dynamic reconstruction approaches, our method operates on casually captured static scenes and does not require dynamic multi-view acquisition or costly physical simulation. Experiments on a newly captured dataset show more plausible water motion than prior methods at low computational cost. We believe that combining static scene reconstruction with efficient motion synthesis opens promising directions for immersive, controllable, and realistic 3D content creation.

    Acknowledgments

    We would like to thank Brian Scotland and Junbo Li for their valuable contributions to our dataset, as well as Philipp Gronek for his assistance with the comparisons. This work was partially funded by the DFG projects “Real-Action VR” (ID 523421583) and “Increasing Realism of Omnidirectional Videos in Virtual Reality” (ID 491805996). We also acknowledge funding from the Lower Saxony Ministry of Science and Culture under grant number ZN3994 within the Lower Saxony “Vorab” of the Volkswagen Foundation and support by the Center for Digital Innovations (ZDIN).

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Dense Flow Computation

    Following Mahapatra and Kulkarni [MK22], we derive dense flow maps Fᵈᵉⁿˢᵉ_1,⋯,N from sparse flow maps Fˢᵖᵃʳˢᵉ_1,⋯,N by spreading their sparse flow with weighted exponential pixel-distance functions defined as

    D(p₁, p₂)=e^-(\lVertp₁-p₂\rVert₂²)/(σ²) .

    		(11)

    Here the L2 Euclidean distance is used in conjunction with a constant σ=0.075H. For each pixel x, sparse flow Fˢᵖᵃʳˢᵉₙ(p) is weighted by D(x, p) based on hint position p. Pixel values are summed up for all sparse hints and normalized to define dense flow maps:

    Fᵈᵉⁿˢᵉₙ(x)=\begincases(∑ᵢ₌₁^|Hₙ|D(x, pᵢ)·Fˢᵖᵃʳˢᵉₙ(pᵢ))/(∑ᵢ₌₁^|Hₙ|D(x, pᵢ)),&ifx∈Sₙ 0,&otherwise\endcases ,

    		(12)

    with pᵢ the i-th hint position in Hₙ. Note that dense flow is only defined for pixels within the segmentation mask of the view Sₙ.

    Appendix B 3D Motion Field Creation

    Algorithm1 outlines our approach for 3D motion field fusion and refinement.

    Appendix C Motion Field Properties

    In Tab.4, we further analyze per scene motion field properties, where grid size is clearly reduced by our refinement and the density of the refined grid does not exceed 5%, enabling memory-efficient, sparse storage. We set the initial number of voxels individually per scene to constrain VRAM during fusion below 16GB. We find that higher resolution grids do not largely benefit animation quality for our tested scenes.

    Appendix D Animation Illustration and Ablations

    In Fig.10 we illustrate a 2D example of the Gaussian deformation and symmetric animation technique. In Fig.11, we evaluate the Unscented Transform-based Gaussian transformation technique. In the top row, only the Gaussian mean is displaced, while covariance remains constant. As a result, elongated Gaussians, not pointing in the direction of fluid motion, create noisy artifacts. We further alter α (see Eq.7) controlling the spread of sigma points around the mean. We find that smaller values produce unrealistic deformations, further introducing blur, while larger values result in moderate deformations following fluid motion.

    To achieve high-quality results in our qualitative comparison, we employ K=60 animation keyframes. However, the use of fewer keyframes can significantly reduce memory consumption. In order to create the desired effect of flowing fluid, Gaussian particles need to travel a sufficient distance through the scene. Since decreasing K results in shorter trajectories, a larger motion regulation r^M, increasing particle displacement per keyframe, can accommodate the effect. If r^M is too large, trajectories might diverge and degenerate, but we find that decreasing to K=8 and increasing r^M accordingly still produces visually plausible animations and maintains smoothness due to keyframe interpolation.

    Appendix E Positional Offsets

    Additional transformation sequences can be defined by utilizing the symmetric animation technique (see Sec.3.3.2). Adding a random per Gaussian positional offset μ^off∈ℝ³ to μ before transforming a Gaussian g forward and backward creates new trajectories similar to A^fw and Aᵇʷ. We sample μ^off uniformly from a spherical shell with restricted maximum length. The transformations are blended with unaltered O^fw and Oᵇʷ to enable the same looping behavior for the new instances. Furthermore, the per Gaussian random animation state offset t^off is applied. This procedure can be repeated to generate multiple offset transformation trajectories of the same g, which is useful for enhancing scene density of sparsely reconstructed fluid regions and enables customization of fluid volume. We find that more than two additional instances increase density to the point where animation detail is lost. With increasing offset extent, the scene appearance degenerates and introduces artifacts, observable in Fig.12.

item.title: 别再用 UV 图集压贴图了：把纹理放进贴着表面的稀疏体素场，码流与 GPU 常驻两套都能用 ｜ Beyond UV Mapping: Mesh Texture Compression via Surface-Aligned Texture Fields
item.description:
一句话：UV 图集的接缝与映射开销限制编码效率；TexF 改用贴表面的稀疏体素组织纹理，复现位置不占码流。

要点：

  • 把纹理属性组织成沿网格表面的稀疏体素，既支持高分辨率纹理，又保留局部三维相关性，还能直接做表面查询
  • 码流压缩复用现有 3D 属性编解码器，体素位置可由解码后的网格重建，不必单独传输
  • GPU 常驻版 3DNTC 用量化 hash 特征加轻量解码器，在表面位置上做随机访问重建；并可微渲染做像素空间精修

为什么值得看：资产管线的纹理压缩一直被 UV 布局绑死。这条路把「纹理压缩」变成「几何附属的属性场压缩」，还能直接跑在 GPU 上——对要压显存又要随机采样的引擎很对味。

中文摘要：网格纹理压缩通常依赖二维 UV 图集，图集的接缝与映射开销会限制编码效率。本文提出 TexF：一种沿网格表面组织的稀疏体素纹理场，既能承载高分辨率纹理，又保留局部三维相关性以便压缩，并支持直接做表面查询。码流压缩直接复用成熟的 3D 属性编解码器，体素位置可由解码后的网格重建、无需单独传输；面向 GPU 常驻的版本 3DNTC 组合量化 hash 特征与轻量解码器，实现表面位置的随机访问重建。再用可微渲染在图像空间精修体素属性与压缩后的神经场。在 MPEG 与 AOM 网格压缩基准上，码流与 GPU 常驻两种模式的率失真都优于代表性 UV 方法。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-09-20

本期推送：2026-10-24

Beyond UV Mapping: Mesh Texture Compression via Surface-Aligned Texture Fields

Abstract

Mesh texture compression typically relies on 2D UV atlases, whose chart discontinuities and mapping overhead can limit coding efficiency. To tackle this challenge, we introduce TexF, a surface-aligned texture field that organizes texture attributes in sparse voxels derived from the mesh surface. This representation supports high-resolution textures while preserving local 3D correlations for compression and enabling direct surface queries. For bitstream compression, TexF reuses established 3D attribute codecs, with voxel locations reconstructed from the decoded mesh without separate transmission. For GPU-resident compression, we develop 3DNTC, which combines quantized hash features with a lightweight decoder for random-access reconstruction at surface positions. Differentiable rendering enables image-space refinement of both voxel attributes and compressed neural fields. Experiments on the MPEG and AOM mesh compression benchmarks demonstrate improved average rate–distortion performance over representative UV-based methods for both bitstream and GPU-resident compression. 3DNTC also supports real-time rendering. The code will be publicly available at https://github.com/yydlmzyz1/TexF.

Index Terms:

3D Mesh, Texture Representation, Compression, Inverse Rendering.

I Introduction

Textured 3D meshes are widely used to represent 3D assets, enabling the depiction of continuous geometric surfaces with high-fidelity visual appearances. With the rapid expansion of immersive media [1] and spatial intelligence [2], the efficient representation and compression of these assets have become essential [3, 4]. While the geometric surface provides the structural foundation, the texture component is a key factor in visual realism and often constitutes a major portion of the overall bitrate. Texture compression is challenging not only because of its data volume, but also because texture must remain aligned with the underlying surface and preserve rendered visual quality.

Existing mesh compression pipelines typically store geometry as polygonal meshes and appearance in separate 2D texture atlases through UV parameterization [5, 6, 7], as illustrated on the left of Fig. 1. Within this paradigm, mature image/video codecs such as HEVC [8, 9] and AV1 [10, 4] produce compact bitstreams for storage and transmission. Hardware-supported texture formats such as ASTC [11] and neural texture compression (NTC) methods [12] reduce GPU-resident memory while supporting random access during rendering. Despite their different coding mechanisms, these methods share the same 2D UV atlas representation. However, UV atlas construction can separate nearby surface regions into disjoint charts, weakening the spatial correlations exploitable by 2D codecs, while also introducing padding, packing, and UV-mapping overhead. Both effects can reduce coding efficiency, particularly for meshes with complex geometry. These limitations motivate alternative ways to organize texture for compression.

Beyond compression, texture representation has long been explored outside the UV domain, primarily for appearance modeling, authoring, and rendering. UV-free methods associate texture with mesh elements or locations in 3D space. Related representations include mesh-attached textures [13, 14], volumetric textures [15, 16, 17], and neural or implicit textures [18, 19]. Some of these efforts also address texture storage through sparse octrees [16, 20], compressed 3D blocks [21], or voxel serialization [22]. Yet these storage reductions do not necessarily translate into better compression than established UV-based pipelines. Inefficient modeling of spatial correlations and additional indexing overhead can offset the savings from removing UV mappings, and even increase storage. These considerations suggest that effective mesh texture compression requires jointly addressing texture organization and mapping overhead. We therefore investigate how mesh surface geometry can guide texture organization and coding in 3D, beyond simply removing UV mappings.

Our central idea is to use the mesh surface itself to determine where texture attributes are stored and how they are accessed. We introduce TexF, a surface-aligned texture field that stores texture attributes only in voxels intersected by the mesh surface (right of Fig. 1). This surface-aligned organization offers three advantages for compact representation and compression. First, surface-localized sparsity supports high-resolution, high-fidelity textures without a dense volume, using sample counts comparable to those of 2D texture maps. Second, texture locations can be derived from the mesh, reducing the storage overhead of separate surface-to-texture mappings and spatial indices. Third, organizing texture attributes directly in 3D preserves their native spatial relationships for compression, avoiding the disruption of spatial coherence caused by UV charting or reordering.

We construct TexF through direct texture transfer from a UV-textured mesh. We develop an efficient, differentiable renderer that queries texture attributes directly at mesh surface positions. The renderer also enables inverse-rendering (IR) refinement [23, 24, 25, 26], using multi-view image-space supervision to reduce transfer and discretization errors.

We exploit TexF’s surface-aligned structure for both bitstream and GPU-resident texture compression. For bitstream compression, we encode voxel attributes directly using established 3D attribute codecs, including Unicorn [27] and G-PCC [28], exploiting spatial correlations in their native 3D neighborhoods. Voxel locations are reconstructed from the decoded mesh, avoiding separate voxel-position coding and UV-mapping overhead. For GPU-resident compression, we develop a neural codec that captures 3D spatial correlations in quantized multiresolution hash features. A compact decoder reconstructs attributes on demand at surface positions, supporting random access during rendering [29, 12].

Experiments on the standard MPEG [30] and AOM [4] benchmarks demonstrate that TexF with Unicorn significantly outperforms the evaluated UV-based pipelines in averaged rate–distortion performance, including those enhanced by UV reparameterization and alternative image codecs. Competitive results with G-PCC further show that these benefits are not confined to a single coding backend. For GPU-resident compression, TexF generally achieves better rate–distortion performance than conventional and neural UV texture compression, while supporting random-access decoding during rendering.

In summary, we present a mesh texture compression framework based on a surface-aligned texture field (TexF). Specifically:

  • •

    TexF stores and accesses texture in a sparse 3D field aligned with the underlying mesh surface, enabling compact, high-resolution, and UV-free representation. An efficient differentiable renderer supports direct surface queries and inverse-rendering refinement.

  • •

    We exploit TexF’s native 3D spatial correlations for both bitstream and GPU-resident compression. Bitstream compression reuses established 3D attribute codecs without separately transmitting voxel locations. GPU-resident compression uses quantized hash features and a lightweight decoder for random-access surface queries without explicit per-voxel lookup entries.

  • •

    We systematically compare TexF with UV-based and serialization-based alternatives, demonstrating improved average rate–distortion performance in both compression settings and analyzing how asset characteristics affect the relative performance of TexF and UV representations.

    • The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Sec. II comprehensively reviews existing work on the representation of mesh texture and its compression. Sec. III presents the proposed method, followed by extensive experiments and a series of promising future directions in Sec. IV. Finally, Sec. V concludes this work

    II Related Work

    Compression of a textured mesh involves both geometry and texture. Geometry coding represents vertex positions and connectivity using methods such as Draco [6]; comprehensive reviews are provided in [5, 31]. Our focus, instead, is mesh texture compression.

    Since the texture representation determines the signal exposed to subsequent coding, we organize prior work according to how texture is associated with the mesh surface, broadly distinguishing UV-based and UV-free approaches. UV atlases remain the prevailing representation in production pipelines, underlying both texture bitstreams for storage and transmission and GPU-resident payloads for rendering. Fig. 2 summarizes the representations, their construction, and the associated compression methods. Here, it is worth noting that UV-free describes how texture is associated with the mesh surface, rather than the domain in which the resulting signal is compressed.

    II-AUV-based Mesh Textures

    UV parameterization and atlas construction. A UV-textured mesh associates its surface with coordinates in a 2D texture domain. Surface parameterization partitions the mesh into charts and unfolds them onto the plane. Parameterization methods seek to limit angular or area distortion [32, 33], while atlas packing arranges the resulting charts in a UV atlas with gutters to improve image utilization and reduce filtering artifacts [34]. When constructing a new atlas, texture baking resamples the source appearance into the new UV layout. The resulting regular 2D images are compatible with mature image/video coding tools and GPU texture formats.

    Bitstream-oriented compression. For storage and transmission, UV-based texture can be encoded using established codecs such as H.265/HEVC [8] and AV1 [10]. MPEG V-DMC [7, 9] organizes mesh textures into video-compatible representations and reuses established video coding tools. Reparameterization [34] and atlas packing can improve texture coding efficiency, but may incur substantial preprocessing cost for complex meshes.

    GPU-resident compression. For runtime GPU memory, block-based image formats derived from block truncation coding [35], including S3TC [36] and ASTC [11], provide fixed-rate storage and hardware-supported random access. Random-access neural texture compression (NTC) [12] instead represents material using quantized latent grids and a compact decoder, enabling on-demand reconstruction from a GPU-resident representation at the cost of per-material optimization.

    Limitations of the UV domain. Despite the practical advantages of UV-based pipelines, chart-based unfolding changes the native surface neighborhoods exposed in the atlas: regions adjacent on the mesh may fall into different charts, weakening correlations across chart boundaries. Chart packing also introduces padding, while the explicit surface-to-atlas mapping requires UV coordinates and associated indices. Constructing a new atlas also incurs preprocessing cost, and texture resampling can introduce distortion before compression. Careful parameterization and packing mitigate these costs but do not remove the dependence on chart layout, motivating complementary representations that preserve appearance directly in 3D space.

    II-BUV-free Mesh Textures

    UV-free texture representations associate appearance directly with mesh elements or locations in the surrounding 3D space, avoiding dependence on a global UV atlas. This long-standing idea has inspired diverse approaches to appearance modeling, authoring, and rendering, whereas its application to mesh texture compression remains comparatively limited.

    II-B1 UV-free Texture Representations

    UV-free texture representations differ primarily in how they associate appearance with the mesh surface.

    Mesh-attached textures. A separate family attaches appearance directly to mesh elements. Per-vertex colors provide the simplest example, although their spatial resolution is limited by the vertex density of the mesh. Per-face methods such as Ptex [13] assign an independent 2D texture to each face and maintain a per-face adjacency map for cross-face filtering. Mesh Colors [14] and Patch Textures [37] associate color samples with mesh elements without explicit UV coordinates. However, their global organization follows mesh connectivity rather than a single regular lattice, complicating the direct reuse of mature image- or volume-based codecs. These systems primarily address parameterization-free authoring and rendering rather than texture compression.

    Volumetric textures. Volumetric texture representations associate appearance directly with positions in 3D space. Early solid textures [15, 38] define appearance procedurally as a function of 3D position and are particularly suited to materials with volumetric patterns, such as wood or stone. Shell Maps [17] instead construct a surface-aligned volumetric parameterization by mapping a tetrahedral shell around the mesh into texture space. Octree-based textures [16, 39, 20] instead organize sampled surface attributes in adaptive octree hierarchies for parameterization-free painting and rendering. TexF instead defines a surface-aligned texture field directly in the mesh coordinate system, with voxel locations derived from the mesh rather than stored in a separate hierarchy.

    Neural and implicit textures. In recent years, neural methods have represented appearance using continuous coordinate functions or learned features. Oechsle et al.’s neural Texture Fields [18] represent appearance as a continuous function f_θ(x,y,z)→RGB conditioned on shape features, avoiding explicit surface parameterization. NeuMesh [40] instead attaches learned geometry and texture features to mesh vertices for neural rendering and editing. In contrast, NeuTex [19] learns a continuous mapping from 3D surface points to a 2D neural texture domain. These neural texture methods primarily target appearance modeling, reconstruction, or editing. TexF instead starts from explicit texture attributes on mesh-derived voxels, providing a common representation for both 3D attribute codecs and GPU-resident neural compression.

    II-B2 UV-free Representations for Mesh Texture Compression

    UV-free representations have been widely studied for appearance modeling, authoring, and rendering, but comparatively few works address mesh texture compression. These works differ in how they organize surface attributes for coding.

    As an early effort, CB3TM [21] retains surface-relevant regions of a solid texture and applies 3D Haar-wavelet coding with coefficient truncation to local 4³ subvolumes for independent reconstruction. Although not mesh-specific, the 3D mode of ASTC [11] provides fixed-rate coding of regular 3D blocks. Both exploit local 3D correlations and support random access, but their dense coding units limit the use of fine-grained surface sparsity.

    Dolonius et al. [22, 41] used octree-derived Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graphs (SVDAGs) to compactly represent voxelized surfaces and address separately stored attributes. The attributes are linearized along Morton or Hilbert curves, then compressed with a custom random-access codec or mapped to 2D for existing image and GPU texture codecs. These methods exploit spatial coherence through the serialized ordering. While SVDAG-based methods use a separate voxel hierarchy for texture access, TexF uses the mesh surface as the common spatial basis for representation, compression, and rendering. This surface-aligned organization supports native 3D attribute coding and direct neural queries at surface positions.

    II-CRelated 3D Coding and Optimization Techniques

    Beyond mesh-texture representations, research on 3D coding and differentiable rendering provides tools that TexF draws on for construction and compression.

    3D spatial coding. Broader volumetric-data research has developed compression methods for regular and sparse 3D signals [11, 42, 43, 44]. These techniques generally target volume data or voxel scenes rather than appearance associated with a separate triangle mesh. Point cloud codecs provide related tools for attributes defined on known 3D support, but do not themselves define a mesh-texture representation or renderer. V-PCC projects point cloud patches into packed 2D images, whereas G-PCC operates on geometry and attributes in the 3D point set [45, 28]. Learned point cloud attribute codecs, such as Unicorn [27], further explore data-driven spatial transforms and entropy models [46, 47]. TexF makes these codecs applicable to mesh textures by organizing attributes on mesh-derived voxels, whose positions can be reconstructed from the decoded mesh without separate transmission.

    Multiresolution hash encoding. Multiresolution hash encoding [29] maps spatial coordinates to trainable features stored in compact hash tables. We adapt this encoding to GPU-resident TexF compression, using quantized features and lightweight decoding inspired by NTC [12]. By replacing explicit voxel attributes with a directly queryable compressed field, the codec avoids storing per-voxel lookup entries.

    Inverse rendering. Inverse rendering optimizes geometry or appearance by propagating image-space supervision through a differentiable rendering process [23, 24, 25, 26]. TexF uses this supervision both to reduce transfer and discretization errors during representation construction and to refine the compressed neural field.

    III Proposed Method

    Conventional mesh texture compression operates on 2D UV atlases. We instead organize texture attributes in a surface-aligned texture field (TexF), whose sparse voxel support is derived from the mesh surface. Thus surface positions can directly query the 3D field, providing a common spatial basis for texture representation, compression, and rendering.

    As illustrated in Fig. 3, we construct TexF by voxelizing the mesh surface and transferring the source texture, then refine its attributes through differentiable rendering to reduce transfer and discretization errors. Based on this representation, we develop two complementary schemes: bitstream compression with established 3D attribute codecs for disk storage and transmission, and GPU-resident neural compression for memory-efficient random access during rendering.

    III-ASurface-aligned TexF Representation and Construction

    TexF associates texture attributes with voxels derived from the mesh surface, preserving spatial locality without UV parameterization. We efficiently construct this support through surface voxelization and initialize its attributes from the source texture.

    III-A1 Surface-aligned TexF Construction

    Given a textured mesh M, we first discretize its canonical axis-aligned bounding box into a K×K×K grid. TexF and the mesh geometry therefore share a common coordinate system, allowing surface points to query the field directly in 3D space without an intermediate parameterization such as UV mapping. The surface-aligned TexF retains only voxels intersecting the mesh surface, referred to as active voxels. Their indices form the active set Q, with q∈ℤ³ and 0≤q

    T={(q,t(q))|q∈Q},

    		(1)

    where t(q) encodes base color (i.e., RGB) by default and can be extended channel-wise to include other physically-based rendering (PBR) material attributes, such as roughness and metallicity.

    A textured mesh is thus represented by its geometry M and the associated TexF T, forming a mesh with TexF. Surface positions query texture directly in their shared 3D coordinate system, without UV coordinates or a separate surface parameterization. Because the voxel support is derived from the mesh and grid configuration, its coordinates need not be separately transmitted. This organization preserves local 3D spatial relationships among texture attributes, supporting direct surface queries and spatially coherent attribute coding, as described in Secs. III-B and III-C.

    Remark. TexF’s spatial structure also offers representational versatility. It naturally shares a voxel grid with grid-based implicit geometry, such as an SDF, for joint geometry–appearance modeling. Its attributes can also be sampled at mesh vertices for vertex-color rendering. Examples are provided in the Supplementary Material.

    III-A2 UV Texture Transfer to TexF

    To support conventional UV-textured assets, we initialize TexF by sampling the mesh surface and transferring attributes from the source texture. For each surface sample, its barycentric coordinates determine both its 3D position and UV coordinate. The UV coordinate is used to sample the source material maps, while the 3D position assigns the retrieved attributes to the corresponding voxel. Attributes assigned to the same voxel are averaged. Conversely, TexF can be baked into a UV texture by rasterizing a target UV layout and querying the field at the corresponding surface positions, enabling compatibility with standard UV rendering pipelines. Voxel discretization and interpolation introduce transfer errors, which we reduce through rendering-driven refinement in Sec. III-B.

    III-BTexF Rendering and Refinement

    III-B1 Differentiable TexF Rendering

    TexF rendering first rasterizes the mesh to determine visible surface positions, then queries the field at these positions to obtain texture attributes. As illustrated in Fig. 4, UV rendering samples a 2D texture through interpolated UV coordinates, whereas TexF queries the field directly at p. For the voxel representation defined in Eq. (1), the color c(p) is obtained by trilinearly interpolating neighboring texture attributes:

    c(p)=∑_i∈ℕ(p)ωᵢt(qᵢ),\vskip-4.26773pt

    		(2)

    where ℕ(p) denotes the set of active grid points within the 2×2×2 neighborhood of p, and the trilinear weights ωᵢ are determined by the query position within the grid cell. This interpolation is mathematically analogous to bilinear sampling in UV rendering, but operates in 3D with weights renormalized over the available voxels. In the rare case that no active corner is available, the nearest active voxel is used as a fallback. We implement this rendering path using differentiable rasterization [48] and sparse-grid interpolation operators [49]. The interpolation in Eq. (2) is differentiable and can be evaluated in parallel, supporting real-time rendering and efficient backpropagation to the voxel attributes. GPU-resident TexF uses the same rasterization stage, but interpolates latent features and decodes them with an MLP to obtain texture attributes (Sec. III-D).

    III-B2 Rendering-driven Optimization

    We use our differentiable renderer to refine texture appearance through inverse rendering. We render reference images {Iᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N from the original lossless UV-textured mesh and corresponding images {Îᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N from the target mesh with TexF under the same views. We minimize the photometric objective

    D=∑ᵢ₌₁^N[∥Îᵢ-Iᵢ∥₁+1-SSIM(Îᵢ,Iᵢ)],\vskip-2.84544pt

    		(3)

    where the ℓ₁ term measures pixel-wise color errors and the SSIM term encourages structural similarity. Starting from the transferred attributes, we optimize t(q) while keeping the mesh geometry and voxel support fixed.

    Image-space supervision accounts for the sampling and interpolation used during rendering, allowing refinement to compensate for errors left by direct texture transfer and voxel discretization. It therefore improves the texture representation without increasing its capacity. This refinement is also efficient, requiring only a modest optimization cost in our experiments. The same objective also optimizes the latent features and decoder parameters of the compressed neural field (Sec. III-D).

    Beyond compression refinement, the differentiable renderer could support mesh texturing directly from multi-view images. Extending it to jointly optimize geometry and appearance is another direction for future work.

    III-CTexF Bitstream Compression

    For disk storage and transmission, we seek a compact entropy-coded texture bitstream [3, 4]. TexF derives voxel locations from the mesh rather than encoding them separately. As illustrated in Fig. 5, mesh geometry is encoded using an existing mesh codec [5, 31, 6]. The encoder and decoder apply the same voxelization procedure to the reconstructed mesh to obtain the voxel set Q. These shared locations establish the correspondence between decoded attributes and TexF voxels, allowing the texture stream to carry coded attributes without per-voxel coordinates.

    To encode the attributes, we leverage established 3D coding tools. Just like UV-based pipelines use image or video codecs such as HEVC [8] and AV1 [10], TexF interfaces with point cloud attribute codecs through its compatible coordinate–attribute structure. Their transform, prediction, and entropy-coding tools can therefore exploit spatial correlations directly in mesh-derived voxel neighborhoods, without requiring a texture-specific codec architecture.

    The interface is codec-agnostic: compatible 3D attribute codecs can be used without changing the TexF representation. We use Unicorn [27] as the primary backend, leveraging its multiscale neural transform and conditional entropy model. We also evaluate conventional RAHT [50]-based attribute coding in G-PCC [28] to examine whether TexF’s compression gains extend across different coding architectures. Beyond these two backends, the same interface allows TexF to benefit from advances in compatible 3D attribute codecs without changing the representation. At the decoder, reconstructed attributes are restored to their corresponding voxel locations, recovering T̂.

    III-DGPU-Resident TexF Compression

    GPU-resident compression aims to reduce texture memory while supporting low-latency random access during rendering [12]. Although TexF is spatially sparse, its explicit attributes and lookup structure can still occupy substantial GPU memory at high resolutions. For example, our uncompressed implementation stores three 8-bit RGB values and a 64-bit lookup key per voxel. We therefore develop 3D Neural Texture Compression (3DNTC), which exploits TexF’s 3D-native organization to compress surface appearance into quantized features and a lightweight decoder. Unlike NTC [12], which decodes texture attributes in the 2D UV domain, 3DNTC reconstructs them directly at continuous mesh surface positions, without UV mapping or explicit per-voxel lookup entries.

    III-D1 Quantized Hash Representation

    3DNTC uses two spatially downsampled hash grids with INT4 features to capture texture variations at different spatial scales, together with a shared four-layer FP16 MLP (Fig. 6). At level i∈{1,2}, the grid resolution is ⌈K/sᵢ⌉, where K is the reference spatial resolution set according to the source texture resolution, and sᵢ is the downsampling factor (e.g., 4 or 8). Following multiresolution hash encoding [29], each level uses a table of 2^hᵢ entries with F feature channels, indexed by hashing integer grid coordinates. These entries store shared latent features, without explicit per-voxel lookup keys. Thus, the downsampling factor sᵢ controls spatial granularity, while hᵢ and F determine latent storage; varying these parameters adjusts the rate–distortion trade-off.

    III-D2 Surface-Query Decoding

    Rasterization provides visible surface positions as in Sec. III-B. For each position p, we hash the eight surrounding grid-corner coordinates at each level and trilinearly interpolate their features. The interpolated features are concatenated across levels into Φ(p)∈ℝ^2F and combined with an 18-dimensional positional encoding γ(p). A single evaluation of the decoder D_θ then reconstructs color:

    t̂(p)=D_θ (Φ(p),γ(p)),

    		(4)

    Interpolating features before decoding yields the attribute directly at p, avoiding separate neural decoding of the eight voxel-corner colors. The decoder has three hidden layers with 64, 48, and 32 channels and hardGELU activations, followed by a linear output layer; its parameters are shared across all surface queries within each asset. Only the packed latent tables and decoder parameters need to remain resident as texture data. Queries are independent and require no sequential entropy decoding, enabling on-demand reconstruction during rendering.

    III-D3 Training and Refinement

    For each asset, we sample continuous surface positions and obtain target attributes from the refined explicit TexF. We jointly optimize the latent tables and MLP to minimize attribute mean squared error, simulating INT4 quantization during training. We then refine both against ground-truth multi-view renderings using Eq. (3), improving rendered fidelity without increasing the payload. At deployment, only the packed latent tables and decoder parameters are needed as GPU-resident texture data. Detailed settings are provided in the Supplementary Material.

    IV Experiments

    In this section, we first present the common experimental settings and assess TexF’s representation fidelity, compactness, and rendering efficiency. We then compare its bitstream and GPU-resident compression performance with UV-based and other alternatives, followed by ablation studies and further analysis.

    IV-AExperimental Settings

    IV-A1 Datasets

    To evaluate performance across diverse geometries and textures, we use eight human models from the MPEG mesh compression benchmark [30] and 32 assets from the AOMedia mesh coding test set [4]. The AOM assets include scanned objects, plants and animals, DCC-created assets, and architectural models. Together, the two benchmarks comprise 40 assets with texture resolutions ranging from 2K to 4K.111 We use 1K, 2K, and 4K to denote resolutions of 1024, 2048, and 4096, respectively. Detailed asset statistics and the complete test sets are provided in the Supplementary Material, and representative assets are shown in Fig. 7.

    IV-A2 Evaluation Protocol and Metrics

    To isolate texture-coding efficiency, all methods use the same geometry and evaluation protocol. Following the common test conditions [30] and MPEG official metrics222https://github.com/MPEGGroup/mpeg-pcc-mmetric[51], we assess quality using renderings from 16 fixed orthographic views distributed on a Fibonacci sphere at 2048×2048 resolution, evaluated using PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS [52] metrics, complemented by point-sampled 3D-PSNR following the standard evaluation procedure. The 16 fixed orthographic evaluation views are held out from rendering-driven optimization, which instead uses independently sampled perspective views.

    We compare only the texture-related payload, since all methods use the same geometry. Rate is measured as bitstream size (KB) or GPU-resident memory (MB). We quantify relative bitrate savings using BD-BR [53] and provide detailed R–D curves. Detailed payload accounting is provided in the corresponding sections. Computational efficiency is evaluated by runtime. We use an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU (48 GB) with Intel Xeon Silver 4309Y CPUs for runtime measurements.

    IV-BRepresentation and Rendering Performance

    Because the representation is the basis for subsequent compression, we first assess the fidelity and compactness of TexF, together with its construction and rendering efficiency. We compare TexF with UV-reparameterized textures (UV-Reparam) generated using UVAtlas [34], a tool commonly used in mesh compression [7, 4] to improve spatial continuity and coding efficiency through chart reparameterization and packing. Both are evaluated against renderings of the source UV-textured mesh, following the evaluation protocol described above. We also examine how rendering-driven refinement improves TexF fidelity.

    IV-B1 Representation Fidelity and Compactness

    We vary the resolutions of TexF and UV-Reparam from 1K to 4K to obtain different representation capacities. Here, K denotes spatial resolution for TexF and atlas resolution for UV-Reparam. Note that equal resolutions do not imply equal capacity. We therefore measure capacity by the actual number of texels: voxels for TexF and pixels for UV-Reparam.

    Although TexF is defined at a spatial resolution of K³, its surface-aligned design stores attributes only in voxels intersecting the mesh surface. Its texel count therefore grows approximately quadratically with K, similar to the scaling of 2D texture maps. This surface-localized sparsity supports resolutions of 4K and beyond. Fig. 8 shows that fidelity improves with capacity for both representations, while TexF generally achieves comparable or higher fidelity than UV-Reparam with fewer texels. Visual comparisons in Fig. 9 further demonstrate its ability to preserve fine texture details.

    Inverse Rendering Refinement. Direct UV-to-TexF texture transfer provides a strong initialization. Inverse rendering (IR) further compensates for transfer errors, improving fidelity without increasing representation capacity. By default, we perform 30 optimization iterations, each using a batch of eight newly sampled perspective views, totaling 240 random views at a rendering resolution of 1024×1024. Cameras look at the object center with a 45^∘ FOV. Azimuth, sine elevation, and distance are drawn from uniform distributions over [0,2π), [-1,1], and [1.2,3.0], respectively. These training views are separate from the 16 fixed orthographic Fibonacci evaluation views mentioned above and differ in both viewing direction and projection.

    As shown in Fig. 8, IR improves PSNR and 3D-PSNR by 1.4 and 1.2 dB on average, alongside higher SSIM and lower LPIPS. Gains in LPIPS and 3D-PSNR extend beyond the objective in Eq. (3). Evaluation with different viewpoints and projection further suggests genuine improvements in texture fidelity, rather than overfitting to specific training views or metrics. The visual comparisons in Fig. 9 also illustrate the texture details recovered by refinement. The improvement is more pronounced at lower resolutions and diminishes at higher resolutions, particularly at 4K, where dense sampling already provides high-fidelity transfer, leaving little room for refinement.

    IV-B2 Representation Construction and Rendering Efficiency

    TexF is constructed through surface voxelization and texture transfer, whereas UVAtlas requires more complex UV reparameterization and atlas packing. As shown in Table I, TexF construction takes less than 1 s on average even at 4K resolution, and remains below 10 s with refinement. By contrast, UVAtlas requires approximately 100 s on MPEG and more than 1600 s on the more complex AOM dataset. Overall, TexF reduces representation construction time by orders of magnitude relative to UVAtlas reparameterization. At high resolutions like 4K, IR can be shortened or omitted to balance fidelity and construction cost.

    Following the evaluation protocol above, we measure rendering throughput at 2048×2048 resolution. TexF averages 190–222 FPS on MPEG and 107–127 FPS on AOM across the 1K–4K resolutions. TexF thus supports real-time rendering through sparse 3D queries, with throughput close to that of UV rendering.

    IV-CBitstream Compression Performance

    We evaluate whether surface-aligned TexF improves texture compression over established UV-based pipelines and whether its gains extend across different 3D coding backends.

    IV-C1 Experimental Configurations

    We denote each configuration by its representation and codec.

  • •

    UV-Source. We retain the source UV parameterization and encode its texture atlas. We use the V-DMC reference software [7, 54], with its default HEVC texture codec [8] as the baseline, and additionally evaluate AV1 [10] and ELIC [55] to assess potential gains from alternative texture codecs. UV mapping data and HEVC textures are encoded following the V-DMC CTC [30].

  • •

    UV-Reparam. We use V-DMC’s default UVAtlas pipeline [34] to reparameterize the mesh and pack its charts. UV mapping and texture coding follow the same settings as UV-Source.

  • •

    TexF. TexF replaces the UV atlas with a surface-aligned representation. We encode its attributes directly in 3D using the released pretrained Unicorn model [27] without retraining as the primary backend (TexF/Unicorn). We additionally encode TexF with conventional G-PCC in its official configuration [28] (TexF/G-PCC) to evaluate its compatibility with different 3D codecs.

  • •

    Serialized. We evaluate serialization followed by 2D coding as an alternative to direct 3D attribute coding, inspired by prior voxel-texturing work [41]. We order and pack the attributes of refined TexF representations into 2D images using Morton or Hilbert curves, then encode them with HEVC. We denote the two variants as Serialized-Morton/HEVC and Serialized-Hilbert/HEVC.

    • All methods use the same original geometry, losslessly coded with V-DMC; we therefore compare only texture-related bitstreams, including UV mapping data for UV-based methods. Detailed codec settings and additional results under lossy geometry are provided in the Supplementary Material.

    IV-C2 Rate–Distortion Performance

    Fig. 10 compares the R–D performance of the different methods, while Table II summarizes their BD-BR results using UV-Source/HEVC as the anchor. With the default HEVC codec, UV reparameterization yields BD-BR savings of approximately 27%–30% on MPEG and 42%–45% on AOM across the four quality metrics, demonstrating the benefit of a more compression-friendly atlas. Replacing HEVC with AV1 or ELIC generally improves coding efficiency further.

    TexF/Unicorn outperforms all evaluated UV configurations across the four metrics on both datasets, including UV-Reparam with AV1 or ELIC. Relative to UV-Source/HEVC, it achieves approximately 46%–49% BD-BR savings on MPEG and 53%–70% on AOM. TexF/G-PCC also delivers substantial savings, particularly under LPIPS, and remains competitive with or better than the strongest UV baselines in most cases. The gains with both Unicorn and G-PCC show that TexF’s compression benefits are not confined to a single coding backend.

    UV-based pipelines must transmit UV mapping data, whereas TexF derives texture locations directly from the shared mesh through its surface-aligned design. For each UV representation, the mapping payload remains fixed across texture bitrate points. As Fig. 12(12(a)) shows, this payload accounts for a larger share at lower texture rates and on the more complex AOM assets. For UV-Source/HEVC on AOM, its share decreases from 82% to 23% as texture bitrate increases. This helps explain TexF’s greater compression gains in these settings and highlights the benefits of avoiding UV mapping.

    Among the serialization baselines in Fig. 10, Serialized-Hilbert outperforms Serialized-Morton, yet both of them remain substantially less efficient than TexF/Unicorn and TexF/G-PCC. These results show that removing UV mapping and applying a mature 2D codec to serialized voxel attributes do not by themselves ensure competitive compression. They highlight the importance of matching texture organization with coding tools that exploit its spatial correlations.

    The visual comparisons in Fig. 11 further illustrate these differences. At comparable rates, TexF preserves coherent surface details more effectively, whereas the UV-based reconstructions exhibit localized blurring and discontinuities around some chart boundaries.
