TexF/Unicorn and UV-Reparam/HEVC use the same decoded mesh. Quality is evaluated against the original assets, and only texture-related bitstreams are compared, since the geometry payload is shared.

    Fig. S2 and Table S4 show that TexF retains substantial bitrate savings under PSNR, SSIM, and 3D-PSNR on both datasets, while LPIPS performance is comparable to the UV baseline on MPEG and improves substantially on AOM. These results indicate that TexF’s compression benefits extend to lossy geometry condition.

    S3-BCompatibility with Implicit Geometry

    TexF can also represent appearance alongside implicit geometry, extending its use beyond the original mesh. We demonstrate this compatibility by coupling TexF with an SDF and rendering the extracted surface through a standard vertex-color pipeline.

    The SDF and TexF share the same grid. After extracting a mesh with Marching Cubes [57], we transfer TexF attributes to its vertices using k-nearest-neighbor interpolation. The rasterizer then interpolates these vertex attributes across triangles, avoiding per-pixel TexF queries (Fig. S3).

    Fig. S4 shows that TexF/Unicorn (SDF) retains an overall texture compression advantage over UV-Reparam/HEVC on MPEG, although its 3D-PSNR advantage diminishes at higher rates. Relative to the default TexF/Unicorn pipeline, SSIM and LPIPS remain close, whereas PSNR and 3D-PSNR decrease. Geometry and interpolation changes may explain these larger pointwise errors despite similar structural and perceptual quality. Only texture bitstreams are compared; geometry coding is outside this experiment.

    This extension supports implicit geometry and vertex-based rendering at some cost in fidelity. The shared grid also suggests a direction for joint geometry and texture compression.

item.title: 位姿图不够用：3DGS 航拍重建里，只优化位姿为什么永远追不上 BA ｜ When pose graphs are not enough: a failure analysis of pose-graph-based camera estimation for Gaussian splatting
item.description:
一句话：专用系统比 COLMAP 快但质量始终不如，作者把原因拆成四条：手调权重、贪心合并、GPS 噪声，以及 SE(3) 边没有尺度自由度。

要点：

  • 针对固定拍摄配方（消费级无人机单栋房产、多高度多圈重叠、带 GPS 与时间戳、每帧与数十帧闭环）做专用系统，而不是通用 SfM 工具
  • 结论很直白：速度赢 COLMAP，质量从未赢过——这是一篇直白的失败复盘
  • 两条形式化层面的病根：SE(3) 边没有尺度自由度，独立缩放的子图一合并就漂；两视图边给不出「一个 3D 点约束所有看到它的帧」的耦合。可行设计要补回 Sim(3) 约束、绝对 GPS 先验、保留结构与不确定性加权

为什么值得看：做 3DGS 采集管线的人最容易在这里省时间：以为位姿图能替代 BA。这篇明确告诉你省不掉，并且列出了四条具体修补方向。

中文摘要：房产外景的高斯孪生是固定配方拍出来的：消费级无人机围绕单栋房产多圈重叠飞行、分段抬升高度、偶尔垂直上升，影像稠密、连续、带 GPS 与时间戳，每面立面都被反复覆盖。这种结构让人以为相机位姿可以用稠密位姿图优化单独求解，未知量远少于联合优化位姿与点云的 BA。作者针对该采集结构做了专用系统来验证，结果速度赢 COLMAP、质量始终没赢，本文是直白的复盘。原因包括手设权重、贪心合并与噪声 GPS 尺度，以及两个形式化缺陷：SE(3) 边没有尺度自由度导致子图合并漂移，两视图边无法表达一个 3D 点对所有观测帧的耦合。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-08

本期推送：2026-10-24

When pose graphs are not enough: a failure analysis of pose-graph-based camera estimation for Gaussian splatting

Abstract

Exterior Gaussian-splat twins for real-estate listings are captured to a fixed recipe: a consumer drone orbits a single property in several overlapping passes at stepped altitudes, with occasional vertical ascents, so the imagery is dense, sequential, GPS- and time-tagged, and revisits each facade from many angles. This structure is tantalizing: it suggests camera poses could be recovered by a dense pose-graph optimization (PGO) whose only unknowns are the poses, far fewer than the joint pose-and-point problem bundle adjustment (BA) solves. PGO is mature in robotics, but almost always as post-processing: it redistributes the drift of an already-decent trajectory once loop closures tie it together. Splatting captures push that regime to its limit, every frame closing loops with dozens of others, raising a clean question: does pose-only optimization reach BA accuracy? We built a system specialized to this capture structure, not a general-purpose SfM tool, to test it. It beat COLMAP on speed but never on quality; this paper is the candid post-mortem. The shortfall arises from several interacting causes, hand-set weights, greedy merging and a noisy GPS ruler, together with two limits inherent to the formulation: SE(3) edges carry no scale degree of freedom, so independently scaled sub-maps drift when merged, and a two-view edge stops short of the coupling one 3D point imposes on every frame that sees it. A viable design must add back Sim(3) constraints, absolute GPS priors, retained structure, and uncertainty-aware weighting.

Keywords:

Pose estimation Gaussian splatting Pose graph optimization Failure analysis Structure from motion

1 Introduction

Gaussian splatting [13] has made high-quality novel-view synthesis of real scenes routine, and with it the need for accurate camera poses at scale. The default recipe passes images through a structure-from-motion (SfM) system, almost always COLMAP[21], before training. For large exterior scenes this SfM step is the bottleneck: robust incremental reconstruction of thousands of drone frames can take hours.

The captures used for exterior splatting are, however, far from the “images-in-the-wild” regime SfM is built for: as above, a home is flown as several dense overlapping orbits, every frame carries GPS, and consecutive frames overlap strongly. It is natural to ask whether this structure lets us avoid the expensive part of SfM. Bundle adjustment [23] jointly refines camera poses and a large point cloud, its cost nominally dominated by the points: each 3D point adds three parameters and there are far more points than cameras. If we could constrain the cameras directly, through a dense graph of pairwise relative-pose measurements, the optimization would touch only the six degrees of freedom per camera and be both smaller and trivially decomposable per sequence.

This intuition can be sharpened, and it is what makes a pose-only formulation tempting rather than naive. Each Gauss–Newton step of bundle adjustment [9] solves a normal-equation system that, with the camera update Δx_c ordered above the landmark update Δxₚ, takes the block form

\beginbmatrixB&E E^⊤&C\endbmatrix\beginbmatrixΔx_c Δxₚ\endbmatrix=\beginbmatrixv w\endbmatrix,

(1)

with a camera block B, a landmark block C, and their coupling E. Because C carries one 3×3 diagonal block per 3D point it is block-diagonal and cheap to invert, so BA does not in fact pay for the landmarks directly: it eliminates Δxₚ by the Schur complement, left-multiplying Eq.1 by [\beginsmallmatrixI&-EC⁻¹ 0&I\endsmallmatrix] to reach the much smaller, pose-only reduced system

(B-EC⁻¹E^⊤) (S) Δx_c=v-EC⁻¹w,

(2)

and only then back-substitutes Δxₚ=C⁻¹(w-E^⊤Δx_c). Forming the reduction and back-substituting are redone at every iteration, so the dominant work is the repeated solve of S, not the landmarks. If BA’s expensive core is already a pose-only system, the attractive idea is to build Sdirectly, as a pose graph of relative-pose constraints, skipping the landmark bookkeeping and marginalization altogether and arriving at the reduced system for free (Fig.1). The core question is whether the S that pose-graph optimization assembles directly approaches the S that BA produces by marginalization, in the limit of increasingly many inter-frame constraints.

There is a further, more principled reason to study this here. Pose-graph optimization is a mature and well-understood tool [11], but in robotics and SLAM [4] it is almost always a back-end refinement: a front end (visual odometry or SLAM) first produces poses of reasonable accuracy, and PGO then uses loop-closure edges to redistribute the accumulated drift into a globally consistent trajectory. Its power grows with the number and diversity of those loop closures. Splatting captures sit at an extreme of that regime: because the imagery is so dense, essentially every frame closes loops with dozens of others, so the pose graph is far richer than the sparse loop-closure graphs PGO is usually handed. This invites a genuine research question, in the limit of an ever-denser loop-closure graph, does pose-only optimization converge to bundle-adjustment accuracy? If it did, the dense structure of splatting captures would be exactly the setting in which to trade BA for PGO. We treat answering this, empirically and then structurally, as the study’s core purpose.

This is the hypothesis we set out to validate: that dense pose-graph optimization, used not as a post-hoc SLAM refinement but as the primary estimation objective, can recover poses of BA-grade quality on these structured, GPS-tagged drone captures, faster and in a cloud-parallel form. We built the system and ran it on self-captured drone scenes and a public benchmark. The strong form of the hypothesis proved false. This paper explains why, using the system’s own design and numbers, and is careful about which parts of the explanation generalize: two of the causes are properties of the pose-only formulation that no parameter setting escapes, while the rest are choices this pipeline made and a better one could revisit. We keep the two apart throughout (Sec.5).

We recall the related landscape (Sec.2), the pipeline (Sec.3) and its outcomes (Sec.4), then give the methodological failure analysis that is our contribution (Sec.5) and the design lessons it implies (Sec.6).

2 Related work

COLMAP[21] is the de facto general-purpose standard for pose estimation in vision and the default front end for splatting. We do not aim to replace it there: we target only the narrow, structured regime of exterior splatting captures, using COLMAP as the reference a specialized pose-only design must match. GLOMAP [19] showed that global SfM can approach incremental accuracy at lower cost, yet COLMAP remains the method of choice when robust registration is required. Theia [22] offers both incremental and global SfM but is chiefly a researcher’s toolkit. Learned, feed-forward estimators such as VGGT [24] and Depth-Anything-3 [16] predict poses, depth and intrinsics in a single pass and are advancing quickly. They make excellent one-shot pose initializers, but as we confirm below they have not yet reached the pose accuracy of a robust system that nonlinearly refines poses.

Our matching front end follows hierarchical localization [20], pairing SuperPoint features [6] with LightGlue [17] and NetVLAD [2] retrieval indexed with FAISS [7], a modern replacement for bag-of-words retrieval [8]. Distributing SfM across machines dates back to Building Rome in a Day [1]. Our design differs in demoting bundle adjustment [23] from the global objective to a per-chunk step and making pose-graph optimization carry the estimation, solved with g2o [14] (GTSAM [5] is the common alternative), and in exploiting GPS and sequential capture. It is the limits of that partial substitution, and of the pure-pose formulation it approximates, that we analyze.

3 The system we built

We summarize the pipeline only enough to make the analysis precise. It is not a general-purpose SfM system but one built expressly around the structure of these captures, dense sequential overlap, per-frame GPS, and multi-orbit coverage; a three-stage divide–compute–merge design (Fig.2).

Chunks.

The image stream is split by timestamp into disjoint chunks (“sequences”), each a continuous imaging run in which every frame overlaps another frame in the same chunk. Chunks larger than 200 frames are subdivided. Chunks are the unit of parallelism.

Intra-sequence PGO.

Within a chunk, images are indexed with NetVLAD [2] in a FAISS [7] store; each frame retrieves visual neighbors plus GPS-proximate geometric neighbors. Retrieved pairs are matched with SuperPoint [6]+LightGlue [17], verified against degeneracy (minimum feature motion, essential-vs-homography inlier test, a 3^∘ median-triangulation-angle floor), and reduced to a relative rotation and an up-to-scale translation from the essential matrix [18]. That translation is scaled by the GPS distance between the two frames. Each verified pair becomes an edge in an SE(3) pose graph solved with g2o [14]; the objective is the standard robust sum of relative-pose residuals,

E= ∑_(i,j)∈𝔼 ρ ([\log(Tⱼ⁻¹TⱼᵢTᵢ)]^∨⊤ Ωⱼᵢ [\log(Tⱼ⁻¹TⱼᵢTᵢ)]^∨),

(3)

with Ωⱼᵢ a hand-set information matrix (high on rotation, low on translation) and ρ a Huber kernel. Each chunk yields a dense graph in which a frame is tied to about 100 others.

Retained bundle adjustment.

The pipeline does not end there, and this is the design’s most consequential compromise. Each chunk’s matches are imported into a COLMAP database and a bundle-adjustment pass refines poses, intrinsics, and points. The points that pass triangulates are then reused: they are what the 3D–2D constraints below are built from. BA is thus removed only globally. It is not run over the full capture, which is where the cost argument of Sec.1 bites, but it survives inside every chunk, and structure survives with it. The system is accordingly BA-reduced, not BA-free, and we return in Sec.5.4 to why the pure-pose design could not shed this last dependency.

Inter-sequence constraints and merge.

Chunks are still disconnected. We form a K×K table whose (i,j) entry holds cross-chunk constraints, 2D–2D essential (GPS-scaled) and 3D–2D perspective-n-point (PnP) [15] edges, the latter resolved against the per-chunk BA points; 3D–3D point-cloud alignment was tried and abandoned as unstable. The final stage greedily merges the pair of chunks with the most constraints: a robust SE(3) average of the pairwise relative transforms (iterated 3σ rejection) pre-aligns one chunk to the other, g2o re-optimizes with the cross-chunk edges enabled, and the two chunks collapse into one. This repeats until a single graph remains. Information matrices encode trust: PnP edges 7× essential edges, intra-sequence edges up-weighted 10× before the merge.

Intended parallelism.

Every intra-sequence solve is independent and each K×K entry is independent, so the front end is designed to run across a cloud cluster.

4 Outcomes

We evaluated the pipeline internally on 40 proprietary drone scenes. Across the set it neither beats COLMAP nor yields metrics useful on their own, so we do not tabulate aggregate numbers that would only restate a uniform shortfall. Instead we elucidate two representative self-captured scenes (houses of 824 and 741 frames) in detail: precisely because they neither beat COLMAP nor behave anomalously, they make a clean test bed for reasoning about why a pose-only, structure-free formulation falls short. We compare against a tuned COLMAP baseline (GPU extraction and matching, vocab-tree matcher, hierarchical mapper), and add the public GauU-Scene V2 [25] drone dataset with lidar ground truth. Tabs.1 and 2 collect the numbers and Fig.3 shows a representative splat pair. The poses agree with COLMAP to 0.5–0.6^∘ and to within about 2 m, in a space where the trajectories themselves span more than 100 m, and the splats are recognizable (Fig.4). Of the two axes the system was built to win, speed and splat quality, the outcome is split. It has real potential to beat COLMAP on speed: the parallel time beats COLMAP by a wide margin. But we had no incentive to pursue that implementation with full vigor, because the splat quality was never comparable to what COLMAP poses produce. On the external dataset one scene failed outright and the rest contained large outliers, though we do report the median here. Sec.5 explains why each of these follows from the method’s design.

5 Why the method fails

We give four causes, each supported by the system’s own design and measurements. They are not of one kind, and separating them matters for how much the reader should conclude.

Two are representational: they follow from what a pose-only formulation can express, hold for any parameter setting, and are argued below from the structure of the estimator rather than from our numbers. SE(3) edges have no scale degree of freedom (Sec.5.2), and a two-view edge cannot encode the simultaneous coupling that one point observed in many views imposes (Sec.5.4). No information matrix, merge order, or initialization repairs either; they bound what the formulation can do.

The other two are implementation choices of this pipeline: sequence-wise ordering and merging (Sec.5.3) and reliance on consumer GPS as the metric ruler (Sec.5.5), together with the hand-set information matrices of Sec.5.6. Better choices exist for each, and we say so as we go.

The honest limit of our evidence is the boundary between these two kinds. Since we ablate none of the four, the analysis locates where a ceiling comes from without showing that our measurements sit at it rather than at a lower floor set by the implementation; a better-engineered pose-only pipeline should beat the numbers in Sec.4, perhaps substantially. What it cannot do is escape the two representational limits, and Sec.6 is written for whoever tries.

5.1 Runtime is not where the method fails

The founding motivation was a runtime argument, and on its own terms it is sound. The cost splits into two parts that scale very differently. The matching front end, per frame, NetVLAD retrieval, SuperPoint+LightGlue against about 100 neighbors, and two-view verification of each pair, is the dominant absolute cost, but it is embarrassingly parallel: every pair is matched and verified independently, so it shards trivially across a cloud fleet and imposes no fundamental serial bottleneck. What does not parallelize is the solver, the global optimization that ties the frames into one consistent model, and that is the fundamental bottleneck a distributable pipeline must attack. Reducing it is exactly what a pose-only formulation sets out to do: shrink the per-step system to the six-DoF cameras (Eq.2) and solve each chunk independently, making the one part that cannot be parallelized as small and as decomposable as possible. In that sense the design targets the right cost. The single-machine (sequential) runtime in Tab.1 does not beat COLMAP, but the parallel time does. Speed, then, is not where this method fails; its failures, examined next, are geometric.

5.2 SE(3) edges cannot represent scale, so merged sub-maps drift

This is the deepest failure. Each intra-sequence graph is metric only up to the GPS scaling applied to its essential-matrix translations, and different chunks acquire slightly different effective scales because their GPS baselines and triangulation geometry differ. The merge then aligns chunks with an SE(3) transform, and Eq.3 lives entirely in SE(3), which has no scale degree of freedom. When two chunks disagree on scale by even a few percent, an SE(3) alignment cannot reconcile them: it trades the error into translation and leaves a residual the optimizer cannot drive to zero. The visible symptom is blur and ghosting at the seams of the merged splat (Fig.3b), and it contributes to the 1.7–2.7 dB PSNR deficit in Tab.1, alongside the GPS noise and weighting choices discussed below, which our measurements cannot separate from it. The argument does not need the attribution: the limitation is visible in the state space itself, before any measurement. Bundle adjustment never encounters this, because 3D points shared across overlapping views implicitly tie their scales together. A pose graph in SE(3) discards that coupling and has no other mechanism to recover it, so scale drift across merges is not a bug to be tuned away; it is unrepresentable in the chosen state space.

Restoring the missing degree of freedom does not rescue the result, and we tried: lifting each merge to Sim(3), which does carry a scale term. Such a merge must estimate one similarity (s,R,t) per sequence boundary from the inter-sequence constraints alone, and with few, wide-baseline shared observations that estimate starts far from its optimum. Compounding this, the GPS-derived constraints conflict: each pulls the boundary toward a different, meter-scale, anisotropically noisy anchor, so the solve settles at a compromise satisfying none of them, metrically plausible but still blurring the seam. The missing scale degree of freedom is therefore necessary but not sufficient.

Under a sequential merge this conflict is structural rather than an artifact of noise levels, and seeing why shows exactly where Sim(3) alone relocates the problem instead of removing it. Scaling an entire sequence together with all of its pose constraints does keep that sequence internally consistent, so once we scale sequence 2 to agree with sequence 1 the pair (1,2) is mutually consistent, and every inter-sequence constraint incident on 2 is scaled to match. An astute reader might expect this rescaling to be absorbed automatically as the next sequence is merged. It is not. When a third sequence is merged against the first two, the inter-pose constraints 3 → 1 and 3 → 2 both carry the raw GPS scale, because that is how sequence 3 was reconstructed. But sequence 2 has already been rescaled to match 1, so 3 → 1 is roughly consistent up to ordinary scale drift while 3 → 2 disagrees by exactly the correction we applied to 2. The optimizer is handed two contradictory statements about the same scale, and no single scalar satisfies both. The similarity that resolved (1,2) thus reappears as a fresh conflict at 3: Sim(3) shifts the scale mismatch along the merge order rather than removing it.

Multi-way synchronization was not attempted.

The contradiction above arises only because the merges happen one after another: each merge aligns the incoming chunk to the partial map so far, so by chunk 3, chunk 2 has already been corrected by its merge with 1 while chunk 3 still carries raw GPS scale. That mismatch, not Sim(3) itself, is what no single scalar can satisfy.

The alternative is to estimate all K chunk similarities at once from the full graph of inter-chunk constraints, so no chunk is corrected before the others are accounted for. We did not try it. Such multi-way Sim(3) synchronization, in the spirit of motion and rotation averaging [10, 12] and similarity synchronization [3], spreads inconsistent pairwise scales in a least-squares sense over all chunks.

The scale component in particular is a linear problem, which is what makes this attractive. Give chunk k an unknown log-scale σₖ=\logsₖ; each cross-chunk constraint between i and j measures a ratio sᵢⱼ and so contributes one equation σⱼ-σᵢ=\logsᵢⱼ. Over the populated entries of the K×K table these stack into an overdetermined linear system in K unknowns whose normal equations are a weighted graph Laplacian, determined up to a single global gauge that GPS, or fixing one chunk, supplies. Rotations follow by rotation averaging and translations are linear once scales and rotations are known, the standard Sim(3) synchronization recipe [3]. Crucially, every chunk’s scale is then set by all of its constraints simultaneously, so a disagreement between 3 → 1 and 3 → 2 is distributed as residual rather than resolved in favour of whichever merge happened first. With K in the tens the solve is negligible beside the matching front end, so it costs nothing the speed argument cares about. We expect this to reduce the seam error materially and regard it as the most promising untried repair, though it redistributes inconsistency rather than supplying the absolute scale the capture lacks.

5.3 Sequence-by-sequence ordering leaves sub-maps ill-conditioned before they merge

This cause and the two that follow are implementation choices, each of which could have been made differently and none of which we ablated. They are worth recording because the divide-and-merge decomposition that makes a pose-only design attractive to parallelize is exactly what makes them tempting.

The pipeline orders images by capture sequence, solves each sequence independently, and only then merges, and the ordering itself is a failure mode, for two compounding reasons. First, some sequences are geometrically degenerate in isolation: a nadir ascent, where the drone rises vertically over a fixed point, supplies almost no translational parallax, so the sub-map is fundamentally unconstrained up to the missing baseline. Solved alone, it has no way to recover the structure a neighbouring oblique sequence would have supplied. Second, to absorb the meter-scale GPS noise each sequence settles into its own local optimum that best trades its observations against its noisy anchors. Because every sub-map made that trade independently, the local optima disagree; when the sequences merge, the cross-sequence constraints are in large mutual conflict, far outside the basin the merge can reconcile, and the global solve settles at a sub-optimal compromise.

The lesson is about ordering, not merging: an image ordering that proceeds strictly sequence-by-sequence guarantees these isolated, separately-converged pieces, and no merge strategy applied afterwards can undo a sub-map that has already converged to the wrong basin. An ideal ordering would never take one sequence to convergence in isolation. Interleaving images across sequences from the start, so that cross-sequence constraints shape each pose before it commits to a local optimum, keeps the whole capture in a single jointly constrained basin rather than assembling it from pre-settled, mutually inconsistent parts, and it costs nothing in parallelism: the chunking that makes the front end shardable is independent of the order in which poses are allowed to influence one another. We did not build that ordering, so we cannot say how much of the merge conflict it would remove; it is the ablation we would run first.

5.4 Removing shared structure removes multi-view consistency

The premise was that pose-only optimization could reach BA-grade quality. But the thing that makes BA’s poses globally consistent is precisely the structure the method discards: a 3D point observed in many frames forces those frames to agree, and BA averages their independent measurement errors into one consistent estimate. A pose graph of pairwise relative transforms has no such shared latent variable; it is only as good as its edges, and edge errors accumulate rather than cancel. Two facts in the system confirm that this coupling could not simply be dropped. First, the pipeline still runs a per-chunk COLMAP bundle adjustment, and the 3D–2D PnP constraints that stitch chunks are derived from the points that BA produced, so structure was reintroduced through the back door. This cuts two ways, and we state both. It is the clearest evidence that the coupling is load-bearing: the design reached for structure exactly where pose-only constraints proved too weak to stitch sub-maps, and no version of the pipeline ran without it. But it also means we never put the pure-pose premise fully on trial, and our negative result is correspondingly bounded. What we have shown to fail is pose-only estimation at the global scale, with BA still supporting each chunk from below; a formulation that removed BA entirely would inherit every weakness catalogued here and lose that support besides, so we expect it to fare worse, but we did not measure it. Second, the one path that tried to use structure-to-structure information directly, the 3D–3D point-cloud alignment edge, was abandoned as unstable. That instability is no accident: projectively triangulated points carry an uncertainty that grows with observation distance and shrinks with disparity, so a point seen from 50 m away is localized far more loosely than one seen from a few meters. A point-cloud alignment that treats every point as equally certain then forces such a loosely-triangulated far point, from one sequence, to line up precisely with a tightly-triangulated near point of the same structure from another; without propagating those per-point uncertainties into the cost, the solve trades a well-localized constraint against a badly-localized one and settles at a poorly-converged compromise. The method’s own choices show that without shared structure the estimate is not consistent enough, and with it the “BA-free” claim no longer holds.

5.5 Consumer GPS is a noisy ruler, not an anchor

GPS plays an outsized role: it is the only metric signal, used to scale each pairwise translation and to select neighbors, yet it enters only as a relative ruler on translations, never as a soft absolute position prior on the nodes. So nothing pins global scale or arrests drift; each chunk’s scale floats independently, exactly the freedom Sec.5.2 cannot later remove.

Worse, the ruler itself is imprecise. These drones carry consumer-grade GNSS (GPS). With an RTK fix the receiver is accurate to a few centimeters, but the captures rarely hold an RTK lock, and without it horizontal position is off by 0.5–1.0 m. That error does not stay contained: fed in as the scale of every essential-matrix translation, it is large relative to the inter-frame baselines it scales, injecting meter-scale noise into precisely the SE(3) translations the merge already cannot correct. Altitude is worse still: on several of these drones the vertical channel comes from a barometric altimeter, so the relative-Z component carries far more uncertainty than the horizontal ones. Feeding a strongly anisotropic, meter-scale, sometimes-biased position signal into an optimizer that treats it as a metric constraint makes the pose graph ill-posed, though not uniformly. The circular orbit sequences are largely safe: their wide, multi-directional baselines triangulate structure, and vertical scale with it, from the imagery. The damage concentrates on the nadir sequences, the near-straight vertical ascents flown looking straight down, where the geometry is degenerate: straight-line motion gives no cross-baseline, and the nadir view aligns the poorly-triangulated depth axis with the vertical, so “the camera climbed” and “the scene grew” are nearly indistinguishable. Vertical scale is then only weakly constrained: the nadir edges resist it little, and the one term that penalizes a wrong vertical scale, the barometric-Z prior, is too noisy to push back. With so little curvature there, Eq.3 is nearly flat, so the estimate can drift far at almost no cost. This is a direct source of the large outliers and outright failure we observed (Tab.2). A pose-only formulation has no shared structure to fall back on when its metric signal is this noisy; bundle adjustment derives scale from the imagery itself and needs GPS only as a weak gauge, so the same fix does it little harm.

5.6 Trust is hand-set, not propagated

Compounding the noise, every constraint’s influence is a hand-chosen information matrix (rotation over translation, PnP 7× essential, refined edges 10×) rather than a value propagated from the data’s uncertainty. Without a data-driven model, a triangulation-noisy or badly-GPS-scaled match cannot be down-weighted against a clean one, the mechanical reason the 3D–3D constraint was unusable and the reason the same fixed weights that worked on the tuning scenes produced large outliers and an outright failure (HAV) on a capture whose noise profile differed. Stability resting on manually balanced trust, over a signal as heteroscedastic as consumer GPS, does not transfer. This is the most fixable of the four causes and the one that most confounds our results: with no learned-weight configuration run, we cannot separate error from the formulation from error from weighting it badly.

6 Lessons

The causes above translate into concrete guidance for anyone drawn to the same shortcut, replacing structure-aware optimization with a cheaper pose-only surrogate on structured captures.

  • 1.

    Two independent speedups, and the front end is the bigger one. Dropping the points for a structure-less, pose-only optimization is genuinely faster than a full bundle adjustment: it removes the most expensive part of the solve, and that saving is real and worth taking. The larger opportunity, though, is the matching front end that dominates absolute cost. It is embarrassingly parallel and shards cleanly across workers, and the levers that matter there are mundane, the retrieval budget per frame, pruning pairs before verification, and GPU-parallel extraction and matching. Both are worth accelerating, but the front end’s gains are far easier to capture, because they come from trivial parallelism rather than from reformulating the estimator, and reformulating the estimator is what costs accuracy.

  • 2.

    If you drop the points, add scale back explicitly. BA’s hidden gift is that shared structure couples the scales of overlapping views. A pose-only formulation must recover that coupling elsewhere, through Sim(3) edges and a Sim(3) merge estimated jointly over all sub-maps rather than pairwise (Sec.5.2). SE(3) pose graphs across independently-scaled sub-maps are a scale trap.

  • 3.

    Use GPS as an absolute prior, not merely a ruler, but model its noise. A soft absolute position constraint on every node pins global scale and arrests drift. It helps only if weighted by its true, anisotropic uncertainty, looser in barometric Z than in the horizontal plane and looser still without an RTK lock, otherwise the meter-scale error re-enters as bias.

  • 4.

    Keep a little structure. A pose graph with zero shared 3D points is on the wrong side of a cliff. Retaining even a small point set, a few times the camera count rather than the hundreds-of-times BA carries, restores multi-view consistency while keeping the problem small, the structured-but-lean middle, not pure PGO, the cost argument should have pointed to.

  • 5.

    Propagate uncertainty; do not hand-tune it. Data-driven information matrices are what make structure-to-structure constraints usable. Fixed trust ratios are a liability that grows with capture diversity.

    • 7 Conclusion

    We asked whether, in the dense loop-closure regime splatting captures uniquely provide, pose-graph optimization could displace bundle adjustment as the estimation objective. For the system we built the answer is no, twice over: it did not match COLMAP’s accuracy, and it did not even dispense with BA to get there, keeping a per-chunk pass whose triangulated points its own cross-chunk constraints are built on.

    The causes divide, and the division is the point. Some are ours to own: a consumer-GPS anchor too noisy and too anisotropic to hold scale, greedy pairwise merging, sequence-by-sequence ordering, and hand-set information matrices. Each is a repairable engineering decision we did not ablate, and a careful reimplementation should beat our numbers. Two causes are not repairable that way. The SE(3) state space cannot represent the scale differences its own GPS-scaled sub-maps introduce, whatever weights the edges carry; and a graph of two-view edges cannot reconstitute the many-view coupling that gives bundle adjustment its consistency. These are properties of the formulation, not settings within it, and they are what a future design has to answer for: Sim(3) constraints estimated jointly rather than pairwise, absolute uncertainty-aware GPS priors, and a thin layer of retained structure. How much of the measured gap those limits account for would take the ablations we did not run; we hope the account still saves the next team the same detour.

    When the approach might be worth revisiting.

    Several failures trace to the noisy metric anchor, not the formulation. Under an RTK fix, position is accurate to a few centimetres in all of (x,y,z), enough to pin scale across merges and stop inter-sequence constraints conflicting at the meter scale. A lightweight distributed pose graph, with a few sparse retained points supplying the coupling pure SE(3)/Sim(3) edges cannot, would then deserve a fresh attempt: the negative result is a scoping one, pose-only, GPS-scaled estimation is the wrong tool for consumer-grade capture.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：专用系统比 COLMAP 快但质量始终不如，作者把原因拆成四条：手调权重、贪心合并、GPS 噪声，以及 SE(3) 边没有尺度自由度。

要点：

  • 针对固定拍摄配方（消费级无人机单栋房产、多高度多圈重叠、带 GPS 与时间戳、每帧与数十帧闭环）做专用系统，而不是通用 SfM 工具
  • 结论很直白：速度赢 COLMAP，质量从未赢过——这是一篇直白的失败复盘
  • 两条形式化层面的病根：SE(3) 边没有尺度自由度，独立缩放的子图一合并就漂；两视图边给不出「一个 3D 点约束所有看到它的帧」的耦合。可行设计要补回 Sim(3) 约束、绝对 GPS 先验、保留结构与不确定性加权

为什么值得看：做 3DGS 采集管线的人最容易在这里省时间：以为位姿图能替代 BA。这篇明确告诉你省不掉，并且列出了四条具体修补方向。

中文摘要：房产外景的高斯孪生是固定配方拍出来的：消费级无人机围绕单栋房产多圈重叠飞行、分段抬升高度、偶尔垂直上升，影像稠密、连续、带 GPS 与时间戳，每面立面都被反复覆盖。这种结构让人以为相机位姿可以用稠密位姿图优化单独求解，未知量远少于联合优化位姿与点云的 BA。作者针对该采集结构做了专用系统来验证，结果速度赢 COLMAP、质量始终没赢，本文是直白的复盘。原因包括手设权重、贪心合并与噪声 GPS 尺度，以及两个形式化缺陷：SE(3) 边没有尺度自由度导致子图合并漂移，两视图边无法表达一个 3D 点对所有观测帧的耦合。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-08

本期推送：2026-10-24

When pose graphs are not enough: a failure analysis of pose-graph-based camera estimation for Gaussian splatting

Abstract

Exterior Gaussian-splat twins for real-estate listings are captured to a fixed recipe: a consumer drone orbits a single property in several overlapping passes at stepped altitudes, with occasional vertical ascents, so the imagery is dense, sequential, GPS- and time-tagged, and revisits each facade from many angles. This structure is tantalizing: it suggests camera poses could be recovered by a dense pose-graph optimization (PGO) whose only unknowns are the poses, far fewer than the joint pose-and-point problem bundle adjustment (BA) solves. PGO is mature in robotics, but almost always as post-processing: it redistributes the drift of an already-decent trajectory once loop closures tie it together. Splatting captures push that regime to its limit, every frame closing loops with dozens of others, raising a clean question: does pose-only optimization reach BA accuracy? We built a system specialized to this capture structure, not a general-purpose SfM tool, to test it. It beat COLMAP on speed but never on quality; this paper is the candid post-mortem. The shortfall arises from several interacting causes, hand-set weights, greedy merging and a noisy GPS ruler, together with two limits inherent to the formulation: SE(3) edges carry no scale degree of freedom, so independently scaled sub-maps drift when merged, and a two-view edge stops short of the coupling one 3D point imposes on every frame that sees it. A viable design must add back Sim(3) constraints, absolute GPS priors, retained structure, and uncertainty-aware weighting.

Keywords:

Pose estimation Gaussian splatting Pose graph optimization Failure analysis Structure from motion

1 Introduction

Gaussian splatting [13] has made high-quality novel-view synthesis of real scenes routine, and with it the need for accurate camera poses at scale. The default recipe passes images through a structure-from-motion (SfM) system, almost always COLMAP[21], before training. For large exterior scenes this SfM step is the bottleneck: robust incremental reconstruction of thousands of drone frames can take hours.

The captures used for exterior splatting are, however, far from the “images-in-the-wild” regime SfM is built for: as above, a home is flown as several dense overlapping orbits, every frame carries GPS, and consecutive frames overlap strongly. It is natural to ask whether this structure lets us avoid the expensive part of SfM. Bundle adjustment [23] jointly refines camera poses and a large point cloud, its cost nominally dominated by the points: each 3D point adds three parameters and there are far more points than cameras. If we could constrain the cameras directly, through a dense graph of pairwise relative-pose measurements, the optimization would touch only the six degrees of freedom per camera and be both smaller and trivially decomposable per sequence.

This intuition can be sharpened, and it is what makes a pose-only formulation tempting rather than naive. Each Gauss–Newton step of bundle adjustment [9] solves a normal-equation system that, with the camera update Δx_c ordered above the landmark update Δxₚ, takes the block form

\beginbmatrixB&E E^⊤&C\endbmatrix\beginbmatrixΔx_c Δxₚ\endbmatrix=\beginbmatrixv w\endbmatrix,

(1)

with a camera block B, a landmark block C, and their coupling E. Because C carries one 3×3 diagonal block per 3D point it is block-diagonal and cheap to invert, so BA does not in fact pay for the landmarks directly: it eliminates Δxₚ by the Schur complement, left-multiplying Eq.1 by [\beginsmallmatrixI&-EC⁻¹ 0&I\endsmallmatrix] to reach the much smaller, pose-only reduced system

(B-EC⁻¹E^⊤) (S) Δx_c=v-EC⁻¹w,

(2)

and only then back-substitutes Δxₚ=C⁻¹(w-E^⊤Δx_c). Forming the reduction and back-substituting are redone at every iteration, so the dominant work is the repeated solve of S, not the landmarks. If BA’s expensive core is already a pose-only system, the attractive idea is to build Sdirectly, as a pose graph of relative-pose constraints, skipping the landmark bookkeeping and marginalization altogether and arriving at the reduced system for free (Fig.1). The core question is whether the S that pose-graph optimization assembles directly approaches the S that BA produces by marginalization, in the limit of increasingly many inter-frame constraints.

There is a further, more principled reason to study this here. Pose-graph optimization is a mature and well-understood tool [11], but in robotics and SLAM [4] it is almost always a back-end refinement: a front end (visual odometry or SLAM) first produces poses of reasonable accuracy, and PGO then uses loop-closure edges to redistribute the accumulated drift into a globally consistent trajectory. Its power grows with the number and diversity of those loop closures. Splatting captures sit at an extreme of that regime: because the imagery is so dense, essentially every frame closes loops with dozens of others, so the pose graph is far richer than the sparse loop-closure graphs PGO is usually handed. This invites a genuine research question, in the limit of an ever-denser loop-closure graph, does pose-only optimization converge to bundle-adjustment accuracy? If it did, the dense structure of splatting captures would be exactly the setting in which to trade BA for PGO. We treat answering this, empirically and then structurally, as the study’s core purpose.

This is the hypothesis we set out to validate: that dense pose-graph optimization, used not as a post-hoc SLAM refinement but as the primary estimation objective, can recover poses of BA-grade quality on these structured, GPS-tagged drone captures, faster and in a cloud-parallel form. We built the system and ran it on self-captured drone scenes and a public benchmark. The strong form of the hypothesis proved false. This paper explains why, using the system’s own design and numbers, and is careful about which parts of the explanation generalize: two of the causes are properties of the pose-only formulation that no parameter setting escapes, while the rest are choices this pipeline made and a better one could revisit. We keep the two apart throughout (Sec.5).

We recall the related landscape (Sec.2), the pipeline (Sec.3) and its outcomes (Sec.4), then give the methodological failure analysis that is our contribution (Sec.5) and the design lessons it implies (Sec.6).

2 Related work

COLMAP[21] is the de facto general-purpose standard for pose estimation in vision and the default front end for splatting. We do not aim to replace it there: we target only the narrow, structured regime of exterior splatting captures, using COLMAP as the reference a specialized pose-only design must match. GLOMAP [19] showed that global SfM can approach incremental accuracy at lower cost, yet COLMAP remains the method of choice when robust registration is required. Theia [22] offers both incremental and global SfM but is chiefly a researcher’s toolkit. Learned, feed-forward estimators such as VGGT [24] and Depth-Anything-3 [16] predict poses, depth and intrinsics in a single pass and are advancing quickly. They make excellent one-shot pose initializers, but as we confirm below they have not yet reached the pose accuracy of a robust system that nonlinearly refines poses.

Our matching front end follows hierarchical localization [20], pairing SuperPoint features [6] with LightGlue [17] and NetVLAD [2] retrieval indexed with FAISS [7], a modern replacement for bag-of-words retrieval [8]. Distributing SfM across machines dates back to Building Rome in a Day [1]. Our design differs in demoting bundle adjustment [23] from the global objective to a per-chunk step and making pose-graph optimization carry the estimation, solved with g2o [14] (GTSAM [5] is the common alternative), and in exploiting GPS and sequential capture. It is the limits of that partial substitution, and of the pure-pose formulation it approximates, that we analyze.

3 The system we built

We summarize the pipeline only enough to make the analysis precise. It is not a general-purpose SfM system but one built expressly around the structure of these captures, dense sequential overlap, per-frame GPS, and multi-orbit coverage; a three-stage divide–compute–merge design (Fig.2).

Chunks.

The image stream is split by timestamp into disjoint chunks (“sequences”), each a continuous imaging run in which every frame overlaps another frame in the same chunk. Chunks larger than 200 frames are subdivided. Chunks are the unit of parallelism.

Intra-sequence PGO.

Within a chunk, images are indexed with NetVLAD [2] in a FAISS [7] store; each frame retrieves visual neighbors plus GPS-proximate geometric neighbors. Retrieved pairs are matched with SuperPoint [6]+LightGlue [17], verified against degeneracy (minimum feature motion, essential-vs-homography inlier test, a 3^∘ median-triangulation-angle floor), and reduced to a relative rotation and an up-to-scale translation from the essential matrix [18]. That translation is scaled by the GPS distance between the two frames. Each verified pair becomes an edge in an SE(3) pose graph solved with g2o [14]; the objective is the standard robust sum of relative-pose residuals,

E= ∑_(i,j)∈𝔼 ρ ([\log(Tⱼ⁻¹TⱼᵢTᵢ)]^∨⊤ Ωⱼᵢ [\log(Tⱼ⁻¹TⱼᵢTᵢ)]^∨),

(3)

with Ωⱼᵢ a hand-set information matrix (high on rotation, low on translation) and ρ a Huber kernel. Each chunk yields a dense graph in which a frame is tied to about 100 others.

Retained bundle adjustment.

The pipeline does not end there, and this is the design’s most consequential compromise. Each chunk’s matches are imported into a COLMAP database and a bundle-adjustment pass refines poses, intrinsics, and points. The points that pass triangulates are then reused: they are what the 3D–2D constraints below are built from. BA is thus removed only globally. It is not run over the full capture, which is where the cost argument of Sec.1 bites, but it survives inside every chunk, and structure survives with it. The system is accordingly BA-reduced, not BA-free, and we return in Sec.5.4 to why the pure-pose design could not shed this last dependency.

Inter-sequence constraints and merge.

Chunks are still disconnected. We form a K×K table whose (i,j) entry holds cross-chunk constraints, 2D–2D essential (GPS-scaled) and 3D–2D perspective-n-point (PnP) [15] edges, the latter resolved against the per-chunk BA points; 3D–3D point-cloud alignment was tried and abandoned as unstable. The final stage greedily merges the pair of chunks with the most constraints: a robust SE(3) average of the pairwise relative transforms (iterated 3σ rejection) pre-aligns one chunk to the other, g2o re-optimizes with the cross-chunk edges enabled, and the two chunks collapse into one. This repeats until a single graph remains. Information matrices encode trust: PnP edges 7× essential edges, intra-sequence edges up-weighted 10× before the merge.

Intended parallelism.

Every intra-sequence solve is independent and each K×K entry is independent, so the front end is designed to run across a cloud cluster.

4 Outcomes

We evaluated the pipeline internally on 40 proprietary drone scenes. Across the set it neither beats COLMAP nor yields metrics useful on their own, so we do not tabulate aggregate numbers that would only restate a uniform shortfall. Instead we elucidate two representative self-captured scenes (houses of 824 and 741 frames) in detail: precisely because they neither beat COLMAP nor behave anomalously, they make a clean test bed for reasoning about why a pose-only, structure-free formulation falls short. We compare against a tuned COLMAP baseline (GPU extraction and matching, vocab-tree matcher, hierarchical mapper), and add the public GauU-Scene V2 [25] drone dataset with lidar ground truth. Tabs.1 and 2 collect the numbers and Fig.3 shows a representative splat pair. The poses agree with COLMAP to 0.5–0.6^∘ and to within about 2 m, in a space where the trajectories themselves span more than 100 m, and the splats are recognizable (Fig.4). Of the two axes the system was built to win, speed and splat quality, the outcome is split. It has real potential to beat COLMAP on speed: the parallel time beats COLMAP by a wide margin. But we had no incentive to pursue that implementation with full vigor, because the splat quality was never comparable to what COLMAP poses produce. On the external dataset one scene failed outright and the rest contained large outliers, though we do report the median here. Sec.5 explains why each of these follows from the method’s design.

5 Why the method fails

We give four causes, each supported by the system’s own design and measurements. They are not of one kind, and separating them matters for how much the reader should conclude.

Two are representational: they follow from what a pose-only formulation can express, hold for any parameter setting, and are argued below from the structure of the estimator rather than from our numbers. SE(3) edges have no scale degree of freedom (Sec.5.2), and a two-view edge cannot encode the simultaneous coupling that one point observed in many views imposes (Sec.5.4). No information matrix, merge order, or initialization repairs either; they bound what the formulation can do.

The other two are implementation choices of this pipeline: sequence-wise ordering and merging (Sec.5.3) and reliance on consumer GPS as the metric ruler (Sec.5.5), together with the hand-set information matrices of Sec.5.6. Better choices exist for each, and we say so as we go.

The honest limit of our evidence is the boundary between these two kinds. Since we ablate none of the four, the analysis locates where a ceiling comes from without showing that our measurements sit at it rather than at a lower floor set by the implementation; a better-engineered pose-only pipeline should beat the numbers in Sec.4, perhaps substantially. What it cannot do is escape the two representational limits, and Sec.6 is written for whoever tries.

5.1 Runtime is not where the method fails

The founding motivation was a runtime argument, and on its own terms it is sound. The cost splits into two parts that scale very differently. The matching front end, per frame, NetVLAD retrieval, SuperPoint+LightGlue against about 100 neighbors, and two-view verification of each pair, is the dominant absolute cost, but it is embarrassingly parallel: every pair is matched and verified independently, so it shards trivially across a cloud fleet and imposes no fundamental serial bottleneck. What does not parallelize is the solver, the global optimization that ties the frames into one consistent model, and that is the fundamental bottleneck a distributable pipeline must attack. Reducing it is exactly what a pose-only formulation sets out to do: shrink the per-step system to the six-DoF cameras (Eq.2) and solve each chunk independently, making the one part that cannot be parallelized as small and as decomposable as possible. In that sense the design targets the right cost. The single-machine (sequential) runtime in Tab.1 does not beat COLMAP, but the parallel time does. Speed, then, is not where this method fails; its failures, examined next, are geometric.

5.2 SE(3) edges cannot represent scale, so merged sub-maps drift

This is the deepest failure. Each intra-sequence graph is metric only up to the GPS scaling applied to its essential-matrix translations, and different chunks acquire slightly different effective scales because their GPS baselines and triangulation geometry differ. The merge then aligns chunks with an SE(3) transform, and Eq.3 lives entirely in SE(3), which has no scale degree of freedom. When two chunks disagree on scale by even a few percent, an SE(3) alignment cannot reconcile them: it trades the error into translation and leaves a residual the optimizer cannot drive to zero. The visible symptom is blur and ghosting at the seams of the merged splat (Fig.3b), and it contributes to the 1.7–2.7 dB PSNR deficit in Tab.1, alongside the GPS noise and weighting choices discussed below, which our measurements cannot separate from it. The argument does not need the attribution: the limitation is visible in the state space itself, before any measurement. Bundle adjustment never encounters this, because 3D points shared across overlapping views implicitly tie their scales together. A pose graph in SE(3) discards that coupling and has no other mechanism to recover it, so scale drift across merges is not a bug to be tuned away; it is unrepresentable in the chosen state space.

Restoring the missing degree of freedom does not rescue the result, and we tried: lifting each merge to Sim(3), which does carry a scale term. Such a merge must estimate one similarity (s,R,t) per sequence boundary from the inter-sequence constraints alone, and with few, wide-baseline shared observations that estimate starts far from its optimum. Compounding this, the GPS-derived constraints conflict: each pulls the boundary toward a different, meter-scale, anisotropically noisy anchor, so the solve settles at a compromise satisfying none of them, metrically plausible but still blurring the seam. The missing scale degree of freedom is therefore necessary but not sufficient.

Under a sequential merge this conflict is structural rather than an artifact of noise levels, and seeing why shows exactly where Sim(3) alone relocates the problem instead of removing it. Scaling an entire sequence together with all of its pose constraints does keep that sequence internally consistent, so once we scale sequence 2 to agree with sequence 1 the pair (1,2) is mutually consistent, and every inter-sequence constraint incident on 2 is scaled to match. An astute reader might expect this rescaling to be absorbed automatically as the next sequence is merged. It is not. When a third sequence is merged against the first two, the inter-pose constraints 3 → 1 and 3 → 2 both carry the raw GPS scale, because that is how sequence 3 was reconstructed. But sequence 2 has already been rescaled to match 1, so 3 → 1 is roughly consistent up to ordinary scale drift while 3 → 2 disagrees by exactly the correction we applied to 2. The optimizer is handed two contradictory statements about the same scale, and no single scalar satisfies both. The similarity that resolved (1,2) thus reappears as a fresh conflict at 3: Sim(3) shifts the scale mismatch along the merge order rather than removing it.

Multi-way synchronization was not attempted.

The contradiction above arises only because the merges happen one after another: each merge aligns the incoming chunk to the partial map so far, so by chunk 3, chunk 2 has already been corrected by its merge with 1 while chunk 3 still carries raw GPS scale. That mismatch, not Sim(3) itself, is what no single scalar can satisfy.

The alternative is to estimate all K chunk similarities at once from the full graph of inter-chunk constraints, so no chunk is corrected before the others are accounted for. We did not try it. Such multi-way Sim(3) synchronization, in the spirit of motion and rotation averaging [10, 12] and similarity synchronization [3], spreads inconsistent pairwise scales in a least-squares sense over all chunks.

The scale component in particular is a linear problem, which is what makes this attractive. Give chunk k an unknown log-scale σₖ=\logsₖ; each cross-chunk constraint between i and j measures a ratio sᵢⱼ and so contributes one equation σⱼ-σᵢ=\logsᵢⱼ. Over the populated entries of the K×K table these stack into an overdetermined linear system in K unknowns whose normal equations are a weighted graph Laplacian, determined up to a single global gauge that GPS, or fixing one chunk, supplies. Rotations follow by rotation averaging and translations are linear once scales and rotations are known, the standard Sim(3) synchronization recipe [3]. Crucially, every chunk’s scale is then set by all of its constraints simultaneously, so a disagreement between 3 → 1 and 3 → 2 is distributed as residual rather than resolved in favour of whichever merge happened first. With K in the tens the solve is negligible beside the matching front end, so it costs nothing the speed argument cares about. We expect this to reduce the seam error materially and regard it as the most promising untried repair, though it redistributes inconsistency rather than supplying the absolute scale the capture lacks.

5.3 Sequence-by-sequence ordering leaves sub-maps ill-conditioned before they merge

This cause and the two that follow are implementation choices, each of which could have been made differently and none of which we ablated. They are worth recording because the divide-and-merge decomposition that makes a pose-only design attractive to parallelize is exactly what makes them tempting.

The pipeline orders images by capture sequence, solves each sequence independently, and only then merges, and the ordering itself is a failure mode, for two compounding reasons. First, some sequences are geometrically degenerate in isolation: a nadir ascent, where the drone rises vertically over a fixed point, supplies almost no translational parallax, so the sub-map is fundamentally unconstrained up to the missing baseline. Solved alone, it has no way to recover the structure a neighbouring oblique sequence would have supplied. Second, to absorb the meter-scale GPS noise each sequence settles into its own local optimum that best trades its observations against its noisy anchors. Because every sub-map made that trade independently, the local optima disagree; when the sequences merge, the cross-sequence constraints are in large mutual conflict, far outside the basin the merge can reconcile, and the global solve settles at a sub-optimal compromise.

The lesson is about ordering, not merging: an image ordering that proceeds strictly sequence-by-sequence guarantees these isolated, separately-converged pieces, and no merge strategy applied afterwards can undo a sub-map that has already converged to the wrong basin. An ideal ordering would never take one sequence to convergence in isolation. Interleaving images across sequences from the start, so that cross-sequence constraints shape each pose before it commits to a local optimum, keeps the whole capture in a single jointly constrained basin rather than assembling it from pre-settled, mutually inconsistent parts, and it costs nothing in parallelism: the chunking that makes the front end shardable is independent of the order in which poses are allowed to influence one another. We did not build that ordering, so we cannot say how much of the merge conflict it would remove; it is the ablation we would run first.

5.4 Removing shared structure removes multi-view consistency

The premise was that pose-only optimization could reach BA-grade quality. But the thing that makes BA’s poses globally consistent is precisely the structure the method discards: a 3D point observed in many frames forces those frames to agree, and BA averages their independent measurement errors into one consistent estimate. A pose graph of pairwise relative transforms has no such shared latent variable; it is only as good as its edges, and edge errors accumulate rather than cancel. Two facts in the system confirm that this coupling could not simply be dropped. First, the pipeline still runs a per-chunk COLMAP bundle adjustment, and the 3D–2D PnP constraints that stitch chunks are derived from the points that BA produced, so structure was reintroduced through the back door. This cuts two ways, and we state both. It is the clearest evidence that the coupling is load-bearing: the design reached for structure exactly where pose-only constraints proved too weak to stitch sub-maps, and no version of the pipeline ran without it. But it also means we never put the pure-pose premise fully on trial, and our negative result is correspondingly bounded. What we have shown to fail is pose-only estimation at the global scale, with BA still supporting each chunk from below; a formulation that removed BA entirely would inherit every weakness catalogued here and lose that support besides, so we expect it to fare worse, but we did not measure it. Second, the one path that tried to use structure-to-structure information directly, the 3D–3D point-cloud alignment edge, was abandoned as unstable. That instability is no accident: projectively triangulated points carry an uncertainty that grows with observation distance and shrinks with disparity, so a point seen from 50 m away is localized far more loosely than one seen from a few meters. A point-cloud alignment that treats every point as equally certain then forces such a loosely-triangulated far point, from one sequence, to line up precisely with a tightly-triangulated near point of the same structure from another; without propagating those per-point uncertainties into the cost, the solve trades a well-localized constraint against a badly-localized one and settles at a poorly-converged compromise. The method’s own choices show that without shared structure the estimate is not consistent enough, and with it the “BA-free” claim no longer holds.

5.5 Consumer GPS is a noisy ruler, not an anchor

GPS plays an outsized role: it is the only metric signal, used to scale each pairwise translation and to select neighbors, yet it enters only as a relative ruler on translations, never as a soft absolute position prior on the nodes. So nothing pins global scale or arrests drift; each chunk’s scale floats independently, exactly the freedom Sec.5.2 cannot later remove.

Worse, the ruler itself is imprecise. These drones carry consumer-grade GNSS (GPS). With an RTK fix the receiver is accurate to a few centimeters, but the captures rarely hold an RTK lock, and without it horizontal position is off by 0.5–1.0 m. That error does not stay contained: fed in as the scale of every essential-matrix translation, it is large relative to the inter-frame baselines it scales, injecting meter-scale noise into precisely the SE(3) translations the merge already cannot correct. Altitude is worse still: on several of these drones the vertical channel comes from a barometric altimeter, so the relative-Z component carries far more uncertainty than the horizontal ones. Feeding a strongly anisotropic, meter-scale, sometimes-biased position signal into an optimizer that treats it as a metric constraint makes the pose graph ill-posed, though not uniformly. The circular orbit sequences are largely safe: their wide, multi-directional baselines triangulate structure, and vertical scale with it, from the imagery. The damage concentrates on the nadir sequences, the near-straight vertical ascents flown looking straight down, where the geometry is degenerate: straight-line motion gives no cross-baseline, and the nadir view aligns the poorly-triangulated depth axis with the vertical, so “the camera climbed” and “the scene grew” are nearly indistinguishable. Vertical scale is then only weakly constrained: the nadir edges resist it little, and the one term that penalizes a wrong vertical scale, the barometric-Z prior, is too noisy to push back. With so little curvature there, Eq.3 is nearly flat, so the estimate can drift far at almost no cost. This is a direct source of the large outliers and outright failure we observed (Tab.2). A pose-only formulation has no shared structure to fall back on when its metric signal is this noisy; bundle adjustment derives scale from the imagery itself and needs GPS only as a weak gauge, so the same fix does it little harm.

5.6 Trust is hand-set, not propagated

Compounding the noise, every constraint’s influence is a hand-chosen information matrix (rotation over translation, PnP 7× essential, refined edges 10×) rather than a value propagated from the data’s uncertainty. Without a data-driven model, a triangulation-noisy or badly-GPS-scaled match cannot be down-weighted against a clean one, the mechanical reason the 3D–3D constraint was unusable and the reason the same fixed weights that worked on the tuning scenes produced large outliers and an outright failure (HAV) on a capture whose noise profile differed. Stability resting on manually balanced trust, over a signal as heteroscedastic as consumer GPS, does not transfer. This is the most fixable of the four causes and the one that most confounds our results: with no learned-weight configuration run, we cannot separate error from the formulation from error from weighting it badly.

6 Lessons

The causes above translate into concrete guidance for anyone drawn to the same shortcut, replacing structure-aware optimization with a cheaper pose-only surrogate on structured captures.

  • 1.

    Two independent speedups, and the front end is the bigger one. Dropping the points for a structure-less, pose-only optimization is genuinely faster than a full bundle adjustment: it removes the most expensive part of the solve, and that saving is real and worth taking. The larger opportunity, though, is the matching front end that dominates absolute cost. It is embarrassingly parallel and shards cleanly across workers, and the levers that matter there are mundane, the retrieval budget per frame, pruning pairs before verification, and GPU-parallel extraction and matching. Both are worth accelerating, but the front end’s gains are far easier to capture, because they come from trivial parallelism rather than from reformulating the estimator, and reformulating the estimator is what costs accuracy.

  • 2.

    If you drop the points, add scale back explicitly. BA’s hidden gift is that shared structure couples the scales of overlapping views. A pose-only formulation must recover that coupling elsewhere, through Sim(3) edges and a Sim(3) merge estimated jointly over all sub-maps rather than pairwise (Sec.5.2). SE(3) pose graphs across independently-scaled sub-maps are a scale trap.

  • 3.

    Use GPS as an absolute prior, not merely a ruler, but model its noise. A soft absolute position constraint on every node pins global scale and arrests drift. It helps only if weighted by its true, anisotropic uncertainty, looser in barometric Z than in the horizontal plane and looser still without an RTK lock, otherwise the meter-scale error re-enters as bias.

  • 4.

    Keep a little structure. A pose graph with zero shared 3D points is on the wrong side of a cliff. Retaining even a small point set, a few times the camera count rather than the hundreds-of-times BA carries, restores multi-view consistency while keeping the problem small, the structured-but-lean middle, not pure PGO, the cost argument should have pointed to.

  • 5.

    Propagate uncertainty; do not hand-tune it. Data-driven information matrices are what make structure-to-structure constraints usable. Fixed trust ratios are a liability that grows with capture diversity.

    • 7 Conclusion

    We asked whether, in the dense loop-closure regime splatting captures uniquely provide, pose-graph optimization could displace bundle adjustment as the estimation objective. For the system we built the answer is no, twice over: it did not match COLMAP’s accuracy, and it did not even dispense with BA to get there, keeping a per-chunk pass whose triangulated points its own cross-chunk constraints are built on.

    The causes divide, and the division is the point. Some are ours to own: a consumer-GPS anchor too noisy and too anisotropic to hold scale, greedy pairwise merging, sequence-by-sequence ordering, and hand-set information matrices. Each is a repairable engineering decision we did not ablate, and a careful reimplementation should beat our numbers. Two causes are not repairable that way. The SE(3) state space cannot represent the scale differences its own GPS-scaled sub-maps introduce, whatever weights the edges carry; and a graph of two-view edges cannot reconstitute the many-view coupling that gives bundle adjustment its consistency. These are properties of the formulation, not settings within it, and they are what a future design has to answer for: Sim(3) constraints estimated jointly rather than pairwise, absolute uncertainty-aware GPS priors, and a thin layer of retained structure. How much of the measured gap those limits account for would take the ablations we did not run; we hope the account still saves the next team the same detour.

    When the approach might be worth revisiting.

    Several failures trace to the noisy metric anchor, not the formulation. Under an RTK fix, position is accurate to a few centimetres in all of (x,y,z), enough to pin scale across merges and stop inter-sequence constraints conflicting at the meter scale. A lightweight distributed pose graph, with a few sparse retained points supplying the coupling pure SE(3)/Sim(3) edges cannot, would then deserve a fresh attempt: the negative result is a scoping one, pose-only, GPS-scaled estimation is the wrong tool for consumer-grade capture.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 致密化别只数「能看到几次」：被完全遮挡的高斯也在计数，正好把阴影里的细节饿死 ｜ Counting Contributions, Not Views: Occlusion-Aware Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting
item.description:
一句话：现有可见性过滤只看高斯是否会出现在视图里，全遮挡也算被观测，稀释平均梯度；改成按真实贡献统计后高斯数少一半。

要点：

  • 问题定位：自适应密度控制（ADC）的统计来自渲染期，视锥可见性过滤只判断「这个高斯是否可能出现在视图里」，完全被遮挡的高斯照样计入观测，稀释平均梯度并在遮挡区域抑制致密化
  • 修法两条：遮挡感知过滤，只统计高斯真正有贡献的视图；把判据里原始的视图计数归一化换成平均贡献归一化
  • 接进 StopThePop 框架：遮挡密集的场景所有画质指标都提升（LPIPS 最多降 6%），高斯数不到视图计数法的一半；长训练计划下数量保持有界，而多数判据会发散

为什么值得看：这类「统计口径错了」的 bug 在自研重建管线上极难靠肉眼看出来。如果你们的 3DGS 在大场景的遮挡区域总是缺细节，先查致密化统计的可见性判据。

中文摘要：3DGS 通过自适应密度控制从稀疏初始化长出稠密场景，而所有致密化决策都依赖渲染期收集的逐高斯统计。本文指出一个根本缺陷：收集统计时用的视锥可见性过滤只检验高斯是否可能出现在某个视图里，而不检验它是否真的对像素有贡献，于是完全被遮挡的高斯依然被算作被观测到，稀释了平均梯度信号，并且恰好在几何被遮挡的地方抑制致密化。作者的修法是加一层遮挡感知过滤，把统计限制在高斯真正有贡献的视图上，同时把判据里原始的视图计数归一化换成平均贡献归一化。两者接进 StopThePop 框架后，在遮挡密集的场景上所有图像质量指标都优于遮挡盲的基线（LPIPS 最多降低 6%），而所需高斯数不到视图计数法的一半。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-19

本期推送：2026-10-24

Counting Contributions, Not Views:
Occlusion-Aware Densification
for 3D Gaussian Splatting

Abstract

3D Gaussian Splatting grows a dense scene from a sparse initialization through adaptive density control (ADC), driven by per-Gaussian statistics gathered during rendering. These statistics pass a frustum-based visibility filter blind to occlusion: fully occluded Gaussians still count as observed, diluting the averaged gradient signal and suppressing densification precisely where geometry is occluded. We correct this with an occlusion-aware filter that restricts densification statistics to views in which a Gaussian actually contributes, and replace the criterion’s raw view-count normalizer with an average-contribution one. Integrated into a StopThePop-based framework, the two together improve every image-quality metric over the occlusion-blind baseline on occlusion-heavy scenes (up to 6% lower LPIPS), at less than half the Gaussians a view-count normalizer requires. Under the longer schedules these large scenes require, the count stays bounded where most criteria diverge, and on smaller benchmarks our method stays competitive at a fraction of the competitors’ count.

Keywords:

Gaussian Splatting Adaptive Density Control Densification 3D Reconstruction Large-Scale Scenes Novel View Synthesis

1 Introduction

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [13] represents a milestone in 3D scene reconstruction and novel-view synthesis. It introduced a large multi-component system, with a tile-based rasterizer and adaptive density control (ADC) purpose-built for the new representation. Follow-up works improve these components largely in isolation, many focusing on ADC, which is essential for growing a dense reconstruction from the sparse initialization. However, we find that the accumulation of the densification statistics at the root of all ADC decisions has a fundamental flaw: the frustum-based visibility filter that gathers them tests only whether a Gaussian could appear in a view, not whether it actually contributes to the rendered image. A fully occluded Gaussian yields zero gradients, yet the filter still counts its view in the criterion’s denominator, dragging the average down and stalling densification wherever geometry is occluded. The resulting under-densification grows with the degree of occlusion and degrades quality most where high detail and occlusion co-occur. Large, occlusion-heavy scenes such as multi-room apartments are affected most severely (Counting Contributions, Not Views:
Occlusion-Aware Densification
for 3D Gaussian Splatting). We correct this with an occlusion-aware visibility filter that updates a Gaussian’s statistics only from views in which it is actually rendered; densification then reaches occluded regions whenever their level of detail requires it.

We further find that normalizing the accumulated gradient by a raw view count does not match the contribution-weighted nature of the tracked gradients. We derive a more natural normalizer that accumulates a Gaussian’s average contribution to each rendered view. To validate our occlusion-aware densification, we build a framework around StopThePop [20] that consolidates established densification improvements from separate prior methods into a strong baseline. We evaluate both changes on this baseline and directly on StopThePop. On the occlusion-heavy Zip-NeRF [2] scenes, the resulting method outperforms StopThePop on all image-quality metrics, reducing LPIPS by up to 12%. Its Gaussian count also stays bounded under the longer schedules these large scenes require, where most competing criteria diverge. On smaller benchmarks, it performs comparably to the state of the art with up to 63% fewer Gaussians. Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to replace the visibility filter itself: the frustum-based test that underlies all densification statistics. Our occlusion-aware filter updates a Gaussian’s statistics only from views in which it is actually rendered, independent of the criterion built on top.

  • •

    We introduce a contribution-based densification criterion that is more closely related to the gradient signal used by ADC, leading to better densification decisions, demonstrated on small- and large-scale scenes.

  • •

    We combine both contributions with established densification improvements and other refinements into a strong framework that does not require per-scene tuning and has fewer hyperparameters (e.g. eliminating the unstable scene extent). We will make the code available to the research community.

    • 2 Background and Related Work

    2.1 Adaptive Density Control

    3D Gaussian Splatting [13] represents a scene as a set of 3D Gaussians, each defined by a 3D mean position, a 3D covariance matrix (parameterized by a rotation and per-axis scale), an opacity o, and a view-dependent color c derived from spherical harmonics [7]. For rendering, each Gaussian is projected onto the image as a 2D footprint with a screen-space mean and radius. Starting from a sparse point cloud, 3DGS grows and prunes its set of Gaussians via adaptive density control (ADC), executed every 100 iterations after a 500-iteration warm-up and disabled after the first half of training. A scene extent E, computed from the training cameras, provides the reference scale for several ADC decisions.

    Criterion.

    During rendering, a frustum-based visibility filter accumulates per-Gaussian statistics: the 2D screen-space positional gradient g_i,v of Gaussian i in view v, the screen-space radius, and a view count M. At each ADC event, a Gaussian is marked for densification if its accumulated gradient magnitude, averaged over the view count, exceeds a predefined threshold (0.0002 by default).

    Densification.

    To resolve the problem of an insufficient number of Gaussians capturing a region’s textural or structural detail (from here on described as under-densification), a marked Gaussian is densified in one of two modes: if it is large relative to the scene extent, it is split into two downscaled children sampled from the parent’s distribution, otherwise it is cloned, i.e. duplicated, in place.

    Pruning.

    Redundant or noisy Gaussians are removed using pruning mechanisms. An opacity prune removes every Gaussian whose opacity oᵢ falls below a predefined threshold (0.005). A size-based prune removes Gaussians whose screen-space radius or world-space scale exceeds a fixed threshold. To clear floater artifacts, 3DGS additionally resets all opacities to near zero (0.01) every 3000 iterations; important Gaussians recover quickly, floaters stay dim and fall to the opacity prune. StopThePop [20] offers a gradual opacity decay as an alternative to the drastic reset. We evaluate both as the (Reset) and (Decay) variants.

    2.2 Adaptive Density Control Improvements

    All of the following ADC improvements inherit the frustum-based visibility filter described above, which counts every in-frustum Gaussian, occluded or not. We make this filter occlusion-aware (Sec.3.1).

    Densification Criterion.

    AbsGS [28] and GOF [29] counter gradient cancellation in the accumulation, which otherwise causes under-densification of high-detail regions. PixelGS [31] instead questions the normalization by the observation count and proposes a pixel-count-weighted mean. Grubert et al.[9] adopt the PixelGS strategy with an ascending threshold that shifts densification earlier. Taming3DGS [18] replaces the threshold with a per-Gaussian multi-term score under a fixed densification budget. However, budget-controlled methods require a target count as input, a value that is not known and that a good densification criterion should find. We propose to normalize a Gaussian’s accumulated gradient by the accumulated average contributions of its rendered views (Sec.3.2), rather than the observation count of 3DGS or the visible-pixel count of PixelGS. We also adopt GOF’s absolute-gradient signal against cancellation.

    Densification Step (Split & Clone).

    GOF observes that clones remain clustered and instead samples the child’s position from the parent’s distribution, while Bulò et al.[22] show that the clone operation introduces an opacity bias. EFA-GS [23] and Deng et al.[4] drop the clone entirely, and Deng et al. additionally propose a geometrically more meaningful split procedure. Grubert et al. address inconsistencies in the scene-extent computation that governs some ADC decisions by also accounting for the input point cloud. Other works replace the densification step more radically [15, 3, 6, 24]. Our experiments also support dropping the clone: we notice large floater clusters due to excessive cloning on scenes where the scene extent is not well matched to the size of detail (Tab.4). We therefore follow the split-only approach of EFA-GS and Deng et al., including the latter’s split procedure. This removes one dependence on the scene extent.

    Pruning.

    Grubert et al. restrict the opacity prune to Gaussians that also contribute little; EAGLES [8] and OC2DGS [21] prune low- or non-contributing Gaussians at intervals long enough to observe every training view; ReLaGS [26] and RadSplat [19] prune by maximum contribution over a full pass, at isolated points of the optimization.
