Due to densification no longer getting suppressed, these floater clusters are amplified. Our criterion reduces the number of floaters and recovers most of the lost quality, while the 3DGS port does not show this degradation as it does not form the floaters into solid clusters.

item.title: 随手拍一圈，车门、引擎盖、后备箱可以随便开合：SwitchSplat 学的是「离散状态」 ｜ SwitchSplat: Learning Discrete Object States from Casually Captured Scenes
item.description:
一句话：静态底图加可独立开关的 slot，每个可交互物体两个二值状态，推理时能渲染训练中从未出现过的状态组合。

要点：

  • base + slot 分解：共享静态底图承载不变场景，每个可交互物体一个 slot，各自持有开/关两个状态
  • 高斯到 slot 的归属完全可微，模型能直接从视频里学出每个状态的几何，不需要人工标注
  • 推理时可自由组合各 slot 状态并从任意新视角渲染；对比之下，4DGS 这类时间条件方法把「什么时候被观测到」和「场景处于什么状态」混为一谈，只能回放见过的序列

为什么值得看：随手拍的重建要变成可用资产，缺的正是「可交互状态」。这种把状态离散化、可组合的表示，比时序动态表示更接近引擎里对可交互物体的建模方式。

中文摘要：3DGS 让高保真重建变得又快又易得，但现有表示都假定世界是静态的。随手拍摄时人自然会与环境交互——开门、拨开关、挪动物体——这些离散状态变化目前没有框架能建模。时间条件的动态方法（如 4DGS）把「何时观测到」与「场景处于哪个状态」混在一起，只能重放见过的序列。SwitchSplat 用 base + slot 分解解决这个问题：一个共享静态底图捕捉不变的场景，每个可交互物体单独占一个 slot，各自持有两个二值状态（开/关）。由于高斯到 slot 的归属完全可微，模型能从视频中直接发现每个状态的几何而无需标注。推理时用户可以自由组合 slot 状态并从任意视角渲染，包括训练中从未见过的组合。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-17

本期推送：2026-10-24

SwitchSplat: Learning Discrete Object States from Casually Captured Scenes

© cc

Abstract.

3D Gaussian Splatting has made high-fidelity 3D reconstruction fast and accessible, yet existing representations assume a static world. This assumption breaks down in casual captures, where a user naturally interacts with the environment – opening doors, toggling switches, or moving objects – introducing discrete state changes that no current framework can model. Time-conditioned dynamic methods such as 4DGS conflate when a state was observed with what state the scene is in, limiting them to replaying seen sequences rather than composing arbitrary object configurations. We present SwitchSplat, the first 3DGS representation to address this gap via a base+slot decomposition: a shared static base captures the invariant scene, while each slot independently holds the two binary states (on/off) of one interactable object. Because the assignment of Gaussians to slots is fully differentiable, the model discovers the geometry of each state directly from video, without manual annotation. At inference, the user can freely combine slot states and render the resulting scene from any viewpoint. We validate SwitchSplat on a new casual-capture dataset and show that it outperforms static and dynamic baselines in novel-view synthesis quality, while uniquely supporting rendering of state combinations never seen during capture. Project page: https://switchsplat.github.io.

Keywords:

Novel View Synthesis, Gaussian Splatting, State-aware Rendering, 360^∘ Capture ††cc-license: by

1. Introduction

In inverse rendering, Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [(Kerbl et al., 2023)] has emerged as the leading representation for real-time, high-fidelity novel-view synthesis, enabling a new generation of interactive applications. Its combination of fast training and efficient rendering has driven broad adoption across academia as well as industry, from Matterport’s digital twins and Niantic Scaniverse’s mobile reconstruction to Meta’s Hyperscape111https://www.meta.com/experiences/meta-horizon-hyperscape-capture-beta/8798130056953686/.

While early 3DGS pipelines required meticulous data acquisition (fixed exposure and white balance, controlled lighting, and a perfectly static scene), recent works like 3DGRT [(Moenne-Loccoz et al., 2024)] and FullCircle [(Foroutan et al., 2026)] have unlocked casual capture: viewpoints need not be carefully curated – made possible by 360^∘ cameras held in a single hand – and the capturer’s pixels are automatically masked out to satisfy the static-scene assumption. This freedom naturally invites users to interact with the environment during capture – opening doors, toggling switches, or repositioning objects – turning the operator into both an active agent and a dynamic distractor within the scene.

Yet no existing reconstruction framework is equipped to handle these interactions. Many contemporary 3D representations enforce a strict static-world assumption: when an operator triggers a discrete state change – opening a door, flipping a switch, relocating an object – the model has no mechanism to account for the resulting geometric variation. As a result, even state-of-the-art pipelines can only represent a single, frozen scene configuration, and capturing multiple stable states requires re-recording the scene from scratch.

One could argue that the natural candidate to address this limitation is the family of 4D Gaussian Splatting methods [(Yang et al., 2024b)], which extend 3DGS to dynamic scenes by conditioning the scene representation on time. However, this design choice fundamentally conflates when a state was observed with what state the scene is in: the model learns to replay a specific sequence of observations, not to understand independent object configurations.

As a result, 4D methods are largely limited to novel-viewpoint synthesis of seen sequences; composing an unseen combination of object states—e.g., door open and light on—is not directly supported, since no single timestamp in the training data corresponds to that configuration. What is needed instead is a representation that de-correlates scene state from time, allowing the user to freely specify both the viewpoint and the desired configuration of each object independently.

To address these challenges, we propose SwitchSplat, a method that learns “state-aware” representations from casual captures featuring human-object interactions; see Figure1. SwitchSplat organizes the scene into a static base – the parts that never change throughout the capture – and a set of slots, one per interactable object. Each slot holds two 3D representations corresponding to the binary states of that object (“on” and “off”). For example, if a room was captured while a closet door was closed for part of the recording and open for another, a single slot would hold both the “off” state (door closed, interior hidden) and the “on” state (door open, interior visible), while the walls, floor, and furniture – unchanged throughout – are handled by the static base. To assign each Gaussian primitive to the right part of the scene, we attach a small learnable score vector that controls how strongly the primitive belongs to the base, or to either state of each slot.

This decomposition avoids data redundancy: without a shared static base, one would need to duplicate the full scene geometry for every slot, with no reusable structure across states. Instead, SwitchSplat shares the base across all configurations and only stores the geometry that actually differs per state.222 This is structurally analogous to PCA-based morphable models [(Blanz and Vetter, 2023)]: the static base plays the role of the mean face, each slot’s on/off representations correspond to the eigenvectors, and the state activations act as the blend-shape coefficients. Because the full pipeline is differentiable end-to-end, the model learns simultaneously which Gaussians belong to which slot and when each slot is active – directly from the input video, without any manual annotation. At inference, the user can query any combination of slot states independently – e.g., closet door open and desk lamp on – and render the resulting scene from any viewpoint.

To summarize our contributions: (1) We identify a novel problem in the 3DGS literature: existing representations cannot model scenes with discrete, user-triggered state changes (e.g., objects that can be opened, switched, or moved), and we show that naïvely applying dynamic methods such as 4DGS fails to address this. (2) We propose SwitchSplat, the first 3DGS representation to address this problem via a base+slot decomposition, where a shared static base captures the invariant scene and each slot independently models the binary states of one interactable object. (3) We demonstrate on a new casual-capture dataset that SwitchSplat improves novel-view synthesis quality over static and dynamic baselines, and uniquely supports rendering arbitrary combinations of object states from unseen viewpoints.

2. Related Work

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [(Kerbl et al., 2023)] has become the dominant representation for novel-view synthesis, optimizing a set of anisotropic Gaussian primitives that render at real-time rates. Extensions beyond the standard perspective-camera model are particularly relevant to our setting: 3DGRT [(Moenne-Loccoz et al., 2024)] reformulates rendering via ray tracing, and 3DGUT [(Wu et al., 2025a)] adds support for highly distorted cameras and secondary rays, enabling casual capture with wide field-of-view sensors. FullCircle [(Foroutan et al., 2026)] further shows that raw dual-fisheye 360^∘ video suffices for high-quality reconstruction, automatically masking the camera operator. Despite these advances, all of these pipelines represent the scene as a single, fixed configuration. When multiple object states are present in the capture—a door open in some frames and closed in others—the model either conflates them into averaged geometry and ghosting artifacts, or learns to discard the minority state as a distractor [(Sabour et al., 2025)]. Either way, only one configuration survives in the final model; there is no mechanism to retain, switch between, or compose multiple stable states at inference time.

Dynamic Gaussian Splatting

A large family of methods extends 3DGS to dynamic scenes by conditioning the representation on time. Dynamic 3D Gaussians [(Luiten et al., 2024)] tracks persistent primitives across frames, while Deformable 3D Gaussians [(Yang et al., 2024a)] and 4DGS [(Wu et al., 2024)] deform a canonical scene over time, with 4DGS using a learned space-time encoding. Spacetime Gaussians [(Li et al., 2024a)] further augments primitives with temporal opacity and parametric motion. Subsequent work improves efficiency, temporal consistency, or geometric accuracy via depth priors [(Yang et al., 2024b; Sun et al., 2024; Duan et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2025b)]. Differently from our method, all of these methods are parameterized by time, not by object state: recovering a specific scene configuration requires locating the right moment in the recording, and rendering a novel combination of states—e.g., two objects in configurations never co-observed—is not supported.

Decomposed Gaussian Splatting

More recent dynamic Gaussian methods, such as SDD-4DGS [(Sun et al., 2025)], observe that applying deformation models to the entire scene is often inefficient, since most real-world scenes are largely static. This motivates methods that decompose scenes into static and dynamic components: GauFRe [(Liang et al., 2025)] combines a static Gaussian component with deformable dynamic Gaussians, while Swift4D [(Wu et al., 2025b)] improves efficiency by passing only dynamic Gaussians through the deformation model. DeGauss [(Wang et al., 2025a)] further uses dynamic-static decomposition to improve robustness to transient distractors. This observation is closely aligned with our setting, since object interactions usually affect only a small part of a 360^∘ environment. In contrast to our method, existing decomposition methods still treat the dynamic component as a temporally varying foreground: they separate dynamic regions from a static background, but provide no mechanism to independently switch or compose object states at inference time.

Controllable Scene Representation

A parallel line of work studies controllable and articulated 3D representations. Pre-Gaussian methods such as Watch It Move [(Noguchi et al., 2022)] discover articulated structure from object motion; PARIS [(Liu et al., 2023)] goes further by decoupling static and movable parts from two multi-view captures of the same scene. Gaussian-based approaches extend this to photorealistic settings: SC-GS [(Huang et al., 2024)] enables motion editing via sparse control points, Template-free Articulated Gaussian Splatting [(Wan et al., 2024)] supports re-posing with super-points, and RigGS [(Yao et al., 2025)] adds rig-based editing and interpolation. ArtGS [(Liu et al., 2025a)] and ArticulatedGS [(Guo et al., 2025)] further focus on part-level modeling of individual objects. Crucially, all of these methods aim to encode object motion or articulation—they model how parts move, rather than discarding motion entirely to focus on the discrete stable configurations of the scene. In contrast, our method treats object interactions as a nuisance to be factored out, retaining only the clean on/off states and ignoring the transient motion between them.

State-aware Scene Reconstruction

Closest to our setting are methods that reconstruct scenes across discrete object states. IGFuse [(Hu et al., 2026)] and RecurGS [(Hu et al., 2025)] address this by using semantic cues to detect state changes and aligning them via rigid transformations. GaussianCut [(Jain et al., 2024)] and DecoupledGaussian [(Wang et al., 2025b)] contribute related tools for object segmentation and scene decomposition. However, all of these methods assume that state changes can be described as rigid motions of segmented object entities—an assumption that breaks down for casual capture, where interaction boundaries are fuzzy and deformations are non-rigid. In contrast, SwitchSplat learns which Gaussians belong to each state directly from photometric supervision, without requiring object masks, or rigid-body assumptions.

3. Method

SwitchSplat learns a state-aware 3D representation from casual captures by decomposing the scene into controllable, state-conditioned components. In the following subsections, we detail our methodology by first formulating our state-conditioned Gaussian primitives and describing their integration within volume rendering (Sec.3.1). We then introduce the parameterization of the differentiable slot-table (Sec.3.2), followed by our slot initialization procedure (Sec.3.3). Finally, we describe our training pipeline and objectives that facilitate granular, state-controlled visualization during inference (Secs.3.4 and 3.5).

Terminology

A slot corresponds to one interactable object and holds two 3D representations for its binary states: “off” (e.g., door closed) and “on” (e.g., door open). A slot activation is a per-frame binary variable indicating which state is currently observed. All parts of the scene that remain constant throughout the capture are handled by the static base, which is shared across all configurations.

3.1. State-aware Gaussian Splat

Each 3D Gaussian primitive in our model is defined by its standard geometric and appearance attributes: mean μ, covariance Σ, opacity α, and view-dependent appearance c. To make our representation state-aware, we augment every Gaussian with a learnable categorical state distribution p=softmax(ℓ) over 1+2K channels, where K is the total number of object slots. These channels comprise a single static base channel ℓ[0], together with a pair of off (ℓ[2k-1]) and on (ℓ[2k]) channels for each slot k∈{1,…,K}. The two channels per slot — rather than one — let the softmax assign each Gaussian to a single configuration, so that disjoint subsets of primitives can independently model the geometry and appearance of an object in each of its two states (see Figure3). This separation is essential because the on/off configurations of an object generally differ not just in appearance, but also in spatial extent — a closed door and an open door, for instance, occupy different parts of the scene — which a single shared primitive simply cannot represent.

Test-time rendering

Assume we have trained our representation, and that we want to render an image corresponding to the slot configuration p̃∈{0,1}^K. This is achieved by computing the probability of each gaussian being present in the scene to be rendered:

(1)

ω(p̃)=p[0]+∑ₖ₌₁^K(p̃[k]·p[2k]+(1-p̃[k])·p[2k-1])

This formulation ensures that “base” Gaussians remain present across all frames, while the presence of the on/off state Gaussians is gated by the probability of the corresponding slot being on. We then gate the opacity of the gaussian by this probability:

(2)

α̃=α·ω(p̃),

which is then used to compute the final RGB color for a ray r via classical volume rendering [(Tagliasacchi and Mildenhall, 2022)]:

Î(r)=∑_i∈H(r)Tᵢ(r)·α̃ᵢ·cᵢ(r), Tᵢ(r)=∏_j

where H(r) represents the set of Gaussians intersected by the ray in depth order and cᵢ(r) denotes the view-dependent color. While p̃ will be selected by the user at test-time, the key question in training our representation lies in how to propagate the gradients from image Îₜ at time t to the (per-Gaussian) state distribution p.

3.2. Differentiable slot table

To achieve this, we exploit the key assumption that, within the video, the activation state of a slot is compactly supported in time. Let us denotes with the per-slot scalar πₖ(t)∈[0,1] the probability of slot k being in its on state at time t. Then, ∀k≠0 we have that πₖ(t) is zero everywhere outside some bounded, closed region. Without loss of generality, let us drop the indexing k, and focus on a single entry π(t). We can satisfy our compact support assumption by explicitly parameterizing π(t) as a smooth window function defined by its temporal endpoints (tₗ,tᵣ)333 To ensure tₗ≤tᵣ in practice we optimize auxiliary free variables u and v, and then remap them to tₗ=\min(u,v) and tᵣ=\max(u,v)., and a temperature parameter rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5) that controls the smoothness of transition; see Figure4.

By defining the midpoint as tₘ=(tₗ+tᵣ)/2, and σ_rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)(t)=σ(t/rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)), the probability of an interaction occurring at time t is computed via the normalized product of two sigmoid functions σ:

(3)π(t)=(σ_rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)(t-tₗ)·σ_rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)(tᵣ-t))/(σ_rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)(tₘ-tₗ)·σ_rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)(tᵣ-tₘ))

Therefore, to model the time window of each object interaction, we treat the state of the k-th slot at time t as a Bernoulli random variable S_k,t∈{0,1}, where S_k,t=1 denotes the slot being in its on state and S_k,t=0 its off state, whose probability mass function (PMF) for a specific state s∈{0,1} is given by:

(4)P(S_k,t=s)=πₖ(t)ˢ(1-πₖ(t))¹⁻ˢ

Train-time rendering

The quantity πₖ(t) defined above is our slot table, which we use to compute the probability of each Gaussian being present in the scene at time t:

(5)ω(t)=p[0]+∑ₖ₌₁^K(πₖ(t)·p[2k]+(1-πₖ(t))·p[2k-1])

from which, like before, we can compute a time-dependent effective opacity for volume rendering the predicted image Îₜ:

(6)α̃(t)=α·ω(t)

This differentiable rendering framework ensures that gradients propagate seamlessly to the slot activation probabilities, Gaussian state memberships, and geometric parameters, enabling stable and efficient joint optimization of the entire scene representation.

3.3. Initialization

In a casual capture setting, neither the total number of slots K, nor the precise slot transition timestamps are known a priori. Requiring the user to annotate them would defeat the very premise of a “casual” capture. To address this, we leverage the reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and in particular GPT 5.6, to provide an approximate initialization for the slot-table. By prompting GPT 5.6 with a sequence of frames, we extract semantically grounded start and end timestamps for each distinct object interaction. These timestamps serve as the initial values for the endpoint parameters (tₗ,tᵣ) in our slot-table. This VLM-informed initialization allows the system to bypass exhaustive temporal searches or complex diagnostics, providing a clean and efficient configuration for final full-resolution training. To facilitate a robust optimization process, we initialize each interaction slot with a high temperature value rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5). This high-temperature initialization ensures that the Bernoulli random variable S_k,t begins with smooth transitions at the boundaries, allowing the gradients to flow more effectively over a wider temporal range during the initial stages of optimization.

3.4. Optimization

Leveraging the initial parameters derived from the VLM-based slot discovery phase, we proceed to optimize our final state-aware scene representation. We build our state-aware framework upon the 3D Gaussian Unscented Transform (3DGUT) architecture [(Wu et al., 2025a)]. Following the 3DGUT pipeline, we initialize the 3D Gaussian primitives using COLMAP-derived point clouds and augment each primitive with the learnable state logits ℓ. To provide an unbiased starting point for optimization, these logits are initialized such that the base/on/off state channels are assigned equal membership probabilities. Throughout this stage, we jointly optimize the geometric attributes of the Gaussians, their state logits, and the temporal parameters of the slot-table (tₗ,tᵣ,rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)). We strictly adhere to the optimization schedule established by 3DGUT, including its specialized densification and pruning protocols. To ensure consistent state behavior during optimization, we modify the standard densification process: whenever a Gaussian primitive is cloned or split, its state logits are inherited by the resultant primitives. This inheritance mechanism ensures that state-aware attributes remain spatially coherent even as the underlying scene geometry increases in complexity.

3.5. Training objective

Beyond the standard L₁ photometric and SSIM losses used to preserve perceptual fidelity, we employ two additional regularizers to mitigate floater artifacts, and prevent the emergence of redundant Gaussian primitives by supervising the optimization process via:

(7)L=L_rgb+λ₁L_SSIM+λ₂L_sparsity+λ₃L_compactness

Sparsity loss

To ensure a parsimonious partitioning of the scene, we regularize the Gaussian primitives to favor the static base state, thereby preventing unnecessary scene regions from being categorized as interactive. This is achieved by applying a negative log-likelihood penalty on the base state probability for all N Gaussians:

(8)L_sparsity=-1/N∑ₙ\logpₙ[0]

Compactness loss

To encourage Gaussians within slots to form spatially cohesive clusters, we first compute the opacity-weighted center of mass for primitives assigned to the on state of slot k:

(9)μ̄ₖ=(∑ₙαₙ·pₙ[2k]·μₙ)/(∑ₙαₙ·pₙ[2k]+ε)

and then penalize the weighted variance [(Sun et al., 2021)] for both the off and on states to encourage local clustering:

(10)L_compactness=1/2K∑_j={0,1}(∑ₙαₙ·pₙ[2k-j]·||μₙ-μ̄ₖ||²)/(∑ₙαₙ·pₙ[2k-j]+ε)

4. Experiments

To validate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm in the absence of an existing dataset with variable object interactions, we collected a custom dataset using a consumer-grade Insta360 X4 dual-fisheye 360^∘ camera. This hardware choice reflects the typical setup of casual users. During capture, we emulated non-expert behaviors, moving through the scene and interacting with objects—transitioning them from resting to active states and back.

Our dataset comprises 12 scenes organized into two groups. The standard set contains 10 casually captured scenes (8 indoor and 2 outdoor), each featuring 3–9 object interactions. The golden set contains 2 additional scenes for which we acquire controlled test sequences with novel camera trajectories and object-state combinations. We preprocess the raw dual-fisheye data following FullCircle [(Foroutan et al., 2026)] to mask the capturer. The calibration is performed in COLMAP using the masked fisheye frames, and then the fisheye images are undistorted into standard pinhole images.

For evaluation, we adhere to standard NeRF procedures, holding out every 8th frame as a test set. Crucially, we exclude test samples that coincide with state transitions (i.e., frames where an object is actively being moved) to reduce noise in our metrics, though these transition frames are retained within the training set to measure whether models can learn robustly from casual capture data. For the golden set sequences, we additionally evaluate novel camera frames, which show state configurations observed during training from new camera trajectories, and novel state-combination frames, which contain object-state configurations not observed during training. This set is used to demonstrate our method’s ability to generalize beyond the training configurations, and provide true state-aware control.

4.1. Baselines

We evaluate our proposed method against several state-of-the-art scene representation baselines. For static modeling, we compare against FullCircle[(Foroutan et al., 2026)], utilizing its underlying 3DGUT[(Wu et al., 2025a)] architecture as our primary reference. To assess performance in dynamic contexts, we benchmark our framework against 4DGS[(Yang et al., 2024b)] and DeGauss[(Wang et al., 2025a)]. For all quantitative and qualitative assessments, we utilize every 8th frame of the captured sequences as our standard evaluation set.

4.2. Quantitative Results

In Table1, we present the quantitative performance of our method relative to both static and dynamic baselines on the undistorted dataset. These results validate our framework’s ability to maintain high-fidelity visual representations while providing granular, state-controlled manipulation. More detailed metrics for all 10 scenes are available in the supplementary material.

4.3. Qualitative Results

Figures5, 6 and 7 illustrate qualitative comparisons between SwitchSplat and baselines. While our method consistently yields high-fidelity renderings, dynamic baselines frequently exhibit pervasive floating artifacts during object interactions. For example, in the “Car” scene (Figure6), both 4DGS and DeGauss generate significant floaters around the hood region. Similarly, in the “Kitchen” environment, these baselines produce substantial noise when the refrigerator is in its on state. Comparable degradations, manifesting as unanchored geometry, are observed during cabinet and wardrobe interactions in the “Flat” scenes. In contrast, SwitchSplat maintains significantly cleaner reconstructions by effectively disentangling static environment components from discrete state-specific changes.

4.4. Golden set comparisons

Beyond the standard held-out evaluation on the original trajectories, we evaluate SwitchSplat on two additional generalization settings: novel camera frames and novel state-combination frames. For two representative scenes, we acquire dedicated test trajectories containing previously unseen camera viewpoints and object-state combinations, and compare against 4DGS and DeGauss. Because 4DGS and DeGauss parameterize scene variation by continuous time rather than a discrete state code, we evaluate both dynamic baselines on the novel-camera and novel state-combination splits using a per-image oracle over time. For each target image, we select the rendering with the highest PSNR for both methods; these results therefore constitute upper bounds. As shown in Figure5, SwitchSplat consistently outperforms the dynamic baselines on novel camera frames and produces sharper reconstructions with fewer structural artifacts. We further evaluate novel state-combination frames, where multiple independently controlled interactions are composed into configurations not observed during training. Quantitative results in Table2 demonstrate that SwitchSplat maintains high reconstruction quality under these unseen configurations, highlighting the compositional generalization enabled by our state-conditioned representation.

4.5. Ablation study

We perform a comprehensive ablation study to evaluate the contribution of individual components within our framework. These experiments are conducted on the “Kitchen 2” scene, which features the golden test set. We report PSNR averaged over three evaluation settings: the standard 8th-frame test set, novel camera frames, and novel state-combination frames, with each configuration further averaged over five independent runs.

Slot representation

We first evaluate the importance of the slot representation. When interaction slots are removed, the model reduces to a scene representation without any of our slot-specific components, including slot optimization and the associated regularization terms. The substantial performance drop in Table3 demonstrates that explicitly introducing interaction slots is essential for modeling state-dependent scene changes.

Slot optimization

We next assess the importance of optimizing the initialized slot parameters. For this ablation, slots are initialized normally via VLM outputs but their parameters are kept fixed throughout training. The observed deterioration in reconstruction quality (Table3) shows that differentiable slot optimization is important for refining the initial estimates according to photometric evidence.

Compactness regularization

The compactness loss encourages state-conditioned Gaussians associated with the same interaction to remain spatially localized, preventing them from dispersing across unrelated regions of the scene. This spatial prior therefore plays an important role in learning coherent state-dependent representations.

Sparsity regularization

Removing the sparsity regularization has a modest effect on average reconstruction quality. The regularizer nevertheless discourages unnecessary assignment of otherwise static Gaussians to interactive states, promoting a more parsimonious state decomposition and reducing spurious state-dependent changes.

5. Conclusion

We presented SwitchSplat, a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that learns state-aware scene representations directly from casual video captures. By decomposing the scene into a shared static base and a set of independently controllable slots, each modeling the binary “on”/“off” states of one interactable object, SwitchSplat decouples scene state from time – enabling a capability that time-conditioned dynamic methods fundamentally cannot provide: free composition of object configurations at inference, including combinations never observed during capture. The slot table is initialized via a VLM and jointly refined end-to-end through differentiable rendering, requiring no manual annotation. Experiments on our new casual-capture dataset show that SwitchSplat outperforms static and dynamic baselines in novel-view synthesis quality, and uniquely generalizes to out-of-distribution camera paths and unseen state combinations.

Limitations and future work

The current model assumes binary object states with the constraints of single-operator capture with one free hand. Extending to continuous or multi-valued states by multiple operators – would broaden the applicability of the framework. The slot count and approximate interaction windows are currently seeded by a VLM; a fully unsupervised discovery of both the number and timing of interactions from raw video remains an open problem. Finally, SwitchSplat focuses on novel-view synthesis; combining our state-aware decomposition with physics-based priors or generative models could enable downstream applications such as scene editing and simulation.

Acknowledgements.

We thank the anonymous reviewers for their helpful comments and suggestions. We also thank Zhihan Zhang, Egor Fokin, and Mingrui Zhao for contributing scenes and objects used in our dataset captures. We thank Lily Goli for her helpful advice and suggestions. This work was supported in part by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC) Discovery Grant [2023-05617], the Canada Foundation for Innovation (CFI) John R. Evans Leaders Fund (JELF), the SFU Visual Computing Research Chair, Google Research, and the Digital Research Alliance of Canada.

（参考文献见原文。）

Appendix A Supplementary Material

The supplementary materials are organized as follows. We first provide additional qualitative video results in the accompanying HTML supplement. To view them locally, open the provided index.html file in a modern web browser. Additional interactive results are available on our project page: https://switchsplat.github.io.

A.1. Dataset Capture and Preprocessing

We captured twelve real-world scenes using an Insta360 X4 dual-fisheye 360 camera, comprising ten standard scenes and two golden scenes. Video frames were extracted at 4 FPS. We use the raw fisheye frames for reconstruction to avoid propagating stitching artifacts into the scene representation. Camera-holder masks are automatically obtained using the FullCircle masking pipeline. These masks, together with the fisheye frames, are passed to COLMAP for camera pose estimation and subsequent image undistortion. Input images are downsampled by a factor of two. An overview of the object-interaction intervals and temporal structure of all twelve scenes is provided in Figure18.

A.2. Benchmark Construction and Evaluation Splits

We evaluate reconstruction and generalization using four evaluation splits.

Base-state test frames. This split contains held-out frames in which all objects remain in their initial base state. It evaluates reconstruction of the canonical scene configuration and provides a natural comparison point for static reconstruction methods.

All standard test frames. For each scene, we hold out every eight frame from the original capture sequence. Frames occurring during object transitions are excluded, such that evaluation is performed only on stable object configurations. The remaining frames constitute our standard test set and cover the object states observed throughout the original capture.

For the two golden scenes, Kitchen 2 and Oslo, we additionally perform controlled recaptures under prescribed binary object states and new camera trajectories, as illustrated in Figure8. These recaptures define two additional evaluation splits.

Novel camera frames. We recapture object-state configurations observed during the original training sequence using new camera trajectories. This split evaluates generalization to novel viewpoints while keeping the scene configuration within the set observed during training.

Novel state-combination frames. We additionally recapture joint object-state configurations that never occurred during the training sequence, again using new camera trajectories. This split evaluates whether the learned representation can compose individually observed object states into previously unseen scene configurations.

Dynamic-baseline evaluation.

DeGauss and 4DGS represent scene variation using a continuous timestamp and cannot directly condition on the prescribed state code of a Golden-set test image. For the novel-camera and novel state-combination splits, we therefore evaluate both methods using the same per-image oracle-over-time protocol. We first evaluate 30 uniformly spaced timestamps over [0,1], then evaluate 8 additional timestamps within a ±0.03 neighborhood of the best coarse prediction. The rendering with the highest PSNR across both stages is retained. PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS are computed from this same selected rendering; SSIM and LPIPS are not independently optimized. Since the ground-truth image is used to select the timestamp, these results should be interpreted as oracle upper bounds.

A.3. Additional Training Details

For fair comparison, all methods use corresponding undistorted pinhole images for both training and rendering, with the camera-holder exclusion masks mapped into the respective undistorted image representation.

We initialize our Gaussians from the COLMAP SfM point cloud and use the same densification and pruning schedule as 3DGUT. Gaussian parameters and state logits are optimized with fused Adam, while the slot-window endpoints and temperatures use a separate Adam optimizer; both optimizers are stepped jointly. SwitchSplat, FullCircle, and 4DGS are trained for 30,000 iterations with batch size 4. DeGauss uses batch size 4 with a 1,000-iteration coarse stage followed by a 30,000-iteration fine stage. The learning rates for opacity and state logits are both 5×10⁻².

The state-sparsity loss has weight 10⁻⁴, starts at iteration 18,000, and ramps linearly over 1,000 iterations. The compactness loss has weight 5×10⁻⁴, starts at iteration 21,000, and also ramps linearly over 1,000 iterations. For each slot, both states are measured relative to the opacity- and assignment-weighted centroid of the active state. After iterations 18,000 and 21,000, we mean-center the state logits and scale them by 0.3, reducing assignment confidence as the corresponding regularizer becomes active.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：静态底图加可独立开关的 slot，每个可交互物体两个二值状态，推理时能渲染训练中从未出现过的状态组合。

要点：

  • base + slot 分解：共享静态底图承载不变场景，每个可交互物体一个 slot，各自持有开/关两个状态
  • 高斯到 slot 的归属完全可微，模型能直接从视频里学出每个状态的几何，不需要人工标注
  • 推理时可自由组合各 slot 状态并从任意新视角渲染；对比之下，4DGS 这类时间条件方法把「什么时候被观测到」和「场景处于什么状态」混为一谈，只能回放见过的序列

为什么值得看：随手拍的重建要变成可用资产，缺的正是「可交互状态」。这种把状态离散化、可组合的表示，比时序动态表示更接近引擎里对可交互物体的建模方式。

中文摘要：3DGS 让高保真重建变得又快又易得，但现有表示都假定世界是静态的。随手拍摄时人自然会与环境交互——开门、拨开关、挪动物体——这些离散状态变化目前没有框架能建模。时间条件的动态方法（如 4DGS）把「何时观测到」与「场景处于哪个状态」混在一起，只能重放见过的序列。SwitchSplat 用 base + slot 分解解决这个问题：一个共享静态底图捕捉不变的场景，每个可交互物体单独占一个 slot，各自持有两个二值状态（开/关）。由于高斯到 slot 的归属完全可微，模型能从视频中直接发现每个状态的几何而无需标注。推理时用户可以自由组合 slot 状态并从任意视角渲染，包括训练中从未见过的组合。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-17

本期推送：2026-10-24

SwitchSplat: Learning Discrete Object States from Casually Captured Scenes

© cc

Abstract.

3D Gaussian Splatting has made high-fidelity 3D reconstruction fast and accessible, yet existing representations assume a static world. This assumption breaks down in casual captures, where a user naturally interacts with the environment – opening doors, toggling switches, or moving objects – introducing discrete state changes that no current framework can model. Time-conditioned dynamic methods such as 4DGS conflate when a state was observed with what state the scene is in, limiting them to replaying seen sequences rather than composing arbitrary object configurations. We present SwitchSplat, the first 3DGS representation to address this gap via a base+slot decomposition: a shared static base captures the invariant scene, while each slot independently holds the two binary states (on/off) of one interactable object. Because the assignment of Gaussians to slots is fully differentiable, the model discovers the geometry of each state directly from video, without manual annotation. At inference, the user can freely combine slot states and render the resulting scene from any viewpoint. We validate SwitchSplat on a new casual-capture dataset and show that it outperforms static and dynamic baselines in novel-view synthesis quality, while uniquely supporting rendering of state combinations never seen during capture. Project page: https://switchsplat.github.io.

Keywords:

Novel View Synthesis, Gaussian Splatting, State-aware Rendering, 360^∘ Capture ††cc-license: by

1. Introduction

In inverse rendering, Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [(Kerbl et al., 2023)] has emerged as the leading representation for real-time, high-fidelity novel-view synthesis, enabling a new generation of interactive applications. Its combination of fast training and efficient rendering has driven broad adoption across academia as well as industry, from Matterport’s digital twins and Niantic Scaniverse’s mobile reconstruction to Meta’s Hyperscape111https://www.meta.com/experiences/meta-horizon-hyperscape-capture-beta/8798130056953686/.

While early 3DGS pipelines required meticulous data acquisition (fixed exposure and white balance, controlled lighting, and a perfectly static scene), recent works like 3DGRT [(Moenne-Loccoz et al., 2024)] and FullCircle [(Foroutan et al., 2026)] have unlocked casual capture: viewpoints need not be carefully curated – made possible by 360^∘ cameras held in a single hand – and the capturer’s pixels are automatically masked out to satisfy the static-scene assumption. This freedom naturally invites users to interact with the environment during capture – opening doors, toggling switches, or repositioning objects – turning the operator into both an active agent and a dynamic distractor within the scene.

Yet no existing reconstruction framework is equipped to handle these interactions. Many contemporary 3D representations enforce a strict static-world assumption: when an operator triggers a discrete state change – opening a door, flipping a switch, relocating an object – the model has no mechanism to account for the resulting geometric variation. As a result, even state-of-the-art pipelines can only represent a single, frozen scene configuration, and capturing multiple stable states requires re-recording the scene from scratch.

One could argue that the natural candidate to address this limitation is the family of 4D Gaussian Splatting methods [(Yang et al., 2024b)], which extend 3DGS to dynamic scenes by conditioning the scene representation on time. However, this design choice fundamentally conflates when a state was observed with what state the scene is in: the model learns to replay a specific sequence of observations, not to understand independent object configurations.

As a result, 4D methods are largely limited to novel-viewpoint synthesis of seen sequences; composing an unseen combination of object states—e.g., door open and light on—is not directly supported, since no single timestamp in the training data corresponds to that configuration. What is needed instead is a representation that de-correlates scene state from time, allowing the user to freely specify both the viewpoint and the desired configuration of each object independently.

To address these challenges, we propose SwitchSplat, a method that learns “state-aware” representations from casual captures featuring human-object interactions; see Figure1. SwitchSplat organizes the scene into a static base – the parts that never change throughout the capture – and a set of slots, one per interactable object. Each slot holds two 3D representations corresponding to the binary states of that object (“on” and “off”). For example, if a room was captured while a closet door was closed for part of the recording and open for another, a single slot would hold both the “off” state (door closed, interior hidden) and the “on” state (door open, interior visible), while the walls, floor, and furniture – unchanged throughout – are handled by the static base. To assign each Gaussian primitive to the right part of the scene, we attach a small learnable score vector that controls how strongly the primitive belongs to the base, or to either state of each slot.

This decomposition avoids data redundancy: without a shared static base, one would need to duplicate the full scene geometry for every slot, with no reusable structure across states. Instead, SwitchSplat shares the base across all configurations and only stores the geometry that actually differs per state.222 This is structurally analogous to PCA-based morphable models [(Blanz and Vetter, 2023)]: the static base plays the role of the mean face, each slot’s on/off representations correspond to the eigenvectors, and the state activations act as the blend-shape coefficients. Because the full pipeline is differentiable end-to-end, the model learns simultaneously which Gaussians belong to which slot and when each slot is active – directly from the input video, without any manual annotation. At inference, the user can query any combination of slot states independently – e.g., closet door open and desk lamp on – and render the resulting scene from any viewpoint.

To summarize our contributions: (1) We identify a novel problem in the 3DGS literature: existing representations cannot model scenes with discrete, user-triggered state changes (e.g., objects that can be opened, switched, or moved), and we show that naïvely applying dynamic methods such as 4DGS fails to address this. (2) We propose SwitchSplat, the first 3DGS representation to address this problem via a base+slot decomposition, where a shared static base captures the invariant scene and each slot independently models the binary states of one interactable object. (3) We demonstrate on a new casual-capture dataset that SwitchSplat improves novel-view synthesis quality over static and dynamic baselines, and uniquely supports rendering arbitrary combinations of object states from unseen viewpoints.

2. Related Work

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [(Kerbl et al., 2023)] has become the dominant representation for novel-view synthesis, optimizing a set of anisotropic Gaussian primitives that render at real-time rates. Extensions beyond the standard perspective-camera model are particularly relevant to our setting: 3DGRT [(Moenne-Loccoz et al., 2024)] reformulates rendering via ray tracing, and 3DGUT [(Wu et al., 2025a)] adds support for highly distorted cameras and secondary rays, enabling casual capture with wide field-of-view sensors. FullCircle [(Foroutan et al., 2026)] further shows that raw dual-fisheye 360^∘ video suffices for high-quality reconstruction, automatically masking the camera operator. Despite these advances, all of these pipelines represent the scene as a single, fixed configuration. When multiple object states are present in the capture—a door open in some frames and closed in others—the model either conflates them into averaged geometry and ghosting artifacts, or learns to discard the minority state as a distractor [(Sabour et al., 2025)]. Either way, only one configuration survives in the final model; there is no mechanism to retain, switch between, or compose multiple stable states at inference time.

Dynamic Gaussian Splatting

A large family of methods extends 3DGS to dynamic scenes by conditioning the representation on time. Dynamic 3D Gaussians [(Luiten et al., 2024)] tracks persistent primitives across frames, while Deformable 3D Gaussians [(Yang et al., 2024a)] and 4DGS [(Wu et al., 2024)] deform a canonical scene over time, with 4DGS using a learned space-time encoding. Spacetime Gaussians [(Li et al., 2024a)] further augments primitives with temporal opacity and parametric motion. Subsequent work improves efficiency, temporal consistency, or geometric accuracy via depth priors [(Yang et al., 2024b; Sun et al., 2024; Duan et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2025b)]. Differently from our method, all of these methods are parameterized by time, not by object state: recovering a specific scene configuration requires locating the right moment in the recording, and rendering a novel combination of states—e.g., two objects in configurations never co-observed—is not supported.

Decomposed Gaussian Splatting

More recent dynamic Gaussian methods, such as SDD-4DGS [(Sun et al., 2025)], observe that applying deformation models to the entire scene is often inefficient, since most real-world scenes are largely static. This motivates methods that decompose scenes into static and dynamic components: GauFRe [(Liang et al., 2025)] combines a static Gaussian component with deformable dynamic Gaussians, while Swift4D [(Wu et al., 2025b)] improves efficiency by passing only dynamic Gaussians through the deformation model. DeGauss [(Wang et al., 2025a)] further uses dynamic-static decomposition to improve robustness to transient distractors. This observation is closely aligned with our setting, since object interactions usually affect only a small part of a 360^∘ environment. In contrast to our method, existing decomposition methods still treat the dynamic component as a temporally varying foreground: they separate dynamic regions from a static background, but provide no mechanism to independently switch or compose object states at inference time.

Controllable Scene Representation

A parallel line of work studies controllable and articulated 3D representations. Pre-Gaussian methods such as Watch It Move [(Noguchi et al., 2022)] discover articulated structure from object motion; PARIS [(Liu et al., 2023)] goes further by decoupling static and movable parts from two multi-view captures of the same scene. Gaussian-based approaches extend this to photorealistic settings: SC-GS [(Huang et al., 2024)] enables motion editing via sparse control points, Template-free Articulated Gaussian Splatting [(Wan et al., 2024)] supports re-posing with super-points, and RigGS [(Yao et al., 2025)] adds rig-based editing and interpolation. ArtGS [(Liu et al., 2025a)] and ArticulatedGS [(Guo et al., 2025)] further focus on part-level modeling of individual objects. Crucially, all of these methods aim to encode object motion or articulation—they model how parts move, rather than discarding motion entirely to focus on the discrete stable configurations of the scene. In contrast, our method treats object interactions as a nuisance to be factored out, retaining only the clean on/off states and ignoring the transient motion between them.

State-aware Scene Reconstruction

Closest to our setting are methods that reconstruct scenes across discrete object states. IGFuse [(Hu et al., 2026)] and RecurGS [(Hu et al., 2025)] address this by using semantic cues to detect state changes and aligning them via rigid transformations. GaussianCut [(Jain et al., 2024)] and DecoupledGaussian [(Wang et al., 2025b)] contribute related tools for object segmentation and scene decomposition. However, all of these methods assume that state changes can be described as rigid motions of segmented object entities—an assumption that breaks down for casual capture, where interaction boundaries are fuzzy and deformations are non-rigid. In contrast, SwitchSplat learns which Gaussians belong to each state directly from photometric supervision, without requiring object masks, or rigid-body assumptions.

3. Method

SwitchSplat learns a state-aware 3D representation from casual captures by decomposing the scene into controllable, state-conditioned components. In the following subsections, we detail our methodology by first formulating our state-conditioned Gaussian primitives and describing their integration within volume rendering (Sec.3.1). We then introduce the parameterization of the differentiable slot-table (Sec.3.2), followed by our slot initialization procedure (Sec.3.3). Finally, we describe our training pipeline and objectives that facilitate granular, state-controlled visualization during inference (Secs.3.4 and 3.5).

Terminology

A slot corresponds to one interactable object and holds two 3D representations for its binary states: “off” (e.g., door closed) and “on” (e.g., door open). A slot activation is a per-frame binary variable indicating which state is currently observed. All parts of the scene that remain constant throughout the capture are handled by the static base, which is shared across all configurations.

3.1. State-aware Gaussian Splat

Each 3D Gaussian primitive in our model is defined by its standard geometric and appearance attributes: mean μ, covariance Σ, opacity α, and view-dependent appearance c. To make our representation state-aware, we augment every Gaussian with a learnable categorical state distribution p=softmax(ℓ) over 1+2K channels, where K is the total number of object slots. These channels comprise a single static base channel ℓ[0], together with a pair of off (ℓ[2k-1]) and on (ℓ[2k]) channels for each slot k∈{1,…,K}. The two channels per slot — rather than one — let the softmax assign each Gaussian to a single configuration, so that disjoint subsets of primitives can independently model the geometry and appearance of an object in each of its two states (see Figure3). This separation is essential because the on/off configurations of an object generally differ not just in appearance, but also in spatial extent — a closed door and an open door, for instance, occupy different parts of the scene — which a single shared primitive simply cannot represent.

Test-time rendering

Assume we have trained our representation, and that we want to render an image corresponding to the slot configuration p̃∈{0,1}^K. This is achieved by computing the probability of each gaussian being present in the scene to be rendered:

(1)

ω(p̃)=p[0]+∑ₖ₌₁^K(p̃[k]·p[2k]+(1-p̃[k])·p[2k-1])

This formulation ensures that “base” Gaussians remain present across all frames, while the presence of the on/off state Gaussians is gated by the probability of the corresponding slot being on. We then gate the opacity of the gaussian by this probability:

(2)

α̃=α·ω(p̃),

which is then used to compute the final RGB color for a ray r via classical volume rendering [(Tagliasacchi and Mildenhall, 2022)]:

Î(r)=∑_i∈H(r)Tᵢ(r)·α̃ᵢ·cᵢ(r), Tᵢ(r)=∏_j

where H(r) represents the set of Gaussians intersected by the ray in depth order and cᵢ(r) denotes the view-dependent color. While p̃ will be selected by the user at test-time, the key question in training our representation lies in how to propagate the gradients from image Îₜ at time t to the (per-Gaussian) state distribution p.

3.2. Differentiable slot table

To achieve this, we exploit the key assumption that, within the video, the activation state of a slot is compactly supported in time. Let us denotes with the per-slot scalar πₖ(t)∈[0,1] the probability of slot k being in its on state at time t. Then, ∀k≠0 we have that πₖ(t) is zero everywhere outside some bounded, closed region. Without loss of generality, let us drop the indexing k, and focus on a single entry π(t). We can satisfy our compact support assumption by explicitly parameterizing π(t) as a smooth window function defined by its temporal endpoints (tₗ,tᵣ)333 To ensure tₗ≤tᵣ in practice we optimize auxiliary free variables u and v, and then remap them to tₗ=\min(u,v) and tᵣ=\max(u,v)., and a temperature parameter rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5) that controls the smoothness of transition; see Figure4.

By defining the midpoint as tₘ=(tₗ+tᵣ)/2, and σ_rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)(t)=σ(t/rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)), the probability of an interaction occurring at time t is computed via the normalized product of two sigmoid functions σ:

(3)π(t)=(σ_rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)(t-tₗ)·σ_rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)(tᵣ-t))/(σ_rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)(tₘ-tₗ)·σ_rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)(tᵣ-tₘ))

Therefore, to model the time window of each object interaction, we treat the state of the k-th slot at time t as a Bernoulli random variable S_k,t∈{0,1}, where S_k,t=1 denotes the slot being in its on state and S_k,t=0 its off state, whose probability mass function (PMF) for a specific state s∈{0,1} is given by:

(4)P(S_k,t=s)=πₖ(t)ˢ(1-πₖ(t))¹⁻ˢ

Train-time rendering

The quantity πₖ(t) defined above is our slot table, which we use to compute the probability of each Gaussian being present in the scene at time t:

(5)ω(t)=p[0]+∑ₖ₌₁^K(πₖ(t)·p[2k]+(1-πₖ(t))·p[2k-1])

from which, like before, we can compute a time-dependent effective opacity for volume rendering the predicted image Îₜ:

(6)α̃(t)=α·ω(t)

This differentiable rendering framework ensures that gradients propagate seamlessly to the slot activation probabilities, Gaussian state memberships, and geometric parameters, enabling stable and efficient joint optimization of the entire scene representation.

3.3. Initialization

In a casual capture setting, neither the total number of slots K, nor the precise slot transition timestamps are known a priori. Requiring the user to annotate them would defeat the very premise of a “casual” capture. To address this, we leverage the reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and in particular GPT 5.6, to provide an approximate initialization for the slot-table. By prompting GPT 5.6 with a sequence of frames, we extract semantically grounded start and end timestamps for each distinct object interaction. These timestamps serve as the initial values for the endpoint parameters (tₗ,tᵣ) in our slot-table. This VLM-informed initialization allows the system to bypass exhaustive temporal searches or complex diagnostics, providing a clean and efficient configuration for final full-resolution training. To facilitate a robust optimization process, we initialize each interaction slot with a high temperature value rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5). This high-temperature initialization ensures that the Bernoulli random variable S_k,t begins with smooth transitions at the boundaries, allowing the gradients to flow more effectively over a wider temporal range during the initial stages of optimization.

3.4. Optimization

Leveraging the initial parameters derived from the VLM-based slot discovery phase, we proceed to optimize our final state-aware scene representation. We build our state-aware framework upon the 3D Gaussian Unscented Transform (3DGUT) architecture [(Wu et al., 2025a)]. Following the 3DGUT pipeline, we initialize the 3D Gaussian primitives using COLMAP-derived point clouds and augment each primitive with the learnable state logits ℓ. To provide an unbiased starting point for optimization, these logits are initialized such that the base/on/off state channels are assigned equal membership probabilities. Throughout this stage, we jointly optimize the geometric attributes of the Gaussians, their state logits, and the temporal parameters of the slot-table (tₗ,tᵣ,rgb(0bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(25bp)=(0,0,0);rgb(75bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5);rgb(100bp)=(0.5,0.5,0.5)). We strictly adhere to the optimization schedule established by 3DGUT, including its specialized densification and pruning protocols. To ensure consistent state behavior during optimization, we modify the standard densification process: whenever a Gaussian primitive is cloned or split, its state logits are inherited by the resultant primitives. This inheritance mechanism ensures that state-aware attributes remain spatially coherent even as the underlying scene geometry increases in complexity.

3.5. Training objective

Beyond the standard L₁ photometric and SSIM losses used to preserve perceptual fidelity, we employ two additional regularizers to mitigate floater artifacts, and prevent the emergence of redundant Gaussian primitives by supervising the optimization process via:

(7)L=L_rgb+λ₁L_SSIM+λ₂L_sparsity+λ₃L_compactness

Sparsity loss

To ensure a parsimonious partitioning of the scene, we regularize the Gaussian primitives to favor the static base state, thereby preventing unnecessary scene regions from being categorized as interactive. This is achieved by applying a negative log-likelihood penalty on the base state probability for all N Gaussians:

(8)L_sparsity=-1/N∑ₙ\logpₙ[0]

Compactness loss

To encourage Gaussians within slots to form spatially cohesive clusters, we first compute the opacity-weighted center of mass for primitives assigned to the on state of slot k:

(9)μ̄ₖ=(∑ₙαₙ·pₙ[2k]·μₙ)/(∑ₙαₙ·pₙ[2k]+ε)

and then penalize the weighted variance [(Sun et al., 2021)] for both the off and on states to encourage local clustering:

(10)L_compactness=1/2K∑_j={0,1}(∑ₙαₙ·pₙ[2k-j]·||μₙ-μ̄ₖ||²)/(∑ₙαₙ·pₙ[2k-j]+ε)

4. Experiments

To validate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm in the absence of an existing dataset with variable object interactions, we collected a custom dataset using a consumer-grade Insta360 X4 dual-fisheye 360^∘ camera. This hardware choice reflects the typical setup of casual users. During capture, we emulated non-expert behaviors, moving through the scene and interacting with objects—transitioning them from resting to active states and back.

Our dataset comprises 12 scenes organized into two groups. The standard set contains 10 casually captured scenes (8 indoor and 2 outdoor), each featuring 3–9 object interactions. The golden set contains 2 additional scenes for which we acquire controlled test sequences with novel camera trajectories and object-state combinations. We preprocess the raw dual-fisheye data following FullCircle [(Foroutan et al., 2026)] to mask the capturer. The calibration is performed in COLMAP using the masked fisheye frames, and then the fisheye images are undistorted into standard pinhole images.

For evaluation, we adhere to standard NeRF procedures, holding out every 8th frame as a test set. Crucially, we exclude test samples that coincide with state transitions (i.e., frames where an object is actively being moved) to reduce noise in our metrics, though these transition frames are retained within the training set to measure whether models can learn robustly from casual capture data. For the golden set sequences, we additionally evaluate novel camera frames, which show state configurations observed during training from new camera trajectories, and novel state-combination frames, which contain object-state configurations not observed during training. This set is used to demonstrate our method’s ability to generalize beyond the training configurations, and provide true state-aware control.

4.1. Baselines

We evaluate our proposed method against several state-of-the-art scene representation baselines. For static modeling, we compare against FullCircle[(Foroutan et al., 2026)], utilizing its underlying 3DGUT[(Wu et al., 2025a)] architecture as our primary reference. To assess performance in dynamic contexts, we benchmark our framework against 4DGS[(Yang et al., 2024b)] and DeGauss[(Wang et al., 2025a)]. For all quantitative and qualitative assessments, we utilize every 8th frame of the captured sequences as our standard evaluation set.

4.2. Quantitative Results

In Table1, we present the quantitative performance of our method relative to both static and dynamic baselines on the undistorted dataset. These results validate our framework’s ability to maintain high-fidelity visual representations while providing granular, state-controlled manipulation. More detailed metrics for all 10 scenes are available in the supplementary material.

4.3. Qualitative Results

Figures5, 6 and 7 illustrate qualitative comparisons between SwitchSplat and baselines. While our method consistently yields high-fidelity renderings, dynamic baselines frequently exhibit pervasive floating artifacts during object interactions. For example, in the “Car” scene (Figure6), both 4DGS and DeGauss generate significant floaters around the hood region. Similarly, in the “Kitchen” environment, these baselines produce substantial noise when the refrigerator is in its on state. Comparable degradations, manifesting as unanchored geometry, are observed during cabinet and wardrobe interactions in the “Flat” scenes. In contrast, SwitchSplat maintains significantly cleaner reconstructions by effectively disentangling static environment components from discrete state-specific changes.

4.4. Golden set comparisons

Beyond the standard held-out evaluation on the original trajectories, we evaluate SwitchSplat on two additional generalization settings: novel camera frames and novel state-combination frames. For two representative scenes, we acquire dedicated test trajectories containing previously unseen camera viewpoints and object-state combinations, and compare against 4DGS and DeGauss. Because 4DGS and DeGauss parameterize scene variation by continuous time rather than a discrete state code, we evaluate both dynamic baselines on the novel-camera and novel state-combination splits using a per-image oracle over time. For each target image, we select the rendering with the highest PSNR for both methods; these results therefore constitute upper bounds. As shown in Figure5, SwitchSplat consistently outperforms the dynamic baselines on novel camera frames and produces sharper reconstructions with fewer structural artifacts. We further evaluate novel state-combination frames, where multiple independently controlled interactions are composed into configurations not observed during training. Quantitative results in Table2 demonstrate that SwitchSplat maintains high reconstruction quality under these unseen configurations, highlighting the compositional generalization enabled by our state-conditioned representation.

4.5. Ablation study

We perform a comprehensive ablation study to evaluate the contribution of individual components within our framework. These experiments are conducted on the “Kitchen 2” scene, which features the golden test set. We report PSNR averaged over three evaluation settings: the standard 8th-frame test set, novel camera frames, and novel state-combination frames, with each configuration further averaged over five independent runs.

Slot representation

We first evaluate the importance of the slot representation. When interaction slots are removed, the model reduces to a scene representation without any of our slot-specific components, including slot optimization and the associated regularization terms. The substantial performance drop in Table3 demonstrates that explicitly introducing interaction slots is essential for modeling state-dependent scene changes.

Slot optimization

We next assess the importance of optimizing the initialized slot parameters. For this ablation, slots are initialized normally via VLM outputs but their parameters are kept fixed throughout training. The observed deterioration in reconstruction quality (Table3) shows that differentiable slot optimization is important for refining the initial estimates according to photometric evidence.

Compactness regularization

The compactness loss encourages state-conditioned Gaussians associated with the same interaction to remain spatially localized, preventing them from dispersing across unrelated regions of the scene. This spatial prior therefore plays an important role in learning coherent state-dependent representations.

Sparsity regularization

Removing the sparsity regularization has a modest effect on average reconstruction quality. The regularizer nevertheless discourages unnecessary assignment of otherwise static Gaussians to interactive states, promoting a more parsimonious state decomposition and reducing spurious state-dependent changes.

5. Conclusion

We presented SwitchSplat, a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that learns state-aware scene representations directly from casual video captures. By decomposing the scene into a shared static base and a set of independently controllable slots, each modeling the binary “on”/“off” states of one interactable object, SwitchSplat decouples scene state from time – enabling a capability that time-conditioned dynamic methods fundamentally cannot provide: free composition of object configurations at inference, including combinations never observed during capture. The slot table is initialized via a VLM and jointly refined end-to-end through differentiable rendering, requiring no manual annotation. Experiments on our new casual-capture dataset show that SwitchSplat outperforms static and dynamic baselines in novel-view synthesis quality, and uniquely generalizes to out-of-distribution camera paths and unseen state combinations.

Limitations and future work

The current model assumes binary object states with the constraints of single-operator capture with one free hand. Extending to continuous or multi-valued states by multiple operators – would broaden the applicability of the framework. The slot count and approximate interaction windows are currently seeded by a VLM; a fully unsupervised discovery of both the number and timing of interactions from raw video remains an open problem. Finally, SwitchSplat focuses on novel-view synthesis; combining our state-aware decomposition with physics-based priors or generative models could enable downstream applications such as scene editing and simulation.

Acknowledgements.

We thank the anonymous reviewers for their helpful comments and suggestions. We also thank Zhihan Zhang, Egor Fokin, and Mingrui Zhao for contributing scenes and objects used in our dataset captures. We thank Lily Goli for her helpful advice and suggestions. This work was supported in part by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC) Discovery Grant [2023-05617], the Canada Foundation for Innovation (CFI) John R. Evans Leaders Fund (JELF), the SFU Visual Computing Research Chair, Google Research, and the Digital Research Alliance of Canada.

（参考文献见原文。）

Appendix A Supplementary Material

The supplementary materials are organized as follows. We first provide additional qualitative video results in the accompanying HTML supplement. To view them locally, open the provided index.html file in a modern web browser. Additional interactive results are available on our project page: https://switchsplat.github.io.

A.1. Dataset Capture and Preprocessing

We captured twelve real-world scenes using an Insta360 X4 dual-fisheye 360 camera, comprising ten standard scenes and two golden scenes. Video frames were extracted at 4 FPS. We use the raw fisheye frames for reconstruction to avoid propagating stitching artifacts into the scene representation. Camera-holder masks are automatically obtained using the FullCircle masking pipeline. These masks, together with the fisheye frames, are passed to COLMAP for camera pose estimation and subsequent image undistortion. Input images are downsampled by a factor of two. An overview of the object-interaction intervals and temporal structure of all twelve scenes is provided in Figure18.

A.2. Benchmark Construction and Evaluation Splits

We evaluate reconstruction and generalization using four evaluation splits.

Base-state test frames. This split contains held-out frames in which all objects remain in their initial base state. It evaluates reconstruction of the canonical scene configuration and provides a natural comparison point for static reconstruction methods.

All standard test frames. For each scene, we hold out every eight frame from the original capture sequence. Frames occurring during object transitions are excluded, such that evaluation is performed only on stable object configurations. The remaining frames constitute our standard test set and cover the object states observed throughout the original capture.

For the two golden scenes, Kitchen 2 and Oslo, we additionally perform controlled recaptures under prescribed binary object states and new camera trajectories, as illustrated in Figure8. These recaptures define two additional evaluation splits.

Novel camera frames. We recapture object-state configurations observed during the original training sequence using new camera trajectories. This split evaluates generalization to novel viewpoints while keeping the scene configuration within the set observed during training.

Novel state-combination frames. We additionally recapture joint object-state configurations that never occurred during the training sequence, again using new camera trajectories. This split evaluates whether the learned representation can compose individually observed object states into previously unseen scene configurations.

Dynamic-baseline evaluation.

DeGauss and 4DGS represent scene variation using a continuous timestamp and cannot directly condition on the prescribed state code of a Golden-set test image. For the novel-camera and novel state-combination splits, we therefore evaluate both methods using the same per-image oracle-over-time protocol. We first evaluate 30 uniformly spaced timestamps over [0,1], then evaluate 8 additional timestamps within a ±0.03 neighborhood of the best coarse prediction. The rendering with the highest PSNR across both stages is retained. PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS are computed from this same selected rendering; SSIM and LPIPS are not independently optimized. Since the ground-truth image is used to select the timestamp, these results should be interpreted as oracle upper bounds.

A.3. Additional Training Details

For fair comparison, all methods use corresponding undistorted pinhole images for both training and rendering, with the camera-holder exclusion masks mapped into the respective undistorted image representation.

We initialize our Gaussians from the COLMAP SfM point cloud and use the same densification and pruning schedule as 3DGUT. Gaussian parameters and state logits are optimized with fused Adam, while the slot-window endpoints and temperatures use a separate Adam optimizer; both optimizers are stepped jointly. SwitchSplat, FullCircle, and 4DGS are trained for 30,000 iterations with batch size 4. DeGauss uses batch size 4 with a 1,000-iteration coarse stage followed by a 30,000-iteration fine stage. The learning rates for opacity and state logits are both 5×10⁻².

The state-sparsity loss has weight 10⁻⁴, starts at iteration 18,000, and ramps linearly over 1,000 iterations. The compactness loss has weight 5×10⁻⁴, starts at iteration 21,000, and also ramps linearly over 1,000 iterations. For each slot, both states are measured relative to the opacity- and assignment-weighted centroid of the active state. After iterations 18,000 and 21,000, we mean-center the state logits and scale them by 0.3, reducing assignment confidence as the corresponding regularizer becomes active.

item.title: 只重载你改的那个方法：Unity 的 MethodReload 把 play 模式迭代从等域重载缩到几秒 ｜ Skipping domain reload: faster iteration using the MethodReload feature
item.description:
一句话：给方法打上 [MethodReload]，改方法体后下一次调用就吃到新实现，IL2CPP 平台也不用每次重出整包。

要点：

  • 用法：在 Project Settings → Pipeline → Editor 的 Method Reload Interpreter Watch 里点 Start Watching；watcher 覆盖整个 Assets 树，但只编译含 MethodReload 属性的 .cs，无关保存不花代价
  • 按方法粒度注入：只有打了标记的方法体可以被替换，调用点、字段与类型布局不动（不能加字段、不能加类），这条约束正是它能安全作用在运行实例上的原因
  • 限制在三个地方：只能换方法体、解释器只实现 C# 子集（await/Task、try/catch、lock、LINQ 查询语法、ref/out/in、多维数组、泛型方法等都不行）、真机上只能调用播放器已暴露的成员；包内自带 Roslyn 分析器在 IDE 里标出违规
  • 真机路径：构建开 Pipeline 驱动的开发版播放器，之后每次保存都用播放器的预处理宏在编辑器里编译并推到所有连接设备，两端都不用重启；同一功能也暴露为 CLI：reload_file_editor_interpreter / reload_file_player_interpreter

为什么值得看：迭代速度是引擎工程的核心指标之一。这套「按方法粒度热更」的思路和 Unity 新推的 pipeline 包绑定，值得关注它会不会变成团队日常的默认工作流。

中文摘要：改一点玩法代码就要等编辑器做完域重载，是 Unity 开发者共同的痛点；在真机上迭代更糟，每次循环都要完整出包。Unity 的答案是 MethodReload，已在 Unite Seoul 台上演示、现以实验包形式提供：在 Project Settings → Pipeline → Editor 打开 Method Reload Interpreter Watch，进入 play 模式或把开发版播放器连上，之后编辑带 [MethodReload] 标记的方法体，运行中的实例会在下一次调用时拾取新实现，离开 play 模式后改动照常编译走完整域重载。它的代价是明确的约束：只换方法体、不改调用点与类型布局；解释器只支持 C# 子集；真机上只能调用播放器已暴露的成员。包内自带 Roslyn 分析器在 IDE 中提示违规，同一能力也可经 Unity CLI 命令调用。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：Unity Blog（English）

原文发布：2026-10-22

本期推送：2026-10-24

Skipping domain reload: faster iteration using the MethodReload feature

Oct 22, 2026Programming and DevOpsProgramming and DevOps

We've all been there: you tweak some gameplay code and then wait for the Editor to complete a domain reload. The process can slow down your iteration time and really drain your creativity. Not to mention the extra time spent iterating on a device, where each cycle requires a full build.

Our answer to this is MethodReload. We demoed it on stage at Unite Seoul and it is available now as an experimental package. In this post we’ll cover how to use MethodReload, what its limitations are, and how it compares to hot reload tools you may already have in your project.

Why we're stuck reloading

A little history helps here, because the reason domain reload exists is also the reason it's hard to get rid of.

Play Mode was built on Mono's AppDomains where code changes kicked off a familiar process: tear down the domain, load the new assemblies, re-JIT, and then resume in the same process. For years that was a genuine superpower, and it's a big part of why iterating in Unity felt fast compared to building a player.

It's also a blunt instrument, meaning that during the reload everything goes away and everything comes back, whether you changed one method or one hundred. Furthermore, IL2CPP doesn’t support domain reloads at all, so every change requires rebuilding the entire player.

You might be asking yourself, “won't CoreCLR fix this?” and the answer is: Not magically. While CoreCLR does away with domain reloads, it still has to reload assemblies, and MethodReload can help here as well.

How to use MethodReload

As mentioned above, MethodReload is available now and it ships in 

com.unity.pipeline
, currently at 
0.7.0-exp.1
.

The process of using MethodReload is fairly simple. Just tag one or more methods with the 

[MethodReload]
attribute, start the watcher, enter Play Mode or attach a development player, and then edit the body of your methods. The running instance picks up the new body on its next call.

Try it out

The fastest way to understand MethodReload is to run it, so if you’d like to test this out yourself, here are some steps to get you started. Note: since this is an experimental feature, the process may change in the future and be different from what is described here

1. Install the package (Unity 6.0+ required).You can either install it through the Unity CLI or use the Package Manager to add the Pipeline package manually using “Install package by technical name” and this string: 

com.unity.pipeline@0.7.0-exp.1
.

2. Tag the methods you iterate on. The attribute has to be there before you enter Play Mode or build a player, because the dispatch check is woven in at compile time. Tagged methods must be 

public
(instance or static) and return 
void
or 
IEnumerator
; anything else is skipped at build time with a warning.

using Unity.Pipeline.MethodReload;
using UnityEngine;

public class Spinner : MonoBehaviour
{
    public float rotationSpeed = 90f;

    [MethodReload]
    public void Update()
    {
        transform.Rotate(Vector3.up, rotationSpeed * Time.deltaTime);
    }
}

While the watcher covers the whole Assets tree, a saved 

.cs
only compiles if it contains a 
MethodReload
attribute, so unrelated saves cost you nothing.

4. If testing in the editor: enter Play Mode.Once running, any tagged code change will be compiled and injected in place. Once you leave play mode, your changes will compile and go through the usual domain reload.

5. If testing on device: plug in a device. Build a development player with the runtime Pipeline driver enabled. Connect the device with Autoconnect Profiler, or attach through the Profiler or Console window. From then on, every save compiles in the Editor using the player's preprocessor defines and pushes to every connected player. No restart is needed in either direction.

    [MethodReload]
    body you cannot use:

  • await
    and 
    Task
    , 
    try
    /
    catch
    /
    finally
    , 
    lock
    , LINQ query syntax, 
    checked
  • decimal
    , 
    dynamic
    , reflection types, threading types
  • ref
    , 
    out
    , and 
    in
    parameters, 
    ref
    returns and locals, multi-dimensional arrays (jagged is fine), generic methods

    • What does work covers most gameplay code : primitives, method calls, loops, delegates, string interpolation, coroutine 

    yield
    , collections. A Roslyn analyzer ships with the package and flags violations in your IDE, on tagged bodies only, so you find out while typing rather than after a push.
