While previous methods [20, 83, 7] impose symmetry as a loss function to guide networks toward symmetric 3D face reconstruction, EGGHead introduces a lightweight Face Symmetry Module that directly mirrors visible Gaussians across the facial symmetry plane to complement occluded regions without additional networks.

3 Method

Problem Formulation.

Given a single source image Iₛ, our goal is to reconstruct a photorealistic head of an unseen subject. To tackle this non-trivial task, we employ the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) pipeline [45]. 3D-GS models a scene with a set of 3D Gaussians, each defined by a 3D covariance matrix Σ and a center (mean) position p:

G(x)=e^-1/2(x-p)ᵀΣ⁻¹(x-p).

(1)

Each Gaussian G is parameterized by G={p,q,s,α,c} where p∈ℝ³ is the center position, q∈ℝ⁴ is the rotation quaternion, s∈ℝ³ is the scaling factor, α∈ℝ¹ is the opacity, and c∈ℝ³ is the color.

Applying 3D-GS to our task is non-trivial, as we aim to render novel views under (1) a single-view setting, (2) a generalizable model without per-subject fine-tuning, and (3) a reduced number of Gaussians rather than a per-pixel allocation. We explain our solution in the following sections.

Architecture.

Fig. 2 illustrates our pipeline. Given a single source image, our approach generates a photorealistic head representation using a fixed Gaussian budget without per-subject optimization. During training, we introduce the Gaussian Allocation Module (GAM) to achieve an effective trade-off between the number of Gaussians and rendering quality (Sec. 3.1). We employ a Gaussian Attribute Regressor to predict Gaussian attribute maps (Sec. 3.2), guided by Voronoi tessellation [11] for more accurate shape computation (Sec. 3.3). The framework is trained to minimize the difference between the rendered and input images (Sec. 3.7). In inference, GAM is replaced with density-based sampling for efficiency (Sec. 3.5), and a Face Symmetry Module completes the occluded regions (Sec. 3.6).

3.1 Gaussian Allocation Module

Our objective is to efficiently allocate a fixed Gaussian budget while preserving rendering quality. We begin by assigning one Gaussian per pixel, compute the error between adjacent Gaussian pairs based on their mean texture difference, and iteratively merge the pair with the lowest error until reaching the target number of Gaussians M. After each merge, all impacted neighboring Gaussians have their mean texture error updated with the newly merged Gaussian. To prevent oversized Gaussians and sparsely covered regions, we set a maximum threshold such that no Gaussian can occupy more than (5*B)/(M) pixels, where B is the number of foreground pixels in the binary face mask.

The resulting positions of these per-pixel Gaussians form a pseudo ground-truth position map in pixel coordinates. In practice, we convert these pseudo ground-truth position maps into continuous density maps and use them to train a network to directly predict a Gaussian position density map given a source image. We then sample our M Gaussians from the predicted density map (See Sec. 3.5). Using the predicted depth map D together with a scaling factor s_img, the sampled Gaussian centers (iₘ,jₘ) can be lifted from the image plane to 3D as:

Mₚ={(s_img(iₘ-cᵢ, jₘ-cⱼ), D_iₘ,jₘ)}ₘ₌₁^M,

(2)

where (cᵢ,cⱼ) is the center of the image.

3.2 Gaussian Attribute Prediction

We aim to model a generalizable function F(Iₛ,D)={Gₘ}ₘ₌₁^M that estimates the attributes of M Gaussians conditioned on each subject.

Following the allocated Gaussians introduced in Sec. 3.1, we formulate their attributes as pixel-wise maps, allowing a 2D CNN to aggregate neighboring information for local coherence and computational efficiency. Specifically, we compute pixel-wise attribute maps M=Mₚ,M_q,Mₛ,M_α,M_c for position, rotation, scale, opacity, and color, respectively.

The position map Mₚ is constructed directly as described in Sec. 3.1, without regression. The rotation map M_q is obtained from covariance matrices computed by the Voronoi tessellation of sampled Gaussians (see Sec. 3.3). The scale map Mₛ is initialized by Voronoi tessellation and refined with the scale adjustment map Mₛ^γ. Similarly, RGB values are directly used as the color map for efficiency and further refined by the color adjustment map M_c^Δ to improve quality. Therefore, only three attribute maps are regressed:

M={Mₛ^γ,M_α,M_c^Δ}.

(3)

To predict the attribute maps, a source image Iₛ∈[0,1]^H×W×3 is fed into an image encoder 𝔼_img. The image feature 𝔼_img(Iₛ) and the depth feature 𝔼ₐₜₜᵣ(D) are concatenated and then passed to the decoder Dₐₜₜᵣ that generates a pixel-wise Gaussian feature:

F=Dₐₜₜᵣ(𝔼_img(Iₛ)||𝔼ₐₜₜᵣ(D)),

(4)

where F ∈ ℝ^H×W×C and ·||· denotes concatenations across all feature levels. Note that we only regress the scale adjusting map Mₛ^γ, the opacity map M_α, and the color adjusting map M_c^Δ, with corresponding prediction heads hₛ, h_α and h_c composed of two convolutional layers:

\beginarray[]cMₛ^γ=\sigmoid(hₛ(F)), M_α=\sigmoid(h_α(F)), [4.0pt] M_c=Iₛ+M_c^Δ=Iₛ+\tanh(h_c(F)).\endarray

(5)

Details of the network architecture are provided in the supplementary materials.

3.3 Capturing 3D Shapes in Sparse Gaussians

In single-view and sparse Gaussian settings, accurately capturing 3D Gaussian shapes via regression is non-trivial due to limited depth information [40]. To address this, we leverage Voronoi tessellation [11] to provide structural guidance. Given Gaussian centers in 3D coordinates P:={p₁,…,p_M} on a surface, a Voronoi tessellation divides the surface into M regions, each containing points closer to one center. Then, the covariance matrix of the resulting 3D polygon captures its spatial variance and orientation.

However, such intrinsic tessellation has O(M²) time complexity, which is prohibitively high for efficient processing. We therefore perform tessellation in 2D with O(M\logM) time complexity, and lift each region R to 3D using the depth. To compute its covariance matrix C, we partition it into N triangles Tᵢ:

R=T₁∪T₂∪⋯∪T_N-1∪T_N,

(6)

where each triangle vertex is lifted to 3D using its corresponding depth value obtained via nearest-neighbor search.

With the barycenter of the region R computed through an area-weighted average of the triangle centers for the constituent triangles, R’s covariance matrix can be assembled by the covariance matrices of the triangles. The resulting covariance matrix reliably represents the geometric structure of the Voronoi region, capturing its spatial distribution and orientation through its eigen decomposition C=R diag[λ₁,λ₂,λ₃] Rᵀ, where λ₁, λ₂, and λ₃ represent the eigenvalues in descending order and R is the rotation matrix assembled from the eigenvectors.

We then assign the scale attributes of Gaussians as:

s₁=k√λ₁, s₂=k√λ₂, s₃=k√λ₃,

(7)

where k denotes the confidence interval, which in our approach is the scale adjusting map Mₛ^γ. Thus, the final scale map Mₛ is represented as:

Mₛ=Mₛ^γ⊙{√λ}ₘ₌₁^M.

(8)

Next, the rotation matrix R is converted to its quaternion representation q∈ℝ⁴. The rotation map M_q is thus:

M_q={(q_w,qₓ,q_y,q_z)}ₘ₌₁^M.

(9)

With all parameters of G={p,q,s,α,c} defined, we render the reconstructed image Iᵣ.

3.4 Refinement Network

High-fidelity facial rendering typically requires a large number of points to capture appearance details [17]. However, our approach reduces the number of Gaussians for efficiency, and to ensure robust generalization across a vast range of identities, we adopt a source-view reconstruction setting instead of video-based supervision. This inherently limits the ability to recover facial details during novel view synthesis. To address this, we introduce a refinement network. To maintain overall efficiency, we adopt a lightweight U-Net style module. The network takes the coarse output Iᵣ and the alpha map I_α obtained via alpha blending of the Gaussians as input and generates the final output Iᵣ^′. Please refer to the supplementary material for more details on the network architecture.

3.5 Density-based Sampling

Density Map Prediction.

During inference, we replace GAM with density-based sampling to improve computational efficiency. Since directly predicting the discrete coordinates of M Gaussians is sensitive to subtle variations, we learn a continuous density map instead. We generate the ground-truth density map M^GT_d by placing Gaussian centers obtained from GAM on a binary map and smoothing it with a 5×5 Gaussian kernel.

Using the resulting density map M^GT_d as ground-truth, we construct a density prediction network that takes an image Iₛ as input and predicts the corresponding density map:

M_d=D_den(𝔼_den(Iₛ)),

(10)

where M_d is the predicted density map, 𝔼_den the density encoder, and D_den is the density decoder.

Adaptive Sampling.

From the predicted density map M_d, we normalize its values to create a probability distribution ℙ(i,j):

ℙ(i,j)=(M_d(i,j))/(∑ᵢ₌₁^H∑ⱼ₌₁^WM_d(i,j)),

(11)

where H and W denote the height and width of the density map. This distribution turns the density map into a likelihood surface, where larger values yield higher sampling probabilities. We then perform Monte Carlo sampling [33]S to obtain a final set of M Gaussian samples:

{(iₘ,jₘ)}ₘ₌₁^M∼S(ℙ(i,j)),

(12)

where (iₘ,jₘ) represents the coordinates of sampled Gaussian centers. This ensures that areas of higher density yield more samples, capturing regions of interest effectively while maintaining variability and robustness against noise.

3.6 Face Symmetry Module

While our method covers visible regions of the head from the input image well, occluded regions also need to be handled to improve the completeness of the reconstructed head. Human faces typically have sufficient bilateral symmetry to serve as a practical prior. We leverage this symmetry to generate the missing side of the head from a single input image. This design avoids the need for diffusion-based multi-view generation [82, 63] or an additional neural network [51, 17], making the method computationally lightweight.

We introduce a Face Symmetry Module to leverage this prior. We first transform the Gaussians into a canonical view using the camera parameters estimated by DECA [24], where the symmetry plane is fixed as x=0. We then mirror the Gaussians across this plane to create a complementary set for the partially occluded side. Directly combining the original and mirrored Gaussians leads to conflicts in overlapping regions, so we assign low opacity to mirrored Gaussians in overlapped regions and increase their opacity with distance. This yields a smooth transition between the two sets and avoids visible seams. Fig. 3 shows the processes described in Sec. 3.5 and Sec. 3.6.

3.7 Training Objective

Our training pipeline follows two parallel branches starting from the same input image Iₛ, each with its own objective.

3.7.1 Density Prediction Network.

Given Iₛ, the network predicts a density map M_d, and is trained with L2 loss between M_d and M^GT_d:

L_den=∥M_d-M_d^GT∥₂².

(13)

3.7.2 Gaussian Attribute Regressor.

We minimize the regressor loss:

L_reg=λ_refL_ref+λ_coarseL_coarse+λ_αL_α,

(14)

which consists of a refinement loss L_ref, a coarse loss L_coarse and an alpha loss L_α. Further details on loss functions can be found in the supplementary material.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets and Baselines.

We train on 30,000 FFHQ [44] images. For evaluation, we use a disjoint set of 1,000 FFHQ images and 1,000 CelebA-HQ [43] images. To train our density prediction network, we generate pseudo ground-truth Gaussian center maps for all training images using our proposed GAM (Sec. 3.1).

For the baselines, we compare EGGHead’s Gaussian representation quality against single-image head reconstruction methods, including the 3D-aware GANs E3DGE [52] and G-NeRF [98], as well as the 3D-GS based method GAGAvatar [17], using the same M=12k Gaussians setting where applicable.

Implementation Details.

Our networks are trained on a single RTX A6000 GPU using PyTorch [72] and the AdamW [62] optimizer with an input image size of 256×256. We train the density prediction network for 100 epochs and the Gaussian attribute regressor for 100k iterations. For depth estimation, we use Sapiens [46].

4.2 Reconstruction Quality

We first evaluate the reconstruction quality of all methods to assess how well each model reproduces the source view. This provides a direct measure of representation power and fidelity before novel-view synthesis. Specifically, we measure the reconstruction error using PSNR, SSIM [88], and LPIPS [95]. In this experiment, we set the number of Gaussians at M=12k for all test images. As shown in Tab. 1, our model achieves the best performance across all metrics. We also qualitatively compare reconstruction quality in Fig. 5. EGGHead captures the subject’s skin tone more accurately and improves the detail of the hair, mouth, and teeth, thanks to our GAM assigning more Gaussians to those regions.

4.3 Novel View Synthesis

We evaluate EGGHead’s novel view synthesis by rendering subjects under unseen viewpoints. Fig. 4 qualitatively compares our results with baselines. All methods produce visually plausible results. However, 3D-aware GANs [52, 98] struggle to maintain color fidelity, particularly in skin tones, hair, ears, and mouth regions, while GAGAvatar [17] suffers from identity inconsistencies due to weak constraints in occluded regions. In contrast, EGGHead preserves fine facial details through effective and efficient Gaussian allocation and better maintains subject identity, synthesizing novel views directly from subject-specific facial information without relying on additional networks.

We also quantitatively evaluate novel view synthesis in Tab. 2. Similar to [14], we compute pairwise identity consistency (ID) across novel views using AdaFace [47] and FID [36] between the generated novel views and real FFHQ/CelebA-HQ images. EGGHead performs best on both metrics for FFHQ and achieves the best ID score for CelebA-HQ, demonstrating superior identity preservation, multi-view consistency, and overall face quality.

We further evaluate on the multi-view NeRSemble dataset [50] to show the generalization capability of our approach. As shown in Fig. 6, our method best preserves identity while synthesizing novel views, whereas the baselines lose fine details (e.g., facial hair, eyes, earrings). We also achieve the best performance across all metrics quantitatively for NeRSemble novel view synthesis (See Tab. 3).

4.4 Efficiency

We compare model efficiency on two fronts: enrollment time and rendering speed, measured on a single RTX A6000 GPU with AMD EPYC 7713 CPU. One key component in the efficiency of head representations is the latency required to prepare them before rendering. As shown in Tab. 4, 3D-aware GANs [52, 98] require several seconds, while ours reduces this cost to around one second. GAGAvatar [17] directly predicts Gaussian attributes during preparations and relies on a neural renderer in each frame, resulting in a short enrollment time. In contrast, our method uses slightly more computation during preparation to predict accurate Gaussian attributes and renders 3× faster, achieving the fastest rendering speed.

4.5 Ablation Studies

We evaluate the effectiveness of our designs in more detail through ablations. All ablations are trained and evaluated on the aforementioned FFHQ dataset.

Sampling Strategy.

We compare our allocation strategy (adaptive sampling) with three alternative sampling strategies (uniform, landmark, and parsing-guided) in reconstruction quality across Gaussian budgets M. Uniform sampling uniformly samples the head region, and landmark sampling allocates more samples around facial landmarks [48]. Parsing-guided sampling leverages face parsing [92] and allocates more Gaussians to targeted regions such as eyes and hair using fixed budgets for each semantic region. We evaluate under three settings of M: 12k, 8k, and 4k. As shown in Tab. 5, our adaptive sampling generally outperforms other strategies, with lower SSIM than uniform sampling. Fig. 7 visualizes improvements in reconstruction quality. Our allocation algorithm captures fine details such as hair strands, eyes, and teeth more faithfully than uniform sampling. Although landmark sampling yields higher facial detail by allocating more samples around facial landmarks, it results in blurred regions elsewhere, such as hair. We also find that a fixed, deterministic budget for each facial semantic region cannot outperform our adaptive sampling that adjusts for each individual. Our method thus utilizes a limited Gaussian budget more effectively.

Voronoi Tessellation.

We found accurately capturing 3D Gaussian shapes in single-view and sparse-Gaussian settings inherently non-trivial. Thus, we leverage Voronoi tessellation to guide the prediction of M_q and Mₛ. To evaluate its influence, we remove this guidance and let the Gaussian attribute regressor directly predict M_q and Mₛ as well. As shown in Fig. 8, with the same training sets, directly regressing Gaussian attributes without tessellation leads to noticeable hole artifacts in the rendered results. Moreover, under sparser Gaussians (M=4k), scale attributes are overly enlarged, causing facial details to become blurred. Without tessellation, the model achieves a PSNR of 18.53 and 18.14 at M=12k and M=4k, respectively. See Adaptive (Ours) in Tab. 5 for results with tessellation. This shows that tessellation greatly improves the robustness of the regressor in predicting Gaussian attributes.

Mirroring Gaussians.

We fill occluded regions by mirroring Gaussians without relying on diffusion-based multi-view generation or an additional network to keep the model lightweight and efficient (see Fig. 9). As the mirrored Gaussians are exclusively added to the occluded regions, our face symmetry module generates novel views without modifying the visible region. Despite its simplicity, it effectively improves completeness under pose variations while preserving the fidelity of visible regions. This design choice aligns with our objective of achieving reliable head reconstruction while minimizing computational overhead.

5 Conclusion

We’ve proposed EGGHead, a single-image generalizable head modeling method that offers fast enrollment and rendering while maintaining high reconstruction quality. Our Gaussian allocation algorithm assigns appropriate numbers of Gaussians to different semantic head regions, preserving visual fidelity even with lower Gaussian budgets. Our feed-forward design combines a Gaussian allocation and density prediction network with a Gaussian attribute regressor, eliminating expensive per-subject optimization typically required in 3D-GS. In addition, Voronoi tessellation-guided attribute prediction improves structural accuracy under sparse single-view settings, while the Face Symmetry Module enhances completeness without additional heavy networks. We hope our method encourages future work on efficient, high-quality, and generalizable Gaussian heads from single images.

Limitations.

Our model does not decompose texture into albedo and illumination and thus cannot support relighting. Moreover, pseudo-ground truth for Gaussian allocation is derived from single in-the-wild FFHQ images. Multi-view images of the same identity would provide more reliable supervision and higher-quality ground truth. Uneven lighting can also challenge the face symmetry assumption, causing incorrect reflection of shadows or overexposed regions under non-diffuse lighting. This can be mitigated by preprocessing the input image with an off-the-shelf delighting method [60, 35] during enrollment. Finally, fully frontal inputs may prevent complete reconstruction of the back of the head, as symmetry-based completion of occluded regions benefits from a partially visible face profile.


Supplementary Material

6 Network Architecture

We describe the architectures of the Gaussian attribute regressor, the density prediction network, and the refinement network. Please refer to Tab. 6, Tab. 7 and Tab. 8 respectively.

Gaussian Attribute Regressor.

The image encoder 𝔼_img and the attribute encoder 𝔼ₐₜₜᵣ share the same architecture, consisting of convolution, 𝔼₁, 𝔼₂, and 𝔼₃. Image and depth features are concatenated and passed to the attribute decoder Dₐₜₜᵣ through skip connections. Each 𝔼 and D stage consists of two residual blocks. hₛ, h_α, and h_c denote the scale, opacity, and color heads, respectively, which operate on the decoded feature to predict the corresponding Gaussian attributes.

Density Prediction Network.

The network follows a U-net-based encoder decoder design. The encoder 𝔼_den consists of four layers, 𝔼₁–𝔼₄, which increase the number of channels from 3 to 256 while downsampling via max pooling. The decoder D_den comprises three layers, D₁–D₃, each upsampling with transposed convolutions and incorporating skip connections from the corresponding encoder layers. Each stage contains two residual blocks, and a final 1×1 convolution followed by Sigmoid generates the density map.

Refinement Network.

The input is constructed by concatenating the coarse image Iᵣ and the alpha map I_α, producing a 4-channel input. The encoder consists of four stages, 𝔼₁–𝔼₄, which increase the channel dimension from 4 to 384 while reducing the spatial resolution. Each stage contains two 3×3 convolutions followed by group normalization and SiLU activation. A bottleneck layer M further processes the latent feature. The decoder comprises three stages, D₁–D₃, each restoring the spatial resolution with skip connections from the encoder. A final 1×1 convolution predicts a 3-channel residual image, which is multiplied by I_α and added to Iᵣ to produce the refined output Iᵣ^′.

7 Regressor Loss

The regressor loss is defined as:

L_reg=λ_refL_ref+λ_coarseL_coarse+λ_αL_α,

(15)

which consists of the refinement loss L_ref, the coarse loss L_coarse and the alpha loss L_α:

L_ref=λ_L₁L₁(Iᵣ^′,Iₛ)+λₛₛᵢₘLₛₛᵢₘ(Iᵣ^′,Iₛ)(16)
+λ_percL_perc(Iᵣ^′,Iₛ),
L_coarse=λ_L₁L₁(Iᵣ,Iₛ)+λₛₛᵢₘLₛₛᵢₘ(Iᵣ,Iₛ),
L_α=L_bce(I_α,Iₘₐₛₖ),

where Iₘₐₛₖ denotes the foreground mask extracted from the input image Iₛ. We set λ_ref=0.7, λ_coarse=0.3, λ_α=0.1, λ_L₁=0.8, λₛₛᵢₘ=0.2 and λ_perc=0.05.

8 Edge-aware Alignment

In addition to Gaussian merging, we incorporate an edge-aware alignment to ensure smoother transitions near internal boundaries in GAM. Specifically, we extract internal edges from the source image using the Canny edge detector [12]. For each Gaussian center, we then compute its distance to the nearest internal edge and determine its symmetric position P̃ across the nearest edge.

P̃=2·proj(P)-P,

(17)

where proj(P) denotes the projection of P onto the nearest edge. We pair P and P̃ across the boundary while preserving the total budget M. This alignment produces smoother transitions along the edges and preserves overall rendering consistency while reducing discontinuities.

9 Density Prediction

We visualize the predicted density maps that are used to sample Gaussian positions. As shown in Fig. 11, the predicted density maps are generally consistent with the GT density maps and assign higher density to detail-sensitive regions, indicating that the density prediction network learns an effective density distribution for adaptive Gaussian allocation. Notably, EGGHead’s density prediction network also handles more extreme expressions well such as “smiling with teeth” and “surprised with mouth open”.

10 Rendering Speed

The 121.19 FPS reported in the main paper includes the refinement network and head mask generation [92] after splatting, and these steps make the final FPS nearly constant regardless of the number of Gaussians. To show the actual rendering efficiency, we measure pure rendering speed without these steps and further evaluate larger Gaussian budgets of 120k, 80k, and 40k, as summarized in Tab. 9. Even with 120k Gaussians, the pure rendering speed reaches 179.91 FPS, exceeding the 121.19 FPS of the full pipeline with M=12k. This shows that EGGHead maintains real-time rendering performance even with larger Gaussian budgets.

11 Expression Editing

Although our framework is trained for source-view reconstruction with static Gaussians, it enables expression editing at inference time by deforming Gaussians bound to the FLAME mesh [55]. Specifically, each Gaussian center is bound to its closest point on the source FLAME mesh and deformed using the displacement between the source and driving meshes. Compared to GAGAvatar [17], EGGHead is able to match the expression in the driving image more closely. For example, in the second driving image shown below, notice that GAGAvatar’s result still has an open mouth whereas EGGHead is able to appropriately close the lips. GAGAvatar also modifies the gaze direction incorrectly (See the first driving image). In terms of efficiency, we find that editing expressions has very little impact on the rendering speed (121.19 FPS →119.21 FPS), and EGGHead remains real-time. The enrollment time increases from 1.54 seconds to 2.14 seconds due to binding and fitting Gaussians to the source mesh, but it remains shorter than those of E3DGE [52] and G-NeRF [98].

12 Additional Gaussian Budget Comparison

To further analyze the efficiency of our adaptive allocation strategy, we compare our method using 12k Gaussians with GAGAvatar [17] using 24k Gaussians, giving GAGAvatar twice the Gaussian budget. As shown in Table 10, our method achieves competitive or better performance while using only half the number of Gaussians. These results show that our adaptive allocation strategy provides a compact and efficient Gaussian representation by focusing the budget on semantically important facial regions.

13 Additional Qualitative Results

We show more qualitative results for the novel view synthesis (See Fig. 13). Thanks to our GAM, EGGHead noticeably improves over the baselines in representing hair texture, eye structure and color, and other facial details such as creases, wrinkles, and dimples. Our face symmetry module further improves reconstruction quality in occluded regions (e.g. recovering the subject’s occluded ear in the fourth row of Fig. 13).

14 Delighting Preprocessing

As discussed in the main paper, uneven lighting can introduce artifacts when mirroring Gaussians across the facial symmetry plane. Fig. 14 illustrates the effect of applying an off-the-shelf delighting method to the input image during enrollment.

15 Licenses and Responsible Use of Human Data

We use three existing datasets in our work: FFHQ [44], CelebA-HQ [43], and NeRSemble [50]. All datasets allow free use for non-commercial research purposes. Aside from the subject faces, none of them contains any additional personally identifiable information or offensive content.

16 Potential Societal Impacts

Creating photorealistic human heads always has the potential for generating malicious edited content of real subjects. We certainly do not condone such misuse. One potential way to address this problem is to train deepfake methods [3, 4, 32, 1, 61, 18, 41, 68] that can distinguish our generated heads from real images using some of our synthesized heads as part of training data.

（参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：高斯头部的开销取决于光栅化多少个高斯、以及准备头部要多久；按语义区域分配预算，两者一起降。

要点：

  • 核心是一个高斯分配算法：在固定预算下，把高斯按语义区域分给头部不同部位，用更少的高斯保住表征力
  • 单次前向完成，避免了 Gaussian 头部方法常见的漫长 enrollment（逐个优化准备）时间
  • 在重建质量、新视角合成与渲染速度三方面都超过此前的单图人脸建模方法

为什么值得看：数字人进游戏或实时应用，卡的是「每个角色准备多久」和「每帧光栅化多少高斯」。把预算分配显式做成算法，比无脑加高斯更适合放进资产流水线。

中文摘要：做照片级人头一直在表征力、效率与泛化性之间取舍：3DMM 这类网格方案渲染高效但表征力受限；NeRF 方案保真度高却牺牲效率；高斯泼溅想两头兼顾，但效率依旧取决于光栅化多少个高斯，而准备头部的 enrollment 时间往往很长。EGGHead 提出一种高斯分配算法：在固定高斯预算下，把高斯高效分配到头部各语义区域，在尽量不影响表征力的前提下减少所需高斯数量。整个模型单次前向即可出结果，在重建质量、新视角合成与渲染速度上都优于此前单图人脸建模方法。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-16

本期推送：2026-10-24

EGGHead: Efficient Generalizable Gaussian Heads from a Single Image

Abstract

Creating photorealistic human heads typically involves trade-offs between representation power, efficiency, and generalizability. Traditional mesh-based solutions relying on 3DMMs generally sacrifice representation power but are efficient to render. On the other hand, NeRF-based methods improve representation power and fidelity while sacrificing efficiency. Gaussian splatting methods attempt to resolve these trade-offs by offering both high representation power and efficiency with real-time rendering. However, their efficiency nonetheless depends on the number of rasterized Gaussians, and the time needed to optimize and prepare the head (the enrollment time) is often high. In light of this, we propose EGGHead, which introduces a novel Gaussian allocation algorithm that efficiently assigns Gaussians to the head’s semantic regions given a fixed Gaussian budget. Our algorithm reduces the number of Gaussians needed while minimizing the impact on representation power. EGGHead operates in a single forward pass and outperforms previous single-image face modeling methods in reconstruction quality, novel view synthesis, and rendering speeds.

1 Introduction

Modeling photorealistic human heads has received widespread attention from the computer vision and graphics communities. It has a wide array of applications, including movie production [31], digital humans in AR/VR [70, 90, 75, 25], and downstream tasks in the face domain [59, 58]. There are several important axes to consider when designing a head reconstruction method, including representation power, the efficiency of the 3D representation, and data requirements. An ideal method produces a high-quality head that captures fine identity details, enables real-time generation and novel view synthesis, and requires minimal data.

Traditional head representation methods adopt mesh-based approaches that rely on 3DMMs [10] to model the face. Although generally efficient to rasterize and render, and despite a plethora of single-image based methods [86, 83, 53, 84, 6], these 3D representations generally lack high representation power due to reliance on PCA bases, carrying over artifacts from intrinsic decomposition into rendering. The follow-up methods [70, 71, 38, 25, 97, 37] relied instead on the implicit NeRF [65] representation, which allowed for higher representation power thanks to per-pixel raytracing, the ability to model view-specific texture variations, and the volumetric rendering design. However, NeRF-based methods sacrifice efficiency since the raytracing inference stage is often costly. More recently, the face modeling community has favored mesh-driven 3D Gaussian Splatting [45] (3D-GS): a hybrid explicit-implicit representation that allows for both high fidelity and real-time rendering.

Gaussian Splatting, however, is not without limitations. While considered a representation that enables real-time rendering, the efficiency is still affected by the number of Gaussians used to represent the head. In practice, high-quality Gaussian heads require a large number of Gaussians to capture fine geometric and appearance details. Reducing the number of Gaussians is thus an important priority, but if done naively will simply reduce the head’s fidelity. To address this trade-off between fidelity and efficiency, we propose a novel Gaussian Allocation Module (GAM), which efficiently allocates a fixed budget of M Gaussians while minimizing the impact on the head’s fidelity.

Moreover, 3D-GS traditionally relies on monocular or multi-view image/video inputs, is trained per subject instead of being generalizable, and requires an expensive optimization for each subject ranging from a few minutes to one hour [73, 16, 90]. GPS-Gaussian [96] resolves some of these limitations by producing a generalizable method that takes a stereo pair of images as input and predicts Gaussian attributes. However, it requires a monocular video as input, since the method depends on the nearest-neighbor stereo pair for each queried viewpoint. Moreover, it makes the naive assumption of assigning one Gaussian to each pixel, which will naturally reduce the rendering speed. We instead reduce this requirement from a monocular video to a single image while also proposing a generalizable method given one image as input. Our novel GAM improves rendering speed by allocating Gaussians over semantic regions rather than on a per-pixel basis, achieving high fidelity with fewer Gaussians. In addition, we employ Voronoi tessellation [11] to guide Gaussian attribute computation in a single-view setting with sparse Gaussians. Finally, we introduce a lightweight, network-free Face Symmetry Module to render occluded face regions, avoiding expensive post-processing networks and diffusion-based multi-view generation during inference.

Our contributions are thus as follows:

\diamond We propose EGGHead, a single-image and generalizable Gaussian head model that outperforms existing approaches in rendering quality and speed while achieving competitive enrollment time.

\diamond We introduce a Gaussian Allocation Module (GAM) that allocates Gaussians under a fixed budget with minimal impact, employ Voronoi tessellation to guide Gaussian shape computation in a single-view setting with sparse Gaussians, and incorporate a lightweight Face Symmetry Module to improve head completeness without relying on additional networks.

\diamond We demonstrate superior head representation capabilities and fidelity among single-image head reconstruction methods, both quantitatively and qualitatively.

2 Related Work

Face Modeling.

Existing 3D face representations include explicit mesh-based methods [84, 57, 83, 56, 39, 58, 86, 53, 6, 77, 59, 8, 9, 85], implicit NeRF-based [65] methods [25, 74, 70, 26, 5, 29, 71, 27, 89, 97, 37, 13, 94, 38], diffusion models conditioned with 3D priors [21, 42], 3D-aware GANs that incorporate triplane representations [2, 52, 14, 30, 22, 91, 79, 76, 80, 19, 93, 34], and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) [45, 75, 17, 73, 64, 16, 78, 90, 15, 81, 87, 49]. Mesh-based 3DMMs [10] enable fast rendering but are limited in fidelity by their PCA basis. NeRF-based methods improve fidelity through view-dependent neural rendering, but require costly ray sampling. 3D-GS offers high-quality real-time rendering, yet its efficiency depends on the number of Gaussians and still requires seconds to minutes of per-subject enrollment. To address this, we introduce EGGHead, a generalizable model that effectively reduces the Gaussian budget.

Generalizable Gaussian Splatting.

Although 3D-GS is traditionally optimized per scene or subject, generalizable 3D-GS methods have recently gained attention. GPS-Gaussian [96] synthesizes unseen identities but assigns one Gaussian per pixel, limiting efficiency. GAGAvatar [17] predicts Gaussians from a single image using FLAME [55] and dual lifting, but its additional neural renderer may compromise identity consistency. Diffusion-based methods [82, 63] achieve high quality but rely on costly multi-view generation. In contrast, EGGHead uses GAM to merge Gaussians in fidelity-insensitive regions, avoiding dense per-pixel allocation, and multi-view generation.

Efficient Gaussian Splatting.

Several methods improve the efficiency of 3D-GS by compressing Gaussian parameters or pruning low-impact Gaussians. Compression methods [54, 67, 66] reduce storage and rendering costs by removing parameter redundancy, while pruning-based methods [23, 28, 69] reduce the Gaussian count. However, they still rely on costly multi-view optimization. In contrast, our GAM operates from a single image and directly allocates a compact set of Gaussians.

Symmetry in Face Modeling.

Face symmetry is a strong prior that preserves the naturally symmetrical structure of human faces, especially in the ill-posed single-image setting where occluded regions rely on face priors to be properly reconstructed. While previous methods [20, 83, 7] impose symmetry as a loss function to guide networks toward symmetric 3D face reconstruction, EGGHead introduces a lightweight Face Symmetry Module that directly mirrors visible Gaussians across the facial symmetry plane to complement occluded regions without additional networks.

3 Method

Problem Formulation.

Given a single source image Iₛ, our goal is to reconstruct a photorealistic head of an unseen subject. To tackle this non-trivial task, we employ the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) pipeline [45]. 3D-GS models a scene with a set of 3D Gaussians, each defined by a 3D covariance matrix Σ and a center (mean) position p:

G(x)=e^-1/2(x-p)ᵀΣ⁻¹(x-p).

(1)

Each Gaussian G is parameterized by G={p,q,s,α,c} where p∈ℝ³ is the center position, q∈ℝ⁴ is the rotation quaternion, s∈ℝ³ is the scaling factor, α∈ℝ¹ is the opacity, and c∈ℝ³ is the color.

Applying 3D-GS to our task is non-trivial, as we aim to render novel views under (1) a single-view setting, (2) a generalizable model without per-subject fine-tuning, and (3) a reduced number of Gaussians rather than a per-pixel allocation. We explain our solution in the following sections.

Architecture.

Fig. 2 illustrates our pipeline. Given a single source image, our approach generates a photorealistic head representation using a fixed Gaussian budget without per-subject optimization. During training, we introduce the Gaussian Allocation Module (GAM) to achieve an effective trade-off between the number of Gaussians and rendering quality (Sec. 3.1). We employ a Gaussian Attribute Regressor to predict Gaussian attribute maps (Sec. 3.2), guided by Voronoi tessellation [11] for more accurate shape computation (Sec. 3.3). The framework is trained to minimize the difference between the rendered and input images (Sec. 3.7). In inference, GAM is replaced with density-based sampling for efficiency (Sec. 3.5), and a Face Symmetry Module completes the occluded regions (Sec. 3.6).

3.1 Gaussian Allocation Module

Our objective is to efficiently allocate a fixed Gaussian budget while preserving rendering quality. We begin by assigning one Gaussian per pixel, compute the error between adjacent Gaussian pairs based on their mean texture difference, and iteratively merge the pair with the lowest error until reaching the target number of Gaussians M. After each merge, all impacted neighboring Gaussians have their mean texture error updated with the newly merged Gaussian. To prevent oversized Gaussians and sparsely covered regions, we set a maximum threshold such that no Gaussian can occupy more than (5*B)/(M) pixels, where B is the number of foreground pixels in the binary face mask.

The resulting positions of these per-pixel Gaussians form a pseudo ground-truth position map in pixel coordinates. In practice, we convert these pseudo ground-truth position maps into continuous density maps and use them to train a network to directly predict a Gaussian position density map given a source image. We then sample our M Gaussians from the predicted density map (See Sec. 3.5). Using the predicted depth map D together with a scaling factor s_img, the sampled Gaussian centers (iₘ,jₘ) can be lifted from the image plane to 3D as:

Mₚ={(s_img(iₘ-cᵢ, jₘ-cⱼ), D_iₘ,jₘ)}ₘ₌₁^M,

(2)

where (cᵢ,cⱼ) is the center of the image.

3.2 Gaussian Attribute Prediction

We aim to model a generalizable function F(Iₛ,D)={Gₘ}ₘ₌₁^M that estimates the attributes of M Gaussians conditioned on each subject.

Following the allocated Gaussians introduced in Sec. 3.1, we formulate their attributes as pixel-wise maps, allowing a 2D CNN to aggregate neighboring information for local coherence and computational efficiency. Specifically, we compute pixel-wise attribute maps M=Mₚ,M_q,Mₛ,M_α,M_c for position, rotation, scale, opacity, and color, respectively.

The position map Mₚ is constructed directly as described in Sec. 3.1, without regression. The rotation map M_q is obtained from covariance matrices computed by the Voronoi tessellation of sampled Gaussians (see Sec. 3.3). The scale map Mₛ is initialized by Voronoi tessellation and refined with the scale adjustment map Mₛ^γ. Similarly, RGB values are directly used as the color map for efficiency and further refined by the color adjustment map M_c^Δ to improve quality. Therefore, only three attribute maps are regressed:

M={Mₛ^γ,M_α,M_c^Δ}.

(3)

To predict the attribute maps, a source image Iₛ∈[0,1]^H×W×3 is fed into an image encoder 𝔼_img. The image feature 𝔼_img(Iₛ) and the depth feature 𝔼ₐₜₜᵣ(D) are concatenated and then passed to the decoder Dₐₜₜᵣ that generates a pixel-wise Gaussian feature:

F=Dₐₜₜᵣ(𝔼_img(Iₛ)||𝔼ₐₜₜᵣ(D)),

(4)

where F ∈ ℝ^H×W×C and ·||· denotes concatenations across all feature levels. Note that we only regress the scale adjusting map Mₛ^γ, the opacity map M_α, and the color adjusting map M_c^Δ, with corresponding prediction heads hₛ, h_α and h_c composed of two convolutional layers:

\beginarray[]cMₛ^γ=\sigmoid(hₛ(F)), M_α=\sigmoid(h_α(F)), [4.0pt] M_c=Iₛ+M_c^Δ=Iₛ+\tanh(h_c(F)).\endarray

(5)

Details of the network architecture are provided in the supplementary materials.

3.3 Capturing 3D Shapes in Sparse Gaussians

In single-view and sparse Gaussian settings, accurately capturing 3D Gaussian shapes via regression is non-trivial due to limited depth information [40]. To address this, we leverage Voronoi tessellation [11] to provide structural guidance. Given Gaussian centers in 3D coordinates P:={p₁,…,p_M} on a surface, a Voronoi tessellation divides the surface into M regions, each containing points closer to one center. Then, the covariance matrix of the resulting 3D polygon captures its spatial variance and orientation.

However, such intrinsic tessellation has O(M²) time complexity, which is prohibitively high for efficient processing. We therefore perform tessellation in 2D with O(M\logM) time complexity, and lift each region R to 3D using the depth. To compute its covariance matrix C, we partition it into N triangles Tᵢ:

R=T₁∪T₂∪⋯∪T_N-1∪T_N,

(6)

where each triangle vertex is lifted to 3D using its corresponding depth value obtained via nearest-neighbor search.

With the barycenter of the region R computed through an area-weighted average of the triangle centers for the constituent triangles, R’s covariance matrix can be assembled by the covariance matrices of the triangles. The resulting covariance matrix reliably represents the geometric structure of the Voronoi region, capturing its spatial distribution and orientation through its eigen decomposition C=R diag[λ₁,λ₂,λ₃] Rᵀ, where λ₁, λ₂, and λ₃ represent the eigenvalues in descending order and R is the rotation matrix assembled from the eigenvectors.

We then assign the scale attributes of Gaussians as:

s₁=k√λ₁, s₂=k√λ₂, s₃=k√λ₃,

(7)

where k denotes the confidence interval, which in our approach is the scale adjusting map Mₛ^γ. Thus, the final scale map Mₛ is represented as:

Mₛ=Mₛ^γ⊙{√λ}ₘ₌₁^M.

(8)

Next, the rotation matrix R is converted to its quaternion representation q∈ℝ⁴. The rotation map M_q is thus:

M_q={(q_w,qₓ,q_y,q_z)}ₘ₌₁^M.

(9)

With all parameters of G={p,q,s,α,c} defined, we render the reconstructed image Iᵣ.

3.4 Refinement Network

High-fidelity facial rendering typically requires a large number of points to capture appearance details [17]. However, our approach reduces the number of Gaussians for efficiency, and to ensure robust generalization across a vast range of identities, we adopt a source-view reconstruction setting instead of video-based supervision. This inherently limits the ability to recover facial details during novel view synthesis. To address this, we introduce a refinement network. To maintain overall efficiency, we adopt a lightweight U-Net style module. The network takes the coarse output Iᵣ and the alpha map I_α obtained via alpha blending of the Gaussians as input and generates the final output Iᵣ^′. Please refer to the supplementary material for more details on the network architecture.

3.5 Density-based Sampling

Density Map Prediction.

During inference, we replace GAM with density-based sampling to improve computational efficiency. Since directly predicting the discrete coordinates of M Gaussians is sensitive to subtle variations, we learn a continuous density map instead. We generate the ground-truth density map M^GT_d by placing Gaussian centers obtained from GAM on a binary map and smoothing it with a 5×5 Gaussian kernel.

Using the resulting density map M^GT_d as ground-truth, we construct a density prediction network that takes an image Iₛ as input and predicts the corresponding density map:

M_d=D_den(𝔼_den(Iₛ)),

(10)

where M_d is the predicted density map, 𝔼_den the density encoder, and D_den is the density decoder.

Adaptive Sampling.

From the predicted density map M_d, we normalize its values to create a probability distribution ℙ(i,j):

ℙ(i,j)=(M_d(i,j))/(∑ᵢ₌₁^H∑ⱼ₌₁^WM_d(i,j)),

(11)

where H and W denote the height and width of the density map. This distribution turns the density map into a likelihood surface, where larger values yield higher sampling probabilities. We then perform Monte Carlo sampling [33]S to obtain a final set of M Gaussian samples:

{(iₘ,jₘ)}ₘ₌₁^M∼S(ℙ(i,j)),

(12)

where (iₘ,jₘ) represents the coordinates of sampled Gaussian centers. This ensures that areas of higher density yield more samples, capturing regions of interest effectively while maintaining variability and robustness against noise.

3.6 Face Symmetry Module

While our method covers visible regions of the head from the input image well, occluded regions also need to be handled to improve the completeness of the reconstructed head. Human faces typically have sufficient bilateral symmetry to serve as a practical prior. We leverage this symmetry to generate the missing side of the head from a single input image. This design avoids the need for diffusion-based multi-view generation [82, 63] or an additional neural network [51, 17], making the method computationally lightweight.

We introduce a Face Symmetry Module to leverage this prior. We first transform the Gaussians into a canonical view using the camera parameters estimated by DECA [24], where the symmetry plane is fixed as x=0. We then mirror the Gaussians across this plane to create a complementary set for the partially occluded side. Directly combining the original and mirrored Gaussians leads to conflicts in overlapping regions, so we assign low opacity to mirrored Gaussians in overlapped regions and increase their opacity with distance. This yields a smooth transition between the two sets and avoids visible seams. Fig. 3 shows the processes described in Sec. 3.5 and Sec. 3.6.

3.7 Training Objective

Our training pipeline follows two parallel branches starting from the same input image Iₛ, each with its own objective.

3.7.1 Density Prediction Network.

Given Iₛ, the network predicts a density map M_d, and is trained with L2 loss between M_d and M^GT_d:

L_den=∥M_d-M_d^GT∥₂².

(13)

3.7.2 Gaussian Attribute Regressor.

We minimize the regressor loss:

L_reg=λ_refL_ref+λ_coarseL_coarse+λ_αL_α,

(14)

which consists of a refinement loss L_ref, a coarse loss L_coarse and an alpha loss L_α. Further details on loss functions can be found in the supplementary material.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets and Baselines.

We train on 30,000 FFHQ [44] images. For evaluation, we use a disjoint set of 1,000 FFHQ images and 1,000 CelebA-HQ [43] images. To train our density prediction network, we generate pseudo ground-truth Gaussian center maps for all training images using our proposed GAM (Sec. 3.1).

For the baselines, we compare EGGHead’s Gaussian representation quality against single-image head reconstruction methods, including the 3D-aware GANs E3DGE [52] and G-NeRF [98], as well as the 3D-GS based method GAGAvatar [17], using the same M=12k Gaussians setting where applicable.

Implementation Details.

Our networks are trained on a single RTX A6000 GPU using PyTorch [72] and the AdamW [62] optimizer with an input image size of 256×256. We train the density prediction network for 100 epochs and the Gaussian attribute regressor for 100k iterations. For depth estimation, we use Sapiens [46].

4.2 Reconstruction Quality

We first evaluate the reconstruction quality of all methods to assess how well each model reproduces the source view. This provides a direct measure of representation power and fidelity before novel-view synthesis. Specifically, we measure the reconstruction error using PSNR, SSIM [88], and LPIPS [95]. In this experiment, we set the number of Gaussians at M=12k for all test images. As shown in Tab. 1, our model achieves the best performance across all metrics. We also qualitatively compare reconstruction quality in Fig. 5. EGGHead captures the subject’s skin tone more accurately and improves the detail of the hair, mouth, and teeth, thanks to our GAM assigning more Gaussians to those regions.

4.3 Novel View Synthesis

We evaluate EGGHead’s novel view synthesis by rendering subjects under unseen viewpoints. Fig. 4 qualitatively compares our results with baselines. All methods produce visually plausible results. However, 3D-aware GANs [52, 98] struggle to maintain color fidelity, particularly in skin tones, hair, ears, and mouth regions, while GAGAvatar [17] suffers from identity inconsistencies due to weak constraints in occluded regions. In contrast, EGGHead preserves fine facial details through effective and efficient Gaussian allocation and better maintains subject identity, synthesizing novel views directly from subject-specific facial information without relying on additional networks.

We also quantitatively evaluate novel view synthesis in Tab. 2. Similar to [14], we compute pairwise identity consistency (ID) across novel views using AdaFace [47] and FID [36] between the generated novel views and real FFHQ/CelebA-HQ images. EGGHead performs best on both metrics for FFHQ and achieves the best ID score for CelebA-HQ, demonstrating superior identity preservation, multi-view consistency, and overall face quality.

We further evaluate on the multi-view NeRSemble dataset [50] to show the generalization capability of our approach. As shown in Fig. 6, our method best preserves identity while synthesizing novel views, whereas the baselines lose fine details (e.g., facial hair, eyes, earrings). We also achieve the best performance across all metrics quantitatively for NeRSemble novel view synthesis (See Tab. 3).

4.4 Efficiency

We compare model efficiency on two fronts: enrollment time and rendering speed, measured on a single RTX A6000 GPU with AMD EPYC 7713 CPU. One key component in the efficiency of head representations is the latency required to prepare them before rendering. As shown in Tab. 4, 3D-aware GANs [52, 98] require several seconds, while ours reduces this cost to around one second. GAGAvatar [17] directly predicts Gaussian attributes during preparations and relies on a neural renderer in each frame, resulting in a short enrollment time. In contrast, our method uses slightly more computation during preparation to predict accurate Gaussian attributes and renders 3× faster, achieving the fastest rendering speed.

4.5 Ablation Studies

We evaluate the effectiveness of our designs in more detail through ablations. All ablations are trained and evaluated on the aforementioned FFHQ dataset.

Sampling Strategy.

We compare our allocation strategy (adaptive sampling) with three alternative sampling strategies (uniform, landmark, and parsing-guided) in reconstruction quality across Gaussian budgets M. Uniform sampling uniformly samples the head region, and landmark sampling allocates more samples around facial landmarks [48]. Parsing-guided sampling leverages face parsing [92] and allocates more Gaussians to targeted regions such as eyes and hair using fixed budgets for each semantic region. We evaluate under three settings of M: 12k, 8k, and 4k. As shown in Tab. 5, our adaptive sampling generally outperforms other strategies, with lower SSIM than uniform sampling. Fig. 7 visualizes improvements in reconstruction quality. Our allocation algorithm captures fine details such as hair strands, eyes, and teeth more faithfully than uniform sampling. Although landmark sampling yields higher facial detail by allocating more samples around facial landmarks, it results in blurred regions elsewhere, such as hair. We also find that a fixed, deterministic budget for each facial semantic region cannot outperform our adaptive sampling that adjusts for each individual. Our method thus utilizes a limited Gaussian budget more effectively.

Voronoi Tessellation.

We found accurately capturing 3D Gaussian shapes in single-view and sparse-Gaussian settings inherently non-trivial. Thus, we leverage Voronoi tessellation to guide the prediction of M_q and Mₛ. To evaluate its influence, we remove this guidance and let the Gaussian attribute regressor directly predict M_q and Mₛ as well. As shown in Fig. 8, with the same training sets, directly regressing Gaussian attributes without tessellation leads to noticeable hole artifacts in the rendered results. Moreover, under sparser Gaussians (M=4k), scale attributes are overly enlarged, causing facial details to become blurred. Without tessellation, the model achieves a PSNR of 18.53 and 18.14 at M=12k and M=4k, respectively. See Adaptive (Ours) in Tab. 5 for results with tessellation. This shows that tessellation greatly improves the robustness of the regressor in predicting Gaussian attributes.

Mirroring Gaussians.

We fill occluded regions by mirroring Gaussians without relying on diffusion-based multi-view generation or an additional network to keep the model lightweight and efficient (see Fig. 9). As the mirrored Gaussians are exclusively added to the occluded regions, our face symmetry module generates novel views without modifying the visible region. Despite its simplicity, it effectively improves completeness under pose variations while preserving the fidelity of visible regions. This design choice aligns with our objective of achieving reliable head reconstruction while minimizing computational overhead.

5 Conclusion

We’ve proposed EGGHead, a single-image generalizable head modeling method that offers fast enrollment and rendering while maintaining high reconstruction quality. Our Gaussian allocation algorithm assigns appropriate numbers of Gaussians to different semantic head regions, preserving visual fidelity even with lower Gaussian budgets. Our feed-forward design combines a Gaussian allocation and density prediction network with a Gaussian attribute regressor, eliminating expensive per-subject optimization typically required in 3D-GS. In addition, Voronoi tessellation-guided attribute prediction improves structural accuracy under sparse single-view settings, while the Face Symmetry Module enhances completeness without additional heavy networks. We hope our method encourages future work on efficient, high-quality, and generalizable Gaussian heads from single images.

Limitations.

Our model does not decompose texture into albedo and illumination and thus cannot support relighting. Moreover, pseudo-ground truth for Gaussian allocation is derived from single in-the-wild FFHQ images. Multi-view images of the same identity would provide more reliable supervision and higher-quality ground truth. Uneven lighting can also challenge the face symmetry assumption, causing incorrect reflection of shadows or overexposed regions under non-diffuse lighting. This can be mitigated by preprocessing the input image with an off-the-shelf delighting method [60, 35] during enrollment. Finally, fully frontal inputs may prevent complete reconstruction of the back of the head, as symmetry-based completion of occluded regions benefits from a partially visible face profile.


Supplementary Material

6 Network Architecture

We describe the architectures of the Gaussian attribute regressor, the density prediction network, and the refinement network. Please refer to Tab. 6, Tab. 7 and Tab. 8 respectively.

Gaussian Attribute Regressor.

The image encoder 𝔼_img and the attribute encoder 𝔼ₐₜₜᵣ share the same architecture, consisting of convolution, 𝔼₁, 𝔼₂, and 𝔼₃. Image and depth features are concatenated and passed to the attribute decoder Dₐₜₜᵣ through skip connections. Each 𝔼 and D stage consists of two residual blocks. hₛ, h_α, and h_c denote the scale, opacity, and color heads, respectively, which operate on the decoded feature to predict the corresponding Gaussian attributes.

Density Prediction Network.

The network follows a U-net-based encoder decoder design. The encoder 𝔼_den consists of four layers, 𝔼₁–𝔼₄, which increase the number of channels from 3 to 256 while downsampling via max pooling. The decoder D_den comprises three layers, D₁–D₃, each upsampling with transposed convolutions and incorporating skip connections from the corresponding encoder layers. Each stage contains two residual blocks, and a final 1×1 convolution followed by Sigmoid generates the density map.

Refinement Network.

The input is constructed by concatenating the coarse image Iᵣ and the alpha map I_α, producing a 4-channel input. The encoder consists of four stages, 𝔼₁–𝔼₄, which increase the channel dimension from 4 to 384 while reducing the spatial resolution. Each stage contains two 3×3 convolutions followed by group normalization and SiLU activation. A bottleneck layer M further processes the latent feature. The decoder comprises three stages, D₁–D₃, each restoring the spatial resolution with skip connections from the encoder. A final 1×1 convolution predicts a 3-channel residual image, which is multiplied by I_α and added to Iᵣ to produce the refined output Iᵣ^′.

7 Regressor Loss

The regressor loss is defined as:

L_reg=λ_refL_ref+λ_coarseL_coarse+λ_αL_α,

(15)

which consists of the refinement loss L_ref, the coarse loss L_coarse and the alpha loss L_α:

L_ref=λ_L₁L₁(Iᵣ^′,Iₛ)+λₛₛᵢₘLₛₛᵢₘ(Iᵣ^′,Iₛ)(16)
+λ_percL_perc(Iᵣ^′,Iₛ),
L_coarse=λ_L₁L₁(Iᵣ,Iₛ)+λₛₛᵢₘLₛₛᵢₘ(Iᵣ,Iₛ),
L_α=L_bce(I_α,Iₘₐₛₖ),

where Iₘₐₛₖ denotes the foreground mask extracted from the input image Iₛ. We set λ_ref=0.7, λ_coarse=0.3, λ_α=0.1, λ_L₁=0.8, λₛₛᵢₘ=0.2 and λ_perc=0.05.

8 Edge-aware Alignment

In addition to Gaussian merging, we incorporate an edge-aware alignment to ensure smoother transitions near internal boundaries in GAM. Specifically, we extract internal edges from the source image using the Canny edge detector [12]. For each Gaussian center, we then compute its distance to the nearest internal edge and determine its symmetric position P̃ across the nearest edge.

P̃=2·proj(P)-P,

(17)

where proj(P) denotes the projection of P onto the nearest edge. We pair P and P̃ across the boundary while preserving the total budget M. This alignment produces smoother transitions along the edges and preserves overall rendering consistency while reducing discontinuities.

9 Density Prediction

We visualize the predicted density maps that are used to sample Gaussian positions. As shown in Fig. 11, the predicted density maps are generally consistent with the GT density maps and assign higher density to detail-sensitive regions, indicating that the density prediction network learns an effective density distribution for adaptive Gaussian allocation. Notably, EGGHead’s density prediction network also handles more extreme expressions well such as “smiling with teeth” and “surprised with mouth open”.

10 Rendering Speed

The 121.19 FPS reported in the main paper includes the refinement network and head mask generation [92] after splatting, and these steps make the final FPS nearly constant regardless of the number of Gaussians. To show the actual rendering efficiency, we measure pure rendering speed without these steps and further evaluate larger Gaussian budgets of 120k, 80k, and 40k, as summarized in Tab. 9. Even with 120k Gaussians, the pure rendering speed reaches 179.91 FPS, exceeding the 121.19 FPS of the full pipeline with M=12k. This shows that EGGHead maintains real-time rendering performance even with larger Gaussian budgets.

11 Expression Editing

Although our framework is trained for source-view reconstruction with static Gaussians, it enables expression editing at inference time by deforming Gaussians bound to the FLAME mesh [55]. Specifically, each Gaussian center is bound to its closest point on the source FLAME mesh and deformed using the displacement between the source and driving meshes. Compared to GAGAvatar [17], EGGHead is able to match the expression in the driving image more closely. For example, in the second driving image shown below, notice that GAGAvatar’s result still has an open mouth whereas EGGHead is able to appropriately close the lips. GAGAvatar also modifies the gaze direction incorrectly (See the first driving image). In terms of efficiency, we find that editing expressions has very little impact on the rendering speed (121.19 FPS →119.21 FPS), and EGGHead remains real-time. The enrollment time increases from 1.54 seconds to 2.14 seconds due to binding and fitting Gaussians to the source mesh, but it remains shorter than those of E3DGE [52] and G-NeRF [98].

12 Additional Gaussian Budget Comparison

To further analyze the efficiency of our adaptive allocation strategy, we compare our method using 12k Gaussians with GAGAvatar [17] using 24k Gaussians, giving GAGAvatar twice the Gaussian budget. As shown in Table 10, our method achieves competitive or better performance while using only half the number of Gaussians. These results show that our adaptive allocation strategy provides a compact and efficient Gaussian representation by focusing the budget on semantically important facial regions.

13 Additional Qualitative Results

We show more qualitative results for the novel view synthesis (See Fig. 13). Thanks to our GAM, EGGHead noticeably improves over the baselines in representing hair texture, eye structure and color, and other facial details such as creases, wrinkles, and dimples. Our face symmetry module further improves reconstruction quality in occluded regions (e.g. recovering the subject’s occluded ear in the fourth row of Fig. 13).

14 Delighting Preprocessing

As discussed in the main paper, uneven lighting can introduce artifacts when mirroring Gaussians across the facial symmetry plane. Fig. 14 illustrates the effect of applying an off-the-shelf delighting method to the input image during enrollment.

15 Licenses and Responsible Use of Human Data

We use three existing datasets in our work: FFHQ [44], CelebA-HQ [43], and NeRSemble [50]. All datasets allow free use for non-commercial research purposes. Aside from the subject faces, none of them contains any additional personally identifiable information or offensive content.

16 Potential Societal Impacts

Creating photorealistic human heads always has the potential for generating malicious edited content of real subjects. We certainly do not condone such misuse. One potential way to address this problem is to train deepfake methods [3, 4, 32, 1, 61, 18, 41, 68] that can distinguish our generated heads from real images using some of our synthesized heads as part of training data.

（参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 给网格上的连续流证明单射：调和函数的 90° 旋转梯度，解一个稀疏线性系统就够 ｜ A Tutte-Like Theorem for Injective Flows on Meshes
item.description:
一句话：类比 Tutte 嵌入，把调和性与单射性连起来：两条流线保证不相交，且流场可微、能在保单射前提下做梯度优化。

要点：

  • 在球面网格上计算离散调和函数，取它旋转 90° 的梯度作为向量场，得到的流是单射的：任意两点沿流推进，轨迹不会相交
  • 核心洞察是离散调和 1-形式的 Poincaré-Hopf 指标刻画，与单射向量场的组合规则相对应
  • 与 Tutte 嵌入一样只需解一个稀疏线性系统；流场可微地依赖 Laplacian 元素，因此能在不违反单射的前提下做无约束梯度优化

为什么值得看：参数化、网格变形、UV 展开里最难处理的就是翻转。这里给了一个「构造即无翻转」的流场，还能上梯度优化——比事后检测加惩罚更干净。

中文摘要：这篇论文证明了一个关于三角网格上由离散向量场定义的连续流是否单射的定理。与 Tutte 嵌入类似，定理把调和性与单射性连了起来：在球面网格上计算离散调和函数，取其旋转 90° 的梯度作为向量场，得到的流是单射的，即两点沿该场推进时轨迹保证不相交。证明的关键在于离散调和 1-形式的 Poincaré-Hopf 指标刻画与单射向量场的组合规则之间的对应。和 Tutte 嵌入一样，这个单射向量场可以通过求解一个稀疏线性系统得到；更重要的是它可微地依赖 Laplacian 的元素，因此能在无约束的梯度优化中始终保持单射性。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-08-06

本期推送：2026-10-24

A Tutte-Like Theorem for Injective Flows on Meshes

Abstract

This work proves a theorem regarding injectivity of continuous flows that are defined via discrete vector fields on triangle meshes. In similar fashion to Tutte’s embedding, the theorem shows a connection between harmonicity and injectivity. Specifically, a discrete harmonic function is computed over a spherical mesh, and its 90^∘-rotated gradients are taken as the vector field. We show that this leads to an injective flow over the mesh, i.e., when two points are advected along the vector field, their trajectories are guaranteed to not intersect. The core insight behind this theorem is that the characterization of the Poincaré-Hopf indices of discrete harmonic 1-forms is paralleled in the combinatorial rules for injective vector fields. Similarly to Tutte’s embedding, the injective vector field can be computed by simply solving a sparse linear system. Furthermore, it is differentiably dependent on the entries of the Laplacian, enabling unconstrained gradient-based optimization of the vector field while preserving injectivity. The advection itself can be computed by a quick and accurate algorithm. We experimentally validate the injectivity of the results, as well as show examples of differentiable optimization, such as computing an injective approximation to a given non-injective vector field, and fitting an injective vector field to satisfy constraints.

1 Introduction

This paper proposes a method for producing discrete, triangle-based tangent vector fields that define injective flows over triangle meshes, i.e., advecting points along the vector field yields continuous trajectories for any given point on the surface, such that the trajectories of any two points do not cross. Figure 1 shows such an advection of randomly sampled points on a mesh, their trajectories traced behind them as faded paths.

The mathematical challenge in ensuring the induced flow is injective lies in the discrete nature of the vector field. Indeed, when considering a continuous vector field, to ensure injectivity it is sufficient to require the vector field to be Lipschitz (per the Picard–Lindelöf theorem). In contrast, discrete, face-based vector fields are piecewise-constant and discontinuous; thus, their injectivity is a much more brittle property, which requires a different, more discrete approach, such as the satisfaction of combinatorial, triangle-based rules [campen2016].

Our main theoretical contribution – Theorem 1 – is akin to a flow-based version of Tutte’s embedding [tutte1963, floater1997parametrization], proving that a specific class of discrete harmonic functions induces injective flows. Specifically, we prove that solving a discrete Laplace equation on a spherical mesh with specific boundary conditions yields a discrete harmonic function whose gradient vectors, rotated by 90^∘, define an injective flow. Geometrically, this implies that each point’s trajectory lies on a fixed level set of the harmonic function. Similarly to Tutte’s embedding, these vector fields can be computed in a simple and efficient manner by solving a sparse linear system.

Theorem 1 is attained through two main insights (Lemmas 1 and 2) regarding a connection between two rather different approaches for injective mappings of triangle meshes: the framework of bijective foliations[campen2016] defines conditions on vector fields to yield injective paths on meshes; however, these conditions are combinatorial, and hence were previously attained by constructing these vector fields in a combinatorial, algorithmic manner. We observe that these conditions for injectivity are exactly reflected in harmonic functions’ specific properties (namely, a discrete Poincaré-Hopf index theorem) that were characterized by Gortler et al. [gortler2006] – see Figure 6, which exhibits the equivalence between the two approaches. This observation, in turn, enables the construction of vector fields that satisfy the injectivity conditions from [campen2016] via harmonic functions.

While we consider the proof our main technical contribution, it holds a secondary practical implication of a differentiable parameterization of injective flows on meshes: any assignment of positive edge weights of the Laplacian matrix modifies the Laplace equation, and hence the resulting vector field and flow, in a differentiable manner. Furthermore, our discrete vector field defines a flow that is piecewise-linear on the triangles of the mesh, leading to simple, efficient and accurate computation, in contrast to techniques that define flows via non-discrete, continuous vector fields [chen2018neural, chen2023riemannianfm]; in order to compute their corresponding flow, one needs to integrate the vector field via quadrature rules, which is both expensive and may lead to inaccuracies.

To verify our theory, we validate the injectivity of our vector field both qualitatively and quantitatively. We additionally show preliminary demonstrations of the utility of a differentiable representation of injective vector fields, by optimizing the injective field to best approximate a given non-injective field, or fitting it to satisfy constraints.

2 Related Works

Vector field design.

Vector field design has been heavily studied in computer graphics and geometry processing [zhang2006vector, degoes2016, vaxman2016]. Similarly to our approach, previous papers have considered vector fields as gradients of functions [diamanti2015integrable] and sought to integrate them [ray2006periodic]. This integration is similar to a flow and is especially common in the context of global parameterization [myles2014robust] and quad-meshing [bommes2013quad]. In these applications, the cases leading to non-injectivity of the flow simply lead to singularities in the parameterization/quad mesh (and not to loss of injectivity of, e.g., the parameterization) – these are in general acceptable, hence those methods usually focus on minimizing the number of such singularities. Many works focus solely on unit-length vector fields [solomon2019optimal, boksebeld2022high, verhoeven2022dev2pq, palmer2024lifting, wang2025power] and their extensions to polyvector fields [palacios2007rotational, bommes2010practical, diamanti2014designing, panozzo2014frame] in which the flow direction can be chosen out of several options at each triangle. Another common goal is optimizing the smoothness of the vector/directional field [fisher2007design, knoppel2013globally], while ensuring adherence to singularity assignment [crane2010]; others optimize for vector fields which produce an as-rigid-as-possible flow [benchen2010killing]. Flows on vector fields additionally have a close connection to geodesics [sharp2019vector, vekhter2019weaving].

Injective maps between meshes.

The flows we compute define a map between a mesh and itself; defining such injective mappings of meshes is a highly researched area. Most previous approaches use a common domain into which the meshes are mapped, thereby defining a mapping by composition of maps into the common domain [kraevoy2004, aigerman2014lifted, aigerman2015seamless, aigerman2016hyperbolic, morreale2021, schmidt2020inter]. Of note is one of the first works on mesh-mesh injective mappings [schreiner2004inter], which directly deals with injectively sliding the vertices of one mesh over the triangles of the other in a sort of ad hoc flow. Bijective maps between domains can also be defined via integral curves [huynh2015], global structural decompositions [nieser2011, bommes2013, hinderink2024], or by auxiliary structures [jiang2020, jiang2021, liu2024]. Lastly, simplicial foliations [campen2016, hinderink2021] can be used for defining vector-aligned slices on surfaces and volumes, and then matching between corresponding slices on two meshes. These slices are in turn created by an injective vector field – we directly use the conditions formulated by [campen2016] and show they hold for specific harmonic functions.

Harmonic functions and injective mappings.

There is a deep connection between harmonic functions over 2-manifolds and injective mappings, with the most central results being the Radó–Kneser–Choquet theorem and its discrete counterpart, Tutte’s embedding [tutte1963, floater1997parametrization, floater2003one]. Tutte’s embedding states that computing two discrete harmonic functions representing the x,y coordinates of a disk-topology mesh, while prescribing the boundary conditions to a convex polygon, yields an injective embedding of the mesh to 2D. This has been extended further into other topologies [gortler2006, aigerman2015orbifold] and non-Euclidean target domains [tsui2013globally, aigerman2016hyperbolic, aigerman2017spherical]. Other methods use more complex harmonic structures for injectivity, which require more careful optimization [bright2017harmonic, hefetz2019subspace]. Previous works have considered the use of harmonic functions and flowing via their gradients for quad-meshing [dong2005harmonic], without considerations of injectivity, and for injective parameterization, but not flows [tong2006designing]. Some use harmonic gradients for constructing maps; however, the injectivity of these is guaranteed only in the smooth setting, relying on the harmonic maps’ infinite smoothness [lin2015interior] and the existence of hessians [xia2010direct]. In contrast, we prove a discrete theorem, showing that injectivity holds directly on the discrete gradients of the discrete harmonic function, for any Laplacian matrix. We further leverage the fact that discrete harmonic functions are defined with respect to any Laplacian matrix defined with positive weights on the mesh’s edges, and optimize the injective vector field via the Laplacian’s entries. Such optimization of the Laplacian in order to control injective maps has been performed before [aigerman2024generative, sun2024tuttenet].

Computing continuous flows.

Computing continuous injective flows is a highly active area, especially in machine learning where it is used for generative techniques [lipman2023]. These flows can be computed in a differentiable process via a neural network that produces a continuous vector field on Euclidean spaces [chen2018neural] and on manifolds [falorsi2020, lou2020, mathieu2020, bose2020, rozen2021, chen2024, benhamu2022]. Some previous works have used such flows to define deformations of 3D shapes [jiang2020shapeflow]. Injectivity is guaranteed as long as the vector field is Lipschitz. In contrast, we focus on piecewise-constant vector fields defined on a piecewise-flat triangle mesh, and on ensuring they still define an injective flow.

3 Problem Setting and Goal

3.1 Preliminaries

We consider sphere-topology manifold triangle meshes M. We will focus on working with oriented half-edgese=(i,j), where, for a triangle (i,j,k), its oriented half-edges follow the triangle’s orientation: (i,j),(j,k),(k,i). Note that each half-edge belongs to exactly one triangle. The twin half-edge of e=(i,j) is denoted \reflectboxe=(j,i). Each such half-edge has its edge normal, defined as the vector obtained by inverting the unit-normalized directed edge vector and rotating it by 90^∘ in the tangent plane of its triangle:

nₑᵗ=-R^90^∘ₜ(vⱼ-vᵢ)/\lVertvᵢ-vⱼ\rVert,

(1)

where R^90^∘ₜ is the matrix that rotates vectors in the tangent plane of triangle t by 90^∘. Note that this normal points inward into the triangle, towards the vertex k opposite to the edge (i,j).

We will consider discrete functions, i.e., an assignment of a scalar zᵢ to each vertex vᵢ of the mesh. We will also use the mesh’s gradient operator ∇, defined via linear finite elements, assigning to each triangle the gradient vector of the affine function interpolating between the three values on the vertices, denoted ∇ₜz.

In standard fashion, we assign a piecewise-constant vector field u over the faces of the mesh, defined by assigning a tangent vector uₜ∈Tₜ to each triangle t of the mesh (see Figure 4). Each half-edge e thus has exactly one corresponding tangent vector, belonging to the triangle t that contains e.

A flow over the mesh is defined for any point p∈M (not necessarily a vertex), assigning it a continuous path pₜ parameterized by a time parameter t∈[0,1] such that the flow starts from p, i.e., p₀=p, and advects that point to somewhere else. The derivative with respect to time t is denoted (∂pₜ)/(∂t). We consider flows with respect to a vector field u such that the flow “agrees” with the vector field inside each triangle, namely, if at time t^* the point p_t^* is strictly inside triangle t – i.e., away from the triangle’s edges – then the speed vector of the point is equal to the vector field assigned to that triangle,

(∂pₜ)/(∂t)(t^*)=uₜ(if $p_t^*∈t$).

(2)

In other words, the vector field defines a flow inside each triangle by advecting each point using the vector field as the temporal derivative, which for a constant vector field reduces to a linear formula:

pₜ=p₀+tuₜ.

(3)

Since the vector field is piecewise-constant, the flow is piecewise-linear, as the inset illustrates.

The question of how to well-define the flow when the point crosses over between triangles (over an edge or a vertex) is equivalent to ensuring the flow is injective. Figure 4 shows examples of flows, where the purple point is flowed to its end position marked by a red X.

To tackle injectivity, we will show that a harmonic function’s gradient field satisfies the combinatorial rules for injectivity from [campen2016]. We next review these rules, and reformulate them into a formulation more suited to our needs, using the notion of edge/vertex fluxes, illustrated in Figure 4.

3.2 Fluxes

We begin by discussing fluxes over edges (which will be subsequently used to also define fluxes over vertices). We say the half-edge e has positive flux if there exists a point inside its corresponding triangle, p∈t, such that the flow defined by uₜ will flow this point to lie on the edge e. Inversely, we say the vector has negative flux with respect to the edge e if there is a point p on the edge e which would flow into the triangle.

We denote the edge flux on the half-edge e as Fₑ∈{+1,-1}. Geometrically, it corresponds to the inverted sign of the dot product of the vector with the edge normal:

Definition 1(Edge flux).

The edge flux Fₑ on edge e is defined as

Fₑ=-sign().

(4)

See Figure 4, top row, where a +/- sign denotes the flux over the corresponding half-edge, the purple point is the starting point p and the red X marks the final point. Note that we assume we do not encounter the case of a vector field parallel to the edge (no point is flowed into or out of that edge, and the inner product is zero).

We now move on to discuss fluxes on vertices. Consider a triangle t, the corresponding vector on the triangle uₜ, and one of the vertices v of that triangle. We say the vector has positive flux with respect to the vertex v if there exists a point on the triangle, p∈t, such that the flow defined by uₜ will flow this point to lie on the vertex v. We say the vector has negative flux with respect to the vertex v if a point starting from the vertex flows into the triangle. Finally, we say there is no flux in all other cases, which essentially correspond to the vertex neither flowing inside nor outside of this triangle.

To formalize these conditions geometrically: note that the vertex lies on the intersection of two of the triangle’s edges, e₁,e₂. Therefore, for a point p to flow to the vertex, it must flow into both edges, hence the vector uₜ must have positive edge flux into both edges sharing that vertex. Similarly, for the vertex to flow into the triangle, the vector uₜ must have negative flux into both edges sharing the vertex.
