In the remaining case (no vertex flux), the vector has positive flux on one edge, and negative flux on the other. See Figure 4, bottom for an illustration of these cases.

Definition 2(Vertex flux).

The flux on vertex v with respect to triangle t is defined via the edge fluxes as:

Fᵗᵥ=\begincases+1&ifF_(v,i)=+1andF_(j,v)=+1 -1&ifF_(v,i)=-1andF_(j,v)=-1 0&ifF_(v,i)=-F_(j,v)\endcases

(5)

3.3 Injectivity Conditions, Defined via Fluxes

Any vector field well-defines a flow in the interior of the triangle, but not necessarily on the boundary of the triangle: two points on two triangles may flow into the same point either on an edge or on a vertex. This is equivalent to non-injectivity. [campen2016] define specific conditions that ensure injectivity, which we review next while reformulating them for our needs.

First, it is immediate to observe (e.g., via Figure 5, left and center) that the vector field is injective over the half-edges e and e iff e has flux (per Definition 1) with a sign opposite to that of e,

Fₑ=-F_\reflectboxe

(6)

The flow of a point p is then defined by the vector with the negative flux, which flows points away from the edge.

Property 1(edge injectivity).

The vector field is injective over a half-edge e, if its flux over that half-edge satisfies Equation (6).

We move on to vertex injectivity. We classify the injectivity on a vertex into three cases:

  • 1.

    If the point p lies on a vertex and is flowed somewhere, for the flow to be well-defined (and injective) there must be exactly one triangle with a vector that has negative flux to the vertex, and one triangle that has positive flux from the vertex. All other triangles have no flux with respect to the vertex. This is the case of a regular injective vertex (see Figure 6, top left). The vector that has outgoing flow with respect to the vertex is chosen to define the flow.

  • 2.

    If the vertex is not flowed and stays in place, then all triangles in the 1-ring have zero vertex flux, implying the flow rotates around the vertex (Figure 6, bottom left). This is a vortex injective vertex.

  • 3.

    All other cases are non-injective vertices.

    • Property 2(Vertex injectivity).

    The vector field is injective over a vertex if its flux on that vertex is either regular injective or vortex injective, per the classification above.

    Our goal is thus to characterize a family of vector fields that satisfy the two above properties for injectivity.

    4 Injective Flows via Harmonic Functions

    Towards producing an injective vector field and proving its injectivity, this section progresses in three steps:

  • 1.

    (Section 4.1) Compute a harmonic function z.

  • 2.

    (Section 4.2) Define a vector field u as the 90^∘-rotated gradient of the harmonic function, and show that its flux F is exactly equal to a 1-form δ defined by z.

  • 3.

    (Section 4.3) Use the 1-form’s properties to show it satisfies the necessary injectivity properties from Section 3.3, thereby showing that F satisfies them as well.

    • 4.1 Computing a Discrete Harmonic 1-Form.

    We define a discrete Laplace equation on the mesh: we choose two vertices to serve as source/target, designated s,t. We also assume to have a Laplacian L, with any desired positive weights wᵢⱼ on each edge (e.g., these can either be positively-clamped cotan weights [pinkall1993], or ones that are optimized). We solve the discrete Laplace equation with boundary conditions defined by s,t and using the Laplacian L:

    \beginarray[]llzᵢ=1&i=s zᵢ=-1&i=t (Lz)ᵢ=0&else\endarray

    		(7)

    Similar to [gortler2006], for any half-edge e=(i,j), we define the 1-form

    δₑ=zⱼ-zᵢ,

    		(8)

    assigning a real number to that half-edge. See Figure 5, right, for an example of such z and the resulting 1-form δ. Note we assume z is such that the 1-form is non-vanishing on any edge (δₑ≠0); otherwise, similarly to the argument made in Appendix A in [gortler2006], we can perturb the 1-form by an infinitesimal amount to make it non-vanishing, without changing any of the assumptions necessary for the proof.

    4.2 Constructing an Injective Vector Field from the Harmonic Function

    We define our vector field on each triangle t as the gradient vector rotated by 90^∘:

    uₜ=R^90^∘∇ₜz,

    		(9)

    which leads to the main theoretical result of this paper:

    Theorem 1.

    The flow induced by the vector field u, defined in Equation (9), is injective.

    The following Section 4.3 proves the above theorem. Similarly to Tutte’s embedding [tutte1963], injectivity holds for a very specific setting: a sphere-topology mesh, with one source and one sink – see Figure 3 for a non-injective example when attempting the same technique on a mesh of a different genus.

    Geometrically, the rotated gradient vector field points in a direction tangent to a level set of z; thus, the resulting injective flow defines a trajectory that marches along a fixed level set of z, in a direction designated by the orientation of the mesh. The source and sink vertices s,t serve as two vortex points (the flow rotates around them and they are stationary). Note, however, that when using Laplacians with random weights (Figure 7, 8) or optimized ones (Figures 10, 11), the level sets become more intricate and enable different flows.

    4.3 Injectivity of the Flow (Proof of Theorem 1)

    We aim to provide a streamlined proof that highlights the key insights leading to the main result; as such, we prove all the necessary lemmas in Appendix A. To prove injectivity of the vector field, we need to prove that the injective properties regarding its fluxF (Section 3.3) hold. The key connection between the harmonic function z and the flux F is that on each edge e, the flux Fₑ is exactly equal to the sign of the 1-form δₑ.

    Lemma 1(flux/1-form equivalence).

    The edge flux of the vector field u defined in Equation (9) is equal on all edges to the 1-form defined in Equation (8):

    Fₑ=sign(δₑ).

    		(10)

    We use this equivalence to prove edge/vertex flux injectivity.

    To prove edge injectivity, we need to prove Property 1 in Section 3.3: Fₑ=-F_\reflectboxe. Per Lemma 1, this is equivalent to proving δₑ=-δ_\reflectboxe. This last equation is immediate to deduce from Equation (8) which implies the anti-symmetry of δ (see also the half-edges shared between the two triangles in Figure 5, right). Hence, we assume the vector field is edge-injective and turn to proving vertex injectivity:

    Theorem 2(Vertex injectivity).

    Let M, z be as above. Then the vector field defined by Equation (9) is vertex-injective as defined in Property 2, Section 3.3.

    To prove this theorem, we draw a connection between the flux conditions of Campen et al. [campen2016] and the behavior of indices of harmonic 1-forms described in  Gortler et al. [gortler2006].

    Proof of Theorem 2.

    We turn to [gortler2006]. We consider their Theorem 3.5 (essentially a discrete Poincaré-Hopf theorem), and interpret it in our scenario. They define an indexind(vₒ) assigning an integer for each vertex vₒ. The index of the vertex vₒ is defined by stepping over its 1-ring edges in order, each oriented in outgoing direction (o,1),(o,2)...,(o,k), and checking how many times the 1-form δ_o,j changes signs, with the index, ind(vₒ), being equal to 1, 0 or -1 based on zero, two, or more than two sign changes, respectively (see Figure 6, right column).

    The proof hinges on the following Lemma 2, which shows an equivalence between the aforementioned index classification and our version (Section 3.3, Property 2) of the classification from Campen et al. [campen2016] of injective and non-injective vertices. Figure 6 portrays this equivalence between the left and right images in each row.

    Lemma 2.

    The vertex v has index 1 iff it is a regular injective vertex, an index 0 iff it is a vortex injective vertex, and index -1 iff it is a non-injective vertex, per the definition in Section 3.3, Property 2.

    Hence, to ensure all vertices are injective, all we need to show is that there are no vertices with ind(v)=-1. We prove a slightly stronger version of this claim using standard arguments [gortler2006]:

    Lemma 3.

    Let M, z and δ be as described above. Then all vertices have index 0, except for the source and sink vertices s,t, which have index 1.

    Thus, no vertex has negative index, entailing that all vertices are injective, and we have proven Theorem 2. ∎

    With this, we have proven that both edge injectivity and vertex injectivity hold, thereby proving Theorem 1 and global injectivity of the flow.

    4.4 Vector Field and Flow computation

    We summarize the vector field construction in Algorithm 1. Each step of this algorithm is differentiable, and thus it provides a differentiable parameterization of injective vector fields, as a function of the Laplacian’s (arbitrary) edge weights Lᵢⱼ.

    Lastly, to flow a given point p∈M on a triangle t with respect to the vector field u for a given amount of time T∈ℝ, we propose a simple, efficient, and accurate algorithm, described in Algorithm 2, which walks on the level sets of z. The flow is piecewise linear and only needs to be evaluated at each intersection point with an edge. The choice of which edge is the next to be intersected, as well as the exact location on the edge on which the intersection happens, can all be easily deduced by simple arithmetic involving the value c of the level set and the values of z on the vertices. Since the algorithm relies on the initial level set to find the intersection points, it does not suffer from accumulated error and can self-correct to always follow the level set (see Table 1).

    5 Results

    As our main contribution is the theoretical Theorem 1, we next empirically verify its correctness, show qualitative examples of injective flows, and also validate the ability of the differentiable pipeline to enable gradient-based optimization. We note that the injectivity of a vector field does not depend on the magnitude of the vectors and hence opt to normalize all vectors to unit norm.

    5.1 Empirical Evidence of Injectivity and Accuracy

    We begin by empirically validating the injectivity of the flows, as well as the accuracy of our advection algorithm, Algorithm 2. We flow a given point for a certain amount of time, and then flip the vector field and flow the resulting point “back in time” – we visualize this experiment in Figure 8 with red/yellow for forward/backward paths, validating injectivity as well as exhibiting the accuracy of the algorithm. For quantitative evaluation, we repeat this process for random source and sink vertices alongside a random initialization of Laplacian weights, sample 100,000 random points, and measure the error between the start point and the point flowed back via the two steps above. We report the aggregated Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Maximum Absolute Error (MXE) in Table 1. No error exceeds 10⁻⁸ on average and 10⁻⁵ at maximum. A few models with triangles that have very small area or are near-degenerate result in less accurate results, mainly because of inaccuracy in numerics of the harmonic equation/gradient operator leading to a slight drift in the calculation of the time it takes to cross an edge.

    5.2 Flows Defined from Different Types of Laplacians

    Theorem 1 guarantees an injective flow for any valid configuration of strictly positive Laplacian weights. In Figure 2 we show flows computed via the cotangent Laplacian [pinkall1993] (clamped to have only positive weights) and via the Mean Value Coordinates (MVC) [floater2003mean] Laplacian. These lead to smooth flows along the harmonic isolines. To show more elaborate flows, Figure 7 shows results for Laplacians with arbitrary entries, which result in more oscillating vector fields and trajectories (see also Figure 8). In all cases, the flows are injective.

    5.3 Discrete Time-Dependent Flows

    In the continuous case, flows are often defined by time-dependent vector fields u(p,t)[chen2018neural]. Following our aim to provide a discrete counterpart of continuous flows, we can produce a time-discrete analogue of the above, where we switch between different harmonic functions discretely, at different time intervals – Figure 9 shows trajectories of points where the harmonic function governing the flow is changed four times. The resulting flow is more elaborate and, as shown on the right, can yield trajectories that intersect, although the flow remains injective (the two points each traverse the intersection point at different moments in time).

    5.4 Gradient-Based Injective Field Optimization

    All steps of Algorithm 1 are differentiable, specifically with respect to the entries of the Laplacian; hence, by leveraging gradient-based optimization, we can effectively optimize the Laplacian edge weights [sun2024tuttenet, aigerman2024generative] thereby optimizing the vector field while maintaining its injectivity. We next show preliminary experiments validating the optimizeability of this representation. We implement the algorithm in PyTorch, which provides automatic differentiation. We use a simple optimization scheme, via the Adam [kingma2015] optimizer with a fixed step size of 0.1, run for 5000 iterations.

    Approximating non-injective vector fields.

    In Figure 10, we show a result of optimizing a randomly-initialized injective vector field to align with a given, non-injective vector field (obtained via [crane2010]), by minimizing the mean squared error (MSE) between the per-face target vectors and the optimized injective field. This leads to an injective vector field that still closely mimics the broader directional trends of the target field, as shown in the blowups.

    Satisfying sparse vector constraints.

    We evaluate the ability of our optimization to satisfy sparse directional constraints across specific faces of a mesh. In Figure 11, black arrows denote ten user-defined constraint vectors. We minimize the MSE loss between the injective vector field and these vectors, exclusively on the constrained faces. We visualize the continuous trajectories passing through five of these constrained faces on the mesh. As shown in the insets of Figure 11(a), the initial vector field (red arrows) naturally deviates from the arbitrary constraints imposed by the target vectors, and is corrected by optimization to achieve near-perfect alignment, sometimes via rather contorted paths.

    6 Conclusion

    Theorem 1 draws a connection between harmonic functions and injective flows and proposes a Tutte-like method for computing them. We hope that in the coming years, this method will find applications within the geometry processing community similar to those of Tutte’s embedding, e.g., producing injective initializations for vector field optimization algorithms, serving as a fast method to construct an injective vector field, or optimizing injective fields.

    While our main contribution is theoretical, on a practical level, our method comes with several limitations, which we hope to solve in future work. First, the method is limited to specific topology and boundary conditions. We believe that extensions to some other specific boundary conditions on specific domains are possible. Furthermore, similarly to Tutte’s embedding, injective extensions to non-euclidean domains [aigerman2016hyperbolic] can lead to a more general and less constrained construction. We also note that we have only shown a few “proof-of-concept” experiments to validate the capability of optimizing the vector field to specific goals, as we focused mainly on the injectivity of the flow, and used PyTorch’s vanilla autodiff with Adam [kingma2015] that does not use adaptive step size nor line search. The current optimization framework is insufficient on its own to optimize for flows that can be used in downstream tasks. As our top future priority, we mark the goal of devising a framework that can output production-ready flows. This requires regularizing the vector fields, e.g., via as-Killing-as-possible [benchen2010killing] or a vector Dirichlet energy  [stein2020simple]. Lastly, our parameterization of injective flows via gradients of a family of harmonic functions does not cover the full space of injective vector fields. As several of our flows are composed (as in Figure 9), the space of injective flows is increased, and we set as important future work to show (both theoretically and practically) that with enough such compositions, any flow can be attained.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Proofs of Lemmas

    Proof of Lemma 1.

    Let e=(i,j) be a half-edge, let t=(i,j,k) be its triangle, and define the edge vector as r⃗=(vⱼ-vᵢ)/(\lVertvᵢ-vⱼ\rVert). In standard linear FEM fashion, consider z as defining an affine function over the triangle, z(p)=aᵀp+b for any point p∈t, uniquely defined as requiring that it interpolates the values zᵢ,zⱼ,zₖ on the vertices, i.e., z(v_α)=z_α,α∈{i,j,k}. We will prove that the sign of the directional derivative (∂z)/(∂r⃗) in the direction r⃗ is equal to both terms in the lemma. First, by restricting z to a one-dimensional function over the edge, we have (∂z)/(∂r⃗)=(zⱼ-zᵢ)/(\lVertvᵢ-vⱼ\rVert)\overset\eqrefeq:1form=(δₑ)/(\lVertvᵢ-vⱼ\rVert); therefore, sign((∂z)/(∂r⃗))=sign(δₑ). Second, a directional derivative is also equal to the inner product between the gradient and the direction, i.e., (∂z)/(∂r⃗)=<∇ₜz,r⃗>. Since applying the same rotation to both vectors does not change their inner product, we have (∂z)/(∂r⃗)==. Thus, we get sign((∂z)/(∂r⃗))=-sign(). Hence, sign(δₑ)=-sign()=Fₑ. ∎

    Proof of Lemma 2.

    We first convert the vertex flux to a more relaxed definition (refer also to Figure 6):

    Definition 3.

    Flux parity: for triangle (o,i,j), we say the triangle has even-parity flux with respect to the vertex o if F_o,i=F_j,o; otherwise, if F_o,i=-F_j,o, we say the triangle has odd-parity flux with respect to the vertex o.

    In other words, positive/negative vertex fluxes are even-parity fluxes, and a zero vertex flux is odd-parity (see Figure 6 for an illustration, where triangles are highlighted in red if they have even-parity flux with respect to the 1-ring’s center vertex). Hence, translating the conditions of Property 2 to parity, it is a necessary condition that two triangles have even-parity flux and the rest have odd-parity flux; the next lemma shows that in fact these two conditions are exactly equivalent, i.e., the parity condition ensures vertex injectivity:

    Lemma 4.

    i) The flux is an injective regular flux over a vertex o iff there are exactly two triangles t¹,t² of the vertex’s 1-ring that have even-parity vertex flux (with respect to o) and all the rest of the triangles have odd-parity vertex flux. ii) The flux is an injective vortex flux iff all triangles have odd-parity vertex flux (with respect to o).

    We prove this lemma later. Now, as illustrated in Figure 6, note that two consecutive edges (o,i),(o,i+1) of the 1-ring correspond to the oriented half-edges (o,i),(i+1,o) of the triangle (o,i,i+1). Hence, if there’s no sign change (F_(o,i)=F_(o,i+1)), then by the anti-symmetry of the 1-form we have F_(o,i)=-F_(i+1,o), i.e., the triangle has odd-parity flux into o. Similarly, if there is a sign change (F_(o,i)=-F_(o,i+1)), then by the anti-symmetry of the 1-form we have F_(o,i)=F_(i+1,o) and the triangle has even-parity flux into o.

    In sum: an index of 1 is defined as no sign changes in the 1-ring, in turn meaning all triangles in the 1-ring have odd-parity flux, which by Lemma 4 entails a vortex injective vertex, as defined in Subsection 3.3 (and vice versa: having all odd-parity flux triangles entails an index of 1).

    Similarly, an index of 0 is defined as exactly two sign changes, hence exactly two triangles of the 1-ring have even-parity flux, which per Lemma 4 entails a regular injective vertex, as defined in Subsection 3.3 (and vice versa: two even-parity triangles entail an index of 0).

    All other numbers of sign changes have negative index, and all correspond to the last remaining case, of a non-injective vertex. With this, we have proven Lemma 2. ∎

    Proof of Lemma 3.

    We begin by reducing the equation in Theorem 3.5 in [gortler2006] to our setting. The original equation stipulates that for a polygonal mesh of genus g with a given 1-form δ,

    ∑_v∈Vind(v) (vertex index)+∑_t∈Tind(t) (face index)=2-2g.

    		(11)

    Aside from the vertex index term (defined in Subsection 4.3), there is an additional face index term; however, it is irrelevant to us: this is computed for polygonal meshes, by walking over the (polygonal) face’s edges and counting how many sign changes occur; for our case this term is always zero since, by definition of δᵢ (Equation (8)), we have that for a triangle with edges e₁,e₂,e₃ it holds that δ₁+δ₂+δ₃=0, entailing exactly two sign changes, thereby leading to zero contribution. Plugging in the genus of the sphere (g=0) to the right-hand side of Equation (11), we get from their theorem that our 1-form δ satisfies

    ∑_v∈Vind(v)=2.

    		(12)

    We note that all vertices except the source and sink satisfy the discrete harmonic equation, and thus it is well-known (and easy to prove) that they satisfy a discrete maximum principle: a vertex o has a vertex vⱼ in its 1-ring with a higher value zₒzₖ. By the definition of δ, Equation (8), this entails δ_(o,j)>0, and δ_(o,k)<0. As such, there must be at least two sign changes transpiring across the edges of the 1-ring of o. Thus the index of all vertices is non-positive, except the source and sink. Since the indices sum to 2, this implies both the source and the sink must have the maximal index, i.e., 1. With that, the sum of the indices of all the other vertices must be exactly zero. Due to non-positivity, this entails that the index of each of those vertices is zero. ∎

    Proof of Lemma 4.

    (⇒) i) Assume the vertex flux is regular injective, i.e., per the definition in Section 3.3, Property 2, there is one triangle t⁺ with positive vertex flux, and one t⁻ with negative vertex flux, and all others with zero vertex flux. Then, by the definition of parity, both t⁺,t⁻ have even-parity vertex flux while the rest have odd-parity vertex flux, as desired. ii) Assume the vertex flux is vortex injective. Then all triangles have zero vertex flux, which has odd parity.

    (⇐) i) Assume that there are exactly two triangles t¹,t² with even-parity vertex flux, with the rest having odd-parity vertex flux. We need to show that the definition of regular injective vertex from Subsection 3.3, Property 2 is satisfied. Odd-parity flux triangles have zero vertex flux; hence, all that remains is to prove that one of t¹,t² has positive vertex flux, and one has negative vertex flux (as opposed to both positive or both negative). Without loss of generality, assume t¹ has positive vertex flux. Due to Equation (5), we have F_(o,i)=F_(i+1,o)=+1. Using the anti-symmetry between a half-edge and its twin (Equation (8)), we have F_i+1,o=-F_o,i+1, entailing F_o,i+1=-1. We consider two cases:

  • 1.

    If (o,i+1) is a half-edge of t², we are done: since t² has even-parity flux, its other edge satisfies F_(i+2,o)=F_(o,i+1)=-1, and thus both have negative edge flux, entailing the vertex flux is negative.

  • 2.

    If the half-edge belongs to a triangle other than t², it is a triangle with odd-parity flux, implying F_(i+2,o)=-F_(o,i+1)=-(-1)=+1. By induction, we can show that when iterating over all triangles until reaching t², for each triangle (o,j,j+1) we have F_(j,o)=1 and F_(o,j+1)=-1. Once we reach t², we are once again in the setting of case 1, and the proof is concluded.

    • ii) Assume all triangles have odd-parity vertex flux; then there are no sign changes, and each triangle must have zero vertex flux, i.e., entailing the vertex flux is vortex injective. ∎
item.content:encoded:
一句话：类比 Tutte 嵌入，把调和性与单射性连起来：两条流线保证不相交，且流场可微、能在保单射前提下做梯度优化。

要点：

  • 在球面网格上计算离散调和函数，取它旋转 90° 的梯度作为向量场，得到的流是单射的：任意两点沿流推进，轨迹不会相交
  • 核心洞察是离散调和 1-形式的 Poincaré-Hopf 指标刻画，与单射向量场的组合规则相对应
  • 与 Tutte 嵌入一样只需解一个稀疏线性系统；流场可微地依赖 Laplacian 元素，因此能在不违反单射的前提下做无约束梯度优化

为什么值得看：参数化、网格变形、UV 展开里最难处理的就是翻转。这里给了一个「构造即无翻转」的流场，还能上梯度优化——比事后检测加惩罚更干净。

中文摘要：这篇论文证明了一个关于三角网格上由离散向量场定义的连续流是否单射的定理。与 Tutte 嵌入类似，定理把调和性与单射性连了起来：在球面网格上计算离散调和函数，取其旋转 90° 的梯度作为向量场，得到的流是单射的，即两点沿该场推进时轨迹保证不相交。证明的关键在于离散调和 1-形式的 Poincaré-Hopf 指标刻画与单射向量场的组合规则之间的对应。和 Tutte 嵌入一样，这个单射向量场可以通过求解一个稀疏线性系统得到；更重要的是它可微地依赖 Laplacian 的元素，因此能在无约束的梯度优化中始终保持单射性。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-08-06

本期推送：2026-10-24

A Tutte-Like Theorem for Injective Flows on Meshes

Abstract

This work proves a theorem regarding injectivity of continuous flows that are defined via discrete vector fields on triangle meshes. In similar fashion to Tutte’s embedding, the theorem shows a connection between harmonicity and injectivity. Specifically, a discrete harmonic function is computed over a spherical mesh, and its 90^∘-rotated gradients are taken as the vector field. We show that this leads to an injective flow over the mesh, i.e., when two points are advected along the vector field, their trajectories are guaranteed to not intersect. The core insight behind this theorem is that the characterization of the Poincaré-Hopf indices of discrete harmonic 1-forms is paralleled in the combinatorial rules for injective vector fields. Similarly to Tutte’s embedding, the injective vector field can be computed by simply solving a sparse linear system. Furthermore, it is differentiably dependent on the entries of the Laplacian, enabling unconstrained gradient-based optimization of the vector field while preserving injectivity. The advection itself can be computed by a quick and accurate algorithm. We experimentally validate the injectivity of the results, as well as show examples of differentiable optimization, such as computing an injective approximation to a given non-injective vector field, and fitting an injective vector field to satisfy constraints.

1 Introduction

This paper proposes a method for producing discrete, triangle-based tangent vector fields that define injective flows over triangle meshes, i.e., advecting points along the vector field yields continuous trajectories for any given point on the surface, such that the trajectories of any two points do not cross. Figure 1 shows such an advection of randomly sampled points on a mesh, their trajectories traced behind them as faded paths.

The mathematical challenge in ensuring the induced flow is injective lies in the discrete nature of the vector field. Indeed, when considering a continuous vector field, to ensure injectivity it is sufficient to require the vector field to be Lipschitz (per the Picard–Lindelöf theorem). In contrast, discrete, face-based vector fields are piecewise-constant and discontinuous; thus, their injectivity is a much more brittle property, which requires a different, more discrete approach, such as the satisfaction of combinatorial, triangle-based rules [campen2016].

Our main theoretical contribution – Theorem 1 – is akin to a flow-based version of Tutte’s embedding [tutte1963, floater1997parametrization], proving that a specific class of discrete harmonic functions induces injective flows. Specifically, we prove that solving a discrete Laplace equation on a spherical mesh with specific boundary conditions yields a discrete harmonic function whose gradient vectors, rotated by 90^∘, define an injective flow. Geometrically, this implies that each point’s trajectory lies on a fixed level set of the harmonic function. Similarly to Tutte’s embedding, these vector fields can be computed in a simple and efficient manner by solving a sparse linear system.

Theorem 1 is attained through two main insights (Lemmas 1 and 2) regarding a connection between two rather different approaches for injective mappings of triangle meshes: the framework of bijective foliations[campen2016] defines conditions on vector fields to yield injective paths on meshes; however, these conditions are combinatorial, and hence were previously attained by constructing these vector fields in a combinatorial, algorithmic manner. We observe that these conditions for injectivity are exactly reflected in harmonic functions’ specific properties (namely, a discrete Poincaré-Hopf index theorem) that were characterized by Gortler et al. [gortler2006] – see Figure 6, which exhibits the equivalence between the two approaches. This observation, in turn, enables the construction of vector fields that satisfy the injectivity conditions from [campen2016] via harmonic functions.

While we consider the proof our main technical contribution, it holds a secondary practical implication of a differentiable parameterization of injective flows on meshes: any assignment of positive edge weights of the Laplacian matrix modifies the Laplace equation, and hence the resulting vector field and flow, in a differentiable manner. Furthermore, our discrete vector field defines a flow that is piecewise-linear on the triangles of the mesh, leading to simple, efficient and accurate computation, in contrast to techniques that define flows via non-discrete, continuous vector fields [chen2018neural, chen2023riemannianfm]; in order to compute their corresponding flow, one needs to integrate the vector field via quadrature rules, which is both expensive and may lead to inaccuracies.

To verify our theory, we validate the injectivity of our vector field both qualitatively and quantitatively. We additionally show preliminary demonstrations of the utility of a differentiable representation of injective vector fields, by optimizing the injective field to best approximate a given non-injective field, or fitting it to satisfy constraints.

2 Related Works

Vector field design.

Vector field design has been heavily studied in computer graphics and geometry processing [zhang2006vector, degoes2016, vaxman2016]. Similarly to our approach, previous papers have considered vector fields as gradients of functions [diamanti2015integrable] and sought to integrate them [ray2006periodic]. This integration is similar to a flow and is especially common in the context of global parameterization [myles2014robust] and quad-meshing [bommes2013quad]. In these applications, the cases leading to non-injectivity of the flow simply lead to singularities in the parameterization/quad mesh (and not to loss of injectivity of, e.g., the parameterization) – these are in general acceptable, hence those methods usually focus on minimizing the number of such singularities. Many works focus solely on unit-length vector fields [solomon2019optimal, boksebeld2022high, verhoeven2022dev2pq, palmer2024lifting, wang2025power] and their extensions to polyvector fields [palacios2007rotational, bommes2010practical, diamanti2014designing, panozzo2014frame] in which the flow direction can be chosen out of several options at each triangle. Another common goal is optimizing the smoothness of the vector/directional field [fisher2007design, knoppel2013globally], while ensuring adherence to singularity assignment [crane2010]; others optimize for vector fields which produce an as-rigid-as-possible flow [benchen2010killing]. Flows on vector fields additionally have a close connection to geodesics [sharp2019vector, vekhter2019weaving].

Injective maps between meshes.

The flows we compute define a map between a mesh and itself; defining such injective mappings of meshes is a highly researched area. Most previous approaches use a common domain into which the meshes are mapped, thereby defining a mapping by composition of maps into the common domain [kraevoy2004, aigerman2014lifted, aigerman2015seamless, aigerman2016hyperbolic, morreale2021, schmidt2020inter]. Of note is one of the first works on mesh-mesh injective mappings [schreiner2004inter], which directly deals with injectively sliding the vertices of one mesh over the triangles of the other in a sort of ad hoc flow. Bijective maps between domains can also be defined via integral curves [huynh2015], global structural decompositions [nieser2011, bommes2013, hinderink2024], or by auxiliary structures [jiang2020, jiang2021, liu2024]. Lastly, simplicial foliations [campen2016, hinderink2021] can be used for defining vector-aligned slices on surfaces and volumes, and then matching between corresponding slices on two meshes. These slices are in turn created by an injective vector field – we directly use the conditions formulated by [campen2016] and show they hold for specific harmonic functions.

Harmonic functions and injective mappings.

There is a deep connection between harmonic functions over 2-manifolds and injective mappings, with the most central results being the Radó–Kneser–Choquet theorem and its discrete counterpart, Tutte’s embedding [tutte1963, floater1997parametrization, floater2003one]. Tutte’s embedding states that computing two discrete harmonic functions representing the x,y coordinates of a disk-topology mesh, while prescribing the boundary conditions to a convex polygon, yields an injective embedding of the mesh to 2D. This has been extended further into other topologies [gortler2006, aigerman2015orbifold] and non-Euclidean target domains [tsui2013globally, aigerman2016hyperbolic, aigerman2017spherical]. Other methods use more complex harmonic structures for injectivity, which require more careful optimization [bright2017harmonic, hefetz2019subspace]. Previous works have considered the use of harmonic functions and flowing via their gradients for quad-meshing [dong2005harmonic], without considerations of injectivity, and for injective parameterization, but not flows [tong2006designing]. Some use harmonic gradients for constructing maps; however, the injectivity of these is guaranteed only in the smooth setting, relying on the harmonic maps’ infinite smoothness [lin2015interior] and the existence of hessians [xia2010direct]. In contrast, we prove a discrete theorem, showing that injectivity holds directly on the discrete gradients of the discrete harmonic function, for any Laplacian matrix. We further leverage the fact that discrete harmonic functions are defined with respect to any Laplacian matrix defined with positive weights on the mesh’s edges, and optimize the injective vector field via the Laplacian’s entries. Such optimization of the Laplacian in order to control injective maps has been performed before [aigerman2024generative, sun2024tuttenet].

Computing continuous flows.

Computing continuous injective flows is a highly active area, especially in machine learning where it is used for generative techniques [lipman2023]. These flows can be computed in a differentiable process via a neural network that produces a continuous vector field on Euclidean spaces [chen2018neural] and on manifolds [falorsi2020, lou2020, mathieu2020, bose2020, rozen2021, chen2024, benhamu2022]. Some previous works have used such flows to define deformations of 3D shapes [jiang2020shapeflow]. Injectivity is guaranteed as long as the vector field is Lipschitz. In contrast, we focus on piecewise-constant vector fields defined on a piecewise-flat triangle mesh, and on ensuring they still define an injective flow.

3 Problem Setting and Goal

3.1 Preliminaries

We consider sphere-topology manifold triangle meshes M. We will focus on working with oriented half-edgese=(i,j), where, for a triangle (i,j,k), its oriented half-edges follow the triangle’s orientation: (i,j),(j,k),(k,i). Note that each half-edge belongs to exactly one triangle. The twin half-edge of e=(i,j) is denoted \reflectboxe=(j,i). Each such half-edge has its edge normal, defined as the vector obtained by inverting the unit-normalized directed edge vector and rotating it by 90^∘ in the tangent plane of its triangle:

nₑᵗ=-R^90^∘ₜ(vⱼ-vᵢ)/\lVertvᵢ-vⱼ\rVert,

(1)

where R^90^∘ₜ is the matrix that rotates vectors in the tangent plane of triangle t by 90^∘. Note that this normal points inward into the triangle, towards the vertex k opposite to the edge (i,j).

We will consider discrete functions, i.e., an assignment of a scalar zᵢ to each vertex vᵢ of the mesh. We will also use the mesh’s gradient operator ∇, defined via linear finite elements, assigning to each triangle the gradient vector of the affine function interpolating between the three values on the vertices, denoted ∇ₜz.

In standard fashion, we assign a piecewise-constant vector field u over the faces of the mesh, defined by assigning a tangent vector uₜ∈Tₜ to each triangle t of the mesh (see Figure 4). Each half-edge e thus has exactly one corresponding tangent vector, belonging to the triangle t that contains e.

A flow over the mesh is defined for any point p∈M (not necessarily a vertex), assigning it a continuous path pₜ parameterized by a time parameter t∈[0,1] such that the flow starts from p, i.e., p₀=p, and advects that point to somewhere else. The derivative with respect to time t is denoted (∂pₜ)/(∂t). We consider flows with respect to a vector field u such that the flow “agrees” with the vector field inside each triangle, namely, if at time t^* the point p_t^* is strictly inside triangle t – i.e., away from the triangle’s edges – then the speed vector of the point is equal to the vector field assigned to that triangle,

(∂pₜ)/(∂t)(t^*)=uₜ(if $p_t^*∈t$).

(2)

In other words, the vector field defines a flow inside each triangle by advecting each point using the vector field as the temporal derivative, which for a constant vector field reduces to a linear formula:

pₜ=p₀+tuₜ.

(3)

Since the vector field is piecewise-constant, the flow is piecewise-linear, as the inset illustrates.

The question of how to well-define the flow when the point crosses over between triangles (over an edge or a vertex) is equivalent to ensuring the flow is injective. Figure 4 shows examples of flows, where the purple point is flowed to its end position marked by a red X.

To tackle injectivity, we will show that a harmonic function’s gradient field satisfies the combinatorial rules for injectivity from [campen2016]. We next review these rules, and reformulate them into a formulation more suited to our needs, using the notion of edge/vertex fluxes, illustrated in Figure 4.

3.2 Fluxes

We begin by discussing fluxes over edges (which will be subsequently used to also define fluxes over vertices). We say the half-edge e has positive flux if there exists a point inside its corresponding triangle, p∈t, such that the flow defined by uₜ will flow this point to lie on the edge e. Inversely, we say the vector has negative flux with respect to the edge e if there is a point p on the edge e which would flow into the triangle.

We denote the edge flux on the half-edge e as Fₑ∈{+1,-1}. Geometrically, it corresponds to the inverted sign of the dot product of the vector with the edge normal:

Definition 1(Edge flux).

The edge flux Fₑ on edge e is defined as

Fₑ=-sign().

(4)

See Figure 4, top row, where a +/- sign denotes the flux over the corresponding half-edge, the purple point is the starting point p and the red X marks the final point. Note that we assume we do not encounter the case of a vector field parallel to the edge (no point is flowed into or out of that edge, and the inner product is zero).

We now move on to discuss fluxes on vertices. Consider a triangle t, the corresponding vector on the triangle uₜ, and one of the vertices v of that triangle. We say the vector has positive flux with respect to the vertex v if there exists a point on the triangle, p∈t, such that the flow defined by uₜ will flow this point to lie on the vertex v. We say the vector has negative flux with respect to the vertex v if a point starting from the vertex flows into the triangle. Finally, we say there is no flux in all other cases, which essentially correspond to the vertex neither flowing inside nor outside of this triangle.

To formalize these conditions geometrically: note that the vertex lies on the intersection of two of the triangle’s edges, e₁,e₂. Therefore, for a point p to flow to the vertex, it must flow into both edges, hence the vector uₜ must have positive edge flux into both edges sharing that vertex. Similarly, for the vertex to flow into the triangle, the vector uₜ must have negative flux into both edges sharing the vertex. In the remaining case (no vertex flux), the vector has positive flux on one edge, and negative flux on the other. See Figure 4, bottom for an illustration of these cases.

Definition 2(Vertex flux).

The flux on vertex v with respect to triangle t is defined via the edge fluxes as:

Fᵗᵥ=\begincases+1&ifF_(v,i)=+1andF_(j,v)=+1 -1&ifF_(v,i)=-1andF_(j,v)=-1 0&ifF_(v,i)=-F_(j,v)\endcases

(5)

3.3 Injectivity Conditions, Defined via Fluxes

Any vector field well-defines a flow in the interior of the triangle, but not necessarily on the boundary of the triangle: two points on two triangles may flow into the same point either on an edge or on a vertex. This is equivalent to non-injectivity. [campen2016] define specific conditions that ensure injectivity, which we review next while reformulating them for our needs.

First, it is immediate to observe (e.g., via Figure 5, left and center) that the vector field is injective over the half-edges e and e iff e has flux (per Definition 1) with a sign opposite to that of e,

Fₑ=-F_\reflectboxe

(6)

The flow of a point p is then defined by the vector with the negative flux, which flows points away from the edge.

Property 1(edge injectivity).

The vector field is injective over a half-edge e, if its flux over that half-edge satisfies Equation (6).

We move on to vertex injectivity. We classify the injectivity on a vertex into three cases:

  • 1.

    If the point p lies on a vertex and is flowed somewhere, for the flow to be well-defined (and injective) there must be exactly one triangle with a vector that has negative flux to the vertex, and one triangle that has positive flux from the vertex. All other triangles have no flux with respect to the vertex. This is the case of a regular injective vertex (see Figure 6, top left). The vector that has outgoing flow with respect to the vertex is chosen to define the flow.

  • 2.

    If the vertex is not flowed and stays in place, then all triangles in the 1-ring have zero vertex flux, implying the flow rotates around the vertex (Figure 6, bottom left). This is a vortex injective vertex.

  • 3.

    All other cases are non-injective vertices.

    • Property 2(Vertex injectivity).

    The vector field is injective over a vertex if its flux on that vertex is either regular injective or vortex injective, per the classification above.

    Our goal is thus to characterize a family of vector fields that satisfy the two above properties for injectivity.

    4 Injective Flows via Harmonic Functions

    Towards producing an injective vector field and proving its injectivity, this section progresses in three steps:

  • 1.

    (Section 4.1) Compute a harmonic function z.

  • 2.

    (Section 4.2) Define a vector field u as the 90^∘-rotated gradient of the harmonic function, and show that its flux F is exactly equal to a 1-form δ defined by z.

  • 3.

    (Section 4.3) Use the 1-form’s properties to show it satisfies the necessary injectivity properties from Section 3.3, thereby showing that F satisfies them as well.

    • 4.1 Computing a Discrete Harmonic 1-Form.

    We define a discrete Laplace equation on the mesh: we choose two vertices to serve as source/target, designated s,t. We also assume to have a Laplacian L, with any desired positive weights wᵢⱼ on each edge (e.g., these can either be positively-clamped cotan weights [pinkall1993], or ones that are optimized). We solve the discrete Laplace equation with boundary conditions defined by s,t and using the Laplacian L:

    \beginarray[]llzᵢ=1&i=s zᵢ=-1&i=t (Lz)ᵢ=0&else\endarray

    		(7)

    Similar to [gortler2006], for any half-edge e=(i,j), we define the 1-form

    δₑ=zⱼ-zᵢ,

    		(8)

    assigning a real number to that half-edge. See Figure 5, right, for an example of such z and the resulting 1-form δ. Note we assume z is such that the 1-form is non-vanishing on any edge (δₑ≠0); otherwise, similarly to the argument made in Appendix A in [gortler2006], we can perturb the 1-form by an infinitesimal amount to make it non-vanishing, without changing any of the assumptions necessary for the proof.

    4.2 Constructing an Injective Vector Field from the Harmonic Function

    We define our vector field on each triangle t as the gradient vector rotated by 90^∘:

    uₜ=R^90^∘∇ₜz,

    		(9)

    which leads to the main theoretical result of this paper:

    Theorem 1.

    The flow induced by the vector field u, defined in Equation (9), is injective.

    The following Section 4.3 proves the above theorem. Similarly to Tutte’s embedding [tutte1963], injectivity holds for a very specific setting: a sphere-topology mesh, with one source and one sink – see Figure 3 for a non-injective example when attempting the same technique on a mesh of a different genus.

    Geometrically, the rotated gradient vector field points in a direction tangent to a level set of z; thus, the resulting injective flow defines a trajectory that marches along a fixed level set of z, in a direction designated by the orientation of the mesh. The source and sink vertices s,t serve as two vortex points (the flow rotates around them and they are stationary). Note, however, that when using Laplacians with random weights (Figure 7, 8) or optimized ones (Figures 10, 11), the level sets become more intricate and enable different flows.

    4.3 Injectivity of the Flow (Proof of Theorem 1)

    We aim to provide a streamlined proof that highlights the key insights leading to the main result; as such, we prove all the necessary lemmas in Appendix A. To prove injectivity of the vector field, we need to prove that the injective properties regarding its fluxF (Section 3.3) hold. The key connection between the harmonic function z and the flux F is that on each edge e, the flux Fₑ is exactly equal to the sign of the 1-form δₑ.

    Lemma 1(flux/1-form equivalence).

    The edge flux of the vector field u defined in Equation (9) is equal on all edges to the 1-form defined in Equation (8):

    Fₑ=sign(δₑ).

    		(10)

    We use this equivalence to prove edge/vertex flux injectivity.

    To prove edge injectivity, we need to prove Property 1 in Section 3.3: Fₑ=-F_\reflectboxe. Per Lemma 1, this is equivalent to proving δₑ=-δ_\reflectboxe. This last equation is immediate to deduce from Equation (8) which implies the anti-symmetry of δ (see also the half-edges shared between the two triangles in Figure 5, right). Hence, we assume the vector field is edge-injective and turn to proving vertex injectivity:

    Theorem 2(Vertex injectivity).

    Let M, z be as above. Then the vector field defined by Equation (9) is vertex-injective as defined in Property 2, Section 3.3.

    To prove this theorem, we draw a connection between the flux conditions of Campen et al. [campen2016] and the behavior of indices of harmonic 1-forms described in  Gortler et al. [gortler2006].

    Proof of Theorem 2.

    We turn to [gortler2006]. We consider their Theorem 3.5 (essentially a discrete Poincaré-Hopf theorem), and interpret it in our scenario. They define an indexind(vₒ) assigning an integer for each vertex vₒ. The index of the vertex vₒ is defined by stepping over its 1-ring edges in order, each oriented in outgoing direction (o,1),(o,2)...,(o,k), and checking how many times the 1-form δ_o,j changes signs, with the index, ind(vₒ), being equal to 1, 0 or -1 based on zero, two, or more than two sign changes, respectively (see Figure 6, right column).

    The proof hinges on the following Lemma 2, which shows an equivalence between the aforementioned index classification and our version (Section 3.3, Property 2) of the classification from Campen et al. [campen2016] of injective and non-injective vertices. Figure 6 portrays this equivalence between the left and right images in each row.

    Lemma 2.

    The vertex v has index 1 iff it is a regular injective vertex, an index 0 iff it is a vortex injective vertex, and index -1 iff it is a non-injective vertex, per the definition in Section 3.3, Property 2.

    Hence, to ensure all vertices are injective, all we need to show is that there are no vertices with ind(v)=-1. We prove a slightly stronger version of this claim using standard arguments [gortler2006]:

    Lemma 3.

    Let M, z and δ be as described above. Then all vertices have index 0, except for the source and sink vertices s,t, which have index 1.

    Thus, no vertex has negative index, entailing that all vertices are injective, and we have proven Theorem 2. ∎

    With this, we have proven that both edge injectivity and vertex injectivity hold, thereby proving Theorem 1 and global injectivity of the flow.

    4.4 Vector Field and Flow computation

    We summarize the vector field construction in Algorithm 1. Each step of this algorithm is differentiable, and thus it provides a differentiable parameterization of injective vector fields, as a function of the Laplacian’s (arbitrary) edge weights Lᵢⱼ.

    Lastly, to flow a given point p∈M on a triangle t with respect to the vector field u for a given amount of time T∈ℝ, we propose a simple, efficient, and accurate algorithm, described in Algorithm 2, which walks on the level sets of z. The flow is piecewise linear and only needs to be evaluated at each intersection point with an edge. The choice of which edge is the next to be intersected, as well as the exact location on the edge on which the intersection happens, can all be easily deduced by simple arithmetic involving the value c of the level set and the values of z on the vertices. Since the algorithm relies on the initial level set to find the intersection points, it does not suffer from accumulated error and can self-correct to always follow the level set (see Table 1).

    5 Results

    As our main contribution is the theoretical Theorem 1, we next empirically verify its correctness, show qualitative examples of injective flows, and also validate the ability of the differentiable pipeline to enable gradient-based optimization. We note that the injectivity of a vector field does not depend on the magnitude of the vectors and hence opt to normalize all vectors to unit norm.

    5.1 Empirical Evidence of Injectivity and Accuracy

    We begin by empirically validating the injectivity of the flows, as well as the accuracy of our advection algorithm, Algorithm 2. We flow a given point for a certain amount of time, and then flip the vector field and flow the resulting point “back in time” – we visualize this experiment in Figure 8 with red/yellow for forward/backward paths, validating injectivity as well as exhibiting the accuracy of the algorithm. For quantitative evaluation, we repeat this process for random source and sink vertices alongside a random initialization of Laplacian weights, sample 100,000 random points, and measure the error between the start point and the point flowed back via the two steps above. We report the aggregated Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Maximum Absolute Error (MXE) in Table 1. No error exceeds 10⁻⁸ on average and 10⁻⁵ at maximum. A few models with triangles that have very small area or are near-degenerate result in less accurate results, mainly because of inaccuracy in numerics of the harmonic equation/gradient operator leading to a slight drift in the calculation of the time it takes to cross an edge.

    5.2 Flows Defined from Different Types of Laplacians

    Theorem 1 guarantees an injective flow for any valid configuration of strictly positive Laplacian weights. In Figure 2 we show flows computed via the cotangent Laplacian [pinkall1993] (clamped to have only positive weights) and via the Mean Value Coordinates (MVC) [floater2003mean] Laplacian. These lead to smooth flows along the harmonic isolines. To show more elaborate flows, Figure 7 shows results for Laplacians with arbitrary entries, which result in more oscillating vector fields and trajectories (see also Figure 8). In all cases, the flows are injective.

    5.3 Discrete Time-Dependent Flows

    In the continuous case, flows are often defined by time-dependent vector fields u(p,t)[chen2018neural]. Following our aim to provide a discrete counterpart of continuous flows, we can produce a time-discrete analogue of the above, where we switch between different harmonic functions discretely, at different time intervals – Figure 9 shows trajectories of points where the harmonic function governing the flow is changed four times. The resulting flow is more elaborate and, as shown on the right, can yield trajectories that intersect, although the flow remains injective (the two points each traverse the intersection point at different moments in time).

    5.4 Gradient-Based Injective Field Optimization

    All steps of Algorithm 1 are differentiable, specifically with respect to the entries of the Laplacian; hence, by leveraging gradient-based optimization, we can effectively optimize the Laplacian edge weights [sun2024tuttenet, aigerman2024generative] thereby optimizing the vector field while maintaining its injectivity. We next show preliminary experiments validating the optimizeability of this representation. We implement the algorithm in PyTorch, which provides automatic differentiation. We use a simple optimization scheme, via the Adam [kingma2015] optimizer with a fixed step size of 0.1, run for 5000 iterations.

    Approximating non-injective vector fields.

    In Figure 10, we show a result of optimizing a randomly-initialized injective vector field to align with a given, non-injective vector field (obtained via [crane2010]), by minimizing the mean squared error (MSE) between the per-face target vectors and the optimized injective field. This leads to an injective vector field that still closely mimics the broader directional trends of the target field, as shown in the blowups.

    Satisfying sparse vector constraints.

    We evaluate the ability of our optimization to satisfy sparse directional constraints across specific faces of a mesh. In Figure 11, black arrows denote ten user-defined constraint vectors. We minimize the MSE loss between the injective vector field and these vectors, exclusively on the constrained faces. We visualize the continuous trajectories passing through five of these constrained faces on the mesh. As shown in the insets of Figure 11(a), the initial vector field (red arrows) naturally deviates from the arbitrary constraints imposed by the target vectors, and is corrected by optimization to achieve near-perfect alignment, sometimes via rather contorted paths.

    6 Conclusion

    Theorem 1 draws a connection between harmonic functions and injective flows and proposes a Tutte-like method for computing them. We hope that in the coming years, this method will find applications within the geometry processing community similar to those of Tutte’s embedding, e.g., producing injective initializations for vector field optimization algorithms, serving as a fast method to construct an injective vector field, or optimizing injective fields.

    While our main contribution is theoretical, on a practical level, our method comes with several limitations, which we hope to solve in future work. First, the method is limited to specific topology and boundary conditions. We believe that extensions to some other specific boundary conditions on specific domains are possible. Furthermore, similarly to Tutte’s embedding, injective extensions to non-euclidean domains [aigerman2016hyperbolic] can lead to a more general and less constrained construction. We also note that we have only shown a few “proof-of-concept” experiments to validate the capability of optimizing the vector field to specific goals, as we focused mainly on the injectivity of the flow, and used PyTorch’s vanilla autodiff with Adam [kingma2015] that does not use adaptive step size nor line search. The current optimization framework is insufficient on its own to optimize for flows that can be used in downstream tasks. As our top future priority, we mark the goal of devising a framework that can output production-ready flows. This requires regularizing the vector fields, e.g., via as-Killing-as-possible [benchen2010killing] or a vector Dirichlet energy  [stein2020simple]. Lastly, our parameterization of injective flows via gradients of a family of harmonic functions does not cover the full space of injective vector fields. As several of our flows are composed (as in Figure 9), the space of injective flows is increased, and we set as important future work to show (both theoretically and practically) that with enough such compositions, any flow can be attained.

    Appendix A Proofs of Lemmas

    Proof of Lemma 1.

    Let e=(i,j) be a half-edge, let t=(i,j,k) be its triangle, and define the edge vector as r⃗=(vⱼ-vᵢ)/(\lVertvᵢ-vⱼ\rVert). In standard linear FEM fashion, consider z as defining an affine function over the triangle, z(p)=aᵀp+b for any point p∈t, uniquely defined as requiring that it interpolates the values zᵢ,zⱼ,zₖ on the vertices, i.e., z(v_α)=z_α,α∈{i,j,k}. We will prove that the sign of the directional derivative (∂z)/(∂r⃗) in the direction r⃗ is equal to both terms in the lemma. First, by restricting z to a one-dimensional function over the edge, we have (∂z)/(∂r⃗)=(zⱼ-zᵢ)/(\lVertvᵢ-vⱼ\rVert)\overset\eqrefeq:1form=(δₑ)/(\lVertvᵢ-vⱼ\rVert); therefore, sign((∂z)/(∂r⃗))=sign(δₑ). Second, a directional derivative is also equal to the inner product between the gradient and the direction, i.e., (∂z)/(∂r⃗)=<∇ₜz,r⃗>. Since applying the same rotation to both vectors does not change their inner product, we have (∂z)/(∂r⃗)==. Thus, we get sign((∂z)/(∂r⃗))=-sign(). Hence, sign(δₑ)=-sign()=Fₑ. ∎

    Proof of Lemma 2.

    We first convert the vertex flux to a more relaxed definition (refer also to Figure 6):

    Definition 3.

    Flux parity: for triangle (o,i,j), we say the triangle has even-parity flux with respect to the vertex o if F_o,i=F_j,o; otherwise, if F_o,i=-F_j,o, we say the triangle has odd-parity flux with respect to the vertex o.

    In other words, positive/negative vertex fluxes are even-parity fluxes, and a zero vertex flux is odd-parity (see Figure 6 for an illustration, where triangles are highlighted in red if they have even-parity flux with respect to the 1-ring’s center vertex). Hence, translating the conditions of Property 2 to parity, it is a necessary condition that two triangles have even-parity flux and the rest have odd-parity flux; the next lemma shows that in fact these two conditions are exactly equivalent, i.e., the parity condition ensures vertex injectivity:

    Lemma 4.

    i) The flux is an injective regular flux over a vertex o iff there are exactly two triangles t¹,t² of the vertex’s 1-ring that have even-parity vertex flux (with respect to o) and all the rest of the triangles have odd-parity vertex flux. ii) The flux is an injective vortex flux iff all triangles have odd-parity vertex flux (with respect to o).

    We prove this lemma later. Now, as illustrated in Figure 6, note that two consecutive edges (o,i),(o,i+1) of the 1-ring correspond to the oriented half-edges (o,i),(i+1,o) of the triangle (o,i,i+1). Hence, if there’s no sign change (F_(o,i)=F_(o,i+1)), then by the anti-symmetry of the 1-form we have F_(o,i)=-F_(i+1,o), i.e., the triangle has odd-parity flux into o. Similarly, if there is a sign change (F_(o,i)=-F_(o,i+1)), then by the anti-symmetry of the 1-form we have F_(o,i)=F_(i+1,o) and the triangle has even-parity flux into o.

    In sum: an index of 1 is defined as no sign changes in the 1-ring, in turn meaning all triangles in the 1-ring have odd-parity flux, which by Lemma 4 entails a vortex injective vertex, as defined in Subsection 3.3 (and vice versa: having all odd-parity flux triangles entails an index of 1).

    Similarly, an index of 0 is defined as exactly two sign changes, hence exactly two triangles of the 1-ring have even-parity flux, which per Lemma 4 entails a regular injective vertex, as defined in Subsection 3.3 (and vice versa: two even-parity triangles entail an index of 0).

    All other numbers of sign changes have negative index, and all correspond to the last remaining case, of a non-injective vertex. With this, we have proven Lemma 2. ∎

    Proof of Lemma 3.

    We begin by reducing the equation in Theorem 3.5 in [gortler2006] to our setting. The original equation stipulates that for a polygonal mesh of genus g with a given 1-form δ,

    ∑_v∈Vind(v) (vertex index)+∑_t∈Tind(t) (face index)=2-2g.

    		(11)

    Aside from the vertex index term (defined in Subsection 4.3), there is an additional face index term; however, it is irrelevant to us: this is computed for polygonal meshes, by walking over the (polygonal) face’s edges and counting how many sign changes occur; for our case this term is always zero since, by definition of δᵢ (Equation (8)), we have that for a triangle with edges e₁,e₂,e₃ it holds that δ₁+δ₂+δ₃=0, entailing exactly two sign changes, thereby leading to zero contribution. Plugging in the genus of the sphere (g=0) to the right-hand side of Equation (11), we get from their theorem that our 1-form δ satisfies

    ∑_v∈Vind(v)=2.

    		(12)

    We note that all vertices except the source and sink satisfy the discrete harmonic equation, and thus it is well-known (and easy to prove) that they satisfy a discrete maximum principle: a vertex o has a vertex vⱼ in its 1-ring with a higher value zₒzₖ. By the definition of δ, Equation (8), this entails δ_(o,j)>0, and δ_(o,k)<0. As such, there must be at least two sign changes transpiring across the edges of the 1-ring of o. Thus the index of all vertices is non-positive, except the source and sink. Since the indices sum to 2, this implies both the source and the sink must have the maximal index, i.e., 1. With that, the sum of the indices of all the other vertices must be exactly zero. Due to non-positivity, this entails that the index of each of those vertices is zero. ∎

    Proof of Lemma 4.

    (⇒) i) Assume the vertex flux is regular injective, i.e., per the definition in Section 3.3, Property 2, there is one triangle t⁺ with positive vertex flux, and one t⁻ with negative vertex flux, and all others with zero vertex flux. Then, by the definition of parity, both t⁺,t⁻ have even-parity vertex flux while the rest have odd-parity vertex flux, as desired. ii) Assume the vertex flux is vortex injective. Then all triangles have zero vertex flux, which has odd parity.

    (⇐) i) Assume that there are exactly two triangles t¹,t² with even-parity vertex flux, with the rest having odd-parity vertex flux. We need to show that the definition of regular injective vertex from Subsection 3.3, Property 2 is satisfied. Odd-parity flux triangles have zero vertex flux; hence, all that remains is to prove that one of t¹,t² has positive vertex flux, and one has negative vertex flux (as opposed to both positive or both negative). Without loss of generality, assume t¹ has positive vertex flux. Due to Equation (5), we have F_(o,i)=F_(i+1,o)=+1. Using the anti-symmetry between a half-edge and its twin (Equation (8)), we have F_i+1,o=-F_o,i+1, entailing F_o,i+1=-1. We consider two cases:

  • 1.

    If (o,i+1) is a half-edge of t², we are done: since t² has even-parity flux, its other edge satisfies F_(i+2,o)=F_(o,i+1)=-1, and thus both have negative edge flux, entailing the vertex flux is negative.

  • 2.

    If the half-edge belongs to a triangle other than t², it is a triangle with odd-parity flux, implying F_(i+2,o)=-F_(o,i+1)=-(-1)=+1. By induction, we can show that when iterating over all triangles until reaching t², for each triangle (o,j,j+1) we have F_(j,o)=1 and F_(o,j+1)=-1. Once we reach t², we are once again in the setting of case 1, and the proof is concluded.

    • ii) Assume all triangles have odd-parity vertex flux; then there are no sign changes, and each triangle must have zero vertex flux, i.e., entailing the vertex flux is vortex injective. ∎

item.title: Walk in Envelopes：用可证明的解上下界改造分支随机游走，别让分支树自己炸掉 ｜ Walk in Envelopes: Efficient Branching Walk-on-Spheres via Certified Solution Bounds
item.description:
一句话：分支强度接近临界阈值时期望粒子数发散；把「繁殖」重参数化成分裂/返回0/返回1 三类事件，无偏且能剪掉冗余分支。

要点：

  • branching WoS 用无网格方式解半线性 PDE，但分支强度接近临界谱阈值时期望粒子数发散，计算树迅速爆炸
  • WiE 不是去剪已有的树，而是用可证明的解上下界重新参数化分支扩散：抑制繁殖、引入受控终止，并给出与包络相关的方差界以保证无偏
  • 用 screened WoS 核做精确拒绝采样实现该变换，配可证明的样条包络与自适应采样；并证明合适的调和包络能让期望繁殖次数有界，而传统 BBM 会发散

为什么值得看：路径追踪里解半线性 PDE（参与介质、非线性散射）本来就靠随机过程，分支一多就没法算。这里给出的是「带证书的方差控制」，和渲染里用控制变量/上界估计降噪是同一套思路。

中文摘要：无网格蒙特卡洛方法（如 Walk-on-Spheres）能在复杂区域上做点查询式的 PDE 求解，扩展到半线性方程则需要处理非线性反应项，常用的概率表示是分支布朗运动——把非线性项换成粒子繁殖事件。但消除时间离散并不消除分支复杂度：每个后代都要再开新的游走，当分支强度接近临界谱阈值时，期望粒子数发散，使本来合法的随机表示变得不可算。Walk in Envelopes 不改动已有树去做剪枝，而是用可证明的解上下界来变换分支扩散：抑制繁殖、引入受控终止，并通过包络相关的方差界保持无偏。作者用标准 screened WoS 核做精确拒绝采样来实现该变换，配可证明的样条包络与自适应采样，并证明合适的调和包络能让期望繁殖次数有界。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-18

本期推送：2026-10-24

Walk in Envelopes: Efficient Branching Walk-on-Spheres via Certified Solution Bounds

© none

Abstract.

Branching Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) solves semilinear PDEs without meshes, but its computational cost grows sharply near critical branching rates. We introduce Walk in Envelopes (WiE), which uses certified solution bounds to transform branching diffusion rather than prune existing trees. The transformation suppresses reproduction, introduces controlled termination, and preserves unbiasedness with an envelope-dependent variance bound. We realize the transformed process through exact rejection sampling using standard screened WoS kernels, supported by certified spline envelopes and adaptive sampling and further prove that suitable harmonic envelopes yield bounded expected reproduction counts even as conventional BBM diverges.

Keywords:

Walk-on-Spheres, Branching Brownian Motion, Semilinear PDEs, Certified Solution Bounds, Monte Carlo Methods

1. Introduction

Grid-free Monte Carlo methods have become an attractive alternative to mesh-based PDE solvers, enabling pointwise solution queries on complex domains without constructing a global discretization [(Sawhney and Crane, 2020)]. While Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) efficiently resolves linear elliptic equations through boundary-hitting processes, extending this paradigm to semilinear PDEs requires handling nonlinear reactions. Branching Brownian motion (BBM) provides a natural probabilistic representation by replacing nonlinear terms with particle reproduction events [(Agarwal and Claisse, 2020)]. Combined with WoS, this yields a grid-free solver for semilinear equations. However, eliminating Brownian time discretization does not eliminate branching complexity: each offspring initiates additional walks, and the expected particle population diverges as the branching intensity approaches a critical spectral threshold. This makes otherwise valid stochastic representations increasingly expensive precisely in strongly nonlinear regimes.

A natural strategy is to exploit approximate solution information to terminate branches whose remaining contributions are sufficiently small. Yet such pruning requires reliable bounds on unresolved subtrees, whose evaluation can itself be expensive. Approximate bounds may also introduce bias, while tighter estimates do not necessarily offset their computation costs. More fundamentally, pruning acts on a branching process that has already been generated, rather than preventing unnecessary reproduction. This motivates a different question: can certified solution information be used to construct an equivalent stochastic process that branches less frequently, without sacrificing correctness?

We introduce Walk in Envelopes (WiE), a branching WoS framework that transforms the stochastic representation using certified lower and upper solution envelopes. Given sub- and supersolutions ℓ≤u≤a, we normalize the unknown solution as v=(u-ℓ)/(a-ℓ). This induces a generalized Doob transform whose diffusion, reproduction, and termination mechanisms are determined by the envelope functions. For binary branching, the reproduction rate becomes λ(a-ℓ), while envelope residuals introduce additional success and failure termination events. The resulting estimator remains unbiased and has variance bounded by (a-ℓ)²/4. Moreover, we characterize its expected reproduction count through an elliptic equation, showing that a suitable harmonic envelope can keep this count uniformly bounded even as conventional BBM approaches its critical divergence threshold. Although branching-process transformations have established mathematical foundations [(Engländer, 2007)], WiE develops them into a certified computational framework for semilinear PDE solving.

The transformed process introduces spatially varying diffusion, which would ordinarily require simulating drifted trajectories. We avoid this difficulty by deriving an exact envelope-aware transition using the original screened WoS exit and Green kernels. Rejection sampling with certified local majorants realizes the transformed distribution without evaluating weighted kernel integrals. To obtain useful envelopes efficiently, we develop monotone refinement of cubic B-spline sub- and supersolutions, using Bernstein constraints to certify PDE inequalities throughout the domain by comparison principle. Adaptive screening, spatially localized rejection bounds, and lazy evaluation further reduce sampling overhead, while a spectral-workload criterion avoids unnecessary preprocessing in inexpensive regimes.

We evaluate WiE on four complex two-dimensional domains across branching intensities and accuracy requirements. Near criticality, WiE achieves 6.9–16.2× improvements in time–variance efficiency and 4.7–14.6× reductions in sampling time at matched accuracy, excluding one-time envelope construction. Its benefits increase with branching intensity, while a workload-aware fallback preserves the efficiency of conventional BBM in easier regimes. We additionally demonstrate extensions to projected walks on manifolds and semilinear parabolic equations.

Our main contributions are:

  • •

    A certified envelope transformation of branching diffusion, with unbiased estimation, variance guarantees, and a spectral characterization of near-critical branching complexity.

  • •

    An exact envelope-aware WoS sampler using existing screened kernels, without explicitly simulating transformed diffusion.

  • •

    A practical solver combining certified spline-envelope refinement, efficient rejection sampling, and workload-aware fallback, with substantial near-critical acceleration.

    • 2. Related Work

    Branching Diffusions and Solution-Guided Transformations.

    BBM represents semilinear reaction–diffusion PDEs, beginning with McKean’s Kolmogorov–Petrovskii–Piskunov representation [(McKean, 1975)]. Branching-diffusion solvers extend to polynomial nonlinearities, gradient dependence via marked particles [(Henry-Labordère et al., 2019)], and elliptic boundary-value problems on bounded domains [(Agarwal and Claisse, 2020)], but face integrability and branching-cost restrictions under strong branching. Process transformations are well established: nonlinear h-transforms alter both motion and reproduction [(Engländer, 2007)], while measure changes and backbone decompositions characterize conditioned branching and near-critical behavior [(Salisbury and Verzani, 2000; Harris et al., 2016)]. These underpin solution-guided representations. Our computational realization uses certified sub- and supersolutions to obtain nonnegative branching and killing rates, with exact sphere-transition sampling requiring neither the unknown solution nor drifted-trajectory simulation.

    Monte Carlo Methods for Nonlinear Equations.

    Monte Carlo solvers avoid global spatial discretization, but nested nonlinear expectations and recursive branching can sharply increase variance and work. Numerical branching methods handle polynomial nonlinear PDEs, subject to representation-dependent convergence and integrability [(Henry-Labordère et al., 2019; Agarwal and Claisse, 2020)]. In graphics, [(Tong and Hachisuka, 2025)] accelerate nonlinear recursive light transport through nonlinear path filtering that reuses intermediate evaluations and neural radiance caching that learns them. For nonlinear radiative boundary conditions, [(Bao et al., 2026)] combine Picard-style iteration with Monte Carlo PDE solvers. These reduce nonlinear integral-equation costs through reuse, approximation, or iteration. Instead, we retain a branching estimator but change its probability law: certified envelopes suppress reproduction, bound its range, and preserve its expectation under stated assumptions. We reduce sample-generation work rather than only accelerate or approximate an existing recursion.

    Walk-on-Spheres and Grid-Free PDE Solvers.

    WoS originated for Dirichlet problems [(Muller, 1956)] and entered geometric computing as a grid-free elliptic PDE solver for point queries [(Sawhney and Crane, 2020)]. Extensions handle spatially varying coefficients via null scattering [(Sawhney et al., 2022)], mixed Neumann–Dirichlet conditions via walk on stars [(Sawhney et al., 2023)], and boundary-integral transport via walk on boundary [(Sugimoto et al., 2023)]. Boundary-value caching reuses estimates across queries [(Miller et al., 2023)], differential WoS computes parameter derivatives [(Miller et al., 2024)], and projected walks solve surface PDEs [(Sugimoto et al., 2024a)]. These advances mainly address linear PDE representations, boundary handling, or stochastic-estimate reuse. For semilinear PDEs, sphere jumps eliminate Brownian time discretization but not branching-tree growth. We target this remaining bottleneck through certified semilinear bounds and a transformed process with weighted exit and interior events sampled using the original screened WoS kernels.

    3. Envelope-Transformed Branching Walks

    3.1. Preliminary: Branching Walk on Spheres

    Branching Brownian motion (BBM) provides a stochastic representation of semilinear elliptic PDEs by interpreting nonlinear reactions as particle branching events. Consider F(u):=Lu+λ(P(u)-u)=0 with Dirichlet condition u|_∂Ω=g, where P(u)=∑ₖ₌₀^Kpₖuᵏ is the offspring generating function and L=1/2Δ. Each particle follows Brownian motion until either reaching the boundary or branching into k independent offspring with probability pₖ at an exponential rate λ. The solution is recovered as u(x)=𝔼[∏_i∈Tg(Xᵢ)], where T is the terminal leaves.

    For probabilistic semilinear elliptic PDEs, Dirichlet values naturally lie in [0,1]. For example, g(y)∈[0,1] may specify the success probability of a particle absorbed at y, in which case u(x) gives the probability that every terminal particle succeeds. This interpretation follows directly from the BBM representation u(x)=𝔼[∏_i∈Lg(Xᵢ)], and ensures 0≤u≤1.

    Branching WoS accelerates this process by replacing Brownian trajectories with sphere transitions. At each particle position x, let B=B(x,r)⊂Ω be the largest inscribed ball, and denote by H_λ and G_λ its screened exit and Green kernels, respectively. Conditioning on whether the particle exits the ball before branching yields the integral equation induced by total expectation:

    (1)

    u(x)=∫_∂BH_λ(x,dy) u(y)+λ∫_BG_λ(x,y)∑ₖ₌₀^Kpₖu(y)ᵏ dy.

    Specifically, the exit probability is q_B=∫_∂BH_λ(x,dy)=1/I₀(r√2λ) in ℝ², where I₀ denotes the modified Bessel function. With probability q_B, the particle jumps uniformly to ∂B and continues walking; otherwise, an interior branching location Y is sampled with density λG_λ(x,y)/(1-q_B), and k∼(pₖ) offspring are added to the active particle queue at Y. The procedure repeats until all particles reach the domain boundary or terminate with zero offspring, producing one Monte Carlo sample from the product of terminal values. Thus, although WoS eliminates explicit trajectory discretization, each sphere transition still requires a branching decision, while every offspring introduces additional walks that must be maintained and evaluated. Canonical results show that BWoS crashes when the particle splitting rate surpasses the boundary-absorbing speed, i.e., λ>λ₁ where λ₁ is the least non-negative eigenvalue of -L in Ω.

    3.2. From Solution Bounds to Branching Processes

    Although WoS eliminates explicit Brownian trajectory discretization, its computational cost still grows with the branching tree. The expected cumulative particle population becomes unbounded as λ approaches the principal Dirichlet eigenvalue λ₁ associated with Ω, motivating the early termination of subtrees whose remaining contributions can be bounded. Let τ denote the first Brownian exit time from Ω, and h(x)=𝔼ₓ[g(B_τ)] the harmonic extension of g. Several bounds follow directly from the BBM representation and its associated linear equations as Theorem 3.1.

    Theorem 3.1 (Probabilistic Solution Bounds).

    For 0<λ<λ₁,P(u)=u² and 0≤g≤1, the solution of F(u)=0 with u|∂Ω=g satisfies \max{L₀(x),L₁(x),L₂(x)}≤u(x)≤U(x), where U=h, and L₀(x)=𝔼ₓ[e^-λτg(Bτ)], L₁(x)=1-𝔼ₓ[e^λτ(1-g(B_τ))], L₂(x)=h(x)-\tfracλ4𝔼ₓ[τ].

    Proof.

    Since F(u)=0 implies Lu=λu(1-u)≥0, the maximum principle gives u≤h=U. For L₀, restrict the BBM expectation to trajectories reaching the boundary before their first branching event; all omitted products are nonnegative, yielding u≥𝔼ₓ[e^-λτg(B_τ)]. For L₁, let q=1-u. Then Lq+λq=λq²≥0. The Feynman–Kac formula gives q(x)=𝔼ₓ[e^λτ(1-g(B_τ))]-λ𝔼ₓ[∫₀^τe^λtq(Bₜ)² dt], hence u≥L₁. Finally, Dynkin’s formula gives h-u=λ𝔼ₓ[∫₀^τu(Bₜ)(1-u(Bₜ)) dt]. Since u(1-u)≤1/4, we obtain u≥L₂. ∎

    These bounds enable early termination of unresolved branching subtrees. Suppose the completed leaves contribute a product ω∈[0,1], while the active frontier contains particles at x₁,…,xₘ. By conditional independence, their remaining expected contribution is R=ω∏ᵢ₌₁ᵐu(xᵢ). With bounds L≤u≤U immediately yield

    (2)

    B⁻:=ω∏ᵢ₌₁ᵐL(xᵢ)≤R≤ω∏ᵢ₌₁ᵐU(xᵢ):=B⁺.

    Thus, whenever B⁺-B⁻≤2ε, the remaining tree can be pruned and replaced by (B⁻+B⁺)/2, introducing at most ε absolute bias in the final expectation, since the conditional expected contribution lies within [B⁻,B⁺].

    Despite their validity, these bounds incur evaluation overhead and exhibit strongly case-dependent efficiency (Fig. 2). L₀ ignores branched trajectories, L₁ deteriorates with large boundary deficits, while L₂ relies on the worst-case bound u(1-u)≤1/4. Consequently, L₂ generally performs best on smooth boundaries, whereas discontinuous binary data defeats most pruning with binary boundary condition. Combining all bounds often increases overhead without proportional savings. This motivates certified envelopes that directly reduce branching rather than repeatedly pruning existing trees.

    3.3. Generalized Envelope Branching

    The preceding pruning strategy uses solution bounds to terminate subtrees after they have been generated, but does not alter the underlying branching dynamics. We instead construct an equivalent branching process whose reproduction and termination rates are determined directly by certified solution envelopes. This can be understood as a generalized Doob’s h-transform, where the envelope width acts as the transforming function.

    For F(u)=0, let ℓ and a be certified sub- and supersolutions satisfying 0≤ℓ≤u≤a≤1, F(ℓ)≥0, and F(a)≤0.
