Define the domain envelop width d:=a-ℓ>0, the normalized solution v=(u-ℓ)/d∈[0,1], and the nonnegative residuals r_ℓ=F(ℓ) and rₐ=-F(a). By substituting u=ℓ+dv and expanding the offspring generating function, we obtain

    P(ℓ+dv)=P(ℓ)+∑ⱼ₌₁^KCⱼvʲ, Cⱼ=(P⁽ʲ⁾(ℓ))/(j!)dʲ≥0.

    The key is that the transformation changes not only the diffusion operator but also the branching mechanism into four parts – drifted diffusion Lᵈv, reduced branching ∑ⱼ₌₂^KλCⱼ(vʲ-v)/d, returning one r_c(1-v)/d and zero (being killed) -rₐv/d in the theorem below.

    Theorem 3.2 (Generalized Envelope Branching).

    With certified envelopes satisfying the conditions above and well-defined and integrable transformed branching process, v=(u-ℓ)/d satisfies

    (3)0=Lᵈv+∑ⱼ₌₂^KλCⱼ/d(vʲ-v)+(r_ℓ)/(d)(1-v)-rₐ/dv,

    where Lᵈ=L+∇\logd·∇. Consequently, the equivalent process branches into j≥2 offspring at rate λCⱼ/d, terminates successfully at rate r_ℓ/d, and terminates unsuccessfully at rate rₐ/d. If W∈[0,1] is its terminal-product estimator, then Z(x)=ℓ(x)+d(x)W is unbiased 𝔼[Z(x)]=u(x) and

    (4)

    Var[Z(x)]≤(u(x)-ℓ(x))(a(x)-u(x))≤d(x)²/4.

    Proof.

    The product rule gives L(dv)=dLᵈv+vLd, where Lᵈv=d⁻¹[L(dv)-vLd]. Since F(a)-F(ℓ)=-rₐ-r_ℓ and P(a)-P(ℓ)=∑ⱼ₌₁^KCⱼ, we have Ld-λd=-r_ℓ-rₐ-λ∑ⱼ₌₁^KCⱼ. Substituting these identities into F(ℓ+dv)=0 yields dLᵈv+r_ℓ(1-v)-rₐv+λ∑ⱼ₌₁^KCⱼ(vʲ-v)=0. The j=1 term vanishes, giving Eq. (3). Its nonnegative rates define the stated branching process, with boundary payoff (g-ℓ)/d∈[0,1]. The branching representation gives 𝔼[W]=v, hence 𝔼[Z]=u. Finally, Z∈[ℓ,a] implies 𝔼[(Z-ℓ)(a-Z)]≥0, which yields Eq. (3). ∎

    Beyond preserving the original PDE solution, it also changes the expected branching complexity. For conventional BBM, the expected number of reproduction events m_B satisfies (-L-λ)m_B=λ, with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. The transformed process instead obeys the following equation.

    Lemma 3.3 (Expected Branching Complexity).

    Let m_ℓ,a(x) denote the expected number of reproduction events in the transformed process, assumed finite. Then H=m_ℓ,ad satisfies H|_∂Ω=0 and

    (5)

    [-L+λ(1-P^′(a))]H=λ[P(a)-P(ℓ)-P^′(ℓ)d].

    Proof.

    Writing bⱼ=λCⱼ/d and κ=(r_ℓ+rₐ)/d, the first-event decomposition gives

    (6)

    -Lᵈm_ℓ,a+[κ-∑ⱼ₌₂^K(j-1)bⱼ]m_ℓ,a=∑ⱼ₌₂^Kbⱼ.

    Multiplying by d and using Ld=λd-r_ℓ-rₐ-λ∑ⱼ₌₁^KCⱼ, together with ∑ⱼ₌₁^KjCⱼ=P^′(a)d and ∑ⱼ₌₂^KCⱼ=P(a)-P(ℓ)-P^′(ℓ)d, yields the stated equation. ∎

    For binary branching, this reduces to [-L+λ(1-2a)]H=λd². Thus, the transformation changes both the source of branching work and the elliptic operator governing its propagation. In particular, narrowing the envelope suppresses the quadratic source term, while the upper envelope controls the effective reproduction potential. These effects explain how WiE can reduce branching complexity even when conventional BBM approaches its critical regime. Also, there exists a harmonic envelope such that the cost of WiE keeps finite as the splitting rate approaches the divergence limit of vanilla WoS in theory as Theorem 3.4 reveals.

    Theorem 3.4 (Bounded near-critical branching with harmonic envelopes).

    Let Ω⊂ℝⁿ be a bounded, connected C^2,α domain, and let λ₁>0 be the principal Dirichlet eigenvalue of -L, where L=1/2Δ. Suppose g∈C^2,α(∂Ω) satisfies 0≤g≤1, g\not≡0, and g\not≡1. Let h be its harmonic extension, Lh=0 in Ω and h=g on ∂Ω. For the binary branching equation Lu+λ(u²-u)=0, choose the certified envelopes ℓ=0 and a=h. Then the expected reproduction count m_λ of the transformed process satisfies

    (7)

    \sup_0<λ<λ₁|m_λ|_L^∞(Ω)<∞.

    In contrast, the expected reproduction count m_λ^BBM of conventional binary BBM diverges as λ↑λ₁: for every fixed x∈Ω, m_λ^BBM(x)=Θ((λ₁-λ)⁻¹).

    Proof.

    The strong maximum principle gives 00 in the interior. By Lemma 3.3, H_λ:=hm_λ solves

    (8)

    A_λH_λ=λh², H_λ|∂Ω=0, Aλ=-L-λ+2λ(1-h).

    We first show that A_λ has a spectral gap uniform up to λ₁. At λ=λ₁, its quadratic form is

    (9)

    ⟨f,A_λ₁f⟩=∥∇f∥₂²/2-λ₁∥f∥₂² (≥0)+2λ₁∫_Ω(1-h)f² dx.

    If its lowest eigenvalue were zero, equality would force f to be a multiple of the positive first Dirichlet eigenfunction φ₁ and simultaneously ∫_Ω(1-h)f² dx=0, contradicting 1-h>0 in Ω. Hence κ:=λ_\min(A_λ₁)>0. Writing t=λ/λ₁ gives A_λ=(1-t)(-L)+tA_λ₁, so the min–max principle yields

    (10)

    λ_\min(A_λ)≥(1-t)λ₁+tκ≥\minλ₁,κ>0.

    Uniform invertibility and standard Dirichlet elliptic estimates therefore imply |H_λ|C¹(Ω̄)≤C, with C independent of λ∈(0,λ₁). Since Hλ=0 on ∂Ω, |H_λ(x)|≤C,dist(x,∂Ω). On the other hand, positivity of h in the interior, the Hopf boundary lemma at points where g=0, and compactness of ∂Ω imply h(x)≥c,dist(x,∂Ω) for some c>0. Thus m_λ=H_λ/h≤C/c throughout Ω, proving the bound. For conventional BBM, (-L-λ)m_λ^BBM=λ with zero Dirichlet boundary data. The isolated principal-eigenvalue resolvent expansion gives

    (11)

    m_λ^BBM(x)=(λ₁⟨1,φ₁⟩φ₁(x))/(λ₁-λ)+Oₓ(1), λ↑λ₁,

    where |φ₁|₂=1. This proves the stated divergence. ∎

    3.4. Walk in Envelopes: Exact Walk-on-Spheres Transition

    The generalized Doob transform introduces a spatially varying drift ∇\logd, seemingly requiring a new sampler for the transformed diffusion, which instead be sampled exactly by reweighting the original WoS transitions, without explicitly simulating drifted trajectories.

    Theorem 3.5 (Exact Envelope-Aware WoS Transition).

    For any certified envelopes 0≤ℓ
    (12)d(x)v(x)=∫_∂BH_λ(x,dy) d(y)v(y)
    +∫_BG_λ(x,y)[r_ℓ(y)+λ∑ⱼ₌₁^KCⱼ(y)v(y)ʲ] dy.

    Moreover, Eq. (12) admits an exact stochastic transition using only the original screened WoS kernels and pointwise envelope evaluations.

    Proof.

    Expanding F(ℓ+dv)=0 using P(ℓ+dv)=P(ℓ)+∑ⱼ₌₁^KCⱼvʲ gives (λ-L)(dv)=r_ℓ+λ∑ⱼ₌₁^KCⱼvʲ. Applying the screened Green representation on B establishes Eq. (12). Set v≡1 on the right-hand side of Eq. (12) and have

    (13)

    λω_I:=r_ℓ+rₐ+λ∑ⱼ₌₁^KCⱼ=λd-Ld.

    Since all terms are nonnegative, ω_I≥0. Applying the screened Green representation to d yields

    (14)

    d(x)=∫_∂BH_λ(x,dy)d(y)+\allowbreakλ\allowbreak∫_BG_λ(x,y)ω_I(y) dy.

    Dividing by d(x) therefore defines a probability distribution over two mutually exclusive outcomes: exiting the sphere with density H_λ(x,dy)d(y)/d(x), or triggering an interior event with density λG_λ(x,y)ω_I(y)/d(x). For an interior event at y, dividing the nonnegative terms in Eq. (13) by λω_I(y) gives

    (15)

    π₊(y):=(r_ℓ(y))/(λω_I(y)), π₋(y):=(rₐ(y))/(λω_I(y)), πⱼ(y):=(Cⱼ(y))/(ω_I(y)).

    These probabilities correspond to successful termination, unsuccessful termination, and j offspring, respectively, with π₊+π₋+∑ⱼπⱼ=1. Multiplying the interior density by each event probability recovers the corresponding integrand in Eq. (12); unsuccessful termination contributes zero. Hence the stochastic transition reproduces the original integral equation exactly. ∎

    The remaining challenge is sampling this distribution without evaluating its weighted integrals. Although Eq. (14) provides the normalizing constant d(x), directly sampling a density proportional to H_λd or G_λω_I would require a new sampler for each spatially varying envelope. Instead, we use rejection sampling to recover these densities from the original WoS proposals.

    Specifically, the target exit and interior transition measures are proportional to H_λ(x,dy)d(y) and λG_λ(x,y)ω_I(y) dy, respectively. We therefore introduce two certified constants M_E≥\sup_∂Bd and M_I≥\sup_Bω_I to dominate these weighted measures by distributions that are already straightforward to sample. Let q_B=∫_∂BH_λ(x,dy) denote the original sphere-exit probability. The corresponding proposal masses are q_BM_E for exits and (1-q_B)M_I for interior events, giving the computable normalization Q_B=q_BM_E+(1-q_B)M_I.

    We first choose an exit proposal with probability q_BM_E/Q_B, otherwise an interior proposal. Its position Y is drawn from H_λ/q_B or λG_λ/(1-q_B), respectively, and accepted with probability d(Y)/M_E or ω_I(Y)/M_I. For example, the joint probability measure of proposing and accepting an exit at y is (q_BM_E)/(Q_B)(H_λ(x,dy))/(q_B)(d(y))/(M_E)=(H_λ(x,dy)d(y))/(Q_B).

    Similarly, the accepted interior measure is λG_λ(x,y)ω_I(y) dy/Q_B. Their total mass is d(x)/Q_B by Eq. (14). Conditioning on acceptance therefore divides both measures by d(x)/Q_B, recovering exactly the target transition probabilities. Thus, the accpetance rate is d(x)/Q_B and rejected candidates can simply be resampled. Notice that neither the target normalization d(x) nor any weighted Green integral needs to be evaluated during sampling.

    3.5. Extensions to Other Semilinear PDEs

    Figure 3 compares projected WiE on a cylinder (top) and heat-ball WiE on the unit square (bottom) with independent finite-difference reference solutions.

    3.5.1. Projected Walk in Envelopes on Manifolds

    For an embedded manifold M⊂ℝⁿ, the envelope transformation extends by replacing L with the Laplace–Beltrami operator L_M=1/2Δ_M, preserving the branching and termination coefficients. Following PWoS [(Sugimoto et al., 2024b)], we approximate intrinsic transitions using ambient Euclidean WoS kernels and the closest-point projection y^*=π(y). Specifically, Eq. (12) becomes

    (16)v_π(x)=(1)/(N_π(x))[∫_∂BH_λ(x,dy) d(y^*)v_π(y^*)
    +∫_BG_λ(x,y)(r_ℓ(y^*)+λ∑ⱼ₌₁^KCⱼ(y^*)v_π(y^*)ʲ) dy],

    where the projected normalization is

    (17)

    N_π(x)=∫_∂BH_λ(x,dy)d(y^*)+λ∫_BG_λ(x,y)ω_I(y^*) dy.

    The rejection sampler from the preceding section applies unchanged, evaluating all envelope-dependent weights at y^* instead of y. Since projected ambient kernels only approximate intrinsic Brownian transitions, N_π(x) need not equal d(x), introducing the same type of geometric approximation as PWoS without requiring intrinsic surface Green kernels.

    3.5.2. Semilinear Parabolic PDEs

    For ∂ₜu=Lu+λ(P(u)-u), replace L by D=L-∂ₜ in the envelope residuals, requiring r_ℓ=Dℓ+λ(P(ℓ)-ℓ)≥0, rₐ=-Da-λ(P(a)-a)≥0, and valid initial/lateral bounds. The coefficients Cⱼ and event rules retain their previous forms, but the interior weight becomes W_λ=λd-Dd=r_ℓ+rₐ+λ∑ⱼCⱼ. Replace each spatial ball by a backward heat ball [(Deaconu et al., 2017)], with elapsed time s and displacement z: H_η={(s,z):0

    Interior locations follow the killed occupation densityq_η(s,z) ds dz=ℙ(Bₛ∈dz, σ>s) ds, rather than the exit distribution: q_η(s,z)=[p(s,z)-(2πη)^-n/2]1_(s,z)∈H_η with p(s,z)=(2πs)^-n/2e^-|z|²/(2s). Let m₀=∫_H_ηq_η ds dz=η(n/n+2)^n/2+1. To sample q_η/m₀, propose S∼Unif(0,η) and Y∼ℕ(0,SIₙ); accept with probability 1_(S,Y)∈H_η[1-(2πη)^-n/2/p(S,Y)]. With M_E≥\sup_∂H_ηd and M_I≥\sup_H_ηW_λ, replace the preceding section’s proposal masses by M_E and m₀M_I (thus Q=M_E+m₀M_I). At (t-S,x+Y), accept exits with e^-λSd/M_E and interiors with e^-λSW_λ/M_I; all offspring and termination rules remain unchanged. At the initial boundary, return (u₀-ℓ)/d.

    4. Efficient Envelope Construction and Sampling

    4.1. Monotone Envelope Refinement for Full Field

    The transformation admits many certified envelopes with different computational costs. We construct tight, reusable bounds for full-field evaluation through four steps: a comparison principle certifies bounds from PDE residuals and boundary conditions; query-weighted envelope width approximates the intractable time–variance objective; conservative affine constraints monotonically refine an initially feasible pair; and cubic B-splines with cellwise Bernstein constraints reduce continuous certification to finite-dimensional linear programs. Certification is preserved throughout, while preprocessing is amortized across repeated queries.

    Lemma 4.1 (Comparison Principle for Certified Envelopes).

    For a bounded Lipschitz domain Ω⊂ℝⁿ, assume λ≥0 and λ\sup_s∈[0,1]\allowbreak(P^′(s)-1)<λ₁. Suppose u,ℓ,a∈C²(Ω)∩C(Ω̄)∩H¹(Ω) take values in [0,1] and satisfy F(u)=0,F(ℓ)≥0,F(a)≤0 and ℓ≤u≤a on ∂Ω. Then ℓ≤u≤a throughout Ω.

    Proof.

    We first prove ℓ≤u. Set w=ℓ-u. Since F(ℓ)-F(u)≥0, subtracting the two PDE residuals gives Lw+λ(P(ℓ)-P(u)-w)≥0. To rewrite the nonlinear difference as a term proportional to w, apply the fundamental theorem of calculus pointwise:

    (18)

    P(ℓ(x))-P(u(x))=∫ᵤ₍ₓ₎^ℓ(x)P^′(s) ds=w(x)∫₀¹P^′(u(x)+tw(x)) dt.

    Define the bounded coefficient q(x)=∫₀¹P^′(u(x)+tw(x)) dt. Because 0≤u,ℓ≤1, every argument of P^′ lies in [0,1], and thus

    (19)

    λ(q(x)-1)≤λ\sup_s∈[0,1](P^′(s)-1)<λ₁.

    It follows that 1/2Δw+λ(q(x)-1)w≥0, w≤0 on∂Ω. We now justify the maximum-principle step rather than assuming it. Let w₊=\max{w,0}. Since w≤0 on the boundary and w∈H¹(Ω), we have w₊∈H₀¹(Ω). Multiplying the last differential inequality by w₊ and integrating by parts gives

    (20)

    0≤-1/2∫_Ω|∇w₊|² dx+λ∫_Ω(q(x)-1)w₊² dx.

    Consequently,

    (21)

    1/2∫_Ω|∇w₊|² dx≤c_*∫_Ωw₊² dx, c_*:=λ\sup_s∈[0,1](P^′(s)-1).

    The variational characterization of the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of -1/2Δ states that, for any φ∈H₀¹(Ω), 1/2∫_Ω|∇φ|² dx≥λ₁∫_Ωφ² dx. Applying this inequality to φ=w₊ yields (λ₁-c_*)∫_Ωw₊² dx≤0. Since λ₁-c_*>0, we obtain w₊=0, hence ℓ≤u.

    To prove u≤a, repeat the same argument with w=u-a. Indeed, F(u)-F(a)≥0, w≤0 on the boundary, and P(u)-P(a)=w∫₀¹P^′(a+t(u-a)) dt. The same upper bound on the resulting zero-order coefficient and the same energy argument show (u-a)₊=0. Thus ℓ≤u≤a in Ω. ∎

    Work-aware envelope optimization.

    Let ℚ⊂Ω denote the evaluation region and let T_ℓ,a(x) and V_ℓ,a(x) be the expected runtime and estimator variance induced by a certified envelope pair (ℓ,a). For full-field evaluation, the ideal envelopes minimize the total cost of reaching a prescribed accuracy ∫_ℚT_ℓ,a(x)V_ℓ,a(x) dμ(x). Here μ describes the distribution of evaluation queries. The objective reflects the time–variance cost of independent Monte Carlo evaluation, but is difficult to optimize directly because T_ℓ,a depends on the entire transformed branching process.

    Fortunately, the envelope width d=a-ℓ provides a tractable surrogate. From Eq. (12), the transformed reproduction coefficients are Cⱼ=P⁽ʲ⁾(ℓ)dʲ/j!. In particular, for binary branching, the probability mass associated with reproduction is proportional to d². Moreover, Eq. (4) bounds the estimator variance by d²/4. These observations motivate minimizing the domain-averaged envelope width which replaces T_ℓ,a(x)V_ℓ,a(x), yielding

    (22)\min_ℓ,a∫_ℚ(a(x)-ℓ(x)) dμ(x),
    s.t.F(ℓ)≥0,F(a)≤0,0≤ℓ≤a≤1,ℓ|_∂Ω≤g≤a|_∂Ω.

    This objective seeks a single pair of reusable envelopes rather than independently optimizing bounds at each evaluation point. While width reduction does not guarantee a proportional runtime improvement, it simultaneously suppresses higher-order reproduction terms and tightens the estimator’s variance bound.

    Monotone certified refinement.

    The optimization in Eq. (22) is nonlinear because the envelope constraints involve the reaction term P. We therefore begin with a feasible pair (ℓ₀,a₀) and construct a sequence of increasingly tight certified envelopes. At iteration t, we seek nonnegative corrections hₜ,jₜ such that

    (23)

    ℓₜ₊₁=ℓₜ+hₜ, aₜ₊₁=aₜ-jₜ.

    The corresponding optimization maximizes the improvement

    (24)\max_hₜ,jₜ≥0∫_ℚ(hₜ+jₜ) dμ,
    s.t.F(ℓₜ+hₜ)≥0, F(aₜ-jₜ)≤0, ℓₜ+hₜ≤aₜ-jₜ,

    together with the original range and boundary constraints. Feasibility at every iteration implies

    (25)

    ℓₜ≤ℓₜ₊₁≤u≤aₜ₊₁≤aₜ, J(ℓₜ₊₁,aₜ₊₁)≤J(ℓₜ,aₜ).

    Thus, refinement never sacrifices a previously certified bound, and every accepted update improves the surrogate objective (Figure 4).

    For a general offspring generating function P(u)=∑ₖ₌₀^Kpₖuᵏ, the nonlinear certification constraints can be converted into affine sufficient conditions by exploiting the convexity of P on [0,1]. Substituting the monotone updates yields

    (26)F(ℓₜ+hₜ)=F(ℓₜ)+[L+λ(P^′(ℓₜ)-1)]hₜ+λR_ℓ(hₜ),
    -F(aₜ-jₜ)=-F(aₜ)+[L+λ(P^′(aₜ)-1)]jₜ-λRₐ(jₜ),

    where the Taylor remainders satisfy

    (27)R_ℓ(hₜ)=∫₀^hₜ(hₜ-s)P^′′(ℓₜ+s) ds≥0,
    Rₐ(jₜ)=∫₀^jₜ(jₜ-s)P^′′(aₜ-s) ds≤Mₜ/2jₜ²,

    with Mₜ(x)=\sup_s∈[ℓₜ(x),aₜ(x)]P^′′(s). Imposing a trust region 0≤jₜ≤δ further gives Rₐ(jₜ)≤Mₜδjₜ/2. Therefore, the original nonlinear certification constraints are guaranteed by

    (28)F(ℓₜ)+[L+λ(P^′(ℓₜ)-1)]hₜ≥0,
    -F(aₜ)+[L+λ(P^′(aₜ)-1-\tfrac12Mₜδ)]jₜ≥0.

    Since ℓₜ, aₜ, and Mₜ are fixed during each iteration, these conditions are affine in hₜ and jₜ. Together with the linear width-reduction objective and monotonicity constraints, they yield a linear program after finite-dimensional representation and continuous certification. Thus, the refinement extends to general offspring distributions while preserving the validity and nesting of the certified envelopes.

    Finite-dimensional certified optimization.

    We represent the envelopes using cubic B-splines, ℓ(x)=∑ᵢcᵢ^ℓφᵢ(x) and a(x)=∑ᵢcᵢᵃφᵢ(x), with their coefficients as optimization variables. Although Eq. (28) is affine in the corrections, it imposes infinitely many spatial constraints. The following theorem provides a finite-dimensional certification. On each spline cell, we express the affine residuals and ordering constraints in the Bernstein basis, enforcing nonnegativity of their coefficients; range and polynomial boundary constraints are handled analogously. These finitely many sufficient linear inequalities certify the PDE constraints throughout the domain while preserving monotone envelope refinement.

    For nonrectangular domains, we may restrict these certificates to a decomposition of each cell intersected with Ω, using tensor-product or triangular Bernstein bases on the resulting pieces. This changes the sufficient finite constraints, while retaining the same globally C² spline representation and continuous PDE inequalities on Ω. Therefore, the resulting refinement is a linear program with continuous, rather than pointwise, certification. The Bernstein constraints yields a conservative feasible set. The envelopes are constructed once and reused across full-field evaluations, amortizing their preprocessing cost over all queries.

    4.2. Efficient Envelope-Aware Sampling

    Although the envelope transformation reduces branching complexity, sampling its spatially varying transition weights introduces additional overhead. We employ three complementary optimizations to reduce this cost while preserving the exact transition law.

    Adaptive screening.

    The screened-kernel representation allows an adjustable parameter μ∈[0,λ]. Using Eq. (3), the interior weight W_μ=λω_I-(λ-μ)d, yielding

    (29)W_μ=r_ℓ+rₐ+λ∑ⱼ₌₂^KCⱼ+[μ-λ+λP^′(ℓ)]d.

    This decomposition shows that changing μ affects only the single-offspring continuation weight, leaving termination and genuine reproduction weights unchanged. Their nonnegativity is preserved by choosing μ_B=λ\max{0,1-P^′(ℓ_B)}, where ℓ_B is a certified lower bound over the sphere. A smaller μ_B increases the sphere-exit probability, potentially reducing expensive interior proposals without altering the represented solution.

    Spatially adaptive majorants.

    Instead of using global rejection bounds, we independently bound the exit and interior weights by M_E≥\sup_∂Bd and M_I≥\sup_BW_μ. Their proposal masses are q_μM_E and m_μM_I, where q_μ=∫_∂BH_μ and m_μ=∫_BG_μ. The corresponding acceptance probabilities are d(y)/M_E and W_μ(y)/M_I. We obtain tight local bounds from the spline cells intersecting each sphere and accelerate their aggregation using range-minimum/maximum queries (RMQ), reducing rejection without changing the accepted distribution.

    Lazy evaluation.

    Even with tighter proposals, computing the exact envelope weights for every candidate is unnecessary. We first compare the rejection threshold against inexpensive local lower and upper bounds: candidates are accepted or rejected immediately when these bounds determine the outcome, and full spline evaluation is performed only otherwise. Green-kernel sampling is deferred until an interior proposal is selected, while reusable kernel quantities are cached. Thus, most inexpensive decisions avoid the cost of exact weight evaluation, and the savings accumulate across repeated transitions in the branching tree.

    Spectral-workload fallback.

    Envelope construction incurs a one-time cost that may outweigh its sampling benefits. Motivated by the near-critical BBM work scaling (1-ρ)⁻¹, where ρ=λ(P^′(1)-1)/λ₁<1, we define a spectral-workload indicator for Q queries at target RMSE ε:

    (30)

    W=Q/ε²ρ/1-ρ.

    We activate WiE only when ρ≥ρ₀ and W≥A, with ρ₀=0.8 and A=10⁸ calibrated empirically across four scenes (Figure 5). This pilot-free criterion avoids unnecessary preprocessing, while imperfect fallback decisions affect efficiency but not correctness.

    5. Experiments

    Our proposed WiE algorithm is evaluated in four non-trivial 2D scenes against canonical branching WoS. The results are illustrated in Figure 6 and the its speedup effects are evaluated with different branching rates. In Table 1, it is clear that WiE naturally appears insignificant with low splitting rate and thus the extra processing cost overwhelms its variance advantage per sample; while its merit become explicit as β/λ₁ grows, it strongly suppresses the splitting rate in simulation by being enveloped, which is consistent across all scenarios. Besides, WiE also achieves the same accuracy using much less time than vanilla branching WoS in high splitting scenes as in Table 2.

    Envelope construction ablation.

    We compare three certified constructions with the same 6×6 bicubic basis: sequential LP optimizes the upper and then lower envelope separately, joint LP minimizes their width together, and monotone refinement further tightens the joint solution by certified nonlinear iterations. The archived three-update configuration in Figure 7 shows that joint optimization improves width over sequential fitting, while refinement additionally reduces it by 5.5% on Engine and 7.2% on Flask without increasing spline resolution. Gains on Lock and Clover are negligible, and tighter envelopes do not uniformly imply lower sampling work. Thus, iteration can improve a fixed representation, but is not a universal substitute for increasing its resolution.

    Spline resolution.

    Table 3(a) examines spatial resolution and geometric certification. The earlier implementation certifies the entire bounding square, including regions outside the PDE domain and inside holes. We instead clip certificate cells to the original polygon: intact or axis-aligned pieces use tensor-product Bernstein coefficients, and oblique pieces use triangular Bernstein coefficients. The envelopes remain globally C² cubic B-splines. We keep the same boundary data, offspring laws, and ρ=λ(P^′(1)-1)/λ̂₁=0.98. For all six non-square domains, we transfer the same k=6 joint initialization exactly to k=12 and 24 before refinement, so the resolution comparison does not change the initial functions. Both coefficient vectors are restricted to [-2,2] to suppress large, weakly constrained exterior modes. This extension constraint is additional to the certified range and PDE conditions inside Ω.

    Refinement iterations.

    We allow up to 12 updates, retaining d≥0.003 and the upper-correction limit 0.075. We stop after two successive width reductions below 10⁻⁶, or return the last valid pair when the LP budget or numerical checks fail; the actual accepted count is reported. If the full polynomial LP accepts no update, we retry from the same initialization using conservative cellwise scalar bounds on the residuals and P^′; both attempts are included in construction cost. Table 4(b) tests the returned pairs with fixed queries, sample count, seeds, and rejection-bound grid. At k=24, the six non-square cases reduce mean width by 53–87% relative to the earlier coarse result. Relative to their common initialization, their sampling time–variance efficiency improves by 2.06–23.13×, while additional construction costs 298–600 CPU seconds. Thus finer envelopes improve sampling in these tests, but need sufficient reuse to offset preprocessing. The L-shaped case attains a smaller mean width at k=12 than at k=24; the latter uses the conservative fallback, and these finite-budget results do not imply monotonic improvement with resolution. These results diagnose envelope construction rather than changing the variable transformation underlying WiE. All cases use the general-PGF kernel; Figure 7 retains the earlier specialized binary implementation.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：分支强度接近临界阈值时期望粒子数发散；把「繁殖」重参数化成分裂/返回0/返回1 三类事件，无偏且能剪掉冗余分支。

要点：

  • branching WoS 用无网格方式解半线性 PDE，但分支强度接近临界谱阈值时期望粒子数发散，计算树迅速爆炸
  • WiE 不是去剪已有的树，而是用可证明的解上下界重新参数化分支扩散：抑制繁殖、引入受控终止，并给出与包络相关的方差界以保证无偏
  • 用 screened WoS 核做精确拒绝采样实现该变换，配可证明的样条包络与自适应采样；并证明合适的调和包络能让期望繁殖次数有界，而传统 BBM 会发散

为什么值得看：路径追踪里解半线性 PDE（参与介质、非线性散射）本来就靠随机过程，分支一多就没法算。这里给出的是「带证书的方差控制」，和渲染里用控制变量/上界估计降噪是同一套思路。

中文摘要：无网格蒙特卡洛方法（如 Walk-on-Spheres）能在复杂区域上做点查询式的 PDE 求解，扩展到半线性方程则需要处理非线性反应项，常用的概率表示是分支布朗运动——把非线性项换成粒子繁殖事件。但消除时间离散并不消除分支复杂度：每个后代都要再开新的游走，当分支强度接近临界谱阈值时，期望粒子数发散，使本来合法的随机表示变得不可算。Walk in Envelopes 不改动已有树去做剪枝，而是用可证明的解上下界来变换分支扩散：抑制繁殖、引入受控终止，并通过包络相关的方差界保持无偏。作者用标准 screened WoS 核做精确拒绝采样来实现该变换，配可证明的样条包络与自适应采样，并证明合适的调和包络能让期望繁殖次数有界。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-18

本期推送：2026-10-24

Walk in Envelopes: Efficient Branching Walk-on-Spheres via Certified Solution Bounds

© none

Abstract.

Branching Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) solves semilinear PDEs without meshes, but its computational cost grows sharply near critical branching rates. We introduce Walk in Envelopes (WiE), which uses certified solution bounds to transform branching diffusion rather than prune existing trees. The transformation suppresses reproduction, introduces controlled termination, and preserves unbiasedness with an envelope-dependent variance bound. We realize the transformed process through exact rejection sampling using standard screened WoS kernels, supported by certified spline envelopes and adaptive sampling and further prove that suitable harmonic envelopes yield bounded expected reproduction counts even as conventional BBM diverges.

Keywords:

Walk-on-Spheres, Branching Brownian Motion, Semilinear PDEs, Certified Solution Bounds, Monte Carlo Methods

1. Introduction

Grid-free Monte Carlo methods have become an attractive alternative to mesh-based PDE solvers, enabling pointwise solution queries on complex domains without constructing a global discretization [(Sawhney and Crane, 2020)]. While Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) efficiently resolves linear elliptic equations through boundary-hitting processes, extending this paradigm to semilinear PDEs requires handling nonlinear reactions. Branching Brownian motion (BBM) provides a natural probabilistic representation by replacing nonlinear terms with particle reproduction events [(Agarwal and Claisse, 2020)]. Combined with WoS, this yields a grid-free solver for semilinear equations. However, eliminating Brownian time discretization does not eliminate branching complexity: each offspring initiates additional walks, and the expected particle population diverges as the branching intensity approaches a critical spectral threshold. This makes otherwise valid stochastic representations increasingly expensive precisely in strongly nonlinear regimes.

A natural strategy is to exploit approximate solution information to terminate branches whose remaining contributions are sufficiently small. Yet such pruning requires reliable bounds on unresolved subtrees, whose evaluation can itself be expensive. Approximate bounds may also introduce bias, while tighter estimates do not necessarily offset their computation costs. More fundamentally, pruning acts on a branching process that has already been generated, rather than preventing unnecessary reproduction. This motivates a different question: can certified solution information be used to construct an equivalent stochastic process that branches less frequently, without sacrificing correctness?

We introduce Walk in Envelopes (WiE), a branching WoS framework that transforms the stochastic representation using certified lower and upper solution envelopes. Given sub- and supersolutions ℓ≤u≤a, we normalize the unknown solution as v=(u-ℓ)/(a-ℓ). This induces a generalized Doob transform whose diffusion, reproduction, and termination mechanisms are determined by the envelope functions. For binary branching, the reproduction rate becomes λ(a-ℓ), while envelope residuals introduce additional success and failure termination events. The resulting estimator remains unbiased and has variance bounded by (a-ℓ)²/4. Moreover, we characterize its expected reproduction count through an elliptic equation, showing that a suitable harmonic envelope can keep this count uniformly bounded even as conventional BBM approaches its critical divergence threshold. Although branching-process transformations have established mathematical foundations [(Engländer, 2007)], WiE develops them into a certified computational framework for semilinear PDE solving.

The transformed process introduces spatially varying diffusion, which would ordinarily require simulating drifted trajectories. We avoid this difficulty by deriving an exact envelope-aware transition using the original screened WoS exit and Green kernels. Rejection sampling with certified local majorants realizes the transformed distribution without evaluating weighted kernel integrals. To obtain useful envelopes efficiently, we develop monotone refinement of cubic B-spline sub- and supersolutions, using Bernstein constraints to certify PDE inequalities throughout the domain by comparison principle. Adaptive screening, spatially localized rejection bounds, and lazy evaluation further reduce sampling overhead, while a spectral-workload criterion avoids unnecessary preprocessing in inexpensive regimes.

We evaluate WiE on four complex two-dimensional domains across branching intensities and accuracy requirements. Near criticality, WiE achieves 6.9–16.2× improvements in time–variance efficiency and 4.7–14.6× reductions in sampling time at matched accuracy, excluding one-time envelope construction. Its benefits increase with branching intensity, while a workload-aware fallback preserves the efficiency of conventional BBM in easier regimes. We additionally demonstrate extensions to projected walks on manifolds and semilinear parabolic equations.

Our main contributions are:

  • •

    A certified envelope transformation of branching diffusion, with unbiased estimation, variance guarantees, and a spectral characterization of near-critical branching complexity.

  • •

    An exact envelope-aware WoS sampler using existing screened kernels, without explicitly simulating transformed diffusion.

  • •

    A practical solver combining certified spline-envelope refinement, efficient rejection sampling, and workload-aware fallback, with substantial near-critical acceleration.

    • 2. Related Work

    Branching Diffusions and Solution-Guided Transformations.

    BBM represents semilinear reaction–diffusion PDEs, beginning with McKean’s Kolmogorov–Petrovskii–Piskunov representation [(McKean, 1975)]. Branching-diffusion solvers extend to polynomial nonlinearities, gradient dependence via marked particles [(Henry-Labordère et al., 2019)], and elliptic boundary-value problems on bounded domains [(Agarwal and Claisse, 2020)], but face integrability and branching-cost restrictions under strong branching. Process transformations are well established: nonlinear h-transforms alter both motion and reproduction [(Engländer, 2007)], while measure changes and backbone decompositions characterize conditioned branching and near-critical behavior [(Salisbury and Verzani, 2000; Harris et al., 2016)]. These underpin solution-guided representations. Our computational realization uses certified sub- and supersolutions to obtain nonnegative branching and killing rates, with exact sphere-transition sampling requiring neither the unknown solution nor drifted-trajectory simulation.

    Monte Carlo Methods for Nonlinear Equations.

    Monte Carlo solvers avoid global spatial discretization, but nested nonlinear expectations and recursive branching can sharply increase variance and work. Numerical branching methods handle polynomial nonlinear PDEs, subject to representation-dependent convergence and integrability [(Henry-Labordère et al., 2019; Agarwal and Claisse, 2020)]. In graphics, [(Tong and Hachisuka, 2025)] accelerate nonlinear recursive light transport through nonlinear path filtering that reuses intermediate evaluations and neural radiance caching that learns them. For nonlinear radiative boundary conditions, [(Bao et al., 2026)] combine Picard-style iteration with Monte Carlo PDE solvers. These reduce nonlinear integral-equation costs through reuse, approximation, or iteration. Instead, we retain a branching estimator but change its probability law: certified envelopes suppress reproduction, bound its range, and preserve its expectation under stated assumptions. We reduce sample-generation work rather than only accelerate or approximate an existing recursion.

    Walk-on-Spheres and Grid-Free PDE Solvers.

    WoS originated for Dirichlet problems [(Muller, 1956)] and entered geometric computing as a grid-free elliptic PDE solver for point queries [(Sawhney and Crane, 2020)]. Extensions handle spatially varying coefficients via null scattering [(Sawhney et al., 2022)], mixed Neumann–Dirichlet conditions via walk on stars [(Sawhney et al., 2023)], and boundary-integral transport via walk on boundary [(Sugimoto et al., 2023)]. Boundary-value caching reuses estimates across queries [(Miller et al., 2023)], differential WoS computes parameter derivatives [(Miller et al., 2024)], and projected walks solve surface PDEs [(Sugimoto et al., 2024a)]. These advances mainly address linear PDE representations, boundary handling, or stochastic-estimate reuse. For semilinear PDEs, sphere jumps eliminate Brownian time discretization but not branching-tree growth. We target this remaining bottleneck through certified semilinear bounds and a transformed process with weighted exit and interior events sampled using the original screened WoS kernels.

    3. Envelope-Transformed Branching Walks

    3.1. Preliminary: Branching Walk on Spheres

    Branching Brownian motion (BBM) provides a stochastic representation of semilinear elliptic PDEs by interpreting nonlinear reactions as particle branching events. Consider F(u):=Lu+λ(P(u)-u)=0 with Dirichlet condition u|_∂Ω=g, where P(u)=∑ₖ₌₀^Kpₖuᵏ is the offspring generating function and L=1/2Δ. Each particle follows Brownian motion until either reaching the boundary or branching into k independent offspring with probability pₖ at an exponential rate λ. The solution is recovered as u(x)=𝔼[∏_i∈Tg(Xᵢ)], where T is the terminal leaves.

    For probabilistic semilinear elliptic PDEs, Dirichlet values naturally lie in [0,1]. For example, g(y)∈[0,1] may specify the success probability of a particle absorbed at y, in which case u(x) gives the probability that every terminal particle succeeds. This interpretation follows directly from the BBM representation u(x)=𝔼[∏_i∈Lg(Xᵢ)], and ensures 0≤u≤1.

    Branching WoS accelerates this process by replacing Brownian trajectories with sphere transitions. At each particle position x, let B=B(x,r)⊂Ω be the largest inscribed ball, and denote by H_λ and G_λ its screened exit and Green kernels, respectively. Conditioning on whether the particle exits the ball before branching yields the integral equation induced by total expectation:

    (1)

    u(x)=∫_∂BH_λ(x,dy) u(y)+λ∫_BG_λ(x,y)∑ₖ₌₀^Kpₖu(y)ᵏ dy.

    Specifically, the exit probability is q_B=∫_∂BH_λ(x,dy)=1/I₀(r√2λ) in ℝ², where I₀ denotes the modified Bessel function. With probability q_B, the particle jumps uniformly to ∂B and continues walking; otherwise, an interior branching location Y is sampled with density λG_λ(x,y)/(1-q_B), and k∼(pₖ) offspring are added to the active particle queue at Y. The procedure repeats until all particles reach the domain boundary or terminate with zero offspring, producing one Monte Carlo sample from the product of terminal values. Thus, although WoS eliminates explicit trajectory discretization, each sphere transition still requires a branching decision, while every offspring introduces additional walks that must be maintained and evaluated. Canonical results show that BWoS crashes when the particle splitting rate surpasses the boundary-absorbing speed, i.e., λ>λ₁ where λ₁ is the least non-negative eigenvalue of -L in Ω.

    3.2. From Solution Bounds to Branching Processes

    Although WoS eliminates explicit Brownian trajectory discretization, its computational cost still grows with the branching tree. The expected cumulative particle population becomes unbounded as λ approaches the principal Dirichlet eigenvalue λ₁ associated with Ω, motivating the early termination of subtrees whose remaining contributions can be bounded. Let τ denote the first Brownian exit time from Ω, and h(x)=𝔼ₓ[g(B_τ)] the harmonic extension of g. Several bounds follow directly from the BBM representation and its associated linear equations as Theorem 3.1.

    Theorem 3.1 (Probabilistic Solution Bounds).

    For 0<λ<λ₁,P(u)=u² and 0≤g≤1, the solution of F(u)=0 with u|∂Ω=g satisfies \max{L₀(x),L₁(x),L₂(x)}≤u(x)≤U(x), where U=h, and L₀(x)=𝔼ₓ[e^-λτg(Bτ)], L₁(x)=1-𝔼ₓ[e^λτ(1-g(B_τ))], L₂(x)=h(x)-\tfracλ4𝔼ₓ[τ].

    Proof.

    Since F(u)=0 implies Lu=λu(1-u)≥0, the maximum principle gives u≤h=U. For L₀, restrict the BBM expectation to trajectories reaching the boundary before their first branching event; all omitted products are nonnegative, yielding u≥𝔼ₓ[e^-λτg(B_τ)]. For L₁, let q=1-u. Then Lq+λq=λq²≥0. The Feynman–Kac formula gives q(x)=𝔼ₓ[e^λτ(1-g(B_τ))]-λ𝔼ₓ[∫₀^τe^λtq(Bₜ)² dt], hence u≥L₁. Finally, Dynkin’s formula gives h-u=λ𝔼ₓ[∫₀^τu(Bₜ)(1-u(Bₜ)) dt]. Since u(1-u)≤1/4, we obtain u≥L₂. ∎

    These bounds enable early termination of unresolved branching subtrees. Suppose the completed leaves contribute a product ω∈[0,1], while the active frontier contains particles at x₁,…,xₘ. By conditional independence, their remaining expected contribution is R=ω∏ᵢ₌₁ᵐu(xᵢ). With bounds L≤u≤U immediately yield

    (2)

    B⁻:=ω∏ᵢ₌₁ᵐL(xᵢ)≤R≤ω∏ᵢ₌₁ᵐU(xᵢ):=B⁺.

    Thus, whenever B⁺-B⁻≤2ε, the remaining tree can be pruned and replaced by (B⁻+B⁺)/2, introducing at most ε absolute bias in the final expectation, since the conditional expected contribution lies within [B⁻,B⁺].

    Despite their validity, these bounds incur evaluation overhead and exhibit strongly case-dependent efficiency (Fig. 2). L₀ ignores branched trajectories, L₁ deteriorates with large boundary deficits, while L₂ relies on the worst-case bound u(1-u)≤1/4. Consequently, L₂ generally performs best on smooth boundaries, whereas discontinuous binary data defeats most pruning with binary boundary condition. Combining all bounds often increases overhead without proportional savings. This motivates certified envelopes that directly reduce branching rather than repeatedly pruning existing trees.

    3.3. Generalized Envelope Branching

    The preceding pruning strategy uses solution bounds to terminate subtrees after they have been generated, but does not alter the underlying branching dynamics. We instead construct an equivalent branching process whose reproduction and termination rates are determined directly by certified solution envelopes. This can be understood as a generalized Doob’s h-transform, where the envelope width acts as the transforming function.

    For F(u)=0, let ℓ and a be certified sub- and supersolutions satisfying 0≤ℓ≤u≤a≤1, F(ℓ)≥0, and F(a)≤0. Define the domain envelop width d:=a-ℓ>0, the normalized solution v=(u-ℓ)/d∈[0,1], and the nonnegative residuals r_ℓ=F(ℓ) and rₐ=-F(a). By substituting u=ℓ+dv and expanding the offspring generating function, we obtain

    P(ℓ+dv)=P(ℓ)+∑ⱼ₌₁^KCⱼvʲ, Cⱼ=(P⁽ʲ⁾(ℓ))/(j!)dʲ≥0.

    The key is that the transformation changes not only the diffusion operator but also the branching mechanism into four parts – drifted diffusion Lᵈv, reduced branching ∑ⱼ₌₂^KλCⱼ(vʲ-v)/d, returning one r_c(1-v)/d and zero (being killed) -rₐv/d in the theorem below.

    Theorem 3.2 (Generalized Envelope Branching).

    With certified envelopes satisfying the conditions above and well-defined and integrable transformed branching process, v=(u-ℓ)/d satisfies

    (3)0=Lᵈv+∑ⱼ₌₂^KλCⱼ/d(vʲ-v)+(r_ℓ)/(d)(1-v)-rₐ/dv,

    where Lᵈ=L+∇\logd·∇. Consequently, the equivalent process branches into j≥2 offspring at rate λCⱼ/d, terminates successfully at rate r_ℓ/d, and terminates unsuccessfully at rate rₐ/d. If W∈[0,1] is its terminal-product estimator, then Z(x)=ℓ(x)+d(x)W is unbiased 𝔼[Z(x)]=u(x) and

    (4)

    Var[Z(x)]≤(u(x)-ℓ(x))(a(x)-u(x))≤d(x)²/4.

    Proof.

    The product rule gives L(dv)=dLᵈv+vLd, where Lᵈv=d⁻¹[L(dv)-vLd]. Since F(a)-F(ℓ)=-rₐ-r_ℓ and P(a)-P(ℓ)=∑ⱼ₌₁^KCⱼ, we have Ld-λd=-r_ℓ-rₐ-λ∑ⱼ₌₁^KCⱼ. Substituting these identities into F(ℓ+dv)=0 yields dLᵈv+r_ℓ(1-v)-rₐv+λ∑ⱼ₌₁^KCⱼ(vʲ-v)=0. The j=1 term vanishes, giving Eq. (3). Its nonnegative rates define the stated branching process, with boundary payoff (g-ℓ)/d∈[0,1]. The branching representation gives 𝔼[W]=v, hence 𝔼[Z]=u. Finally, Z∈[ℓ,a] implies 𝔼[(Z-ℓ)(a-Z)]≥0, which yields Eq. (3). ∎

    Beyond preserving the original PDE solution, it also changes the expected branching complexity. For conventional BBM, the expected number of reproduction events m_B satisfies (-L-λ)m_B=λ, with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. The transformed process instead obeys the following equation.

    Lemma 3.3 (Expected Branching Complexity).

    Let m_ℓ,a(x) denote the expected number of reproduction events in the transformed process, assumed finite. Then H=m_ℓ,ad satisfies H|_∂Ω=0 and

    (5)

    [-L+λ(1-P^′(a))]H=λ[P(a)-P(ℓ)-P^′(ℓ)d].

    Proof.

    Writing bⱼ=λCⱼ/d and κ=(r_ℓ+rₐ)/d, the first-event decomposition gives

    (6)

    -Lᵈm_ℓ,a+[κ-∑ⱼ₌₂^K(j-1)bⱼ]m_ℓ,a=∑ⱼ₌₂^Kbⱼ.

    Multiplying by d and using Ld=λd-r_ℓ-rₐ-λ∑ⱼ₌₁^KCⱼ, together with ∑ⱼ₌₁^KjCⱼ=P^′(a)d and ∑ⱼ₌₂^KCⱼ=P(a)-P(ℓ)-P^′(ℓ)d, yields the stated equation. ∎

    For binary branching, this reduces to [-L+λ(1-2a)]H=λd². Thus, the transformation changes both the source of branching work and the elliptic operator governing its propagation. In particular, narrowing the envelope suppresses the quadratic source term, while the upper envelope controls the effective reproduction potential. These effects explain how WiE can reduce branching complexity even when conventional BBM approaches its critical regime. Also, there exists a harmonic envelope such that the cost of WiE keeps finite as the splitting rate approaches the divergence limit of vanilla WoS in theory as Theorem 3.4 reveals.

    Theorem 3.4 (Bounded near-critical branching with harmonic envelopes).

    Let Ω⊂ℝⁿ be a bounded, connected C^2,α domain, and let λ₁>0 be the principal Dirichlet eigenvalue of -L, where L=1/2Δ. Suppose g∈C^2,α(∂Ω) satisfies 0≤g≤1, g\not≡0, and g\not≡1. Let h be its harmonic extension, Lh=0 in Ω and h=g on ∂Ω. For the binary branching equation Lu+λ(u²-u)=0, choose the certified envelopes ℓ=0 and a=h. Then the expected reproduction count m_λ of the transformed process satisfies

    (7)

    \sup_0<λ<λ₁|m_λ|_L^∞(Ω)<∞.

    In contrast, the expected reproduction count m_λ^BBM of conventional binary BBM diverges as λ↑λ₁: for every fixed x∈Ω, m_λ^BBM(x)=Θ((λ₁-λ)⁻¹).

    Proof.

    The strong maximum principle gives 00 in the interior. By Lemma 3.3, H_λ:=hm_λ solves

    (8)

    A_λH_λ=λh², H_λ|∂Ω=0, Aλ=-L-λ+2λ(1-h).

    We first show that A_λ has a spectral gap uniform up to λ₁. At λ=λ₁, its quadratic form is

    (9)

    ⟨f,A_λ₁f⟩=∥∇f∥₂²/2-λ₁∥f∥₂² (≥0)+2λ₁∫_Ω(1-h)f² dx.

    If its lowest eigenvalue were zero, equality would force f to be a multiple of the positive first Dirichlet eigenfunction φ₁ and simultaneously ∫_Ω(1-h)f² dx=0, contradicting 1-h>0 in Ω. Hence κ:=λ_\min(A_λ₁)>0. Writing t=λ/λ₁ gives A_λ=(1-t)(-L)+tA_λ₁, so the min–max principle yields

    (10)

    λ_\min(A_λ)≥(1-t)λ₁+tκ≥\minλ₁,κ>0.

    Uniform invertibility and standard Dirichlet elliptic estimates therefore imply |H_λ|C¹(Ω̄)≤C, with C independent of λ∈(0,λ₁). Since Hλ=0 on ∂Ω, |H_λ(x)|≤C,dist(x,∂Ω). On the other hand, positivity of h in the interior, the Hopf boundary lemma at points where g=0, and compactness of ∂Ω imply h(x)≥c,dist(x,∂Ω) for some c>0. Thus m_λ=H_λ/h≤C/c throughout Ω, proving the bound. For conventional BBM, (-L-λ)m_λ^BBM=λ with zero Dirichlet boundary data. The isolated principal-eigenvalue resolvent expansion gives

    (11)

    m_λ^BBM(x)=(λ₁⟨1,φ₁⟩φ₁(x))/(λ₁-λ)+Oₓ(1), λ↑λ₁,

    where |φ₁|₂=1. This proves the stated divergence. ∎

    3.4. Walk in Envelopes: Exact Walk-on-Spheres Transition

    The generalized Doob transform introduces a spatially varying drift ∇\logd, seemingly requiring a new sampler for the transformed diffusion, which instead be sampled exactly by reweighting the original WoS transitions, without explicitly simulating drifted trajectories.

    Theorem 3.5 (Exact Envelope-Aware WoS Transition).

    For any certified envelopes 0≤ℓ
    (12)d(x)v(x)=∫_∂BH_λ(x,dy) d(y)v(y)
    +∫_BG_λ(x,y)[r_ℓ(y)+λ∑ⱼ₌₁^KCⱼ(y)v(y)ʲ] dy.

    Moreover, Eq. (12) admits an exact stochastic transition using only the original screened WoS kernels and pointwise envelope evaluations.

    Proof.

    Expanding F(ℓ+dv)=0 using P(ℓ+dv)=P(ℓ)+∑ⱼ₌₁^KCⱼvʲ gives (λ-L)(dv)=r_ℓ+λ∑ⱼ₌₁^KCⱼvʲ. Applying the screened Green representation on B establishes Eq. (12). Set v≡1 on the right-hand side of Eq. (12) and have

    (13)

    λω_I:=r_ℓ+rₐ+λ∑ⱼ₌₁^KCⱼ=λd-Ld.

    Since all terms are nonnegative, ω_I≥0. Applying the screened Green representation to d yields

    (14)

    d(x)=∫_∂BH_λ(x,dy)d(y)+\allowbreakλ\allowbreak∫_BG_λ(x,y)ω_I(y) dy.

    Dividing by d(x) therefore defines a probability distribution over two mutually exclusive outcomes: exiting the sphere with density H_λ(x,dy)d(y)/d(x), or triggering an interior event with density λG_λ(x,y)ω_I(y)/d(x). For an interior event at y, dividing the nonnegative terms in Eq. (13) by λω_I(y) gives

    (15)

    π₊(y):=(r_ℓ(y))/(λω_I(y)), π₋(y):=(rₐ(y))/(λω_I(y)), πⱼ(y):=(Cⱼ(y))/(ω_I(y)).

    These probabilities correspond to successful termination, unsuccessful termination, and j offspring, respectively, with π₊+π₋+∑ⱼπⱼ=1. Multiplying the interior density by each event probability recovers the corresponding integrand in Eq. (12); unsuccessful termination contributes zero. Hence the stochastic transition reproduces the original integral equation exactly. ∎

    The remaining challenge is sampling this distribution without evaluating its weighted integrals. Although Eq. (14) provides the normalizing constant d(x), directly sampling a density proportional to H_λd or G_λω_I would require a new sampler for each spatially varying envelope. Instead, we use rejection sampling to recover these densities from the original WoS proposals.

    Specifically, the target exit and interior transition measures are proportional to H_λ(x,dy)d(y) and λG_λ(x,y)ω_I(y) dy, respectively. We therefore introduce two certified constants M_E≥\sup_∂Bd and M_I≥\sup_Bω_I to dominate these weighted measures by distributions that are already straightforward to sample. Let q_B=∫_∂BH_λ(x,dy) denote the original sphere-exit probability. The corresponding proposal masses are q_BM_E for exits and (1-q_B)M_I for interior events, giving the computable normalization Q_B=q_BM_E+(1-q_B)M_I.

    We first choose an exit proposal with probability q_BM_E/Q_B, otherwise an interior proposal. Its position Y is drawn from H_λ/q_B or λG_λ/(1-q_B), respectively, and accepted with probability d(Y)/M_E or ω_I(Y)/M_I. For example, the joint probability measure of proposing and accepting an exit at y is (q_BM_E)/(Q_B)(H_λ(x,dy))/(q_B)(d(y))/(M_E)=(H_λ(x,dy)d(y))/(Q_B).

    Similarly, the accepted interior measure is λG_λ(x,y)ω_I(y) dy/Q_B. Their total mass is d(x)/Q_B by Eq. (14). Conditioning on acceptance therefore divides both measures by d(x)/Q_B, recovering exactly the target transition probabilities. Thus, the accpetance rate is d(x)/Q_B and rejected candidates can simply be resampled. Notice that neither the target normalization d(x) nor any weighted Green integral needs to be evaluated during sampling.

    3.5. Extensions to Other Semilinear PDEs

    Figure 3 compares projected WiE on a cylinder (top) and heat-ball WiE on the unit square (bottom) with independent finite-difference reference solutions.

    3.5.1. Projected Walk in Envelopes on Manifolds

    For an embedded manifold M⊂ℝⁿ, the envelope transformation extends by replacing L with the Laplace–Beltrami operator L_M=1/2Δ_M, preserving the branching and termination coefficients. Following PWoS [(Sugimoto et al., 2024b)], we approximate intrinsic transitions using ambient Euclidean WoS kernels and the closest-point projection y^*=π(y). Specifically, Eq. (12) becomes

    (16)v_π(x)=(1)/(N_π(x))[∫_∂BH_λ(x,dy) d(y^*)v_π(y^*)
    +∫_BG_λ(x,y)(r_ℓ(y^*)+λ∑ⱼ₌₁^KCⱼ(y^*)v_π(y^*)ʲ) dy],

    where the projected normalization is

    (17)

    N_π(x)=∫_∂BH_λ(x,dy)d(y^*)+λ∫_BG_λ(x,y)ω_I(y^*) dy.

    The rejection sampler from the preceding section applies unchanged, evaluating all envelope-dependent weights at y^* instead of y. Since projected ambient kernels only approximate intrinsic Brownian transitions, N_π(x) need not equal d(x), introducing the same type of geometric approximation as PWoS without requiring intrinsic surface Green kernels.

    3.5.2. Semilinear Parabolic PDEs

    For ∂ₜu=Lu+λ(P(u)-u), replace L by D=L-∂ₜ in the envelope residuals, requiring r_ℓ=Dℓ+λ(P(ℓ)-ℓ)≥0, rₐ=-Da-λ(P(a)-a)≥0, and valid initial/lateral bounds. The coefficients Cⱼ and event rules retain their previous forms, but the interior weight becomes W_λ=λd-Dd=r_ℓ+rₐ+λ∑ⱼCⱼ. Replace each spatial ball by a backward heat ball [(Deaconu et al., 2017)], with elapsed time s and displacement z: H_η={(s,z):0

    Interior locations follow the killed occupation densityq_η(s,z) ds dz=ℙ(Bₛ∈dz, σ>s) ds, rather than the exit distribution: q_η(s,z)=[p(s,z)-(2πη)^-n/2]1_(s,z)∈H_η with p(s,z)=(2πs)^-n/2e^-|z|²/(2s). Let m₀=∫_H_ηq_η ds dz=η(n/n+2)^n/2+1. To sample q_η/m₀, propose S∼Unif(0,η) and Y∼ℕ(0,SIₙ); accept with probability 1_(S,Y)∈H_η[1-(2πη)^-n/2/p(S,Y)]. With M_E≥\sup_∂H_ηd and M_I≥\sup_H_ηW_λ, replace the preceding section’s proposal masses by M_E and m₀M_I (thus Q=M_E+m₀M_I). At (t-S,x+Y), accept exits with e^-λSd/M_E and interiors with e^-λSW_λ/M_I; all offspring and termination rules remain unchanged. At the initial boundary, return (u₀-ℓ)/d.

    4. Efficient Envelope Construction and Sampling

    4.1. Monotone Envelope Refinement for Full Field

    The transformation admits many certified envelopes with different computational costs. We construct tight, reusable bounds for full-field evaluation through four steps: a comparison principle certifies bounds from PDE residuals and boundary conditions; query-weighted envelope width approximates the intractable time–variance objective; conservative affine constraints monotonically refine an initially feasible pair; and cubic B-splines with cellwise Bernstein constraints reduce continuous certification to finite-dimensional linear programs. Certification is preserved throughout, while preprocessing is amortized across repeated queries.

    Lemma 4.1 (Comparison Principle for Certified Envelopes).

    For a bounded Lipschitz domain Ω⊂ℝⁿ, assume λ≥0 and λ\sup_s∈[0,1]\allowbreak(P^′(s)-1)<λ₁. Suppose u,ℓ,a∈C²(Ω)∩C(Ω̄)∩H¹(Ω) take values in [0,1] and satisfy F(u)=0,F(ℓ)≥0,F(a)≤0 and ℓ≤u≤a on ∂Ω. Then ℓ≤u≤a throughout Ω.

    Proof.

    We first prove ℓ≤u. Set w=ℓ-u. Since F(ℓ)-F(u)≥0, subtracting the two PDE residuals gives Lw+λ(P(ℓ)-P(u)-w)≥0. To rewrite the nonlinear difference as a term proportional to w, apply the fundamental theorem of calculus pointwise:

    (18)

    P(ℓ(x))-P(u(x))=∫ᵤ₍ₓ₎^ℓ(x)P^′(s) ds=w(x)∫₀¹P^′(u(x)+tw(x)) dt.

    Define the bounded coefficient q(x)=∫₀¹P^′(u(x)+tw(x)) dt. Because 0≤u,ℓ≤1, every argument of P^′ lies in [0,1], and thus

    (19)

    λ(q(x)-1)≤λ\sup_s∈[0,1](P^′(s)-1)<λ₁.

    It follows that 1/2Δw+λ(q(x)-1)w≥0, w≤0 on∂Ω. We now justify the maximum-principle step rather than assuming it. Let w₊=\max{w,0}. Since w≤0 on the boundary and w∈H¹(Ω), we have w₊∈H₀¹(Ω). Multiplying the last differential inequality by w₊ and integrating by parts gives

    (20)

    0≤-1/2∫_Ω|∇w₊|² dx+λ∫_Ω(q(x)-1)w₊² dx.

    Consequently,

    (21)

    1/2∫_Ω|∇w₊|² dx≤c_*∫_Ωw₊² dx, c_*:=λ\sup_s∈[0,1](P^′(s)-1).

    The variational characterization of the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of -1/2Δ states that, for any φ∈H₀¹(Ω), 1/2∫_Ω|∇φ|² dx≥λ₁∫_Ωφ² dx. Applying this inequality to φ=w₊ yields (λ₁-c_*)∫_Ωw₊² dx≤0. Since λ₁-c_*>0, we obtain w₊=0, hence ℓ≤u.

    To prove u≤a, repeat the same argument with w=u-a. Indeed, F(u)-F(a)≥0, w≤0 on the boundary, and P(u)-P(a)=w∫₀¹P^′(a+t(u-a)) dt. The same upper bound on the resulting zero-order coefficient and the same energy argument show (u-a)₊=0. Thus ℓ≤u≤a in Ω. ∎

    Work-aware envelope optimization.

    Let ℚ⊂Ω denote the evaluation region and let T_ℓ,a(x) and V_ℓ,a(x) be the expected runtime and estimator variance induced by a certified envelope pair (ℓ,a). For full-field evaluation, the ideal envelopes minimize the total cost of reaching a prescribed accuracy ∫_ℚT_ℓ,a(x)V_ℓ,a(x) dμ(x). Here μ describes the distribution of evaluation queries. The objective reflects the time–variance cost of independent Monte Carlo evaluation, but is difficult to optimize directly because T_ℓ,a depends on the entire transformed branching process.

    Fortunately, the envelope width d=a-ℓ provides a tractable surrogate. From Eq. (12), the transformed reproduction coefficients are Cⱼ=P⁽ʲ⁾(ℓ)dʲ/j!. In particular, for binary branching, the probability mass associated with reproduction is proportional to d². Moreover, Eq. (4) bounds the estimator variance by d²/4. These observations motivate minimizing the domain-averaged envelope width which replaces T_ℓ,a(x)V_ℓ,a(x), yielding

    (22)\min_ℓ,a∫_ℚ(a(x)-ℓ(x)) dμ(x),
    s.t.F(ℓ)≥0,F(a)≤0,0≤ℓ≤a≤1,ℓ|_∂Ω≤g≤a|_∂Ω.

    This objective seeks a single pair of reusable envelopes rather than independently optimizing bounds at each evaluation point. While width reduction does not guarantee a proportional runtime improvement, it simultaneously suppresses higher-order reproduction terms and tightens the estimator’s variance bound.

    Monotone certified refinement.

    The optimization in Eq. (22) is nonlinear because the envelope constraints involve the reaction term P. We therefore begin with a feasible pair (ℓ₀,a₀) and construct a sequence of increasingly tight certified envelopes. At iteration t, we seek nonnegative corrections hₜ,jₜ such that

    (23)

    ℓₜ₊₁=ℓₜ+hₜ, aₜ₊₁=aₜ-jₜ.

    The corresponding optimization maximizes the improvement

    (24)\max_hₜ,jₜ≥0∫_ℚ(hₜ+jₜ) dμ,
    s.t.F(ℓₜ+hₜ)≥0, F(aₜ-jₜ)≤0, ℓₜ+hₜ≤aₜ-jₜ,

    together with the original range and boundary constraints. Feasibility at every iteration implies

    (25)

    ℓₜ≤ℓₜ₊₁≤u≤aₜ₊₁≤aₜ, J(ℓₜ₊₁,aₜ₊₁)≤J(ℓₜ,aₜ).

    Thus, refinement never sacrifices a previously certified bound, and every accepted update improves the surrogate objective (Figure 4).

    For a general offspring generating function P(u)=∑ₖ₌₀^Kpₖuᵏ, the nonlinear certification constraints can be converted into affine sufficient conditions by exploiting the convexity of P on [0,1]. Substituting the monotone updates yields

    (26)F(ℓₜ+hₜ)=F(ℓₜ)+[L+λ(P^′(ℓₜ)-1)]hₜ+λR_ℓ(hₜ),
    -F(aₜ-jₜ)=-F(aₜ)+[L+λ(P^′(aₜ)-1)]jₜ-λRₐ(jₜ),

    where the Taylor remainders satisfy

    (27)R_ℓ(hₜ)=∫₀^hₜ(hₜ-s)P^′′(ℓₜ+s) ds≥0,
    Rₐ(jₜ)=∫₀^jₜ(jₜ-s)P^′′(aₜ-s) ds≤Mₜ/2jₜ²,

    with Mₜ(x)=\sup_s∈[ℓₜ(x),aₜ(x)]P^′′(s). Imposing a trust region 0≤jₜ≤δ further gives Rₐ(jₜ)≤Mₜδjₜ/2. Therefore, the original nonlinear certification constraints are guaranteed by

    (28)F(ℓₜ)+[L+λ(P^′(ℓₜ)-1)]hₜ≥0,
    -F(aₜ)+[L+λ(P^′(aₜ)-1-\tfrac12Mₜδ)]jₜ≥0.

    Since ℓₜ, aₜ, and Mₜ are fixed during each iteration, these conditions are affine in hₜ and jₜ. Together with the linear width-reduction objective and monotonicity constraints, they yield a linear program after finite-dimensional representation and continuous certification. Thus, the refinement extends to general offspring distributions while preserving the validity and nesting of the certified envelopes.

    Finite-dimensional certified optimization.

    We represent the envelopes using cubic B-splines, ℓ(x)=∑ᵢcᵢ^ℓφᵢ(x) and a(x)=∑ᵢcᵢᵃφᵢ(x), with their coefficients as optimization variables. Although Eq. (28) is affine in the corrections, it imposes infinitely many spatial constraints. The following theorem provides a finite-dimensional certification. On each spline cell, we express the affine residuals and ordering constraints in the Bernstein basis, enforcing nonnegativity of their coefficients; range and polynomial boundary constraints are handled analogously. These finitely many sufficient linear inequalities certify the PDE constraints throughout the domain while preserving monotone envelope refinement.

    For nonrectangular domains, we may restrict these certificates to a decomposition of each cell intersected with Ω, using tensor-product or triangular Bernstein bases on the resulting pieces. This changes the sufficient finite constraints, while retaining the same globally C² spline representation and continuous PDE inequalities on Ω. Therefore, the resulting refinement is a linear program with continuous, rather than pointwise, certification. The Bernstein constraints yields a conservative feasible set. The envelopes are constructed once and reused across full-field evaluations, amortizing their preprocessing cost over all queries.

    4.2. Efficient Envelope-Aware Sampling

    Although the envelope transformation reduces branching complexity, sampling its spatially varying transition weights introduces additional overhead. We employ three complementary optimizations to reduce this cost while preserving the exact transition law.

    Adaptive screening.

    The screened-kernel representation allows an adjustable parameter μ∈[0,λ]. Using Eq. (3), the interior weight W_μ=λω_I-(λ-μ)d, yielding

    (29)W_μ=r_ℓ+rₐ+λ∑ⱼ₌₂^KCⱼ+[μ-λ+λP^′(ℓ)]d.

    This decomposition shows that changing μ affects only the single-offspring continuation weight, leaving termination and genuine reproduction weights unchanged. Their nonnegativity is preserved by choosing μ_B=λ\max{0,1-P^′(ℓ_B)}, where ℓ_B is a certified lower bound over the sphere. A smaller μ_B increases the sphere-exit probability, potentially reducing expensive interior proposals without altering the represented solution.

    Spatially adaptive majorants.

    Instead of using global rejection bounds, we independently bound the exit and interior weights by M_E≥\sup_∂Bd and M_I≥\sup_BW_μ. Their proposal masses are q_μM_E and m_μM_I, where q_μ=∫_∂BH_μ and m_μ=∫_BG_μ. The corresponding acceptance probabilities are d(y)/M_E and W_μ(y)/M_I. We obtain tight local bounds from the spline cells intersecting each sphere and accelerate their aggregation using range-minimum/maximum queries (RMQ), reducing rejection without changing the accepted distribution.

    Lazy evaluation.

    Even with tighter proposals, computing the exact envelope weights for every candidate is unnecessary. We first compare the rejection threshold against inexpensive local lower and upper bounds: candidates are accepted or rejected immediately when these bounds determine the outcome, and full spline evaluation is performed only otherwise. Green-kernel sampling is deferred until an interior proposal is selected, while reusable kernel quantities are cached. Thus, most inexpensive decisions avoid the cost of exact weight evaluation, and the savings accumulate across repeated transitions in the branching tree.

    Spectral-workload fallback.

    Envelope construction incurs a one-time cost that may outweigh its sampling benefits. Motivated by the near-critical BBM work scaling (1-ρ)⁻¹, where ρ=λ(P^′(1)-1)/λ₁<1, we define a spectral-workload indicator for Q queries at target RMSE ε:

    (30)

    W=Q/ε²ρ/1-ρ.

    We activate WiE only when ρ≥ρ₀ and W≥A, with ρ₀=0.8 and A=10⁸ calibrated empirically across four scenes (Figure 5). This pilot-free criterion avoids unnecessary preprocessing, while imperfect fallback decisions affect efficiency but not correctness.

    5. Experiments

    Our proposed WiE algorithm is evaluated in four non-trivial 2D scenes against canonical branching WoS. The results are illustrated in Figure 6 and the its speedup effects are evaluated with different branching rates. In Table 1, it is clear that WiE naturally appears insignificant with low splitting rate and thus the extra processing cost overwhelms its variance advantage per sample; while its merit become explicit as β/λ₁ grows, it strongly suppresses the splitting rate in simulation by being enveloped, which is consistent across all scenarios. Besides, WiE also achieves the same accuracy using much less time than vanilla branching WoS in high splitting scenes as in Table 2.

    Envelope construction ablation.

    We compare three certified constructions with the same 6×6 bicubic basis: sequential LP optimizes the upper and then lower envelope separately, joint LP minimizes their width together, and monotone refinement further tightens the joint solution by certified nonlinear iterations. The archived three-update configuration in Figure 7 shows that joint optimization improves width over sequential fitting, while refinement additionally reduces it by 5.5% on Engine and 7.2% on Flask without increasing spline resolution. Gains on Lock and Clover are negligible, and tighter envelopes do not uniformly imply lower sampling work. Thus, iteration can improve a fixed representation, but is not a universal substitute for increasing its resolution.

    Spline resolution.

    Table 3(a) examines spatial resolution and geometric certification. The earlier implementation certifies the entire bounding square, including regions outside the PDE domain and inside holes. We instead clip certificate cells to the original polygon: intact or axis-aligned pieces use tensor-product Bernstein coefficients, and oblique pieces use triangular Bernstein coefficients. The envelopes remain globally C² cubic B-splines. We keep the same boundary data, offspring laws, and ρ=λ(P^′(1)-1)/λ̂₁=0.98. For all six non-square domains, we transfer the same k=6 joint initialization exactly to k=12 and 24 before refinement, so the resolution comparison does not change the initial functions. Both coefficient vectors are restricted to [-2,2] to suppress large, weakly constrained exterior modes. This extension constraint is additional to the certified range and PDE conditions inside Ω.

    Refinement iterations.

    We allow up to 12 updates, retaining d≥0.003 and the upper-correction limit 0.075. We stop after two successive width reductions below 10⁻⁶, or return the last valid pair when the LP budget or numerical checks fail; the actual accepted count is reported. If the full polynomial LP accepts no update, we retry from the same initialization using conservative cellwise scalar bounds on the residuals and P^′; both attempts are included in construction cost. Table 4(b) tests the returned pairs with fixed queries, sample count, seeds, and rejection-bound grid. At k=24, the six non-square cases reduce mean width by 53–87% relative to the earlier coarse result. Relative to their common initialization, their sampling time–variance efficiency improves by 2.06–23.13×, while additional construction costs 298–600 CPU seconds. Thus finer envelopes improve sampling in these tests, but need sufficient reuse to offset preprocessing. The L-shaped case attains a smaller mean width at k=12 than at k=24; the latter uses the conservative fallback, and these finite-budget results do not imply monotonic improvement with resolution. These results diagnose envelope construction rather than changing the variable transformation underlying WiE. All cases use the general-PGF kernel; Figure 7 retains the earlier specialized binary implementation.

item.title: 像素图动画也能双向外推：三个专家模型分管「上一帧 / 中间 / 下一帧」，只用 280 组样本 ｜ Neural Controlled Directional Frame Generation for Sprite Animation
item.description:
一句话：外推和插值质量几乎一样，单模型 206MB、单次确定性生成，比通用视频模型基线好 17–57%。

要点：

  • 三个专家模型共用同一套 U-Net 编解码结构，分别按不同时间顺序训练：previous（帧 2,3→1）、middle（1,3→2）、next（1,2→3）
  • 面向像素图的域内改造：RGBA 感知处理、多尺度光流细化、pixel-shuffle 上采样、alpha 门控混合
  • 数据只要 280 组精选 sprite 三元组；42 组测试上 FLIP 为 0.265 / 0.258 / 0.271，外推与插值无显著退化，比通用基线好 17–57%，且是确定性单次生成、便于进生产流程

为什么值得看：2D 像素游戏的美术流水线长期缺「往前推一帧/往后倒一帧」的工具，通用视频模型的随机采样又不能进生产。这套按方向拆分的做法，是可落地的最小改动方案。

中文摘要：Sprite 动画在游戏开发中依然普遍，但生产流程需要的远不止传统中间帧补全：动画师还要向前外推预测动作延续，以及向后外推用于编辑和反向拆解已有 sprite sheet。现有神经插值方法只能补两张相邻关键帧之间的中间帧；统一视频生成模型要么面向自然视频、采用不符合生产要求的随机扩散采样，要么只做插值不处理外推。本文用三个共享同一 U-Net 编解码结构的专家模型分管三个方向，并加入 RGBA 感知处理、多尺度光流细化、pixel-shuffle 上采样与 alpha 门控混合等领域改造。仅用 280 组精选 sprite 三元组即可训练，42 组测试上 FLIP 分别为 0.265、0.258、0.271，外推相对插值无显著退化。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-19

本期推送：2026-10-24

Neural Controlled Directional Frame Generation for Sprite Animation

Abstract

Sprite-based animation remains prevalent in video game development, but production workflows require capabilities beyond traditional in-betweening. While existing neural interpolation methods can generate intermediate frames between two close keyframes, animators also need forward extrapolation to predict motion continuations and backward extrapolation for editing and reverse-engineering existing sprite sheets. Current unified video generation models either operate on natural video content with stochastic diffusion sampling incompatible with production requirements, or focus exclusively on interpolation without addressing extrapolation tasks. We present a deep learning approach for controlled directional frame generation in sprite animation using three specialized expert models that share identical U-Net encoder-decoder architectures and a number of domain-specific modifications, including RGBA-aware processing, multi-scale flow refinement, pixel-shuffle upsampling, and alpha-gated blending. Each model is trained on different temporal orderings of the same curated dataset: previous (frames 2,3→1), middle (frames 1,3→2), and next (frames 1,2→3). Following data-centric AI principles, we demonstrate that only 280 carefully curated sprite triplets enable effective training for all three directional tasks without requiring massive generic datasets. Evaluation on 42 test triplets using the FLIP perceptual metric shows that all three models achieve comparable quality—previous (0.265), middle (0.258), and next (0.271)—with no significant degradation for extrapolation versus interpolation, outperforming general-purpose baselines by 17-57%. With deterministic single-pass generation and compact model size (206 MB per model), our method provides the first practical solution for controllable any-position frame generation specifically tailored for pixel art sprite animation workflows, validating that quality-over-quantity data curation enables specialized deep learning for niche visual domains.

Index Terms:

Sprite Animation, Directional Frame Generation, Controllable Frame Synthesis, Neural Image Synthesis, Pixel Art, Game Development

I Introduction

Sprite-based animation remains a cornerstone of modern video game development, valued for its distinct aesthetic appeal, computational efficiency, and rapid prototyping capabilities [1, 2]. While neural frame interpolation has shown promise for automating sprite in-betweening tasks, production workflows continue to face significant limitations when animators require capabilities beyond simple interpolation. Generating the middle frame between two keyframes addresses a substantial portion of animation workload, but practical animation pipelines frequently require directional frame generation: predicting the next frame in a motion sequence or inferring previous frames during editing and reverse-engineering tasks.

Consider three common scenarios in sprite animation production. First, forward extrapolation (next-frame generation): an animator has drawn a character’s initial pose and mid-motion keyframe but needs the system to predict the natural continuation frame that completes the motion arc. Second, backward extrapolation (previous-frame generation): when editing or reverse-engineering existing sprite sheets, animators may have only the latter frames of a sequence and need to reconstruct plausible preceding poses. Third, interpolation (middle-frame generation): the traditional in-betweening task of generating transitional frames between two established keyframes [3]. Existing sprite interpolation methods address only the third scenario, leaving forward and backward generation entirely manual or reliant on general-purpose video prediction methods unsuited to pixel art characteristics.

This paper presents a neural architecture for controlled directional frame generation in sprite animation (Figure 1). Rather than training a single unified model with masked conditioning [4], we train three specialized expert models sharing identical U-Net encoder-decoder architectures [5] but operating on different temporal orderings:

  • •

    Previous model: Given frames (t+1,t+2), generates frame t (backward extrapolation)

  • •

    Middle model: Given frames (t,t+2), generates frame t+1 (interpolation)

  • •

    Next model: Given frames (t,t+1), generates frame t+2 (forward extrapolation)

    • Each model is trained deterministically on sprite animation triplets, preserving the sharp edges, transparency, and palette constraints characteristic of pixel art. At generation time, the user provides two frames and selects the desired temporal direction (previous/middle/next), and the corresponding specialized model produces the output frame with consistent, reproducible results.

    Our approach diverges from unified video generation models in three key design decisions. First, domain specialization: training exclusively on pixel art sprites preserves hard edges, limited palettes, and transparency, rather than optimizing for photorealistic video. Second, architectural separation: three expert models allow each to specialize in its specific temporal task previous, middle, or next rather than learning a single set of parameters for all three via masking. Third, deterministic generation: avoiding diffusion-based stochasticity ensures reproducible outputs, which are critical for production workflows where artists require identical results when regenerating frames.

    The primary contributions of this work are:

  • •

    First directional frame generation system for pixel art: To our knowledge, no prior work enables previous, middle, and next frame generation from two input frames specifically for sprite animation. Current cartoon interpolation methods [6] and prior sprite-specific work [7] address only the middle case, while unified video models [4] target natural video, not stylized pixel art.

  • •

    Three-expert-model architecture: We demonstrate that training three specialized models (one per direction) with identical architecture but different frame orderings achieves comparable quality across all three tasks (mean FLIP error ∼0.26) while maintaining deterministic generation. This contrasts with unified masked conditioning approaches that introduce stochasticity or require substantially more training data.

  • •

    Empirical validation on sprite animation: Evaluation on 42 test triplets from curated sprite datasets shows that our previous, middle, and next models achieve perceptual quality (FLIP metric [8]) matching or exceeding general-purpose video interpolation baselines, demonstrating that directional control need not sacrifice quality.

  • •

    Practical pipeline integration: By providing deterministic and controllable generation, our approach addresses real production constraints faced by indie game developers working with limited computational resources and requiring reproducible animation workflows.

    • While prior work demonstrated that domain-specific training improves sprite interpolation over general video methods [7], this work extends controllability to encompass the full spectrum of directional frame generation required by animation pipelines. The three-expert-model design enables practical deployment: each model is compact (206MB storage) and deterministic, meeting the operational requirements of game development studios.

    Our work aligns with the emerging data-centric AI paradigm[9, 10], which emphasizes that systematic data quality improvements often yield greater performance gains than architectural innovations, especially for specialized domains. Like our prior sprite interpolation work [7], we demonstrate that small, carefully curated datasets can outperform massive, noisy collections when domain-specific quality criteria guide data selection [11, 12, 13]. This principle is particularly relevant for sprite animation: unlike general video where diversity scales with quantity (millions of YouTube clips), sprite animation exhibits discrete, learnable patterns (walk cycles, attacks, idles) that saturate with hundreds of high-quality examples rather than requiring millions of noisy samples. Our 280-triplet dataset—the same used for sprite interpolation [7]—was curated with explicit quality criteria: diverse animation styles (pixel art to HD sprites), motion categories (rigid, articulated, deformable), resolution ranges (32×32 to 256×256), and edge-case coverage (extreme poses, fast motion, occlusions). Each triplet was manually validated to ensure the middle frame is a genuine artist-drawn in-between. By training three models on different temporal orderings of this same curated dataset (previous: frames 2,3→1; middle: frames 1,3→2; next: frames 1,2→3), we demonstrate that quality-over-quantity data curation enables multiple directional tasks from a single dataset. This data-centric approach [14] validates that careful selection of what to learn from matters more than how much to learn from, a critical advantage for specialized domains where massive datasets do not exist.

    The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews video frame synthesis methods, animation automation techniques, and the gap in controllable sprite generation. Section III details the three-model architecture, training procedure, and dataset methodology. Section IV presents quantitative and qualitative evaluation demonstrating comparable performance across all three directional tasks. Section V discusses limitations and future directions for controllable sprite animation synthesis.

    II Related Work

    We organize existing work into four categories: video frame interpolation and generation methods, cartoon and stylized animation techniques, deep learning architectures for image synthesis, and gap analysis positioning our contribution. Each category illuminates different aspects of the directional frame generation problem and highlights why existing solutions are insufficient for controllable sprite animation.

    II-AVideo Frame Interpolation and Generation

    Classical video frame interpolation relies on optical flow estimation to compute dense correspondence fields between frames [15]. Early deep learning approaches like FlowNet[16] demonstrated that convolutional networks could learn optical flow from data, inspiring flow-based interpolation methods. Super SloMo[17] introduced bidirectional optical flow with visibility maps for high-quality multi-frame interpolation, while Deep Voxel Flow[18] synthesized frames by learning to flow pixels through 3D voxel representations, enabling both interpolation and extrapolation. However, these methods assume motion smoothness and photometric consistency, which fail for sprite animation’s discrete color transitions, hard edges, and transparent regions [19].

    State-of-the-art frame interpolation methods (2021-2024) have achieved impressive results on natural video benchmarks. RIFE (Real-Time Intermediate Flow Estimation) [20] introduced IFRNet, a lightweight architecture for real-time interpolation using privileged distillation, achieving strong performance on standard benchmarks while maintaining inference speeds suitable for interactive applications. FLAVR[21] demonstrated that flow-agnostic 3D U-Net architectures can achieve competitive results without explicit optical flow estimation, learning temporal representations directly from multi-frame inputs. More recently, GIMM-VFI[22] employed implicit neural representations for motion modeling, achieving state-of-the-art performance on Vimeo90K and other natural video datasets through generalizable motion priors. Domain-specific interpolation has also advanced: Deep Animation Video Interpolation in the Wild [23] specifically addressed challenges in animation interpolation (large motion, temporal discontinuities, stylized content) through anisotropic synthesis and motion-aware synthesis networks. However, these methods were trained on natural video or photorealistic animation datasets (hundreds of thousands to millions of frames), optimized for smooth gradients and continuous motion. When applied to pixel art sprites with hard edges, discrete palettes, and 32×32 to 256×256 resolutions, they exhibit the same artifacts as earlier methods: edge blur, palette violations, and loss of pixel-perfect precision. Furthermore, all these methods focus exclusively on interpolation, and none address the forward/backward extrapolation needed for directional frame generation.

    A critical development for our work is MCVD (Masked Conditional Video Diffusion) [4], which demonstrated that a single unified diffusion model trained with random temporal masking can perform interpolation, forward extrapolation, backward extrapolation, and unconditional generation by conditioning on different frame subsets. MCVD randomly masks past frames, future frames, or both during training, enabling the same model to predict missing frames in any temporal position. While this unified approach is elegant, it presents three fundamental limitations for sprite animation workflows. First, MCVD operates on natural video content—its architecture, training procedure, and evaluation focus exclusively on photorealistic datasets (e.g., BAIR robot pushing, Kinetics-600), not stylized pixel art with sharp edges, limited palettes, and transparency. Second, as a diffusion model, MCVD uses stochastic sampling: generating the same frame multiple times produces different outputs due to the inherent randomness in the denoising process. Production animation pipelines require deterministic, reproducible results—artists expect identical outputs when regenerating a frame with the same inputs. Third, diffusion models incur substantial computational costs, requiring iterative denoising over 50-1000 steps and training on millions of video frames. Our approach addresses these gaps by training three specialized deterministic models on sprite-specific data, ensuring reproducibility and efficiency.

    Recent diffusion-based video generation methods like DynamiCrafter [24] have demonstrated image-to-video capabilities using pretrained video diffusion priors.
