    Increasing the number of auxiliary cameras steadily improves every metric relying on persistent world state: grounding, memory, and consistency on Solaris, and all three revisit tasks in MAC-Bench, while movement and building performance remain flat (fig.6). This selective improvement confirms that performance gains stem specifically from expanded spatial visual coverage rather than generic model capacity scaling, which would otherwise uniformly elevate all capabilities. Gains naturally plateau once visual coverage saturates.

    Effect of latent compression.

    In cross-scene transfer experiments (decoding residual codes with a different “control” anchor latent), higher compression lowers PSNR but systematically suppresses donor background leakage. Crucially, spatial placement precision and identity preservation of the transferred mover (Import IoU and Mover Id.) improve up to 8× compression—peaking at 26.7 and 0.66, respectively, before degrading at 16× (fig.7). Compression is thus more than an efficiency knob: an informational bottleneck too narrow to encode static background forces the model to allocate capacity to dynamic elements, causing dynamic-static disentanglement to naturally emerge from the constraint itself. We therefore adopt 8× compression by default (fig.7).

    5 Conclusion

    We introduced OverSeer, a multi-agent video world model that jointly generates egocentric agent views and fixed-pose auxiliary views as a lightweight proxy for a world-centric state. These views substantially improve consistency when agents separate and later reunite, and δ-VAE makes them cheap to model by encoding only changes relative to a static reference. We hope this simple yet effective design will pave the way for world models that simulate shared environments beyond what any single agent sees.

    6 Acknowledgement

    The authors would like to thank Tomas Jakab, Zeren Jiang, Zijian Zhou, Mengmeng Xu, and Wonbong Jang for their insightful feedback.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Dataset Curation Pipelines

    Data.

    The three domains are three separate datasets, and we train one model on each. Minecraft and Doom are collected by us; the real captures are an existing dataset that we re-use in the same two-agent, many-camera arrangement. In all three, a clip is 241 frames of every view at once, sampled at 20 frames per second (12 s), 576×320 per view in Minecraft and in the captures and 480×320 in Doom.

    Minecraft.

    The gameplay is collected with the Solaris engine [(Savva et al., 2026)]: two Mineflayer bots play a two-player episode on a Minecraft 1.21 server and each view is recorded from a real Minecraft client, so the frames are the game’s own graphics and every frame carries the bot’s ground-truth action. The bots explore by a potential field, walls pushing them away and unvisited ground pulling them in, which keeps the pair moving over new terrain instead of circling one spot, and each episode is additionally labeled with one of eleven interaction modes (mining, building, fighting, chasing, exploring, reuniting and so on). We extend the engine with six fixed auxiliary cameras. They are placed in a second pass: the episode is played once to establish the terrain, then the six cameras are sampled at random in the free space around the agents’ starting area and the episode is captured with them. Placement therefore follows the ground the episode covers rather than aiming at one point; measured over 200 episodes, a camera sits a median 4.9 blocks above the agents and 3.0 blocks from the nearest point of their path, tilted 52 degrees down with a 70 degree field of view, and while a single camera has an agent in its frustum in about half of the frames, some camera has one in 90% of them. Every view is recorded at 1280×720 and 20 frames per second. We collect 20,000 episodes of outdoor terrain and 11,000 of village worlds, 264 frames each.

    Doom.

    Doom episodes are played with Doom [(ZDoom developers, 2025)] on the 68 maps of Freedoom Phase 1 and Phase 2 [(The Freedoom project, 2024)], two marines and eight fixed auxiliary cameras per episode, and the marines are driven by the same potential-field exploration controller as the Minecraft bots. Every view is recorded at 1024×768 and 30 frames per second with a 120-degree field of view. The eight cameras sit about 100 map units (3 m) above eye height, four tilted 10 degrees down and four 28 degrees, and between them they see the marines almost everywhere they walk, which is what the maps’ corridors and halls allow: a single camera has a marine in its frustum in about 85% of the frames. We train on 20,000 traversal episodes and hold out a separate set of 4,000 arena episodes, in which the two marines start 128 map units apart facing each other, for evaluation.

    Real captures.

    The real sequences come from Replay [(Shapovalov et al., 2023)], 68 scenes of acted social interaction of about five minutes each, filmed by twelve temporally synchronized, geometrically and color-calibrated cameras. We use eight of them in the arrangement the two games are built on: the two head-mounted cameras, which move with their wearers, are the agent views, and six static cameras are the auxiliary views. Unlike the games this gives real people, real cameras, and measured poses: every camera comes with a per-frame camera-to-world pose and pinhole intrinsics; the static cameras hold still to within 5 mm and a wearer covers 3 to 4 m in a clip. We hold out 45 clips of 241 frames, drawn from 35 of the scenes, and train on the rest of the dataset.

    MAC-Bench.

    Table3 lists the task specifications. In all tasks, the agents begin mutually visible and lose sight of each other mid-episode. In Dynamic Event, the scripted event is placed at the midpoint between the agents and is one of sprouting crops, a standing creeper, or a plank cube that ignites at frame 20. Doom uses the two reunite tasks on six Freedoom maps with 1047-unit walks (32 units per block), with the partner 84^∘ off-axis at the midpoint. We use 32 episodes per task in Minecraft and 100 per task in Doom. For VLM accuracy, Claude Opus 5 is given the generated frames and answers the task query for each agent;

    An episode counts as correct only if the answers for both agents match the ground truth. FID is computed between generated and ground-truth agent frames. During evaluation, accuracy is averaged over 5 independent runs of 32 episodes; episodes with failed generation or unparsable judge output are excluded.

    Appendix B Auxiliary Camera Pose Sampling

    As described in section3.2, OverSeer requires auxiliary camera poses c in eq.3 but no auxiliary images at inference time. During training, auxiliary camera poses and their corresponding videos are provided by the dataset. At inference time, we sample the poses as follows.

    Scene-Independent Pose Prior.

    We define a canonical coordinate system whose origin is the initial position of the first agent. Candidate auxiliary camera poses are sampled relative to this coordinate system from a scene-independent camera-pose prior. The horizontal offset from the origin, camera height, yaw, and pitch are modeled as Gaussian variables whose parameters are estimated from the training camera poses. Camera height is constrained to be non-negative, and roll is fixed to zero.

    Coverage-Based Selection.

    We sample a candidate set of poses ℂ from this prior and greedily select K cameras to maximize geometric field-of-view coverage. Let Ω denote a bounded discretized volume in the canonical coordinate system, and let F(c)⊆Ω denote the cells geometrically covered by the camera frustum associated with pose c. The computation of F(c) depends only on camera geometry and does not use scene occupancy or occlusion information. Let ℝₖ denote the region covered by the first k selected cameras, with ℝ₀=∅. We greedily select

    cₖ₊₁=\arg\max_c∈ℂ|F(c)∖ℝₖ|, ℝₖ₊₁=ℝₖ∪F(cₖ₊₁),(6)

    until K cameras are selected. Since both candidate sampling and coverage computation depend only on the canonical coordinate system and camera geometry, this procedure requires no additional scene-specific visual or geometric input.

    Appendix C More Ablations

    Feature alignment loss.

    Table4 ablates L_align. Removing it slightly improves δ-VAE reconstruction (25.1 vs. 24.7 dB PSNR) and FID, but lowers VLM accuracy on all three MAC-Bench tasks, by 2.4–4.5 points. Without alignment, the residual code spends its capacity on reconstructing the whole frame; with it, the code is pushed towards dynamic regions, which is what the world model needs to keep revisited scenes consistent. Reconstruction fidelity is thus not a sufficient proxy for how useful a compressed representation is downstream, in line with the compression trend in section4.2.

    Appendix D Implementation Details

    By applying 2×2 spatial (s=2) and 2× temporal (τ=2) compression rates, the δ-VAE reduces the auxiliary view representation from 864 tokens per frame (at 576×384 resolution) to just 108 tokens, achieving an 8× overall bandwidth reduction. OverSeer jointly generates both agents’ egocentric streams and K auxiliary views (K=6 by default for Minecraft and K=8 for Doom) over a 241-frame horizon, conditioned on the initial frame of agent views and both agents’ action sequences. Built upon Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [(Wan et al., 2025)], the model is fully fine-tuned per domain for 20k steps using Adam with a learning rate of 10⁻⁴ and a batch size of 64 across 64 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs. Training incorporates diffusion forcing and causal masking over a context window of 12 latent frames (48 RGB frames), with autoregressive rollout used during inference.

    For training the δ-VAE, we use Adam with a learning rate of 10⁻⁴ and we set λ_rec=1, λ_KL=10⁻⁵, and λ_align=10⁻³.

    Appendix E Limitations and Future Work

    OverSeer’s benefits depend on auxiliary coverage. Regions far from the sampled cameras, as in Reunite Far, remain harder to keep consistent. Short-horizon egocentric capabilities such as movement do not benefit from auxiliary views. Aggressive residual compression also trades some fidelity and, in fast-changing scenes such as Doom, consistency for efficiency. Promising directions include adaptive or learned camera placement that follows agents into unexplored regions, auxiliary views that are re-anchored for unbounded worlds, and scaling to larger agent populations. More broadly, we hope this work encourages treating the output space of world models, meaning what they choose to render and not only what they condition on, as a first-class design axis for building coherent, shared simulated worlds.

    Appendix F Prompts

    F.1 The judge

    Every question in both benchmarks is asked of the same judge, Claude Opus 5, in one turn: the frame or the pair of frames first, then the question, under the system prompt “You are a helpful assistant that evaluates Minecraft screenshots.” Thinking is adaptive at low effort. The answer is reduced to its first non-empty line, lowercased and stripped of quotes and trailing punctuation, and validated by exact match against the expected word, so every prompt ends by naming the words it accepts. An episode counts as correct only if every question about it is answered correctly.

    Revisiting benchmark.

    The two reunite tasks ask only about the partner, in one sentence:

    Here is a Minecraft/Doom screenshot. Is there another player visible on-screen? Answer with a single word: "yes", "no".

    It is put to each agent’s own view at four moments read off the recorded trajectory: the first generated frame, the frame of maximum separation, the midpoint of the way back, and the rendezvous, which makes eight questions per episode. The judge sees one frame and this sentence, with no description of the task and no earlier frame, so nothing but the frame can decide the answer; the expected answer comes from the poses, the partner counting as visible when it lies well inside the view cone and within 20 blocks and as not visible when it lies outside the cone or beyond 35 blocks, with the judge’s own answer on the ground-truth frame standing in for the band between the two. The dynamic events add two more question shapes. The outcome question names the states the event can be in, one set per event kind; for the creeper,

    Here is a Minecraft screenshot. What is visible where the creeper stood: a creeper still standing, a crater or hole blasted into the ground, or flat undamaged ground? Answer with a single word from "creeper", "crater", "flat".

    with “sprouts”/“wheat”/“none” for the growing crops, “intact”/“burning”/“partly burnt”/“gone” for the burning plank cube. The progression question shows the first and the return frame together:

    Here are two Minecraft screenshots from roughly the same viewpoint, the first taken earlier and the second later. In this scene {process}. Compared with the first image, is that process further along in the second image (progressed), at the same stage (same), or at an earlier stage than in the first image (reverted)? Answer with a single word: "progressed", "same", "reverted".

    where {process} is a phrase for the event, for instance “a creeper explodes, disappears, and leaves a crater blasted into the ground”. Each event kind also has a presence question asked at the first generated frame (“Is there a creeper (green four-legged hostile mob) visible on-screen?” and its equivalents).

    One sentence we add.

    Claude reads the viewer’s own first-person arm in the corner of a sharp frame as another player. Where that matters, we append, to every prompt and identically in both passes,

    The large blocky shape in the bottom-right corner is the viewer’s own first-person arm and held item, not another player.

    The prompt actually used is recorded in every result file.

    F.2 Action prompts

    Actions reach the model as language. Each of the 28 entries of the action vocabulary is written as one English sentence, encoded once by the text encoder, and stored as a table of token sequences; at training and at inference the sentence of the frame’s action is looked up and its tokens are used as the frame’s conditioning context. Table5 lists the sentences.

    Per frame exactly one entry is chosen. The keyboard flags score one when pressed; the mouse contributes through its yaw and pitch, whose sign picks turning left or right and looking up or down and whose magnitude is clipped to one; if nothing scores above zero, the frame is idle. The highest score wins, so a frame that both walks and turns is conditioned on the stronger of the two. The conditioning frame’s tokens are zeroed, since it is given rather than generated, and during training the whole action context is dropped with a fixed probability so that the model can be sampled with classifier-free guidance on the actions.

item.title: 游戏不会停下来等你推理：RealtimeBench 测的是「动作晚到一步」的代价 ｜ The World Won't Wait: Evaluating and Teaching Agents Under a Live Clock
item.description:
一句话：暂停时更聪明的模型一开跑就输给更快的模型；TORSI 让慢教师在间隙写指令、快学生实战中不调教师。

要点：

  • RealtimeBench 含 6 类游戏共 180 个任务，评测期间游戏持续运行；成对评测显示暂停时 GPT-6.1-sol 强于更快的 Jev，不暂停就反过来
  • TORSI（双时间尺度离线递归自我改进）：慢教师在两次尝试之间复盘失败、在暂停的游戏里验证修正，再给快学生写出可复用指令
  • 快学生实战中不向教师发请求；两轮把 Jev 的平均分从 13.51 提到 24.19（0–100 进度分），六类游戏全面提升，另外三个模型不重训也涨

为什么值得看：只要引擎里有实时循环，agent 的延迟就是能力的一部分。这套「离线教师 + 在线学生」的分工，对任何要做实时 NPC 或实时玩法 agent 的架构都直接适用。

中文摘要：LLM 智能体能解决复杂的交互任务，但推理与工具调用都要花时间，在持续变化的环境里，本来正确的动作可能到得太晚。作者提出 RealtimeBench，覆盖 6 类游戏共 180 个任务，评测时让游戏在推理期间继续运行。成对评测显示：游戏暂停时 GPT-6.1-sol 强于更快的 Jev，游戏不暂停时两者顺序反转。为此提出 TORSI：慢教师在两次尝试之间研究失败、在暂停的游戏里检验修正，然后把可复用的指令写给快学生；学生实战中不调用教师，是否采纳更新由验证分数决定。两轮之后 Jev 的平均分从 13.51 升到 24.19，六类游戏全部提升，另外三个模型在不重训的情况下也受益。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·智能体+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-14

本期推送：2026-10-24

The World Won’t Wait: Evaluating and Teaching Agents Under a Live Clock

Abstract

Large language model (LLM) agents can solve complex interactive tasks, yet reasoning and tool calls take time. In continuously changing environments, an otherwise correct action may arrive too late. We introduce RealtimeBench, with 180 tasks across six game types, to evaluate agents while games continue running during inference. Paired evaluations show that GPT-6.1-sol outperforms the faster Jev when games are paused, but falls behind when they keep running. We propose Two-Timescale Offline Recursive Self-Improvement (TORSI): a slow teacher studies failures and tests corrections in paused games between attempts, then writes reusable instructions for a fast student. The student acts without teacher calls during gameplay, and validation scores determine which updates are adopted. Two rounds raise Jev’s average test score from 13.51 to 24.19 on a 0–100 progress scale, improving all six game types. The instructions also improve average scores for three other models without retuning. These findings point toward real-time intelligence: enabling powerful LLM agents to remain effective in a continuously changing world by organizing deliberation, learning, and action across timescales.

1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents can solve complex interactive tasks by combining reasoning with tool use. Bringing these capabilities into continuously changing environments presents a fundamental challenge: reasoning and tool calls take time, and the world can change before an agent finishes deciding what to do. An action that was appropriate when the agent observed the environment may arrive too late to be useful.

Real-time games provide controlled simulations of such dynamic environments, where agents must plan and act while the world keeps changing. Playing them well tests a core requirement for real-time intelligence: making good decisions and acting on them in time. For example, Mario may continue moving toward an enemy while the model decides whether to jump. If the command arrives after the collision, even a sensible decision cannot prevent failure (Figure 1).

However, game evaluations that pause during model responses remove these consequences of decision latency, so their scores may not predict performance when the game keeps moving. Prior work studies latency-sensitive decisions and games that continue during model computation [(Kang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Wen et al., 2026)]. Building on these efforts, we investigate how continued evolution during inference affects agent performance across different game mechanics. Comparing the same agent and tasks under different clocks allows us to examine when good action selection translates into effective real-time control.

To study this relationship, we introduce RealtimeBench, 180 tasks across six game types, including Mario, Snake, and Tetris. Models receive text descriptions of the current state and select from legal actions. While a response is pending, the game keeps running with the previous control still active. We also evaluate the same tasks with the game paused during each response or running faster. Scores measure in-game progress on a 0–100 scale, distinguishing partial achievement even when agents cannot complete a task or the game has no discrete completion condition.

These clock comparisons reveal how timing changes model performance. GPT-6.1-sol, which takes about 19 seconds per response, outperforms Jev, a faster decision model, in five of six game types when games are paused. When games keep running, their average scores are 1.51 and 13.51, respectively. Yet faster responses alone are insufficient: no evaluated model averages more than 16.62 (Table 1). We therefore investigate how a slower model’s reasoning can improve a fast model’s decisions without requiring the agent to wait for the slow model during gameplay.

To this end, we propose Two-Timescale Offline Recursive Self-Improvement (TORSI), which places action selection and learning on different timescales. A fast student chooses actions during gameplay, and a slow teacher studies its failures between attempts. The teacher tests corrections in paused environments and writes reusable instructions that the student follows in later games, without further teacher calls (Figure 5). Instructions replace the current version only when they improve scores on separate validation tasks. The next round then addresses the updated student’s remaining failures.

After two teaching rounds, the adopted instructions raise Jev’s average test score from 13.51 to 24.19, improving all six game types. The same instructions improve average scores for three other models without retuning, although some game-specific regressions remain. Together, RealtimeBench and TORSI investigate how deliberation, learning, and action can be organized to support real-time intelligence. The benchmark measures what happens when the world continues to change during reasoning; the method explores how slow deliberation between attempts can improve fast action within it.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    RealtimeBench: We introduce a shared evaluation framework with 180 tasks across six game types and matched paused, live, and accelerated clocks. Explicit clock controls support consistent comparisons of response speed and performance under real-time conditions.

  • •

    Strong reasoning versus fast response: We highlight the tension between reasoning capability and timely action as a central practical challenge for real-time agents, motivating the separation of deliberation and execution across timescales.

  • •

    TORSI: We propose a method that iteratively turns offline LLM reasoning and practice into reusable guidance for a fast actor, with validation-gated updates and no teacher calls during gameplay.

    • 2 Related Work

    Game benchmarks and time.

    SmartPlay, BALROG, and lmgame-Bench evaluate agents through step-based interaction [(Wu et al., 2024; Paglieri et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026)]. VideoGameBench includes both live and paused evaluation [(Zhang et al., 2025)], while Real-Time Reasoning Gym studies agents in continuously evolving environments [(Wen et al., 2026)]. RealtimeBench explicitly controls the clock to support consistent comparisons between methods. This makes it easier to analyze how response speed affects task performance and whether a method remains effective under real-time conditions (Appendix A, Table 6).

    Acting while the world moves.

    Real-time and delayed reinforcement learning study evolution during action selection [(Ramstedt and Pal, 2019; Derman et al., 2021)]. For large models, approaches include latency–quality trade-offs and time-budget adaptation [(Kang et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2026)], asynchronous inference [(Riemer et al., 2025)], and overlapping inference with action execution [(Black et al., 2025)]. Hybrid agents combine fast control with slower planning during deployment [(Lin et al., 2023; Christakopoulou et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2026; Bjorck et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025)].

    In games, GameSense uses VLMs to develop execution modules for real-time games [(Lu et al., 2025)]. TORSI keeps actor weights and interfaces fixed, revising guidance through offline practice and validation. Decision models such as Jev, Clef, and StartLux score predefined choices [(Almeida, 2026; Deußer et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; startlux-models, 2026)], making them candidates for the fast actor.

    Improvement without weight updates.

    Agents learn through reflection, distilled insights, and skill libraries [(Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024)]. GEPA evolves prompts from execution feedback, ACE refines reusable context, and AHE revises agent components [(Agrawal et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026)]. Recuris and RSIAgent explicitly iterate improvement through validated memory updates and verified environment knowledge [(Yu et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026)]. TORSI adds offline practice for live-clock control, iterating guidance updates from the current student’s failures.

    3 RealtimeBench

    RealtimeBench evaluates how well agents can act in games that continue running while they decide what to do.

    3.1 Live-Clock Protocol

    RealtimeBench keeps the game running while the agent selects an action from the current observation. The previous accepted control remains active during inference, so the observed state may be outdated when the new action takes effect.

    We distinguish response latency from action age. For request i, let tᵢᵒ be the observation time, tᵢʳ the response time, and tᵢᵃ the action-application time. Response latency measures the wait for a response; action age also includes any delay before the selected action is applied:

    Lᵢ=tᵢʳ-tᵢᵒ, Aᵢ=tᵢᵃ-tᵢᵒ.

    		(1)

    The two differ when a response must wait for an eligible game tick or scheduled action. Outcomes follow the state at tᵢᵃ (Figure 1(b)).

    Each game type declares its own wall-clock pacing; real-time evaluation therefore means continued evolution during inference, rather than a common frame rate across games. Paused and accelerated conditions change pacing without changing the underlying game physics.

    3.2 Game Types and Tasks

    The benchmark spans six game types with different control demands: platforming (Mario), navigation and food collection (Snake), falling-piece placement (Tetris), obstacle avoidance (Temple), steering and shooting (River), and timing flap actions (Bird; Figure 2).

    Within each game type, a task fixes the game version, seed or stage, difficulty, action interface, and budget; an episode is one execution of that task, ending at game termination or the budget. Settings and clocks for each game type are listed in Table 7.

    For development and evaluation, each game type has 30 tasks: ten feedback, ten validation, and ten test tasks, giving 180 tasks in total. Feedback tasks provide experience for developing an agent; validation tasks compare candidate updates; test tasks are held out from adaptation and used exclusively for final reporting.

    Across these tasks, agents receive structured text descriptions rather than raw pixels. The harness, the code connecting the model and game, constructs observations and legal action choices, queries the model, and applies its response (Figure 3). It may compute geometry and timing features from the current state, but cannot inspect future states or search the simulator during scored play. Table 8 in Appendix A summarizes the observations and action interfaces for each game type.

    3.3 Scoring

    We score these tasks by progress rather than binary completion for two reasons. Some games have no single completion condition and are naturally scored by points or survival progress. Even when completion is defined, a binary score cannot distinguish partial progress when successful completion is rare. Progress scores let us compare agents that improve without reaching a terminal goal.

    To put progress on a shared scale, we report the native outcome (e.g., lines or points) and a normalized score for episode e in game type f:

    q(e)=100\min((p(e))/(R_f),1),

    		(2)

    where p(e) is peak progress, unaffected by later failure, and R_f is a game type reference target: 3200 pixels (Mario), 85 food (Snake), 260 lines (Tetris), 130,000 points (Temple), 11,000 points (River), and 25 pipes (Bird). Targets are shared across models and conditions.

    On this scale, a score of 100 means reaching the reference target, not necessarily winning the native game. Normalization provides a shared scale, not equal difficulty. A score for a game type is the mean over its tasks; Avg (or Average) is the unweighted mean across the six game types.

    3.4 Clock Sensitivity

    We next examine whether an agent’s performance with a paused game carries over to a continuously running game. We compare a fast decision model, Jev, with a slower reasoning LLM, GPT-6.1-sol, under matched tasks and different clocks.

    Both models use unchanged instructions on the ten test tasks per game type; GPT-6.1-sol uses medium reasoning effort. We evaluate four clocks: Paused, which freezes the game during inference; Current, the declared live clock; and 1.5× and 2× faster clocks. Seeds, instructions, legal actions, objectives, and budgets are fixed; pacing and the clock fields shown to the agent change together.

    Pausing changes the comparison.

    GPT-6.1-sol outperforms Jev in five game types when paused, but under the live clock its mean score is 1.51 versus Jev’s 13.51 (Figure 4). GPT-6.1-sol scores lower live than paused in all six game types; Jev does so in five, with Bird as the exception. Within-model comparisons reveal the outcome cost of allowing the game to evolve during inference.

    Sensitivity varies by game type.

    Faster clocks generally reduce scores, but individual changes are not monotonic. Bird’s relative robustness at moderate speeds may reflect its interface, which executes flap schedules planned in advance; this is an interpretation rather than an isolated causal test. Temple drops sharply from Paused to Current. Together, the controls show why an agent that reasons well with a paused clock may still need better decisions under live timing.

    4 TORSI: Two-Timescale Offline Recursive Self-Improvement

    GPT-6.1-sol outperforms Jev in most paused games but falls behind under the live clock. Motivated by this observation, we propose TORSI, which combines their strengths by using GPT-6.1-sol to develop guidance offline and Jev to act on it during gameplay without teacher calls.

    4.1 Two-Timescale Agent

    TORSI follows four steps (Figure 5): collect the student’s failures on feedback tasks, practice corrections offline, propose guidance, and compare the frozen candidate with the current guidance on validation tasks. Accepted guidance starts the next round. Test tasks evaluate the resulting agent and never select updates.

    For game type f and round k, the student follows π_F(·;hₖ^(f)), where hₖ^(f) contains prompt instructions and conditional action rules; h₀^(f) is the initial guidance. Only guidance changes; weights, observations, legal actions, physics, clocks, objectives, budgets, scoring, and splits remain fixed. The student chooses every action without teacher calls. The teacher explores saved feedback states offline; the deployed student cannot inspect future states.

    4.2 Learning from Feedback and Offline Practice

    Each round starts by running the current student on feedback tasks under the live clock. The resulting trajectories D^(f,k) record observations, responses, response latency, action age, and outcomes, with screenshots aligned to requests.

    Using these trajectories, the teacher examines timing errors, misunderstood mechanics, and failing plans. Trajectories show what happened, but not the outcomes of untried alternatives. Teacher practice tests alternative action sequences from saved feedback states in paused or slowed environments. This access is restricted to offline learning and excludes test states.

    Student practice then checks whether the lesson works at the fast student’s live latency. The student tries draft guidance on feedback tasks, and the teacher revises it using the resulting trajectories. Successful and failed trials both enter the practice evidence B^(f,k).

    4.3 Turning Practice into Reusable Guidance

    The teacher combines the current guidance with this feedback and practice evidence to propose revised guidance, using update procedure Tₖ for round k:

    h̃ₖ₊₁^(f)=Tₖ(hₖ^(f),D^(f,k),B^(f,k)).

    		(3)

    A practiced action sequence fits a particular state; reusable guidance explains how to choose actions in other states. For example, a Mario instruction can specify releasing the jump button before initiating another jump, allowing the student to apply the rule whenever the relevant state occurs.

    To deliver these rules to the student, guidance uses fixed fields for skill instructions, action-specific instructions, and conditional rules (Table 9). Rules use current observation features, such as board height, visible hazards, and timing cues, and remain concise for action selection.

    4.4 Validation-Gated Rounds

    To select an update, each candidate is frozen before evaluation on the game type’s validation tasks. It replaces the current guidance only if its mean validation score is strictly higher; the current guidance stays unchanged for ties or rejected candidates. Adoption is decided separately for each game type using identical observation and action interfaces. Feedback supports learning, validation decides adoption, and test supports final reporting.

    Subsequent rounds collect new feedback from the current student: adopted guidance changes its remaining failures, while rejection preserves the current guidance.

    5 Experiments

    We evaluate baseline models, TORSI improvement, alternative adaptation methods, and cross-model transfer. The clock controls appear in §3.4. TORSI pairs Jev with GPT-6.1-sol (medium reasoning effort) as the offline teacher; Base denotes Jev with its initial guidance.

    5.1 Benchmark Evaluation

    For the baseline comparison, models receive the same state information and legal choices under identical clocks and budgets. Decision models score choices; LLMs return a choice. Table 1 reports scores on ten test tasks per game type, mean response latency, and API cost per task.

    Decision-model mean scores range from 1.65 to 16.62, with mean response latencies below one second. GPT-6.1-sol scores 1.51 with a latency of 18.97 seconds, while MiMo v2.6 Ultra Speed and DeepSeek v4.1 Flash, both promoted for faster inference [(Xiaomi MiMo, 2026; DeepSeek, 2026)], score 5.95 and 2.44 with latencies of 1.60 and 7.72 seconds, respectively. Even these speed-oriented LLMs achieve limited progress under these real-time evaluation conditions.

    5.2 TORSI Improvement Rounds

    After two rounds, the validation-selected guidance raises Jev’s mean test score from 13.51 to 24.19, a gain of 10.68 points, with improvements in all six game types (Table 2).

    Round selection.

    R1 and R2 denote guidance from the first and second rounds. R1 improves test scores in all six game types. R2 improves both splits for Snake, Tetris, River, and Bird, but fails the validation gate for Mario and Temple. Adopted therefore uses R1 for those two game types and R2 for the other four, selected by validation rather than test performance. Scores average three runs.

    An illustrated Mario example in Appendix A (Figure 6) follows the first round from feedback and offline practice to held-out gameplay.

    Roles of offline practice.

    To understand how practice contributes to these gains, we compare variants with and without teacher and student practice. All one-round variants in Table 3 generate guidance from failures. Without practice, the adopted mean test score is 13.08, versus Base’s 13.51. Teacher-only and student-only practice give 14.14 and 13.07; combining both gives 19.35.

    Testing alternatives and checking their live execution are complementary here, although practice budgets are not matched across variants.

    5.3 Comparison with Other Adaptation Methods

    For comparison with TORSI, we adapt ACE, AHE, and GEPA to the same Jev student, offline teacher, task splits, live-clock evaluation, and validation adoption rule [(Zhang et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026; Agrawal et al., 2026)]. Editable components and search configurations differ (Appendix B.1), so this comparison evaluates the adapted configurations without matched budgets.

    In this comparison, TORSI achieves the highest adopted mean test score, 24.19, compared with 13.22 for ACE, 16.59 for AHE, and 14.52 for GEPA (Table 4). Where no update is adopted, the table uses Base scores in the average. Total API expenditure over the update process is $24.39 for TORSI and $20.99–$27.49 for the alternatives. These total adaptation costs differ from per-task API fees and response latency.

    5.4 Cross-Model Generalization

    We evaluate whether guidance developed with Jev generalizes to other models without further adaptation. We apply the final guidance unchanged, keeping the same tasks and clocks (Table 5). MiMo uses an action-selection adapter that returns a valid choice from the provided list. StartLux 4B’s mean score rises from 12.22 to 25.05, StartLux 27B’s from 16.62 to 20.43, and MiMo’s mean score from 5.95 to 7.30.

    Transfer gains vary across models: StartLux 4B and MiMo improve in all six game types, while StartLux 27B improves in four but regresses in Tetris and Temple. These tests use the same game types and do not evaluate guidance transfer to previously unseen environments.

    6 Conclusion

    Real-time intelligence requires both capable decisions and timely action. RealtimeBench provides a shared evaluation framework for studying this requirement and comparing future approaches. TORSI demonstrates one such approach: a powerful LLM reasons and practices offline, turning its experience into reusable guidance that the fast Jev actor applies during live interaction. Improvements across all six game types, together with gains from transferring the guidance to other models, suggest that this combination can extend beyond a single actor. This points toward a promising paradigm for real-time intelligence, in which stronger LLMs continually improve fast actors without requiring those actors to wait for teacher inference during live gameplay.

    Limitations

    Structured observations.

    RealtimeBench does not evaluate actors operating directly from raw visual observations. Actors receive structured state descriptions, so the benchmark omits errors and delays introduced by visual perception. This limits the applicability of our findings to end-to-end visual agents. Nevertheless, all evaluated decision models and LLMs receive the same state information and legal action choices, so the reported comparisons remain informative about decision-making under inference delay within this shared interface.

    Access to offline practice.

    TORSI relies on saved states or resettable environments for teacher practice. Such access may be unavailable in physical or irreversible interactions, limiting direct application beyond simulation. Our experiments therefore establish the method’s effectiveness where offline practice is available; extending it to other settings would require an appropriate mechanism for testing proposed corrections.

    Generalization and experimental scope.

    Our experiments cover six game types and two improvement rounds, with guidance developed separately for each game type. Cross-model transfer retains the same environments and produces some game-specific regressions; it does not establish transfer to unseen environments or sustained improvement over many rounds. The observed gains nevertheless provide evidence that guidance can be reused across the evaluated actors without retuning.

    Ethical Considerations

    More capable and responsive agents could make automated interaction easier to scale, creating opportunities for misuse such as unfair gameplay or unauthorized actions on digital services. Teacher-generated guidance may carry over errors or harmful instructions from the underlying models, while a fast actor can apply them repeatedly before human intervention. Reusing the same guidance across models could further spread these risks.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Benchmark and Guidance Details

    Intended use.

    RealtimeBench is intended for research and evaluation of latency-sensitive agents in controlled game environments. TORSI is intended to study how offline teacher guidance improves real-time control within these environments.

    Underlying implementations.

    Mario uses gym-super-mario-bros (9.1.0) and nes-py (9.0.1), whose emulator core derives from SimpleNES. Temple uses Three.js (0.180.0), while River and Bird use Pygame-based implementations. Snake and Tetris use deterministic Python and JavaScript game engines, respectively. Software sources are listed in Appendix C.

    Benchmark-specific task construction.

    We construct RealtimeBench through explicit task specifications over six game families. Each task fixes the game version, seed or stage, difficulty, observation and action interfaces, and episode budget. Task configurations span platform layouts, board geometry and hazards, falling-piece sequences and gravity, running speed, starting lives, and pipe-gap width. These specifications support paired evaluations under different clocks while keeping task identity and game physics fixed. Feedback, validation, and test tasks serve distinct roles in experience collection, update selection, and final evaluation.

    Live-clock adaptation and timing-aware interfaces.

    Our execution framework couples asynchronous model inference with continuously advancing game state and game-specific action semantics. It records observation, response, and action-application times, allowing response latency and action age to be measured separately. The adapters connect structured observations to executable controls, including timestamped button plans, scheduled turns, piece placements, steering decisions, and flap schedules. For Snake, our adapter extends the underlying engine with configurable task presets, current-grid topology features, response-delay information, and joint direction-and-turn-timing decisions. Turn timing is anchored to the observation tick, making the consequences of inference delay explicit in action execution.

    Evaluation and traceability.

    We define a shared progress-based evaluation procedure while retaining each game’s native outcome. Scores use game-specific reference targets that remain fixed across models and clock conditions, followed by task-level and game-level aggregation. Recorded states and action logs support checking episode outcomes. The task manifest identifies underlying game sources and revisions, while Tables 7–8 document task settings, clocks, observations, and action interfaces. The release includes task definitions, per-episode outcomes, frozen agent specifications, reusable guidance, and replay logs, making the evaluated system and its execution conditions explicit.

    Table 9 and Figure 7 illustrate guidance formats and representative lessons.

    Figure 6 uses native Mario scenes and poses replayed from archived feedback, teacher practice, and held-out episodes. Poses are aligned using recorded camera positions and enlarged for visibility.

    Two improving student-practice examples are shown; the archived three-task practice screen left the guidance unchanged. The held-out Before/After panels show the initial student (Base) and the student with round-1 guidance (R1) on the same task. These examples illustrate the full guidance update rather than isolate the effect of an individual rule.

    Appendix B Additional Experimental Results

    B.1 Adaptation Comparison Protocol

    All methods use Jev as the real-time student and GPT-6.1-sol with medium reasoning effort as the offline teacher. Each game type has ten feedback, ten validation, and ten test tasks. Game physics, clocks, scoring, observations, and legal action interfaces remain fixed. The teacher is never queried during scored play. A frozen candidate is adopted only if its mean validation score strictly exceeds that of the current agent; test tasks are used solely for final evaluation.

    Table 10 summarizes how each method’s optimization mechanism is adapted to the RealtimeBench setting, and Table 11 lists the corresponding search configurations and stopping conditions. All methods use repeated task-level rollouts on the same ten feedback tasks as their interaction unit.

    Episode budgets count student executions of feedback tasks, including repeated executions of the same task; validation and test evaluations are accounted for separately.

    B.2 Response Latency

    Model execution.

    Our local inference hardware consists of NVIDIA L20Y GPUs. All local models run on a single GPU without tensor or pipeline parallelism, e.g., GLiClass (0.4B), Open-Jev-2B (2B), JevK5 (4B), Clef-flash (9B), Clef (27B), and StartLux (4B and 27B). Local inference incurs no API fees; its compute cost is the wall-clock response time reported in Table 13, and no additional compute budget was imposed on local runs. Among the API-based models, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash is queried with thinking mode disabled to reduce response latency, and MiMo v2.6 Ultra Speed exposes no thinking interface, so it is called through the official API with the provider’s default decoding settings.

    Decision models have median response times below two seconds in every game type. In Snake, all of them except StartLux 27B (0.86 s) stay below the 667 ms tick. MiMo has a low median but a long tail, reaching 13.64 s at P95 in Mario. GPT-6.1-sol’s game type medians range from 5 to 31 s, during which the live environment continues evolving.

    B.3 Token Usage and Computational Cost

    Table 14 reports token usage and API cost for the recorded task runs. In Table 4, token counts are in millions (with reasoning tokens included in output) and API costs are totals over the full update process. Jev costs are estimated at $0.042/M input tokens, with free output; teacher costs use $2/M input tokens and $10/M output tokens. GPUs were used only to serve open-source models during evaluation, totaling 46.47 GPU-hours.

    B.4 Model Sources

    Official model cards document the evaluated GLiClass checkpoint,111Hugging Face: knowledgator/gliclass-instruct-large-v1.0 JevK5,222Hugging Face: alibiserikbay/JevK5 Open-Jev-2B,333Hugging Face: ZefanCai/Open-Jev-2B mini-Jev,444Hugging Face: samatv256/mini-Jev and StartLux 27B.555Hugging Face: startlux-models/StartLux-Decision-27B Official API documentation lists MiMo v2.6 Ultra Speed666mimo.mi.com/docs/en-US/api/chat/openai-api and DeepSeek v4.1 Flash.777api-docs.deepseek.com/quick_start/pricing/

    Appendix C Software Sources

    Mario emulator stack. Mario uses Christian Kauten’s gym-super-mario-bros (9.1.0)888GitHub: Kautenja/gym-super-mario-bros and nes-py (9.0.1),999GitHub: Kautenja/nes-py with an emulator core derived from Amish Kumar Naidu and contributors’ SimpleNES.101010GitHub: amhndu/SimpleNES

    Rendering frameworks. Temple uses Three.js (0.180.0, r180).111111GitHub: mrdoob/three.js River and Bird use Pygame-based implementations, with sources maintained by the Pygame121212GitHub: pygame/pygame and Pygame Community Edition131313GitHub: pygame-community/pygame-ce contributor communities.

    Game implementations. The original Super Mario Bros. game is by Nintendo.141414Nintendo: Super Mario Bros. Snake adapts iammusham’s jev-snake (revision a935107),151515GitHub: iammusham/jev-snake and Tetris adapts trungdq88’s jev-tetris (a0b411c).161616GitHub: trungdq88/jev-tetris Temple adapts Mukhsin Mukhtorov’s Night Relay (1e53984).171717GitHub: Mukhsin0508/night-relay River uses Ashkan Aazami’s river-run-typesafe (8cf0429),181818GitHub: ashaazami/river-run-typesafe and Bird uses leftspace89’s JevBird (1e5fd13).191919GitHub: leftspace89/JevBird
item.content:encoded:
一句话：暂停时更聪明的模型一开跑就输给更快的模型；TORSI 让慢教师在间隙写指令、快学生实战中不调教师。

要点：

  • RealtimeBench 含 6 类游戏共 180 个任务，评测期间游戏持续运行；成对评测显示暂停时 GPT-6.1-sol 强于更快的 Jev，不暂停就反过来
  • TORSI（双时间尺度离线递归自我改进）：慢教师在两次尝试之间复盘失败、在暂停的游戏里验证修正，再给快学生写出可复用指令
  • 快学生实战中不向教师发请求；两轮把 Jev 的平均分从 13.51 提到 24.19（0–100 进度分），六类游戏全面提升，另外三个模型不重训也涨

为什么值得看：只要引擎里有实时循环，agent 的延迟就是能力的一部分。这套「离线教师 + 在线学生」的分工，对任何要做实时 NPC 或实时玩法 agent 的架构都直接适用。

中文摘要：LLM 智能体能解决复杂的交互任务，但推理与工具调用都要花时间，在持续变化的环境里，本来正确的动作可能到得太晚。作者提出 RealtimeBench，覆盖 6 类游戏共 180 个任务，评测时让游戏在推理期间继续运行。成对评测显示：游戏暂停时 GPT-6.1-sol 强于更快的 Jev，游戏不暂停时两者顺序反转。为此提出 TORSI：慢教师在两次尝试之间研究失败、在暂停的游戏里检验修正，然后把可复用的指令写给快学生；学生实战中不调用教师，是否采纳更新由验证分数决定。两轮之后 Jev 的平均分从 13.51 升到 24.19，六类游戏全部提升，另外三个模型在不重训的情况下也受益。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·智能体+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-14

本期推送：2026-10-24

The World Won’t Wait: Evaluating and Teaching Agents Under a Live Clock

Abstract

Large language model (LLM) agents can solve complex interactive tasks, yet reasoning and tool calls take time. In continuously changing environments, an otherwise correct action may arrive too late. We introduce RealtimeBench, with 180 tasks across six game types, to evaluate agents while games continue running during inference. Paired evaluations show that GPT-6.1-sol outperforms the faster Jev when games are paused, but falls behind when they keep running. We propose Two-Timescale Offline Recursive Self-Improvement (TORSI): a slow teacher studies failures and tests corrections in paused games between attempts, then writes reusable instructions for a fast student. The student acts without teacher calls during gameplay, and validation scores determine which updates are adopted. Two rounds raise Jev’s average test score from 13.51 to 24.19 on a 0–100 progress scale, improving all six game types. The instructions also improve average scores for three other models without retuning. These findings point toward real-time intelligence: enabling powerful LLM agents to remain effective in a continuously changing world by organizing deliberation, learning, and action across timescales.

1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents can solve complex interactive tasks by combining reasoning with tool use. Bringing these capabilities into continuously changing environments presents a fundamental challenge: reasoning and tool calls take time, and the world can change before an agent finishes deciding what to do. An action that was appropriate when the agent observed the environment may arrive too late to be useful.

Real-time games provide controlled simulations of such dynamic environments, where agents must plan and act while the world keeps changing. Playing them well tests a core requirement for real-time intelligence: making good decisions and acting on them in time. For example, Mario may continue moving toward an enemy while the model decides whether to jump. If the command arrives after the collision, even a sensible decision cannot prevent failure (Figure 1).

However, game evaluations that pause during model responses remove these consequences of decision latency, so their scores may not predict performance when the game keeps moving. Prior work studies latency-sensitive decisions and games that continue during model computation [(Kang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Wen et al., 2026)]. Building on these efforts, we investigate how continued evolution during inference affects agent performance across different game mechanics. Comparing the same agent and tasks under different clocks allows us to examine when good action selection translates into effective real-time control.

To study this relationship, we introduce RealtimeBench, 180 tasks across six game types, including Mario, Snake, and Tetris. Models receive text descriptions of the current state and select from legal actions. While a response is pending, the game keeps running with the previous control still active. We also evaluate the same tasks with the game paused during each response or running faster. Scores measure in-game progress on a 0–100 scale, distinguishing partial achievement even when agents cannot complete a task or the game has no discrete completion condition.

These clock comparisons reveal how timing changes model performance. GPT-6.1-sol, which takes about 19 seconds per response, outperforms Jev, a faster decision model, in five of six game types when games are paused. When games keep running, their average scores are 1.51 and 13.51, respectively. Yet faster responses alone are insufficient: no evaluated model averages more than 16.62 (Table 1). We therefore investigate how a slower model’s reasoning can improve a fast model’s decisions without requiring the agent to wait for the slow model during gameplay.

To this end, we propose Two-Timescale Offline Recursive Self-Improvement (TORSI), which places action selection and learning on different timescales. A fast student chooses actions during gameplay, and a slow teacher studies its failures between attempts. The teacher tests corrections in paused environments and writes reusable instructions that the student follows in later games, without further teacher calls (Figure 5). Instructions replace the current version only when they improve scores on separate validation tasks. The next round then addresses the updated student’s remaining failures.

After two teaching rounds, the adopted instructions raise Jev’s average test score from 13.51 to 24.19, improving all six game types. The same instructions improve average scores for three other models without retuning, although some game-specific regressions remain. Together, RealtimeBench and TORSI investigate how deliberation, learning, and action can be organized to support real-time intelligence. The benchmark measures what happens when the world continues to change during reasoning; the method explores how slow deliberation between attempts can improve fast action within it.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    RealtimeBench: We introduce a shared evaluation framework with 180 tasks across six game types and matched paused, live, and accelerated clocks. Explicit clock controls support consistent comparisons of response speed and performance under real-time conditions.

  • •

    Strong reasoning versus fast response: We highlight the tension between reasoning capability and timely action as a central practical challenge for real-time agents, motivating the separation of deliberation and execution across timescales.

  • •

    TORSI: We propose a method that iteratively turns offline LLM reasoning and practice into reusable guidance for a fast actor, with validation-gated updates and no teacher calls during gameplay.

    • 2 Related Work

    Game benchmarks and time.

    SmartPlay, BALROG, and lmgame-Bench evaluate agents through step-based interaction [(Wu et al., 2024; Paglieri et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026)]. VideoGameBench includes both live and paused evaluation [(Zhang et al., 2025)], while Real-Time Reasoning Gym studies agents in continuously evolving environments [(Wen et al., 2026)]. RealtimeBench explicitly controls the clock to support consistent comparisons between methods. This makes it easier to analyze how response speed affects task performance and whether a method remains effective under real-time conditions (Appendix A, Table 6).

    Acting while the world moves.

    Real-time and delayed reinforcement learning study evolution during action selection [(Ramstedt and Pal, 2019; Derman et al., 2021)]. For large models, approaches include latency–quality trade-offs and time-budget adaptation [(Kang et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2026)], asynchronous inference [(Riemer et al., 2025)], and overlapping inference with action execution [(Black et al., 2025)]. Hybrid agents combine fast control with slower planning during deployment [(Lin et al., 2023; Christakopoulou et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2026; Bjorck et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025)].

    In games, GameSense uses VLMs to develop execution modules for real-time games [(Lu et al., 2025)]. TORSI keeps actor weights and interfaces fixed, revising guidance through offline practice and validation. Decision models such as Jev, Clef, and StartLux score predefined choices [(Almeida, 2026; Deußer et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; startlux-models, 2026)], making them candidates for the fast actor.

    Improvement without weight updates.

    Agents learn through reflection, distilled insights, and skill libraries [(Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024)]. GEPA evolves prompts from execution feedback, ACE refines reusable context, and AHE revises agent components [(Agrawal et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026)]. Recuris and RSIAgent explicitly iterate improvement through validated memory updates and verified environment knowledge [(Yu et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026)]. TORSI adds offline practice for live-clock control, iterating guidance updates from the current student’s failures.

    3 RealtimeBench

    RealtimeBench evaluates how well agents can act in games that continue running while they decide what to do.

    3.1 Live-Clock Protocol

    RealtimeBench keeps the game running while the agent selects an action from the current observation. The previous accepted control remains active during inference, so the observed state may be outdated when the new action takes effect.

    We distinguish response latency from action age. For request i, let tᵢᵒ be the observation time, tᵢʳ the response time, and tᵢᵃ the action-application time. Response latency measures the wait for a response; action age also includes any delay before the selected action is applied:

    Lᵢ=tᵢʳ-tᵢᵒ, Aᵢ=tᵢᵃ-tᵢᵒ.

    		(1)

    The two differ when a response must wait for an eligible game tick or scheduled action. Outcomes follow the state at tᵢᵃ (Figure 1(b)).

    Each game type declares its own wall-clock pacing; real-time evaluation therefore means continued evolution during inference, rather than a common frame rate across games. Paused and accelerated conditions change pacing without changing the underlying game physics.

    3.2 Game Types and Tasks

    The benchmark spans six game types with different control demands: platforming (Mario), navigation and food collection (Snake), falling-piece placement (Tetris), obstacle avoidance (Temple), steering and shooting (River), and timing flap actions (Bird; Figure 2).

    Within each game type, a task fixes the game version, seed or stage, difficulty, action interface, and budget; an episode is one execution of that task, ending at game termination or the budget. Settings and clocks for each game type are listed in Table 7.

    For development and evaluation, each game type has 30 tasks: ten feedback, ten validation, and ten test tasks, giving 180 tasks in total. Feedback tasks provide experience for developing an agent; validation tasks compare candidate updates; test tasks are held out from adaptation and used exclusively for final reporting.

    Across these tasks, agents receive structured text descriptions rather than raw pixels. The harness, the code connecting the model and game, constructs observations and legal action choices, queries the model, and applies its response (Figure 3). It may compute geometry and timing features from the current state, but cannot inspect future states or search the simulator during scored play. Table 8 in Appendix A summarizes the observations and action interfaces for each game type.

    3.3 Scoring

    We score these tasks by progress rather than binary completion for two reasons. Some games have no single completion condition and are naturally scored by points or survival progress. Even when completion is defined, a binary score cannot distinguish partial progress when successful completion is rare. Progress scores let us compare agents that improve without reaching a terminal goal.

    To put progress on a shared scale, we report the native outcome (e.g., lines or points) and a normalized score for episode e in game type f:

    q(e)=100\min((p(e))/(R_f),1),

    		(2)

    where p(e) is peak progress, unaffected by later failure, and R_f is a game type reference target: 3200 pixels (Mario), 85 food (Snake), 260 lines (Tetris), 130,000 points (Temple), 11,000 points (River), and 25 pipes (Bird). Targets are shared across models and conditions.

    On this scale, a score of 100 means reaching the reference target, not necessarily winning the native game. Normalization provides a shared scale, not equal difficulty. A score for a game type is the mean over its tasks; Avg (or Average) is the unweighted mean across the six game types.

    3.4 Clock Sensitivity

    We next examine whether an agent’s performance with a paused game carries over to a continuously running game. We compare a fast decision model, Jev, with a slower reasoning LLM, GPT-6.1-sol, under matched tasks and different clocks.

    Both models use unchanged instructions on the ten test tasks per game type; GPT-6.1-sol uses medium reasoning effort. We evaluate four clocks: Paused, which freezes the game during inference; Current, the declared live clock; and 1.5× and 2× faster clocks. Seeds, instructions, legal actions, objectives, and budgets are fixed; pacing and the clock fields shown to the agent change together.

    Pausing changes the comparison.

    GPT-6.1-sol outperforms Jev in five game types when paused, but under the live clock its mean score is 1.51 versus Jev’s 13.51 (Figure 4). GPT-6.1-sol scores lower live than paused in all six game types; Jev does so in five, with Bird as the exception. Within-model comparisons reveal the outcome cost of allowing the game to evolve during inference.

    Sensitivity varies by game type.

    Faster clocks generally reduce scores, but individual changes are not monotonic. Bird’s relative robustness at moderate speeds may reflect its interface, which executes flap schedules planned in advance; this is an interpretation rather than an isolated causal test. Temple drops sharply from Paused to Current. Together, the controls show why an agent that reasons well with a paused clock may still need better decisions under live timing.

    4 TORSI: Two-Timescale Offline Recursive Self-Improvement

    GPT-6.1-sol outperforms Jev in most paused games but falls behind under the live clock. Motivated by this observation, we propose TORSI, which combines their strengths by using GPT-6.1-sol to develop guidance offline and Jev to act on it during gameplay without teacher calls.

    4.1 Two-Timescale Agent

    TORSI follows four steps (Figure 5): collect the student’s failures on feedback tasks, practice corrections offline, propose guidance, and compare the frozen candidate with the current guidance on validation tasks. Accepted guidance starts the next round. Test tasks evaluate the resulting agent and never select updates.

    For game type f and round k, the student follows π_F(·;hₖ^(f)), where hₖ^(f) contains prompt instructions and conditional action rules; h₀^(f) is the initial guidance. Only guidance changes; weights, observations, legal actions, physics, clocks, objectives, budgets, scoring, and splits remain fixed. The student chooses every action without teacher calls. The teacher explores saved feedback states offline; the deployed student cannot inspect future states.

    4.2 Learning from Feedback and Offline Practice

    Each round starts by running the current student on feedback tasks under the live clock. The resulting trajectories D^(f,k) record observations, responses, response latency, action age, and outcomes, with screenshots aligned to requests.

    Using these trajectories, the teacher examines timing errors, misunderstood mechanics, and failing plans. Trajectories show what happened, but not the outcomes of untried alternatives. Teacher practice tests alternative action sequences from saved feedback states in paused or slowed environments. This access is restricted to offline learning and excludes test states.

    Student practice then checks whether the lesson works at the fast student’s live latency. The student tries draft guidance on feedback tasks, and the teacher revises it using the resulting trajectories. Successful and failed trials both enter the practice evidence B^(f,k).

    4.3 Turning Practice into Reusable Guidance

    The teacher combines the current guidance with this feedback and practice evidence to propose revised guidance, using update procedure Tₖ for round k:

    h̃ₖ₊₁^(f)=Tₖ(hₖ^(f),D^(f,k),B^(f,k)).

    		(3)

    A practiced action sequence fits a particular state; reusable guidance explains how to choose actions in other states. For example, a Mario instruction can specify releasing the jump button before initiating another jump, allowing the student to apply the rule whenever the relevant state occurs.

    To deliver these rules to the student, guidance uses fixed fields for skill instructions, action-specific instructions, and conditional rules (Table 9). Rules use current observation features, such as board height, visible hazards, and timing cues, and remain concise for action selection.

    4.4 Validation-Gated Rounds

    To select an update, each candidate is frozen before evaluation on the game type’s validation tasks. It replaces the current guidance only if its mean validation score is strictly higher; the current guidance stays unchanged for ties or rejected candidates. Adoption is decided separately for each game type using identical observation and action interfaces. Feedback supports learning, validation decides adoption, and test supports final reporting.

    Subsequent rounds collect new feedback from the current student: adopted guidance changes its remaining failures, while rejection preserves the current guidance.

    5 Experiments

    We evaluate baseline models, TORSI improvement, alternative adaptation methods, and cross-model transfer. The clock controls appear in §3.4. TORSI pairs Jev with GPT-6.1-sol (medium reasoning effort) as the offline teacher; Base denotes Jev with its initial guidance.

    5.1 Benchmark Evaluation

    For the baseline comparison, models receive the same state information and legal choices under identical clocks and budgets. Decision models score choices; LLMs return a choice. Table 1 reports scores on ten test tasks per game type, mean response latency, and API cost per task.

    Decision-model mean scores range from 1.65 to 16.62, with mean response latencies below one second. GPT-6.1-sol scores 1.51 with a latency of 18.97 seconds, while MiMo v2.6 Ultra Speed and DeepSeek v4.1 Flash, both promoted for faster inference [(Xiaomi MiMo, 2026; DeepSeek, 2026)], score 5.95 and 2.44 with latencies of 1.60 and 7.72 seconds, respectively. Even these speed-oriented LLMs achieve limited progress under these real-time evaluation conditions.

    5.2 TORSI Improvement Rounds

    After two rounds, the validation-selected guidance raises Jev’s mean test score from 13.51 to 24.19, a gain of 10.68 points, with improvements in all six game types (Table 2).

    Round selection.

    R1 and R2 denote guidance from the first and second rounds. R1 improves test scores in all six game types. R2 improves both splits for Snake, Tetris, River, and Bird, but fails the validation gate for Mario and Temple. Adopted therefore uses R1 for those two game types and R2 for the other four, selected by validation rather than test performance. Scores average three runs.

    An illustrated Mario example in Appendix A (Figure 6) follows the first round from feedback and offline practice to held-out gameplay.

    Roles of offline practice.

    To understand how practice contributes to these gains, we compare variants with and without teacher and student practice. All one-round variants in Table 3 generate guidance from failures. Without practice, the adopted mean test score is 13.08, versus Base’s 13.51. Teacher-only and student-only practice give 14.14 and 13.07; combining both gives 19.35.

    Testing alternatives and checking their live execution are complementary here, although practice budgets are not matched across variants.

    5.3 Comparison with Other Adaptation Methods

    For comparison with TORSI, we adapt ACE, AHE, and GEPA to the same Jev student, offline teacher, task splits, live-clock evaluation, and validation adoption rule [(Zhang et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026; Agrawal et al., 2026)]. Editable components and search configurations differ (Appendix B.1), so this comparison evaluates the adapted configurations without matched budgets.

    In this comparison, TORSI achieves the highest adopted mean test score, 24.19, compared with 13.22 for ACE, 16.59 for AHE, and 14.52 for GEPA (Table 4). Where no update is adopted, the table uses Base scores in the average. Total API expenditure over the update process is $24.39 for TORSI and $20.99–$27.49 for the alternatives. These total adaptation costs differ from per-task API fees and response latency.

    5.4 Cross-Model Generalization

    We evaluate whether guidance developed with Jev generalizes to other models without further adaptation. We apply the final guidance unchanged, keeping the same tasks and clocks (Table 5). MiMo uses an action-selection adapter that returns a valid choice from the provided list. StartLux 4B’s mean score rises from 12.22 to 25.05, StartLux 27B’s from 16.62 to 20.43, and MiMo’s mean score from 5.95 to 7.30.

    Transfer gains vary across models: StartLux 4B and MiMo improve in all six game types, while StartLux 27B improves in four but regresses in Tetris and Temple. These tests use the same game types and do not evaluate guidance transfer to previously unseen environments.

    6 Conclusion

    Real-time intelligence requires both capable decisions and timely action. RealtimeBench provides a shared evaluation framework for studying this requirement and comparing future approaches. TORSI demonstrates one such approach: a powerful LLM reasons and practices offline, turning its experience into reusable guidance that the fast Jev actor applies during live interaction. Improvements across all six game types, together with gains from transferring the guidance to other models, suggest that this combination can extend beyond a single actor. This points toward a promising paradigm for real-time intelligence, in which stronger LLMs continually improve fast actors without requiring those actors to wait for teacher inference during live gameplay.

    Limitations

    Structured observations.

    RealtimeBench does not evaluate actors operating directly from raw visual observations. Actors receive structured state descriptions, so the benchmark omits errors and delays introduced by visual perception. This limits the applicability of our findings to end-to-end visual agents. Nevertheless, all evaluated decision models and LLMs receive the same state information and legal action choices, so the reported comparisons remain informative about decision-making under inference delay within this shared interface.

    Access to offline practice.

    TORSI relies on saved states or resettable environments for teacher practice. Such access may be unavailable in physical or irreversible interactions, limiting direct application beyond simulation. Our experiments therefore establish the method’s effectiveness where offline practice is available; extending it to other settings would require an appropriate mechanism for testing proposed corrections.

    Generalization and experimental scope.

    Our experiments cover six game types and two improvement rounds, with guidance developed separately for each game type. Cross-model transfer retains the same environments and produces some game-specific regressions; it does not establish transfer to unseen environments or sustained improvement over many rounds. The observed gains nevertheless provide evidence that guidance can be reused across the evaluated actors without retuning.

    Ethical Considerations

    More capable and responsive agents could make automated interaction easier to scale, creating opportunities for misuse such as unfair gameplay or unauthorized actions on digital services. Teacher-generated guidance may carry over errors or harmful instructions from the underlying models, while a fast actor can apply them repeatedly before human intervention. Reusing the same guidance across models could further spread these risks.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Benchmark and Guidance Details

    Intended use.

    RealtimeBench is intended for research and evaluation of latency-sensitive agents in controlled game environments. TORSI is intended to study how offline teacher guidance improves real-time control within these environments.

    Underlying implementations.

    Mario uses gym-super-mario-bros (9.1.0) and nes-py (9.0.1), whose emulator core derives from SimpleNES. Temple uses Three.js (0.180.0), while River and Bird use Pygame-based implementations. Snake and Tetris use deterministic Python and JavaScript game engines, respectively. Software sources are listed in Appendix C.

    Benchmark-specific task construction.

    We construct RealtimeBench through explicit task specifications over six game families. Each task fixes the game version, seed or stage, difficulty, observation and action interfaces, and episode budget. Task configurations span platform layouts, board geometry and hazards, falling-piece sequences and gravity, running speed, starting lives, and pipe-gap width. These specifications support paired evaluations under different clocks while keeping task identity and game physics fixed. Feedback, validation, and test tasks serve distinct roles in experience collection, update selection, and final evaluation.

    Live-clock adaptation and timing-aware interfaces.

    Our execution framework couples asynchronous model inference with continuously advancing game state and game-specific action semantics. It records observation, response, and action-application times, allowing response latency and action age to be measured separately. The adapters connect structured observations to executable controls, including timestamped button plans, scheduled turns, piece placements, steering decisions, and flap schedules. For Snake, our adapter extends the underlying engine with configurable task presets, current-grid topology features, response-delay information, and joint direction-and-turn-timing decisions. Turn timing is anchored to the observation tick, making the consequences of inference delay explicit in action execution.

    Evaluation and traceability.

    We define a shared progress-based evaluation procedure while retaining each game’s native outcome. Scores use game-specific reference targets that remain fixed across models and clock conditions, followed by task-level and game-level aggregation. Recorded states and action logs support checking episode outcomes. The task manifest identifies underlying game sources and revisions, while Tables 7–8 document task settings, clocks, observations, and action interfaces. The release includes task definitions, per-episode outcomes, frozen agent specifications, reusable guidance, and replay logs, making the evaluated system and its execution conditions explicit.

    Table 9 and Figure 7 illustrate guidance formats and representative lessons.

    Figure 6 uses native Mario scenes and poses replayed from archived feedback, teacher practice, and held-out episodes. Poses are aligned using recorded camera positions and enlarged for visibility.

    Two improving student-practice examples are shown; the archived three-task practice screen left the guidance unchanged. The held-out Before/After panels show the initial student (Base) and the student with round-1 guidance (R1) on the same task. These examples illustrate the full guidance update rather than isolate the effect of an individual rule.

    Appendix B Additional Experimental Results

    B.1 Adaptation Comparison Protocol

    All methods use Jev as the real-time student and GPT-6.1-sol with medium reasoning effort as the offline teacher. Each game type has ten feedback, ten validation, and ten test tasks. Game physics, clocks, scoring, observations, and legal action interfaces remain fixed. The teacher is never queried during scored play. A frozen candidate is adopted only if its mean validation score strictly exceeds that of the current agent; test tasks are used solely for final evaluation.

    Table 10 summarizes how each method’s optimization mechanism is adapted to the RealtimeBench setting, and Table 11 lists the corresponding search configurations and stopping conditions. All methods use repeated task-level rollouts on the same ten feedback tasks as their interaction unit.

    Episode budgets count student executions of feedback tasks, including repeated executions of the same task; validation and test evaluations are accounted for separately.

    B.2 Response Latency

    Model execution.

    Our local inference hardware consists of NVIDIA L20Y GPUs. All local models run on a single GPU without tensor or pipeline parallelism, e.g., GLiClass (0.4B), Open-Jev-2B (2B), JevK5 (4B), Clef-flash (9B), Clef (27B), and StartLux (4B and 27B). Local inference incurs no API fees; its compute cost is the wall-clock response time reported in Table 13, and no additional compute budget was imposed on local runs. Among the API-based models, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash is queried with thinking mode disabled to reduce response latency, and MiMo v2.6 Ultra Speed exposes no thinking interface, so it is called through the official API with the provider’s default decoding settings.

    Decision models have median response times below two seconds in every game type. In Snake, all of them except StartLux 27B (0.86 s) stay below the 667 ms tick. MiMo has a low median but a long tail, reaching 13.64 s at P95 in Mario. GPT-6.1-sol’s game type medians range from 5 to 31 s, during which the live environment continues evolving.

    B.3 Token Usage and Computational Cost

    Table 14 reports token usage and API cost for the recorded task runs. In Table 4, token counts are in millions (with reasoning tokens included in output) and API costs are totals over the full update process. Jev costs are estimated at $0.042/M input tokens, with free output; teacher costs use $2/M input tokens and $10/M output tokens. GPUs were used only to serve open-source models during evaluation, totaling 46.47 GPU-hours.

    B.4 Model Sources

    Official model cards document the evaluated GLiClass checkpoint,111Hugging Face: knowledgator/gliclass-instruct-large-v1.0 JevK5,222Hugging Face: alibiserikbay/JevK5 Open-Jev-2B,333Hugging Face: ZefanCai/Open-Jev-2B mini-Jev,444Hugging Face: samatv256/mini-Jev and StartLux 27B.555Hugging Face: startlux-models/StartLux-Decision-27B Official API documentation lists MiMo v2.6 Ultra Speed666mimo.mi.com/docs/en-US/api/chat/openai-api and DeepSeek v4.1 Flash.777api-docs.deepseek.com/quick_start/pricing/

    Appendix C Software Sources

    Mario emulator stack. Mario uses Christian Kauten’s gym-super-mario-bros (9.1.0)888GitHub: Kautenja/gym-super-mario-bros and nes-py (9.0.1),999GitHub: Kautenja/nes-py with an emulator core derived from Amish Kumar Naidu and contributors’ SimpleNES.101010GitHub: amhndu/SimpleNES

    Rendering frameworks. Temple uses Three.js (0.180.0, r180).111111GitHub: mrdoob/three.js River and Bird use Pygame-based implementations, with sources maintained by the Pygame121212GitHub: pygame/pygame and Pygame Community Edition131313GitHub: pygame-community/pygame-ce contributor communities.

    Game implementations. The original Super Mario Bros. game is by Nintendo.141414Nintendo: Super Mario Bros. Snake adapts iammusham’s jev-snake (revision a935107),151515GitHub: iammusham/jev-snake and Tetris adapts trungdq88’s jev-tetris (a0b411c).161616GitHub: trungdq88/jev-tetris Temple adapts Mukhsin Mukhtorov’s Night Relay (1e53984).171717GitHub: Mukhsin0508/night-relay River uses Ashkan Aazami’s river-run-typesafe (8cf0429),181818GitHub: ashaazami/river-run-typesafe and Bird uses leftspace89’s JevBird (1e5fd13).191919GitHub: leftspace89/JevBird

item.title: Interaction-as-a-Judge：判断一个游戏做没做好，让会用电脑的 agent 真的去玩一遍 ｜ Interaction-as-a-Judge
item.description:
一句话：只看代码与单测会漏掉人一眼就看出的问题；让 computer-use agent 直接操作应用，偏好预测 65.6%→69.1%。

要点：

  • 评测范式改为让 computer-use agent 直接与应用交互，而不是静态分析代码或跑单测
  • 发布两份数据集：6858 对「应用 + 人类偏好 + 对应 agent 轨迹」，以及 222 个带人工核验需求标注的应用
