  • 预测人类偏好从 65.6% 升到 69.1%，需求核验从 77.0% 升到 81.6%，且随交互预算增加有 scaling 收益

为什么值得看：对「agent 做出来的游戏/工具」来说，可交互性是唯一真正的验收标准。这套方法把评测从「读代码」推到「动手玩」，也顺带能用来改进生成。

中文摘要：编码智能体现在要产出复杂的交互式应用，比如网站、桌面程序和游戏。人类是交互式地评估这些应用的，而当前自动化的 LLM 评测主要看代码分析与单元测试，这种错配会让 LLM 评委漏掉用户一眼就能看出的失败。本文研究「交互即裁判」：让 computer-use agent 直接与应用交互来评测。作者发布了两份互补数据集——6858 对应用与人类偏好及对应 agent 轨迹，以及 222 个经人工核验需求标注的应用。相对非交互方式，该方法在预测人类偏好上从 65.6% 提升到 69.1%，在需求核验上从 77.0% 提升到 81.6%，并观察到随交互规模增长的收益。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·智能体+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-13

本期推送：2026-10-24

Interaction-as-a-Judge

Abstract

Coding agents are tasked with producing sophisticated interactive applications such as websites, desktop applications, and games. While humans assess these applications interactively, current automated LLM evaluations primarily focus on code analysis and unit tests. This mismatch can cause LLM judges to miss failures that are immediately apparent to human users. We study Interaction-as-a-Judge, an evaluation paradigm where computer-use agents (CUAs) directly interact with an application. We demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can improve both evaluation and generation of interactive applications. To this end, we collect and release two complementary datasets: 6,858 pairs of applications with human preferences and corresponding agent traces, and 222 applications with human-verified requirement labels. Relative to standard non-interactive approaches, we find that Interaction-as-a-Judge improves evaluation in terms of predicting human preferences (65.6%→69.1%) and requirement verification (77.0%→81.6%). We also observe scaling benefits: across both preference alignment and requirement verification, higher-quality interactions improve performance. Finally, through both inference- and training-time experiments, we demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can also improve the quality of generated artifacts. At inference time, Interaction-as-a-Judge repairs 75.5% of broken requirements within five attempts, compared to 55.4% for code-only self-feedback. At training time, using Interaction-as-a-Judge as a reward signal improves win-rate over the base model by 6.7pp while reducing both generated code length by 35.7% and build failure rates by 7.2pp compared to a code-only reward signal.

1Carnegie Mellon University2Arena3University of California, Berkeley4University of California, Los Angeles

1.  Introduction

As coding agents improve, so does the complexity of the software artifacts they produce and, in turn, the difficulty of evaluating those artifacts. Correctness and preference are often difficult to assess from code alone. For example, a game may compile while still failing behaviorally: player animations may not match movement, scene transitions may freeze the application, or interactions may lack the visual and temporal feedback needed to feel responsive and intentional. A natural method for evaluation—and the way most humans evaluate software—is simply to interact with and visually inspect the final product. Yet most current LLM-as-a-Judge [(Zheng et al., 2023; Chiang et al., 2024)] and Agent-as-a-Judge [(Zhuge et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025)] methods still rely on static or unimodal inspection of software artifacts. Properly evaluating such artifacts requires moving beyond static inspection to active interaction.

In this work, we study the use of interaction traces to improve evaluation accuracy and in turn improve generation quality. Concretely, a computer-use agent (CUA) interacts with an application and produces a multimodal interaction trace which can be used to evaluate the quality of the application, or optionally, provide feedback for improving it. We call this evaluation paradigm “Interaction-as-a-Judge”, by analogy with LLM-as-a-Judge [(Zheng et al., 2023)]. While some prior work has explored this paradigm in different application settings [(Bian et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026)], we are the first to systematically study it in a controlled fashion. Specifically, we investigate how dimensions such as interaction strategy and agent capability affect evaluation accuracy for both pairwise human preference prediction and correctness verification. We further show that these evaluation signals can improve generation using simple and standard methods at both inference and training time, namely inference-time scaling and reinforcement learning with a learned reward model.

To study Interaction-as-a-Judge, we introduce two datasets: ArenaPreferences and ArenaCorrectness. ArenaPreferences is a set of 6,858 agentic code traces across seven different categories of web development (games, simulations, reference-based designs, content-creation tools, brand sites, consumer apps, and data applications). Alongside the agent traces, each data point contains a prompt, two websites generated from the prompt, and labeled human preferences. ArenaCorrectness is a set of 67 high-quality game development traces with 828 conversation turns. We hand-label 412 requirements across various versions of each game as the game develops by interpreting requirements from a user’s prompt and feedback. Requirements are then hand-verified as working or broken depending on if the requirement is successfully implemented.

We find that Interaction-as-a-Judge increases alignment with human preferences for both in-context LLM judges and trained reward models. On ArenaPreferences, adding interaction traces on top of code significantly improves overall in-context LLM judge accuracy by up to 3.5 percentage points (65.6% to 69.1%) and by 1.5 percentage points (67.6% to 69.1%) when compared to adding only static visual information. Fine-tuning a reward model with interaction traces improves accuracy from 68.2% to 70.2% and outperforms in-context LLM judges. We find that higher quality computer-use results in the best overall performance, although even a random heuristic can capture non-trivial gains. On ArenaCorrectness, Interaction-as-a-Judge improves requirement verification accuracy from 77.0% for a code-only Agent-as-a-Judge [(Zhuge et al., 2024)] to 81.6%. Interaction-as-a-Judge also scales with model capability: accuracy increases from 76.4% with GPT 5.6 Luna to 81.6% with GPT 5.6 Sol when each serves as both the CUA and the judge.

We show that these evaluation gains also improve generation. At inference-time, we use Interaction-as-a-Judge in a self-feedback loop where an agent iteratively attempts to repair broken requirements and evaluates its repairs using Interaction-as-a-Judge. Compared with code-only feedback, adding interaction to the feedback mechanism increases the percentage of initially broken requirements successfully repaired within five attempts from 55.4% to 75.5%. We also use a reward model trained solely on interaction traces, without code, to post-train a generation model through reinforcement learning. Relative to using a code-only reward model, this method reduces the build failure rate by 7.2 percentage points and reduces code-context growth—a known problem in code reward models [(Wang et al., 2026)]—by 35.7%, while achieving comparable generation quality. Additionally, we show that websites generated by this post-training recipe attain a 6.7pp higher win rate against the base model.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We study Interaction-as-a-Judge for both preference judgements and correctness verification and release two datasets—ArenaPreferences and ArenaCorrectness—for further research into both Interaction-as-a-Judge and agentic generation of interactive applications more broadly.

  • •

    We show that Interaction-as-a-Judge improves evaluation capabilities. Interaction-as-a-Judge improves overall alignment with human preferences for both in-context LLM judges and trained reward models. Additionally, Interaction-as-a-Judge improves an agent’s ability to verify requirements when compared to a code-only agentic judge.

  • •

    We demonstrate how Interaction-as-a-Judge can be used to improve generation through both inference-time scaling and reinforcement learning training. Interaction-as-a-Judge improves the number of successful repairs in an iterative self-feedback loop and improves trained model quality when used as a reward signal.

    • 2.  Tasks and Datasets

    We study Interaction-as-a-Judge under two complementary settings: human preferences and correctness verification. Human preferences are useful when quality is subjective or difficult to capture with explicit requirements, while correctness verification is appropriate when desired behavior can be specified objectively. In many applications, both are necessary. For example, a software application may satisfy its functional requirements while still differing substantially in usability or visual quality. The inverse can also be true, where an application is visually preferable, but functionally broken. Effective evaluation methods should therefore be able to assess both correctness and preference.

    2.1.  Preferences

    For pairwise preferences, a judge is given a shared prompt and two candidate outputs and must predict which output would be preferred by a human user [(Zheng et al., 2023)]. We focus on pairwise comparisons in this work rather than other preference tasks such as single answer grading (e.g., predicting a Likert scale score), but our approach is not restricted to pairwise comparisons.

    ArenaPreferences.

    We release ArenaPreferences, a dataset of 6,858 pairwise comparisons across seven categories of web development. We collect our dataset from Arena’s Code Arena where real users prompt two hidden models and vote for their preferred website. Each datapoint in ArenaPreferences contains the user’s prompt, both agentic traces, both final websites, and the ground truth user label. We categorize websites into games, simulations, reference-based designs, content-creation tools, brand sites, consumer product, and data applications following the original leaderboard categories. To ensure that the dataset is high quality, we filter such that all ties are removed, websites are built with React, outputs build successfully, outputs contain ≥5% character difference, and users spent at least 60 seconds and up to 10 minutes interacting with the websites. All personally identifiable information (PII) has been de-identified through a PII filtering process. To our understanding, this is the largest collection of pairwise agentic web development traces and websites released for open source use. We provide further dataset details in Appendix B.

    2.2.  Correctness

    We consider two types of correctness verification: requirement verification and requirement discovery. In requirement verification, the judge is given an application, its code, and a set of explicit requirements, such as “Mario must defeat a Goomba when jumping on it.” The judge must determine whether each requirement is working or broken for that application. In requirement discovery, the judge is given the application and its code but no explicit list of requirements. It must first identify the relevant requirements automatically and then determine whether those requirements are working.

    ArenaCorrectness.

    We create ArenaCorrectness, a dataset containing 67 game development traces with 828 user turns and labeled with 412 requirements across 222 versions of various games. We collect our dataset from Arena’s Agent Mode where users can request a random agent to do tasks such as web search, software development, or image generation. We focus on game development as games are highly interactive and also challenging software development tasks [(Chi et al., 2026)].

    To generate requirements from user traces, we analyze the user trace for specific complaints, and extract the complaint into a broken requirement which is linked to a specific version of the game matching when the user complaint occurred. For example, a user complaint indicating that the player falls through platforms would be annotated as a requirement indicating that the player must be able to stand on platforms. We use GPT 5.6 Luna to label, analyze, and then annotate each complaint as a requirement. A human annotator then reviews each game to verify that the requirements are sensible and broken in the game version. To extract working requirement labels, we take our existing broken requirements, and check to see if the user either explicitly confirms a fix or does not revisit this complaint. We use GPT 5.6 Luna for initial annotation and verify via human annotation. In total, we annotate 323 broken and 89 working requirements. We provide further dataset details in Appendix B.

    3.  Interaction-as-a-Judge

    Interaction-as-a-Judge is an evaluation paradigm which uses computer-use interaction traces to improve downstream evaluation accuracy. Interaction-as-a-Judge consists of an interaction component and a judge component. These two components can be either the same LLM, different LLMs, or a mixture of LLMs and other methods. For example, a cheap computer-use heuristic paired with an LLM judge, or an LLM-based CUA paired with a trained reward model.

    3.1.  Interaction

    Following [Koh et al. (2024)], we model interaction with the environment as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). We define the environment as 𝔼=(S,A,Ω,f) where S is the state space, A is the action space, and Ω is the observation space. In our work, oₜ∈Ω is a visual representation of the application (a screenshot), but the Document Object Model (DOM) is also commonly used. An action aₜ∈A induces a deterministic transition f:S×A→S. To interact with the environment, we define an interaction policy π that determines the sequence of actions taken in the environment. Executing π in the environment produces an interaction trace τ=((oₜ,ρₜ,aₜ))ₜ₌₀ᵀ, where oₜ, ρₜ, and aₜ denote the observation, agent reasoning, and action at timestep t, respectively. We allow ρₜ=∅ when no explicit reasoning is produced. Actions include standard computer inputs such as moving the mouse, clicking, and typing—the full action space is in Appendix A.2.

    There are multiple approaches to interact with a software application environment, with the primary trade-off being between adaptivity and inference cost. We consider three interaction strategies that vary in how frequently they query a model and observe the resulting environment state.

    Iterative computer-use.

    The most general approach is to use a computer-use agent that iteratively observes and acts in the environment. We represent the agent as a policy π_θⁱᵗᵉʳ, where at timestep t it selects an action (aₜ,ρₜ)∼π_θⁱᵗᵉʳ(τ_

    One-shot computer-use.

    A sufficiently capable agent could in principle predict the sequence of actions to take from only the initial state without observing the intermediate outcomes of its actions. We represent this as a policy π_θᵒⁿᵉ that, given the initial observation o₀, reasons and then predicts an entire action sequence (a_0:T,ρ)=π_θᵒⁿᵉ(o₀,i) to be executed sequentially in the environment up to timestep T. This requires only a single model query, substantially reducing inference cost [(Wang et al., 2026)], but prevents the agent from adapting when the environment evolves differently from its prediction. When application code c is available, we additionally provide it to the agent for planning, giving (a_0:T,ρ)=π_θᵒⁿᵉ(o₀,i,c).

    Heuristic computer-use.

    The cheapest alternative is to forgo model-based action selection entirely. In this work, we consider a simple heuristic policy πʰᵉᵘʳ that selects an action uniformly at random. To make this interaction more effective, we restrict the policy to a candidate set ℂ(oₜ)⊆A of interactions that are likely to induce meaningful changes in the environment, such as clicking buttons or typing in text boxes, giving aₜ∼πʰᵉᵘʳ(oₜ)=Unif(ℂ(oₜ)). Because this incurs no model inference cost, the policy can select an action after every environment transition. Despite its simplicity, this can produce substantial interaction when ℂ(oₜ) can be effectively identified, but is less effective for environments such as games, where meaningful interactions are difficult to enumerate automatically.

    3.2.  Judging

    After the interaction trace τ is generated, the judge uses the trace to inform its downstream judgement. We study both an off-the-shelf LLM, which we use for both predicting human preferences and verifying correctness, and a trained reward model, which we use for predicting human preferences. A key benefit of using off-the-shelf LLMs is that it allows interaction-as-a-judge to leverage frontier capabilities without needing to train a custom model, which is often infeasible without data and compute resources. However, a reward model trained on sufficient in-domain data can achieve higher accuracy and reduce inference costs.

    LLM Judge.

    For human preferences, an off-the-shelf LLM judge takes in the user request, source code for each website, and an interaction trace for each website and outputs a judgement indicating which website is better. Due to known position bias [(Zheng et al., 2023)], every battle is judged twice with sides swapped (AB and BA) and accuracy is the mean judge-human agreement of both passes. For requirement verification, the judge takes in the user request, the source code, the interaction trace, and a requirements list and labels each requirement as working, broken, or unverifiable. Requirement discovery is similar except no requirement list is given and the judge must output a list of potential requirements itself. For judges that accept video natively, we convert o_0:T∈τ to video; otherwise, we pass in each frame as an image. Actions and reasoning are passed in directly as text sequences.

    Reward Model.

    We train our reward model r_θ by adding a scalar reward head and optimizing over a standard Bradley–Terry loss [(Bradley and Terry, 1952)]:

    L_BT(θ)=-𝔼_(x,y_w,yₗ,τ_w,τₗ)∼D[\logσ (r_θ(x,y_w,τ_w)-r_θ(x,yₗ,τₗ))]

    where x is the user prompt, y_w and yₗ are the source code for the winner and loser respectively, and τ_w and τₗ are the traces. This is similar to standard reward model training [(Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022)] with the addition of interaction trace information.

    4. Interaction-as-a-Judge for Evaluation

    We measure the extent to which evaluation via Interaction-as-a-Judge aligns with human preferences and verified correctness. In our main experiments, all interaction traces consist of 30 actions. For iterative and one-shot computer-use, we use GPT 5.6 Luna with medium reasoning as our computer-use agent. Unless specified, Interaction-as-a-Judge includes code as input. Games differ from other categories due to their real-time input and difficulty in identifying meaningful candidate interactions (e.g., lack of buttons). We describe our harness, action space, and changes for games in Appendix A.

    4.1.  Human Preferences

    We evaluate the effectiveness of Interaction-as-a-Judge for judging human preferences using ArenaPreferences (Figure 3). We compare Interaction-as-a-Judge against two static-evidence judges: a code-only judge and a code and screenshot judge. The code-only judge receives only the code as input, making it functionally identical to either LLM-as-a-Judge [(Zheng et al., 2023)] or a standard code reward model. The code and screenshot judge receives the code and a full page screenshot of the landing page. This same screenshot is also given as input to Interaction-as-a-Judge approaches. We also vary the amount of code received between the full code capped at 32k tokens and just the core App.tsx file to study the effects of code on Interaction-as-a-Judge. Additional information such as category breakdowns can be found in Appendix B.

    To train our reward model, we fine-tune Qwen-3.5-9B [(Qwen Team, 2026)] as our base model and train on a private dataset of 20,160 human preference pairs. This dataset is structurally identical to ArenaPreferences, but is temporally disjoint consisting of data prior to ArenaPreferences, mirroring how data collection occurs in real settings. This means that the reward model is evaluated on newer, more advanced outputs not seen in the training data. For the visual component of the interaction trace, we input it directly as video and freeze the video encoder weights during training.

    For our LLM judge, we use Gemini 3 Flash and GPT 5.6 Luna with xhigh reasoning. Both were chosen due to their cost-effectiveness with Gemini 3 Flash being chosen due to its native video capabilities and GPT 5.6 Luna being the main computer-use model used throughout the paper. To account for ordering bias in LLM-as-a-Judge approaches, we evaluate both orderings and take the average of the results.

    Interaction-as-a-Judge increases alignment with human preferences. We find that for both a trained reward model and an LLM Judge, adding interaction improves judge alignment with human preferences (Figure 3). Adding visual information through a screenshot improves performance over code and adding interaction improves performance further. We see the largest gap in Gemini 3 Flash as a judge where accuracy improves from 65.6%→69.1% between code only and iterative Interaction-as-a-Judge. GPT 5.6 Luna as a judge is the sole exception where we do not see any statistical differences between any approach. We speculate that for pairwise preferences, GPT 5.6 Luna is both optimized for code and also unable to properly utilize visual information given its strong code-only performance and degradation when adding even a single screenshot. Finally, our trained reward model (70.8%) is able to outperform an off-the-shelf LLM judge (69.1%).

    Interaction alone is sufficient information for training a reward model. We find that training a reward model on the interaction traces alone (without code) provides comparable performance to a code reward model. Iterative computer-use without code performs only slightly worse than a code reward model trained on the entire code context (69.0% vs 69.7%), and performs comparably to Interaction-as-a-Judge with code when using Gemini 3 Flash as a judge. This opens doors to training reward models on data where the application is accessible, but code is inaccessible. In general, Interaction-as-a-Judge judgements remain robust as code context decreases, seeing small decreases between seeing the full source code versus only the core App.tsx file. However, both one-shot and heuristic computer-use degrade more compared to iterative computer-use when no code is available.

    Interaction quality affects alignment with human preferences. We observe that iterative computer-use consistently performs the best across all experiments. Due to its ability to respond to new state changes in the environment, iterative computer-use generates the highest-quality traces among the three approaches. Additionally, we find that higher-quality interaction at inference can compensate for lower-quality traces at training time. We take our reward model trained on heuristic computer-use and run inference using iterative computer-use instead. We find that performance increases across almost every single category (Appendix F, Figure 12). The inverse is not true—a reward model trained on iterative computer-use degrades when using heuristic computer-use traces at inference time.

    4.2.  Correctness Verification

    We evaluate Interaction-as-a-Judge on its ability to both verify and discover requirements using our ArenaCorrectness dataset (Figure 4). For requirement verification, we give the agent the code, the game as an interactable application, and the list of requirements which can be either all broken or all working. The agent is asked to label each requirement as working, broken, or unverifiable. For requirement discovery, we focus only on broken requirements and ask the agent to list out all possible broken requirements that require repair without passing in the original requirements list. We compare Interaction-as-a-Judge against a code only Agent-as-a-Judge [(Zhuge et al., 2024)]. We use the GPT 5.6 model family (Luna, Terra, Sol) all with medium reasoning to measure varying model capabilities.

    Interaction-as-a-Judge outperforms code only requirement verification. We find that across all models, Interaction-as-a-Judge performs better than a code only Agent-as-a-Judge. This is primarily because Interaction-as-a-Judge is significantly better at verifying broken requirements (71.1%) compared to a code only Agent-as-a-Judge (63.0%). We find that both approaches perform comparably for verifying working requirements at 92.1% and 91.0% for Interaction-as-a-Judge and code-only Agent-as-a-Judge respectively.

    Interaction-as-a-Judge scales with model capability. We see in Figure 4 that broken requirement verification performance continues to improve as the overall capability of the model improves going from 65.2% with GPT 5.6 Luna to 68.0% with GPT 5.6 Terra and 71.1% with GPT 5.6 Sol.

    5. Interaction-as-a-Judge for Generation

    5.1.  Inference-time Scaling

    We evaluate whether interaction-based self-feedback improves an agent’s ability to repair broken requirements (Figure 5). An effective inference time strategy is to iteratively repair and verify the resulting application. Regardless of implementation capabilities, self-verification capability becomes important for determining whether the repairs are correct or incorrect. We use the games with broken requirements in ArenaCorrectness as our task list. We ask the agent to repair the broken requirements for each game and self-verify across five iterations. We compare Interaction-as-a-Judge against a code only Agent-as-a-Judge and use GPT 5.6 Luna with medium reasoning as the agent for both approaches. After all iterations are complete, we use a more capable model (GPT 5.6 Sol) with Interaction-as-a-Judge and code-only Agent-as-a-Judge to determine if the repairs were successful or not. We measure success per requirement and report repair success rate after each iteration.

    Interaction-as-a-Judge repairs more broken requirements than a code only Agent-as-a-Judge.

    After five iterations, Interaction-as-a-Judge successfully repairs 75.5% of initially broken requirements, compared to 55.4% for code-only self-feedback, an improvement of 20.1 percentage points (Figure 5, middle). This improvement persists even when using GPT 5.6 Sol as a code-only Agent-as-a-Judge (Figure 5, left), highlighting the improvements Interaction-as-a-Judge provides. We see in Figure 5 that Interaction-as-a-Judge not only improves faster but also outperforms the code-only judge within its first iteration. Additionally, the self-reported accuracy gap between GPT 5.6 Luna and GPT 5.6 Sol is significantly less for Interaction-as-a-Judge compared to a code only Agent-as-a-Judge (Figure 5, right), suggesting a lower false positive rate when using Interaction-as-a-Judge.

    5.2.  Training

    We study the potential of Interaction-as-a-Judge at training time to improve downstream performance in generating interactive applications. Specifically, we explore using an interaction-only reward model as the reward signal for post-training via reinforcement learning (Figure 6). We start our training from Qwen-3.5-9B and use DAPO [(Yu et al., 2025)] as our learning algorithm. We use the same interaction only reward model we trained in Section 4.1 and compare against a code only reward model. We use heuristic computer-use to reduce costs and training time. We train on a set of 14k internal prompts that are not used for reward model training which cover all categories except for games as heuristic computer-use has difficulty playing games. We sample 600 examples uniformly from the six categories in ArenaPreferences as our test set. Since our reward model training data is cleaned to remove any failures, failures are out of distribution for both models. To account for this, we add penalties for any website that fails to build or render at all. Detailed hyperparameters can be found in Appendix G.

    Interaction-as-a-Judge allows for successful reinforcement learning training without code.

    Overall, we observe that each model scores higher on their respective reward models, but interaction improves neutral objectives by reducing code generated and increasing successful builds. Code only reward models are known to have length bias [(Wang et al., 2026)]—we observe that training on the interaction reward model generates 35.7% less code than the code reward model. On our test set, Interaction-as-a-Judge also increases the build success rate from 81.3% to 88.5% compared to a code only reward model, reducing the build failure rate by 7.2 percentage points (18.7%→11.5%). We use an internal auto-rubrics based judge based on [Kao et al. (2026)] calibrated to Arena’s data and leaderboard to compare each trained model against Qwen-3.5-9B. Among websites that build and render successfully, the model trained using Interaction-as-a-Judge achieves a win-rate gain of 6.72pp over the base model (Figure 6). Based on our internal calibrations, this is equivalent to over a 50 point increase on Arena’s leaderboard, which would be a statistically significant improvement to the model in Arena’s leaderboard. This evaluation measures quality conditioned on successful generations and therefore understates the benefit of using Interaction-as-a-Judge as a reward signal. The ability to train a model via reinforcement learning with an interaction only reward model opens the door to data collection opportunities where application access is available, but code access is not.

    6.  Related Work

    The two most related families of work are other LLM-based judging strategies and existing instances where CUAs have been used for evaluation or generation. Unlike prior work, our work differs from the latter in that interaction is the central focus of our study, rather than one component of a larger pipeline. Specifically, we conduct the first systematic study spanning (i) the effects of varying interaction strategies and model capabilities on evaluation performance, (ii) measuring Interaction-as-a-Judge’s alignment with human preferences and correctness, and (iii) its use for both inference-time scaling and post-training. Below, we outline the connections more specifically.

    LLM-as-a-Judge and Agent-as-a-Judge.

    LLM-as-a-Judge uses language models to approximate human judgments of generated outputs [(Zheng et al., 2023)]. For software development, the evidence needed to judge requirement satisfaction can be distributed across a project and its development history. Agent-as-a-Judge [(Zhuge et al., 2024)] addresses this by gathering and inspecting project files and development trajectories before judging. Interactive applications introduce a further source of evidence: the behavior observed when a user operates the software. Computer-use agents provide a means to collect this evidence by interacting with desktop and web interfaces [(Xie et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Koh et al., 2024)]. Interaction-as-a-Judge extends these judging paradigms to this new source of evidence: rather than inspecting only static artifacts, the judge conditions on traces produced by a computer-use agent operating the application.

    Interactive evaluation.

    Recent works have attempted to use computer-use as part of their evaluation pipeline. ArtifactsBench [(Zhang et al., 2025)] and GameCraft-Bench [(Luo et al., 2026)] ground judgments in heuristically generated screenshots and replayed gameplay, respectively. AppEvalPilot [(Bian et al., 2025)] generates and executes test cases using a computer-use agent and validates its judgments against human assessments of functional requirements. In these works, interaction is used as a method of evaluation rather than the focus of study, and it remains unclear how computer-use model capabilities and methods of interaction affect evaluation performance. WebDevJudge [(Li et al., 2025)], which benchmarks LLM and multimodal judges for web development, illustrates the importance of understanding these capabilities as it finds that its standalone GUI-agent workflow actually underperforms its strongest static judges due to errors arising during planning and execution.

    Interaction feedback and reward learning.

    Interaction evidence can also guide the generation process that produces an application. WebGen-Agent [(Lu et al., 2025)] incorporates screenshot feedback and iterative computer-use testing into website refinement. For reinforcement learning, it sums screenshot-based appearance scores and GUI-testing scores, and introduces Step-GRPO to assign advantages separately to each refinement step. [Wang et al. (2026)] use one-shot computer-use: a model plans the full action sequence upfront, and a rubric-based judge scores the recorded execution to provide training rewards, reducing code-length exploitation compared to static judges. Both approaches obtain their reward signals from model-generated assessments of appearance or functionality. We provide an alternative and potentially simpler solution by training a reward model on human preferences [(Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022)] using interaction traces and then using its predictions as outcome rewards in DAPO.

    7.  Conclusion

    Limitations and Future Work.

    While we study some common approaches to computer-use, we believe that better computer-use models and methods could further improve evaluation and generation, especially considering our observation that better computer-use traces lead to better performance. Currently, one of the biggest bottlenecks to computer-use remains cost. For example, we were mostly limited to experiments with GPT 5.6 Luna as our computer use agent due to pricing. More capable and affordable computer-use agents will likely improve Interaction-as-a-Judge capabilities and are worth studying as well. For training, there is the possibility of using the same model for both generation and computer-use and improving them both simultaneously as better applications and better traces both improve reward modeling scores. We leave this as potential future work.

    Conclusion

    We study Interaction-as-a-Judge, an evaluation paradigm that uses computer-use traces to improve evaluation and downstream generation. We study the use of Interaction-as-a-Judge for both human preferences and correctness verification, releasing two datasets—ArenaPreferences and ArenaCorrectness—to facilitate such studies. We demonstrate how Interaction-as-a-Judge improves alignment with human preferences for both reward model training and LLM judges and improves a model’s ability to label requirements as working or broken. We show how Interaction-as-a-Judge can be used for inference-time scaling through an iterative self-feedback loop. Lastly, we illustrate how you can use a reward model trained on only interaction traces, with no code, as the reward signal for standard reinforcement learning training.

    Acknowledgements

    We thank Yewon Kim for help with designing Figure 1 and Seth Karten for initial discussions that led to this work. This work was supported in part by the National Science Foundation grants IIS1705121, IIS1838017, IIS2046613, IIS2112471, and funding from Datadog. This material is based upon work supported by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research under award number FA9550-25-C-B010 in the amount of $129,600. Any opinions, findings and conclusions or recommendations expressed in this material are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily reflect the views of any of these funding agencies.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix

    Appendix A Interaction Harness and Action Space

    A.1.  Browser Environment and Observations

    For preference prediction, we render each candidate in a separate Chromium browser context using Playwright. Applications run inside an iframe with a 1280×800 viewport and device scale factor one. Mouse coordinates are measured in pixels relative to the top-left corner of the application iframe. Each tool response contains a screenshot of the application, the viewport dimensions, cursor position, held keys, and execution status. The interactive agent receives the original user request and these observations. The one-shot agent additionally receives application source code when constructing its action sequence. For pairwise preferences, the agents explore each candidate independently and then the preference judge subsequently compares the resulting evidence for both candidates. For correctness verification, the same agent explores and judges the candidate in one continuous workflow.

    Interaction budget and timing.

    The main preference experiments use a budget of 30 interaction steps per candidate. A step is one tool invocation, which can itself contain several low-level input events: for example, a click includes a mouse press and release, while press_keys executes a sequence of key presses. The full action space is defined in Table 1. The budget does not count individual keystrokes or model reasoning tokens. The computer-use agent is allowed to exit early if it determines that its goal is complete.

    For games, a JavaScript timing shim wraps animation frames, timers, and application clocks. The game is paused between actions, and ordinary actions advance its clock by 500 ms. Key holds and waits advance the requested duration, capped by the per-step budget. This separates model inference latency from simulated game time. The timing shim advances in small increments so that animation callbacks can execute between inputs. Other web applications run in real time and are allowed to settle after an action.

    A.2.  Action Space

    Table 1 gives the interaction tools shared by iterative and one-shot preference agents. The iterative agent selects tools after observing their results. The one-shot agent emits a list of the same tool names and arguments, which the harness executes sequentially without intermediate model feedback. Typing and scrolling use keyboard events; they do not require separate text-entry or scroll tools.

    Coordinates, interpolation counts, and durations are integer arguments. Key names follow Playwright conventions, including ArrowLeft, Space, Enter, and letter keys.

    A.3.  Heuristic Interaction

    For non-gaming applications, the heuristic enumerates visible, enabled controls in the current viewport: links, buttons, input fields, text areas, selects, summaries, elements with relevant accessibility roles, click handlers, or a non-negative tab index. It excludes hidden and off-screen controls, deduplicates controls by their center coordinates, and retains at most 200 candidates. Candidate controls are sampled uniformly. A text field is clicked before entering a phrase drawn from a fixed small vocabulary, and a PageDown action is sampled with probability 0.12 to reveal additional content. If no candidates are found, the policy falls back to pixel and keyboard actions.

    A.4.  Games

    Games differ from other categories in two ways. First, games often require real-time input, so we construct a web harness that freezes games between interactions and plays actions out for up to 500 milliseconds (i.e., 2 actions per second). Second, since games typically do not have clear interaction candidates (e.g., buttons), heuristic computer-use actions are drawn uniformly from a 12-element action space consisting of four click actions, three key-sequence actions, two key-hold actions, and one each of mouse movement, drag, and double click. Coordinates are sampled uniformly within the viewport. Keyboard actions are sampled from the four arrow keys, Space, Enter, and w, a, s, and d.

    Appendix B Dataset Details and Evaluation Protocol

    The 6,858-battles in ArenaPreferences are selected from a time period of one month (July 2026). They exclude unknown countries and the fixed set of EU27 countries, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, and Liechtenstein. Both candidate source records must declare the react-vite-tailwind template and a successful upstream build. Both sides must contain more than 5% character difference.

    ArenaPreferences contains 6,858 battles across seven categories: 1,288 games, 904 simulations, 753 reference-based designs, 1,020 content-creation tools, 1,246 brand sites, 949 data applications, and 698 consumer applications. The reward-model training and validation ID lists contain 20,160 and 4,460 battles, respectively. The training pool precedes the evaluation pool in time.

    The traces in ArenaCorrectness were collected between June 5 and June 26, 2026. Of its 412 requirements, 323 are labeled broken and 89 working. Each of the 222 game versions corresponds to the application state after a specific user turn of its source trace, and repaired variants of a version are included for requirements that users later confirmed fixed.

    Table 2 reports summary statistics for both datasets. Lines of code exclude lockfiles. Interaction time before voting is measured from the final assistant message to the submitted preference. Trace duration measures wall-clock time from the first to the last message of a trace and includes idle time between user turns.

    Appendix C Category Level Results

    Figures 7 and 8 expand the LLM-judge comparison. Figures 9 and 10 give the corresponding reward-model results under the two code representations. All bars measure agreement with the original human preferences. The overall panels weight categories by their number of battles rather than assigning each category equal weight. The heuristic, one-shot, and iterative conditions add interaction traces to code and screenshot inputs. Bold values indicate positive paired gains over code+screenshot with p<0.05, calculated using a two-sided paired test. Across 28 category comparisons, iterative interaction significantly outperformed code+screenshot in 14, significantly underperformed in one, and showed no statistically significant difference in 13. Across the four approaches, simulations and games show the largest average accuracy gains from iterative interaction over code+screenshot (+2.81 and +1.74 percentage points, respectively). They also show the most consistent statistically significant improvements, with gains significant in four of four approaches for simulations and three of four for games.

    Appendix D Reward-Model Training

    We fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B with a scalar reward head evaluated at a trailing classification token. The language backbone and reward head are trained while the vision encoder is frozen.

    Code representations.

    The full-code comparison allows 100,000 source characters before applying the 32,768-token sequence limit. Its source pipeline removes lockfiles, selects files under the character budget, and orders the selected files from smaller to larger with the main application file placed last. This ordering is specified independently of the test outcomes. The App.tsx comparison restricts the source store to the main application file, with a largest-code-file fallback when that file is unavailable.

    Visual processing.

    Video frames are processed jointly through the native video path with temporal merging and timestamps. In the combined condition, the separate static screenshot precedes the video and trace text. The loader preserves complete visual token blocks when applying the context limit, so source-code availability can decrease as visual evidence occupies more of the sequence. Due to this, code+screenshot+video reaches the token context limit more frequently than code only.

    Appendix E Additional Reward Modeling Experiments

    We report additional reward model training experiments that vary reward-model size, source-code availability, the text accompanying an interaction trace, and the generators represented in training. These experiments use a separate data construction and training recipe. Interaction traces are generated using GPT 5.4 Mini rather than GPT 5.6 Luna. We distinguish them from the main test results throughout.

    E.1.  Shared Setup and Evaluation Populations

    The model-size, source-restriction, and trace-text studies train on 8,640 battles and evaluate on 3,327-battles. All data points are from the gaming category. All models use one epoch, learning rate 2×10⁻⁶, global batch size 32, a frozen vision encoder, and the pairwise reward objective described in Appendix D.

    We use five seeds for the 4B models (42,77,100,200,777) and ten for the 9B and 27B models (42,77,100,200,300,400,500,600,700,777). Tables report means and sample standard deviations across seeds.

    Interaction-as-a-Judge exceeds the code-only condition at all three sizes, by 1.39, 1.55, and 1.61 percentage points, respectively. The 4B and 9B Interaction-as-a-Judge models have similar mean agreement, while the 27B model is higher. Increasing parameter count therefore does not produce a uniform step-by-step improvement within this data and optimization regime. Interaction-as-a-Judge also exceeds the screenshot condition at each size, although the size of the difference varies.

    E.2.  Actions and Reasoning as Judge Input

    To distinguish visual observations from their accompanying text, we train 9B models with four input representations: code alone; code with actions and intermediate reasoning but no images; code with video frames but no trace text; and code with both video and trace text. The visual conditions share the same frames. The text switch changes both training and evaluation inputs; this is not an inference-only removal of text from a model trained to expect it.

    Adding trace text changes mean agreement by only +0.03 points without video and -0.03 points with video. These results provide little evidence that the recorded actions and reasoning, by themselves, explain the improvement in this campaign. This does not imply that the text itself is uninformative in every setting; in our unofficial observations we have seen reward model scores vary depending on changes to the trace text.

    E.3.  Spatial Resolution

    We evaluate spatial resolution in a separate gaming study using Qwen3.5-9B reward models with no source-code input. Models are trained for one epoch with the same settings as before. We vary the token cap.

    Screenshot agreement remains between 64.85% and 65.27% across the tested caps (Figure 11, left). The Qwen3.5-9B video encoder combines every two frames into one temporal block, so a token cap of 128 per block corresponds to a total visual token cap of 128×13=1,664 for a 26-frame trace. Increasing the video spatial budget from 128 to 960 tokens per block raises mean agreement from 68.25% to 69.29%. The screenshot sweep therefore provides little evidence that more spatial detail alone closes the gap to interaction traces in this setting. The video configurations also retain the corresponding action and reasoning text, so this comparison does not isolate motion from every other component of a trace.

    E.4.  Trace-prefix Length

    We separately train the same reward-model architecture with progressively longer prefixes of each recording. The loader retains the first F images in chronological order and the associated action and reasoning text. At five frames per second, a prefix of F frames nominally spans 0.2(F-1) seconds. The spatial budget is held at 960 tokens per temporal block. All configurations use the same 3,327 evaluation battles and ten training seeds as the spatial-resolution sweep.

    Mean agreement increases from 64.37% with the initial frame to 69.29% with the full 26-frame prefix (Figure 11, right). Much of this improvement is already present after four frames (67.84%), with smaller gains from later observations.

    Appendix F Interaction Policies and Generalization

    F.1.  Cross-policy Evaluation on the Preference Benchmark

    We cross-evaluate reward models trained without source code using recordings from different interaction policies (Table 7). Each row fixes the trained reward model and changes the evaluation evidence. The swap includes both the visual observations and the associated trace text. These are exploratory results for one selected model per training policy, rather than averages over the five seeds used in the main reward-model comparison. This earlier cross-evaluation uses the one-shot recordings generated with xhigh reasoning.

    Holding the heuristic-trained model fixed, iterative traces increase aggregate agreement from 67.95% to 68.85%. Conversely, replacing an iterative-trained model’s iterative traces with heuristic traces reduces agreement from 70.07% to 67.29%. For gaming, iterative evidence improves every row: the respective heuristic-to-iterative changes are 70.81%→73.23%, 68.87%→74.01%, and 70.03%→75.02%.

    F.2.  Transfer between Gaming Recording Pipelines

    We fix each code+interaction reward model from Table 5 and replace its original GPT 5.4 Mini recordings with recordings from Qwen3.5-27B. The two evaluation sets share all 3,327 battle IDs and human labels. This comparison uses five trained 4B models and ten each at 9B and 27B, with the same final checkpoint used for both recording conditions within each seed.

    Replacing the recordings reduces mean agreement by 3.12, 2.73, and 2.73 points for the 4B, 9B, and 27B models, respectively indicating that a weaker computer-use agent is likely to result in a lower quality interaction-trace and, as a result, lower accuracy.

    Appendix G Reinforcement-Learning Configuration and Evaluation

    We present our hyperparemeter used for DAPO training. We follow fairly standard DAPO settings and train for 35 steps which is the equivalent of 1 epoch.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：只看代码与单测会漏掉人一眼就看出的问题；让 computer-use agent 直接操作应用，偏好预测 65.6%→69.1%。

要点：

  • 评测范式改为让 computer-use agent 直接与应用交互，而不是静态分析代码或跑单测
  • 发布两份数据集：6858 对「应用 + 人类偏好 + 对应 agent 轨迹」，以及 222 个带人工核验需求标注的应用
  • 预测人类偏好从 65.6% 升到 69.1%，需求核验从 77.0% 升到 81.6%，且随交互预算增加有 scaling 收益

为什么值得看：对「agent 做出来的游戏/工具」来说，可交互性是唯一真正的验收标准。这套方法把评测从「读代码」推到「动手玩」，也顺带能用来改进生成。

中文摘要：编码智能体现在要产出复杂的交互式应用，比如网站、桌面程序和游戏。人类是交互式地评估这些应用的，而当前自动化的 LLM 评测主要看代码分析与单元测试，这种错配会让 LLM 评委漏掉用户一眼就能看出的失败。本文研究「交互即裁判」：让 computer-use agent 直接与应用交互来评测。作者发布了两份互补数据集——6858 对应用与人类偏好及对应 agent 轨迹，以及 222 个经人工核验需求标注的应用。相对非交互方式，该方法在预测人类偏好上从 65.6% 提升到 69.1%，在需求核验上从 77.0% 提升到 81.6%，并观察到随交互规模增长的收益。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·智能体+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-13

本期推送：2026-10-24

Interaction-as-a-Judge

Abstract

Coding agents are tasked with producing sophisticated interactive applications such as websites, desktop applications, and games. While humans assess these applications interactively, current automated LLM evaluations primarily focus on code analysis and unit tests. This mismatch can cause LLM judges to miss failures that are immediately apparent to human users. We study Interaction-as-a-Judge, an evaluation paradigm where computer-use agents (CUAs) directly interact with an application. We demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can improve both evaluation and generation of interactive applications. To this end, we collect and release two complementary datasets: 6,858 pairs of applications with human preferences and corresponding agent traces, and 222 applications with human-verified requirement labels. Relative to standard non-interactive approaches, we find that Interaction-as-a-Judge improves evaluation in terms of predicting human preferences (65.6%→69.1%) and requirement verification (77.0%→81.6%). We also observe scaling benefits: across both preference alignment and requirement verification, higher-quality interactions improve performance. Finally, through both inference- and training-time experiments, we demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can also improve the quality of generated artifacts. At inference time, Interaction-as-a-Judge repairs 75.5% of broken requirements within five attempts, compared to 55.4% for code-only self-feedback. At training time, using Interaction-as-a-Judge as a reward signal improves win-rate over the base model by 6.7pp while reducing both generated code length by 35.7% and build failure rates by 7.2pp compared to a code-only reward signal.

1Carnegie Mellon University2Arena3University of California, Berkeley4University of California, Los Angeles

1.  Introduction

As coding agents improve, so does the complexity of the software artifacts they produce and, in turn, the difficulty of evaluating those artifacts. Correctness and preference are often difficult to assess from code alone. For example, a game may compile while still failing behaviorally: player animations may not match movement, scene transitions may freeze the application, or interactions may lack the visual and temporal feedback needed to feel responsive and intentional. A natural method for evaluation—and the way most humans evaluate software—is simply to interact with and visually inspect the final product. Yet most current LLM-as-a-Judge [(Zheng et al., 2023; Chiang et al., 2024)] and Agent-as-a-Judge [(Zhuge et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025)] methods still rely on static or unimodal inspection of software artifacts. Properly evaluating such artifacts requires moving beyond static inspection to active interaction.

In this work, we study the use of interaction traces to improve evaluation accuracy and in turn improve generation quality. Concretely, a computer-use agent (CUA) interacts with an application and produces a multimodal interaction trace which can be used to evaluate the quality of the application, or optionally, provide feedback for improving it. We call this evaluation paradigm “Interaction-as-a-Judge”, by analogy with LLM-as-a-Judge [(Zheng et al., 2023)]. While some prior work has explored this paradigm in different application settings [(Bian et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026)], we are the first to systematically study it in a controlled fashion. Specifically, we investigate how dimensions such as interaction strategy and agent capability affect evaluation accuracy for both pairwise human preference prediction and correctness verification. We further show that these evaluation signals can improve generation using simple and standard methods at both inference and training time, namely inference-time scaling and reinforcement learning with a learned reward model.

To study Interaction-as-a-Judge, we introduce two datasets: ArenaPreferences and ArenaCorrectness. ArenaPreferences is a set of 6,858 agentic code traces across seven different categories of web development (games, simulations, reference-based designs, content-creation tools, brand sites, consumer apps, and data applications). Alongside the agent traces, each data point contains a prompt, two websites generated from the prompt, and labeled human preferences. ArenaCorrectness is a set of 67 high-quality game development traces with 828 conversation turns. We hand-label 412 requirements across various versions of each game as the game develops by interpreting requirements from a user’s prompt and feedback. Requirements are then hand-verified as working or broken depending on if the requirement is successfully implemented.

We find that Interaction-as-a-Judge increases alignment with human preferences for both in-context LLM judges and trained reward models. On ArenaPreferences, adding interaction traces on top of code significantly improves overall in-context LLM judge accuracy by up to 3.5 percentage points (65.6% to 69.1%) and by 1.5 percentage points (67.6% to 69.1%) when compared to adding only static visual information. Fine-tuning a reward model with interaction traces improves accuracy from 68.2% to 70.2% and outperforms in-context LLM judges. We find that higher quality computer-use results in the best overall performance, although even a random heuristic can capture non-trivial gains. On ArenaCorrectness, Interaction-as-a-Judge improves requirement verification accuracy from 77.0% for a code-only Agent-as-a-Judge [(Zhuge et al., 2024)] to 81.6%. Interaction-as-a-Judge also scales with model capability: accuracy increases from 76.4% with GPT 5.6 Luna to 81.6% with GPT 5.6 Sol when each serves as both the CUA and the judge.

We show that these evaluation gains also improve generation. At inference-time, we use Interaction-as-a-Judge in a self-feedback loop where an agent iteratively attempts to repair broken requirements and evaluates its repairs using Interaction-as-a-Judge. Compared with code-only feedback, adding interaction to the feedback mechanism increases the percentage of initially broken requirements successfully repaired within five attempts from 55.4% to 75.5%. We also use a reward model trained solely on interaction traces, without code, to post-train a generation model through reinforcement learning. Relative to using a code-only reward model, this method reduces the build failure rate by 7.2 percentage points and reduces code-context growth—a known problem in code reward models [(Wang et al., 2026)]—by 35.7%, while achieving comparable generation quality. Additionally, we show that websites generated by this post-training recipe attain a 6.7pp higher win rate against the base model.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We study Interaction-as-a-Judge for both preference judgements and correctness verification and release two datasets—ArenaPreferences and ArenaCorrectness—for further research into both Interaction-as-a-Judge and agentic generation of interactive applications more broadly.

  • •

    We show that Interaction-as-a-Judge improves evaluation capabilities. Interaction-as-a-Judge improves overall alignment with human preferences for both in-context LLM judges and trained reward models. Additionally, Interaction-as-a-Judge improves an agent’s ability to verify requirements when compared to a code-only agentic judge.

  • •

    We demonstrate how Interaction-as-a-Judge can be used to improve generation through both inference-time scaling and reinforcement learning training. Interaction-as-a-Judge improves the number of successful repairs in an iterative self-feedback loop and improves trained model quality when used as a reward signal.

    • 2.  Tasks and Datasets

    We study Interaction-as-a-Judge under two complementary settings: human preferences and correctness verification. Human preferences are useful when quality is subjective or difficult to capture with explicit requirements, while correctness verification is appropriate when desired behavior can be specified objectively. In many applications, both are necessary. For example, a software application may satisfy its functional requirements while still differing substantially in usability or visual quality. The inverse can also be true, where an application is visually preferable, but functionally broken. Effective evaluation methods should therefore be able to assess both correctness and preference.

    2.1.  Preferences

    For pairwise preferences, a judge is given a shared prompt and two candidate outputs and must predict which output would be preferred by a human user [(Zheng et al., 2023)]. We focus on pairwise comparisons in this work rather than other preference tasks such as single answer grading (e.g., predicting a Likert scale score), but our approach is not restricted to pairwise comparisons.

    ArenaPreferences.

    We release ArenaPreferences, a dataset of 6,858 pairwise comparisons across seven categories of web development. We collect our dataset from Arena’s Code Arena where real users prompt two hidden models and vote for their preferred website. Each datapoint in ArenaPreferences contains the user’s prompt, both agentic traces, both final websites, and the ground truth user label. We categorize websites into games, simulations, reference-based designs, content-creation tools, brand sites, consumer product, and data applications following the original leaderboard categories. To ensure that the dataset is high quality, we filter such that all ties are removed, websites are built with React, outputs build successfully, outputs contain ≥5% character difference, and users spent at least 60 seconds and up to 10 minutes interacting with the websites. All personally identifiable information (PII) has been de-identified through a PII filtering process. To our understanding, this is the largest collection of pairwise agentic web development traces and websites released for open source use. We provide further dataset details in Appendix B.

    2.2.  Correctness

    We consider two types of correctness verification: requirement verification and requirement discovery. In requirement verification, the judge is given an application, its code, and a set of explicit requirements, such as “Mario must defeat a Goomba when jumping on it.” The judge must determine whether each requirement is working or broken for that application. In requirement discovery, the judge is given the application and its code but no explicit list of requirements. It must first identify the relevant requirements automatically and then determine whether those requirements are working.

    ArenaCorrectness.

    We create ArenaCorrectness, a dataset containing 67 game development traces with 828 user turns and labeled with 412 requirements across 222 versions of various games. We collect our dataset from Arena’s Agent Mode where users can request a random agent to do tasks such as web search, software development, or image generation. We focus on game development as games are highly interactive and also challenging software development tasks [(Chi et al., 2026)].

    To generate requirements from user traces, we analyze the user trace for specific complaints, and extract the complaint into a broken requirement which is linked to a specific version of the game matching when the user complaint occurred. For example, a user complaint indicating that the player falls through platforms would be annotated as a requirement indicating that the player must be able to stand on platforms. We use GPT 5.6 Luna to label, analyze, and then annotate each complaint as a requirement. A human annotator then reviews each game to verify that the requirements are sensible and broken in the game version. To extract working requirement labels, we take our existing broken requirements, and check to see if the user either explicitly confirms a fix or does not revisit this complaint. We use GPT 5.6 Luna for initial annotation and verify via human annotation. In total, we annotate 323 broken and 89 working requirements. We provide further dataset details in Appendix B.

    3.  Interaction-as-a-Judge

    Interaction-as-a-Judge is an evaluation paradigm which uses computer-use interaction traces to improve downstream evaluation accuracy. Interaction-as-a-Judge consists of an interaction component and a judge component. These two components can be either the same LLM, different LLMs, or a mixture of LLMs and other methods. For example, a cheap computer-use heuristic paired with an LLM judge, or an LLM-based CUA paired with a trained reward model.

    3.1.  Interaction

    Following [Koh et al. (2024)], we model interaction with the environment as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). We define the environment as 𝔼=(S,A,Ω,f) where S is the state space, A is the action space, and Ω is the observation space. In our work, oₜ∈Ω is a visual representation of the application (a screenshot), but the Document Object Model (DOM) is also commonly used. An action aₜ∈A induces a deterministic transition f:S×A→S. To interact with the environment, we define an interaction policy π that determines the sequence of actions taken in the environment. Executing π in the environment produces an interaction trace τ=((oₜ,ρₜ,aₜ))ₜ₌₀ᵀ, where oₜ, ρₜ, and aₜ denote the observation, agent reasoning, and action at timestep t, respectively. We allow ρₜ=∅ when no explicit reasoning is produced. Actions include standard computer inputs such as moving the mouse, clicking, and typing—the full action space is in Appendix A.2.

    There are multiple approaches to interact with a software application environment, with the primary trade-off being between adaptivity and inference cost. We consider three interaction strategies that vary in how frequently they query a model and observe the resulting environment state.

    Iterative computer-use.

    The most general approach is to use a computer-use agent that iteratively observes and acts in the environment. We represent the agent as a policy π_θⁱᵗᵉʳ, where at timestep t it selects an action (aₜ,ρₜ)∼π_θⁱᵗᵉʳ(τ_

    One-shot computer-use.

    A sufficiently capable agent could in principle predict the sequence of actions to take from only the initial state without observing the intermediate outcomes of its actions. We represent this as a policy π_θᵒⁿᵉ that, given the initial observation o₀, reasons and then predicts an entire action sequence (a_0:T,ρ)=π_θᵒⁿᵉ(o₀,i) to be executed sequentially in the environment up to timestep T. This requires only a single model query, substantially reducing inference cost [(Wang et al., 2026)], but prevents the agent from adapting when the environment evolves differently from its prediction. When application code c is available, we additionally provide it to the agent for planning, giving (a_0:T,ρ)=π_θᵒⁿᵉ(o₀,i,c).

    Heuristic computer-use.

    The cheapest alternative is to forgo model-based action selection entirely. In this work, we consider a simple heuristic policy πʰᵉᵘʳ that selects an action uniformly at random. To make this interaction more effective, we restrict the policy to a candidate set ℂ(oₜ)⊆A of interactions that are likely to induce meaningful changes in the environment, such as clicking buttons or typing in text boxes, giving aₜ∼πʰᵉᵘʳ(oₜ)=Unif(ℂ(oₜ)). Because this incurs no model inference cost, the policy can select an action after every environment transition. Despite its simplicity, this can produce substantial interaction when ℂ(oₜ) can be effectively identified, but is less effective for environments such as games, where meaningful interactions are difficult to enumerate automatically.

    3.2.  Judging

    After the interaction trace τ is generated, the judge uses the trace to inform its downstream judgement. We study both an off-the-shelf LLM, which we use for both predicting human preferences and verifying correctness, and a trained reward model, which we use for predicting human preferences. A key benefit of using off-the-shelf LLMs is that it allows interaction-as-a-judge to leverage frontier capabilities without needing to train a custom model, which is often infeasible without data and compute resources. However, a reward model trained on sufficient in-domain data can achieve higher accuracy and reduce inference costs.

    LLM Judge.

    For human preferences, an off-the-shelf LLM judge takes in the user request, source code for each website, and an interaction trace for each website and outputs a judgement indicating which website is better. Due to known position bias [(Zheng et al., 2023)], every battle is judged twice with sides swapped (AB and BA) and accuracy is the mean judge-human agreement of both passes. For requirement verification, the judge takes in the user request, the source code, the interaction trace, and a requirements list and labels each requirement as working, broken, or unverifiable. Requirement discovery is similar except no requirement list is given and the judge must output a list of potential requirements itself. For judges that accept video natively, we convert o_0:T∈τ to video; otherwise, we pass in each frame as an image. Actions and reasoning are passed in directly as text sequences.

    Reward Model.

    We train our reward model r_θ by adding a scalar reward head and optimizing over a standard Bradley–Terry loss [(Bradley and Terry, 1952)]:

    L_BT(θ)=-𝔼_(x,y_w,yₗ,τ_w,τₗ)∼D[\logσ (r_θ(x,y_w,τ_w)-r_θ(x,yₗ,τₗ))]

    where x is the user prompt, y_w and yₗ are the source code for the winner and loser respectively, and τ_w and τₗ are the traces. This is similar to standard reward model training [(Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022)] with the addition of interaction trace information.

    4. Interaction-as-a-Judge for Evaluation

    We measure the extent to which evaluation via Interaction-as-a-Judge aligns with human preferences and verified correctness. In our main experiments, all interaction traces consist of 30 actions. For iterative and one-shot computer-use, we use GPT 5.6 Luna with medium reasoning as our computer-use agent. Unless specified, Interaction-as-a-Judge includes code as input. Games differ from other categories due to their real-time input and difficulty in identifying meaningful candidate interactions (e.g., lack of buttons). We describe our harness, action space, and changes for games in Appendix A.

    4.1.  Human Preferences

    We evaluate the effectiveness of Interaction-as-a-Judge for judging human preferences using ArenaPreferences (Figure 3). We compare Interaction-as-a-Judge against two static-evidence judges: a code-only judge and a code and screenshot judge. The code-only judge receives only the code as input, making it functionally identical to either LLM-as-a-Judge [(Zheng et al., 2023)] or a standard code reward model. The code and screenshot judge receives the code and a full page screenshot of the landing page. This same screenshot is also given as input to Interaction-as-a-Judge approaches. We also vary the amount of code received between the full code capped at 32k tokens and just the core App.tsx file to study the effects of code on Interaction-as-a-Judge. Additional information such as category breakdowns can be found in Appendix B.

    To train our reward model, we fine-tune Qwen-3.5-9B [(Qwen Team, 2026)] as our base model and train on a private dataset of 20,160 human preference pairs. This dataset is structurally identical to ArenaPreferences, but is temporally disjoint consisting of data prior to ArenaPreferences, mirroring how data collection occurs in real settings. This means that the reward model is evaluated on newer, more advanced outputs not seen in the training data. For the visual component of the interaction trace, we input it directly as video and freeze the video encoder weights during training.

    For our LLM judge, we use Gemini 3 Flash and GPT 5.6 Luna with xhigh reasoning. Both were chosen due to their cost-effectiveness with Gemini 3 Flash being chosen due to its native video capabilities and GPT 5.6 Luna being the main computer-use model used throughout the paper. To account for ordering bias in LLM-as-a-Judge approaches, we evaluate both orderings and take the average of the results.

    Interaction-as-a-Judge increases alignment with human preferences. We find that for both a trained reward model and an LLM Judge, adding interaction improves judge alignment with human preferences (Figure 3). Adding visual information through a screenshot improves performance over code and adding interaction improves performance further. We see the largest gap in Gemini 3 Flash as a judge where accuracy improves from 65.6%→69.1% between code only and iterative Interaction-as-a-Judge. GPT 5.6 Luna as a judge is the sole exception where we do not see any statistical differences between any approach. We speculate that for pairwise preferences, GPT 5.6 Luna is both optimized for code and also unable to properly utilize visual information given its strong code-only performance and degradation when adding even a single screenshot. Finally, our trained reward model (70.8%) is able to outperform an off-the-shelf LLM judge (69.1%).

    Interaction alone is sufficient information for training a reward model. We find that training a reward model on the interaction traces alone (without code) provides comparable performance to a code reward model. Iterative computer-use without code performs only slightly worse than a code reward model trained on the entire code context (69.0% vs 69.7%), and performs comparably to Interaction-as-a-Judge with code when using Gemini 3 Flash as a judge. This opens doors to training reward models on data where the application is accessible, but code is inaccessible. In general, Interaction-as-a-Judge judgements remain robust as code context decreases, seeing small decreases between seeing the full source code versus only the core App.tsx file. However, both one-shot and heuristic computer-use degrade more compared to iterative computer-use when no code is available.

    Interaction quality affects alignment with human preferences. We observe that iterative computer-use consistently performs the best across all experiments. Due to its ability to respond to new state changes in the environment, iterative computer-use generates the highest-quality traces among the three approaches. Additionally, we find that higher-quality interaction at inference can compensate for lower-quality traces at training time. We take our reward model trained on heuristic computer-use and run inference using iterative computer-use instead. We find that performance increases across almost every single category (Appendix F, Figure 12). The inverse is not true—a reward model trained on iterative computer-use degrades when using heuristic computer-use traces at inference time.

    4.2.  Correctness Verification

    We evaluate Interaction-as-a-Judge on its ability to both verify and discover requirements using our ArenaCorrectness dataset (Figure 4). For requirement verification, we give the agent the code, the game as an interactable application, and the list of requirements which can be either all broken or all working. The agent is asked to label each requirement as working, broken, or unverifiable. For requirement discovery, we focus only on broken requirements and ask the agent to list out all possible broken requirements that require repair without passing in the original requirements list. We compare Interaction-as-a-Judge against a code only Agent-as-a-Judge [(Zhuge et al., 2024)]. We use the GPT 5.6 model family (Luna, Terra, Sol) all with medium reasoning to measure varying model capabilities.

    Interaction-as-a-Judge outperforms code only requirement verification. We find that across all models, Interaction-as-a-Judge performs better than a code only Agent-as-a-Judge. This is primarily because Interaction-as-a-Judge is significantly better at verifying broken requirements (71.1%) compared to a code only Agent-as-a-Judge (63.0%). We find that both approaches perform comparably for verifying working requirements at 92.1% and 91.0% for Interaction-as-a-Judge and code-only Agent-as-a-Judge respectively.

    Interaction-as-a-Judge scales with model capability. We see in Figure 4 that broken requirement verification performance continues to improve as the overall capability of the model improves going from 65.2% with GPT 5.6 Luna to 68.0% with GPT 5.6 Terra and 71.1% with GPT 5.6 Sol.

    5. Interaction-as-a-Judge for Generation

    5.1.  Inference-time Scaling

    We evaluate whether interaction-based self-feedback improves an agent’s ability to repair broken requirements (Figure 5). An effective inference time strategy is to iteratively repair and verify the resulting application. Regardless of implementation capabilities, self-verification capability becomes important for determining whether the repairs are correct or incorrect. We use the games with broken requirements in ArenaCorrectness as our task list. We ask the agent to repair the broken requirements for each game and self-verify across five iterations. We compare Interaction-as-a-Judge against a code only Agent-as-a-Judge and use GPT 5.6 Luna with medium reasoning as the agent for both approaches. After all iterations are complete, we use a more capable model (GPT 5.6 Sol) with Interaction-as-a-Judge and code-only Agent-as-a-Judge to determine if the repairs were successful or not. We measure success per requirement and report repair success rate after each iteration.

    Interaction-as-a-Judge repairs more broken requirements than a code only Agent-as-a-Judge.

    After five iterations, Interaction-as-a-Judge successfully repairs 75.5% of initially broken requirements, compared to 55.4% for code-only self-feedback, an improvement of 20.1 percentage points (Figure 5, middle). This improvement persists even when using GPT 5.6 Sol as a code-only Agent-as-a-Judge (Figure 5, left), highlighting the improvements Interaction-as-a-Judge provides. We see in Figure 5 that Interaction-as-a-Judge not only improves faster but also outperforms the code-only judge within its first iteration. Additionally, the self-reported accuracy gap between GPT 5.6 Luna and GPT 5.6 Sol is significantly less for Interaction-as-a-Judge compared to a code only Agent-as-a-Judge (Figure 5, right), suggesting a lower false positive rate when using Interaction-as-a-Judge.

    5.2.  Training

    We study the potential of Interaction-as-a-Judge at training time to improve downstream performance in generating interactive applications. Specifically, we explore using an interaction-only reward model as the reward signal for post-training via reinforcement learning (Figure 6). We start our training from Qwen-3.5-9B and use DAPO [(Yu et al., 2025)] as our learning algorithm. We use the same interaction only reward model we trained in Section 4.1 and compare against a code only reward model. We use heuristic computer-use to reduce costs and training time. We train on a set of 14k internal prompts that are not used for reward model training which cover all categories except for games as heuristic computer-use has difficulty playing games. We sample 600 examples uniformly from the six categories in ArenaPreferences as our test set. Since our reward model training data is cleaned to remove any failures, failures are out of distribution for both models. To account for this, we add penalties for any website that fails to build or render at all. Detailed hyperparameters can be found in Appendix G.

    Interaction-as-a-Judge allows for successful reinforcement learning training without code.

    Overall, we observe that each model scores higher on their respective reward models, but interaction improves neutral objectives by reducing code generated and increasing successful builds. Code only reward models are known to have length bias [(Wang et al., 2026)]—we observe that training on the interaction reward model generates 35.7% less code than the code reward model. On our test set, Interaction-as-a-Judge also increases the build success rate from 81.3% to 88.5% compared to a code only reward model, reducing the build failure rate by 7.2 percentage points (18.7%→11.5%). We use an internal auto-rubrics based judge based on [Kao et al. (2026)] calibrated to Arena’s data and leaderboard to compare each trained model against Qwen-3.5-9B. Among websites that build and render successfully, the model trained using Interaction-as-a-Judge achieves a win-rate gain of 6.72pp over the base model (Figure 6). Based on our internal calibrations, this is equivalent to over a 50 point increase on Arena’s leaderboard, which would be a statistically significant improvement to the model in Arena’s leaderboard. This evaluation measures quality conditioned on successful generations and therefore understates the benefit of using Interaction-as-a-Judge as a reward signal.
