The ability to train a model via reinforcement learning with an interaction only reward model opens the door to data collection opportunities where application access is available, but code access is not.

    6.  Related Work

    The two most related families of work are other LLM-based judging strategies and existing instances where CUAs have been used for evaluation or generation. Unlike prior work, our work differs from the latter in that interaction is the central focus of our study, rather than one component of a larger pipeline. Specifically, we conduct the first systematic study spanning (i) the effects of varying interaction strategies and model capabilities on evaluation performance, (ii) measuring Interaction-as-a-Judge’s alignment with human preferences and correctness, and (iii) its use for both inference-time scaling and post-training. Below, we outline the connections more specifically.

    LLM-as-a-Judge and Agent-as-a-Judge.

    LLM-as-a-Judge uses language models to approximate human judgments of generated outputs [(Zheng et al., 2023)]. For software development, the evidence needed to judge requirement satisfaction can be distributed across a project and its development history. Agent-as-a-Judge [(Zhuge et al., 2024)] addresses this by gathering and inspecting project files and development trajectories before judging. Interactive applications introduce a further source of evidence: the behavior observed when a user operates the software. Computer-use agents provide a means to collect this evidence by interacting with desktop and web interfaces [(Xie et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Koh et al., 2024)]. Interaction-as-a-Judge extends these judging paradigms to this new source of evidence: rather than inspecting only static artifacts, the judge conditions on traces produced by a computer-use agent operating the application.

    Interactive evaluation.

    Recent works have attempted to use computer-use as part of their evaluation pipeline. ArtifactsBench [(Zhang et al., 2025)] and GameCraft-Bench [(Luo et al., 2026)] ground judgments in heuristically generated screenshots and replayed gameplay, respectively. AppEvalPilot [(Bian et al., 2025)] generates and executes test cases using a computer-use agent and validates its judgments against human assessments of functional requirements. In these works, interaction is used as a method of evaluation rather than the focus of study, and it remains unclear how computer-use model capabilities and methods of interaction affect evaluation performance. WebDevJudge [(Li et al., 2025)], which benchmarks LLM and multimodal judges for web development, illustrates the importance of understanding these capabilities as it finds that its standalone GUI-agent workflow actually underperforms its strongest static judges due to errors arising during planning and execution.

    Interaction feedback and reward learning.

    Interaction evidence can also guide the generation process that produces an application. WebGen-Agent [(Lu et al., 2025)] incorporates screenshot feedback and iterative computer-use testing into website refinement. For reinforcement learning, it sums screenshot-based appearance scores and GUI-testing scores, and introduces Step-GRPO to assign advantages separately to each refinement step. [Wang et al. (2026)] use one-shot computer-use: a model plans the full action sequence upfront, and a rubric-based judge scores the recorded execution to provide training rewards, reducing code-length exploitation compared to static judges. Both approaches obtain their reward signals from model-generated assessments of appearance or functionality. We provide an alternative and potentially simpler solution by training a reward model on human preferences [(Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022)] using interaction traces and then using its predictions as outcome rewards in DAPO.

    7.  Conclusion

    Limitations and Future Work.

    While we study some common approaches to computer-use, we believe that better computer-use models and methods could further improve evaluation and generation, especially considering our observation that better computer-use traces lead to better performance. Currently, one of the biggest bottlenecks to computer-use remains cost. For example, we were mostly limited to experiments with GPT 5.6 Luna as our computer use agent due to pricing. More capable and affordable computer-use agents will likely improve Interaction-as-a-Judge capabilities and are worth studying as well. For training, there is the possibility of using the same model for both generation and computer-use and improving them both simultaneously as better applications and better traces both improve reward modeling scores. We leave this as potential future work.

    Conclusion

    We study Interaction-as-a-Judge, an evaluation paradigm that uses computer-use traces to improve evaluation and downstream generation. We study the use of Interaction-as-a-Judge for both human preferences and correctness verification, releasing two datasets—ArenaPreferences and ArenaCorrectness—to facilitate such studies. We demonstrate how Interaction-as-a-Judge improves alignment with human preferences for both reward model training and LLM judges and improves a model’s ability to label requirements as working or broken. We show how Interaction-as-a-Judge can be used for inference-time scaling through an iterative self-feedback loop. Lastly, we illustrate how you can use a reward model trained on only interaction traces, with no code, as the reward signal for standard reinforcement learning training.

    Acknowledgements

    We thank Yewon Kim for help with designing Figure 1 and Seth Karten for initial discussions that led to this work. This work was supported in part by the National Science Foundation grants IIS1705121, IIS1838017, IIS2046613, IIS2112471, and funding from Datadog. This material is based upon work supported by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research under award number FA9550-25-C-B010 in the amount of $129,600. Any opinions, findings and conclusions or recommendations expressed in this material are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily reflect the views of any of these funding agencies.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix

    Appendix A Interaction Harness and Action Space

    A.1.  Browser Environment and Observations

    For preference prediction, we render each candidate in a separate Chromium browser context using Playwright. Applications run inside an iframe with a 1280×800 viewport and device scale factor one. Mouse coordinates are measured in pixels relative to the top-left corner of the application iframe. Each tool response contains a screenshot of the application, the viewport dimensions, cursor position, held keys, and execution status. The interactive agent receives the original user request and these observations. The one-shot agent additionally receives application source code when constructing its action sequence. For pairwise preferences, the agents explore each candidate independently and then the preference judge subsequently compares the resulting evidence for both candidates. For correctness verification, the same agent explores and judges the candidate in one continuous workflow.

    Interaction budget and timing.

    The main preference experiments use a budget of 30 interaction steps per candidate. A step is one tool invocation, which can itself contain several low-level input events: for example, a click includes a mouse press and release, while press_keys executes a sequence of key presses. The full action space is defined in Table 1. The budget does not count individual keystrokes or model reasoning tokens. The computer-use agent is allowed to exit early if it determines that its goal is complete.

    For games, a JavaScript timing shim wraps animation frames, timers, and application clocks. The game is paused between actions, and ordinary actions advance its clock by 500 ms. Key holds and waits advance the requested duration, capped by the per-step budget. This separates model inference latency from simulated game time. The timing shim advances in small increments so that animation callbacks can execute between inputs. Other web applications run in real time and are allowed to settle after an action.

    A.2.  Action Space

    Table 1 gives the interaction tools shared by iterative and one-shot preference agents. The iterative agent selects tools after observing their results. The one-shot agent emits a list of the same tool names and arguments, which the harness executes sequentially without intermediate model feedback. Typing and scrolling use keyboard events; they do not require separate text-entry or scroll tools.

    Coordinates, interpolation counts, and durations are integer arguments. Key names follow Playwright conventions, including ArrowLeft, Space, Enter, and letter keys.

    A.3.  Heuristic Interaction

    For non-gaming applications, the heuristic enumerates visible, enabled controls in the current viewport: links, buttons, input fields, text areas, selects, summaries, elements with relevant accessibility roles, click handlers, or a non-negative tab index. It excludes hidden and off-screen controls, deduplicates controls by their center coordinates, and retains at most 200 candidates. Candidate controls are sampled uniformly. A text field is clicked before entering a phrase drawn from a fixed small vocabulary, and a PageDown action is sampled with probability 0.12 to reveal additional content. If no candidates are found, the policy falls back to pixel and keyboard actions.

    A.4.  Games

    Games differ from other categories in two ways. First, games often require real-time input, so we construct a web harness that freezes games between interactions and plays actions out for up to 500 milliseconds (i.e., 2 actions per second). Second, since games typically do not have clear interaction candidates (e.g., buttons), heuristic computer-use actions are drawn uniformly from a 12-element action space consisting of four click actions, three key-sequence actions, two key-hold actions, and one each of mouse movement, drag, and double click. Coordinates are sampled uniformly within the viewport. Keyboard actions are sampled from the four arrow keys, Space, Enter, and w, a, s, and d.

    Appendix B Dataset Details and Evaluation Protocol

    The 6,858-battles in ArenaPreferences are selected from a time period of one month (July 2026). They exclude unknown countries and the fixed set of EU27 countries, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, and Liechtenstein. Both candidate source records must declare the react-vite-tailwind template and a successful upstream build. Both sides must contain more than 5% character difference.

    ArenaPreferences contains 6,858 battles across seven categories: 1,288 games, 904 simulations, 753 reference-based designs, 1,020 content-creation tools, 1,246 brand sites, 949 data applications, and 698 consumer applications. The reward-model training and validation ID lists contain 20,160 and 4,460 battles, respectively. The training pool precedes the evaluation pool in time.

    The traces in ArenaCorrectness were collected between June 5 and June 26, 2026. Of its 412 requirements, 323 are labeled broken and 89 working. Each of the 222 game versions corresponds to the application state after a specific user turn of its source trace, and repaired variants of a version are included for requirements that users later confirmed fixed.

    Table 2 reports summary statistics for both datasets. Lines of code exclude lockfiles. Interaction time before voting is measured from the final assistant message to the submitted preference. Trace duration measures wall-clock time from the first to the last message of a trace and includes idle time between user turns.

    Appendix C Category Level Results

    Figures 7 and 8 expand the LLM-judge comparison. Figures 9 and 10 give the corresponding reward-model results under the two code representations. All bars measure agreement with the original human preferences. The overall panels weight categories by their number of battles rather than assigning each category equal weight. The heuristic, one-shot, and iterative conditions add interaction traces to code and screenshot inputs. Bold values indicate positive paired gains over code+screenshot with p<0.05, calculated using a two-sided paired test. Across 28 category comparisons, iterative interaction significantly outperformed code+screenshot in 14, significantly underperformed in one, and showed no statistically significant difference in 13. Across the four approaches, simulations and games show the largest average accuracy gains from iterative interaction over code+screenshot (+2.81 and +1.74 percentage points, respectively). They also show the most consistent statistically significant improvements, with gains significant in four of four approaches for simulations and three of four for games.

    Appendix D Reward-Model Training

    We fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B with a scalar reward head evaluated at a trailing classification token. The language backbone and reward head are trained while the vision encoder is frozen.

    Code representations.

    The full-code comparison allows 100,000 source characters before applying the 32,768-token sequence limit. Its source pipeline removes lockfiles, selects files under the character budget, and orders the selected files from smaller to larger with the main application file placed last. This ordering is specified independently of the test outcomes. The App.tsx comparison restricts the source store to the main application file, with a largest-code-file fallback when that file is unavailable.

    Visual processing.

    Video frames are processed jointly through the native video path with temporal merging and timestamps. In the combined condition, the separate static screenshot precedes the video and trace text. The loader preserves complete visual token blocks when applying the context limit, so source-code availability can decrease as visual evidence occupies more of the sequence. Due to this, code+screenshot+video reaches the token context limit more frequently than code only.

    Appendix E Additional Reward Modeling Experiments

    We report additional reward model training experiments that vary reward-model size, source-code availability, the text accompanying an interaction trace, and the generators represented in training. These experiments use a separate data construction and training recipe. Interaction traces are generated using GPT 5.4 Mini rather than GPT 5.6 Luna. We distinguish them from the main test results throughout.

    E.1.  Shared Setup and Evaluation Populations

    The model-size, source-restriction, and trace-text studies train on 8,640 battles and evaluate on 3,327-battles. All data points are from the gaming category. All models use one epoch, learning rate 2×10⁻⁶, global batch size 32, a frozen vision encoder, and the pairwise reward objective described in Appendix D.

    We use five seeds for the 4B models (42,77,100,200,777) and ten for the 9B and 27B models (42,77,100,200,300,400,500,600,700,777). Tables report means and sample standard deviations across seeds.

    Interaction-as-a-Judge exceeds the code-only condition at all three sizes, by 1.39, 1.55, and 1.61 percentage points, respectively. The 4B and 9B Interaction-as-a-Judge models have similar mean agreement, while the 27B model is higher. Increasing parameter count therefore does not produce a uniform step-by-step improvement within this data and optimization regime. Interaction-as-a-Judge also exceeds the screenshot condition at each size, although the size of the difference varies.

    E.2.  Actions and Reasoning as Judge Input

    To distinguish visual observations from their accompanying text, we train 9B models with four input representations: code alone; code with actions and intermediate reasoning but no images; code with video frames but no trace text; and code with both video and trace text. The visual conditions share the same frames. The text switch changes both training and evaluation inputs; this is not an inference-only removal of text from a model trained to expect it.

    Adding trace text changes mean agreement by only +0.03 points without video and -0.03 points with video. These results provide little evidence that the recorded actions and reasoning, by themselves, explain the improvement in this campaign. This does not imply that the text itself is uninformative in every setting; in our unofficial observations we have seen reward model scores vary depending on changes to the trace text.

    E.3.  Spatial Resolution

    We evaluate spatial resolution in a separate gaming study using Qwen3.5-9B reward models with no source-code input. Models are trained for one epoch with the same settings as before. We vary the token cap.

    Screenshot agreement remains between 64.85% and 65.27% across the tested caps (Figure 11, left). The Qwen3.5-9B video encoder combines every two frames into one temporal block, so a token cap of 128 per block corresponds to a total visual token cap of 128×13=1,664 for a 26-frame trace. Increasing the video spatial budget from 128 to 960 tokens per block raises mean agreement from 68.25% to 69.29%. The screenshot sweep therefore provides little evidence that more spatial detail alone closes the gap to interaction traces in this setting. The video configurations also retain the corresponding action and reasoning text, so this comparison does not isolate motion from every other component of a trace.

    E.4.  Trace-prefix Length

    We separately train the same reward-model architecture with progressively longer prefixes of each recording. The loader retains the first F images in chronological order and the associated action and reasoning text. At five frames per second, a prefix of F frames nominally spans 0.2(F-1) seconds. The spatial budget is held at 960 tokens per temporal block. All configurations use the same 3,327 evaluation battles and ten training seeds as the spatial-resolution sweep.

    Mean agreement increases from 64.37% with the initial frame to 69.29% with the full 26-frame prefix (Figure 11, right). Much of this improvement is already present after four frames (67.84%), with smaller gains from later observations.

    Appendix F Interaction Policies and Generalization

    F.1.  Cross-policy Evaluation on the Preference Benchmark

    We cross-evaluate reward models trained without source code using recordings from different interaction policies (Table 7). Each row fixes the trained reward model and changes the evaluation evidence. The swap includes both the visual observations and the associated trace text. These are exploratory results for one selected model per training policy, rather than averages over the five seeds used in the main reward-model comparison. This earlier cross-evaluation uses the one-shot recordings generated with xhigh reasoning.

    Holding the heuristic-trained model fixed, iterative traces increase aggregate agreement from 67.95% to 68.85%. Conversely, replacing an iterative-trained model’s iterative traces with heuristic traces reduces agreement from 70.07% to 67.29%. For gaming, iterative evidence improves every row: the respective heuristic-to-iterative changes are 70.81%→73.23%, 68.87%→74.01%, and 70.03%→75.02%.

    F.2.  Transfer between Gaming Recording Pipelines

    We fix each code+interaction reward model from Table 5 and replace its original GPT 5.4 Mini recordings with recordings from Qwen3.5-27B. The two evaluation sets share all 3,327 battle IDs and human labels. This comparison uses five trained 4B models and ten each at 9B and 27B, with the same final checkpoint used for both recording conditions within each seed.

    Replacing the recordings reduces mean agreement by 3.12, 2.73, and 2.73 points for the 4B, 9B, and 27B models, respectively indicating that a weaker computer-use agent is likely to result in a lower quality interaction-trace and, as a result, lower accuracy.

    Appendix G Reinforcement-Learning Configuration and Evaluation

    We present our hyperparemeter used for DAPO training. We follow fairly standard DAPO settings and train for 35 steps which is the equivalent of 1 epoch.

item.title: 别人也在动、你不操作世界也变：LLM 当「事件世界模型」能撑到哪一步 ｜ From Single-Actor Environments to Multi-Actor Event Worlds: Can LLMs Be Event World Models?
item.description:
一句话：给全所有角色的动作，微调加数据就能预测得不错；只给自己的动作，别人影响越大就越崩。

要点：

  • 把「多角色各自决策、即使你不行动世界也在演化、只能从事件日志部分观测」的系统形式化为 event world
  • 用人类 Diplomatic 对局与 Polymarket 真实交易构建互补基准：先比较「给 / 不给其他角色动作」的预测差异，再测多步 rollout、对从未发生动作的预测、以及能否帮到 agent 决策
  • 结论：给全所有角色录制的动作时，微调与更多数据都能改善预测；只给智能体自己的动作时，其他角色影响强的场景会明显失败，模型更大、历史更长帮助有限

为什么值得看：要拿 LLM 当玩法或经济系统的世界模型，先要认清它只在「所有参与者的动作都可见」时可靠。做多人游戏模拟时这个边界比精度数字更重要。

中文摘要：世界模型帮助智能体在行动前评估后果，但很多真实系统有多个各自决策的参与者，智能体不行动时世界也会演化，而且只能通过事件日志部分观测。作者把这类系统形式化为「事件世界」，并追问大语言模型能否根据日志与智能体提议的动作预测未来观测。基准分别取自人类 Diplomacy 对局与 Polymarket 的真实交易，用层级化框架先比较给出与不给出其他参与者动作时的预测，再检验多步 rollout、对从未发生动作的预测以及对智能体决策的实际帮助。结果显示：给出所有参与者录制的动作时，微调与更多数据能改善预测；只给智能体自己的动作时，若其他参与者影响很大，模型会明显失手，更大的模型与更长的历史也帮助有限。

From Single-Actor Environments to Multi-Actor Event Worlds:
Can LLMs Be Event World Models?

Abstract

World models help agents assess the consequences of their actions before acting. Many real systems, however, involve multiple actors who make their own decisions, can evolve even when the agent takes no action, and are only partially observed through event logs. We formalize these systems as event worlds and ask whether large language models can predict future observations from the log and the agent’s proposed actions. We build complementary benchmarks from human Diplomacy games and real Polymarket trades. Our hierarchical framework compares prediction with and without other actors’ actions, then tests multi-step rollouts, predictions for actions never taken, and usefulness to agents. Fine-tuning and more data improve prediction when all actors’ recorded actions are given. With only the agent’s action, models struggle when other actors strongly affect the outcome, and larger models and longer histories help little. This gap also limits multi-step prediction and agent decisions, with models overestimating plan success. Yet imagined experience and initialization from world models can still improve policy learning. Anticipating other actors’ actions remains a central challenge for event world modeling. 111 Code: github.com/LingFengGold/EventWorld

1 Introduction

World models simulate how an environment changes in response to an agent’s actions [(Hafner et al., 2025a; Hafner et al., 2025b)]. Such models enable agents to anticipate the consequences of their actions before acting and learn from imagined experience [(Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Gu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026b)]. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have been used as world models in text, web, and tool environments [(Wang et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024; Ruan et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026b; Zuo et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a)]. These studies mainly use environments such as ALFWorld [(Shridhar et al., 2020)], WebShop [(Yao et al., 2022)], and StableToolBench [(Guo et al., 2024b)]. In these environments, the agent is the only decision maker, or actor. We thus refer to them as single-actor environments. They advance only through the agent’s actions and return an observation after each step (Figure 1a).

However, many real systems evolve through the decisions of multiple actors and are only partially observed through event logs. In healthcare, a doctor prescribes medication, but the illness continues to evolve and the patient may miss doses between visits. In a market, a trader places an order, but prices also change as other traders buy and sell, while their beliefs may change as news comes. In an online auction, a bidder makes an offer, but can lose the lead when someone else bids. In each system, we focus on one actor, the agent, whose decisions we aim to support.

We call such systems event worlds (Figure 1b). They are driven by more than one actor, can evolve even when the agent takes no action, and are known only through event logs that reveal part of the underlying state. An event log is a sequence of time-stamped records of actions and observations. An event world model predicts the observation at a chosen time horizon, given the event log and the agent’s proposed actions. The other actors’ actions during this interval are unknown to the agent.

An event world model can help an agent assess the consequences of its actions before acting, especially when testing alternatives in the real system is costly or restricted. Event logs record such systems at scale. However, prediction from event logs remains difficult, because they reveal only part of the state and leave the other actors’ future actions unknown. Event logs also contain heterogeneous records of actions and observations. LLMs have the potential to understand these records. Knowledge from pretraining may also help predict how these systems evolve and how the actors behave. We thus ask: Can LLMs be event world models?

To study this question, we construct two complementary event world benchmarks from human game records of Diplomacy[(Paquette et al., 2019)] and trade logs of Polymarket[(Wang et al., 2026)]. We turn these multi-actor event logs into prediction tasks from one agent’s perspective, separating its actions from those of the other actors. Diplomacy’s rules engine additionally allows us to check the outcomes of actions never taken and evaluate agents beyond the recorded games. Polymarket tests prediction in a real market whose order book is unobserved and for which no engine is available to check actions never taken.

To evaluate comprehensively whether LLMs can serve as event world models, we propose a hierarchical evaluation framework (Figure 2). Each level asks more of LLMs than the level below it. First, we evaluate how well LLMs predict future observations given the event log and every actor’s recorded action (Section 6.1). Second, we provide only the agent’s action alongside the event log, so the models also have to anticipate what the other actors will do (Section 6.2). Third, we test situations not in the event log, such as predicting several steps ahead using the models’ own predictions and assessing the consequences of actions never taken (Section 6.3). Finally, we ask whether LLMs help an agent act by planning, by choosing among candidate actions, or by imagining games for the agent to learn from (Section 6.4).

Our experiments show that (1) fine-tuning and more data improve prediction when every actor’s actions are given. (2) However, given only the agent’s own action, predictions remain less accurate, especially when other actors’ actions have a large effect on the outcome, and this gap remains even with larger LLMs. (3) Rollouts accumulate errors, and fine-tuned LLMs predict the effects of actions never taken far less accurately without the other actors’ actions. (4) The same gap affects agent decisions, with LLMs overestimating plan success and providing less help in choosing actions when only the agent’s action is known. (5) Nevertheless, LLMs as event world models support policy learning through imagined experience and world-model initialization. These findings highlight anticipating the other actors’ actions as the central open problem of event world modeling.

Our main contributions are as follows.

  • (a)

    We define event worlds and event world models, providing a unified formulation for predicting future observations from event logs and an agent’s proposed actions in partially observed systems with multiple actors.

  • (b)

    We construct two complementary benchmarks and propose a hierarchical evaluation framework covering prediction with and without the other actors’ actions, simulation of situations not in the event log, and usefulness to agents.

  • (c)

    We systematically evaluate prompted and fine-tuned LLMs, identifying their capabilities and limitations as event world models and providing empirical insights to guide future research.

    • 2 Related Work

    LLM world models predict future observations and support planning and policy learning in text, web, and tool environments [(Wang et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026b; Zuo et al., 2026; Chu et al., 2026)]. We extend their evaluation from single-actor interaction to multi-actor event logs. Visual world models typically predict frames or trajectories sampled at regular intervals [(Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2025a; Bruce et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2023; Montali et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024)], whereas event logs may record actions and observations at irregular times. Many multi-agent benchmarks generate interactions using LLM agents in predefined environments [(Guo et al., 2024a; Zhu et al., 2025)], while our prediction tasks use human game records and real market logs. Event forecasting predicts future events from historical records [(Shi et al., 2023; Halawi et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2026)]. Our task additionally conditions on the agent’s proposed action. Market and clinical simulators [(Coletta et al., 2022; Li et al., 2025; Mu et al., 2026)] are particularly close, predicting outcomes following trades or treatments. We build on these domain-specific studies with a unified formulation and evaluation, examining how other actors’ unknown actions affect prediction and agent usefulness. More details are in Appendix A.

    3 Problem Definition

    This section formalizes the event world and the agent that acts in the event world, introduces the event world model that serves the agent, and derives two tasks.

    Event World.

    An event world is driven by a set of actors I with |I|≥2, can evolve even when the agent takes no action, and is known only through its event log. Its state Sₜ=(Oₜ,Xₜ) at time t consists of the latest observationOₜ of the world and a hidden part Xₜ, such as the actors’ intentions, unrecorded actions, or the world’s internal conditions. The state evolves as Sₜ₊₁∼P(·|Sₜ,Aₜ₊₁), where Aₜ₊₁ are all actors’ recorded actions at step t+1, possibly none. Actions and observations need not occur at every time step, whereas Xₜ can evolve at every step. Thus, even when the agent takes no action, the state can evolve through the other actors’ actions or through changes in Xₜ alone. The event log Hₜ=(A_≤t,O_≤t) records the actions and observations up to t.

    Agent in an Event World.

    We take the view of one actor i, the agent, defined as

    A:Hₜ→Aⁱₜ₊₁,(1)
    Hₜ=(Aⁱ_≤t, A⁻ⁱ_≤t, O_≤t),

    where Aⁱ_≤t and A⁻ⁱ_≤t are the agent’s own actions and the other actors’ recorded actions up to t. At time t, the agent uses Hₜ to choose its next action Aⁱₜ₊₁, which could be empty, meaning that it waits. The other actors choose theirs at the same time.

    Event World Model.

    An agent chooses Aⁱₜ₊₁ better if it can foresee what its actions lead to. An event world model makes this prediction,

    W:{Hₜ,Aⁱ; Δ}→Ô_t+Δ,

    		(2)

    where Aⁱ=Aⁱ_(t, t+Δ] are the actions the agent proposes in the interval (t,t+Δ], Δ is a time horizon chosen by the modeler, and Ô_t+Δ is the predicted O_t+Δ.

    Two Tasks.

    At each decision pointt, we compare two prediction tasks. In Task S (agent’s action only), the model receives the event log and the agent’s proposed actions, as in Eq. (2). In Task J (joint action), it also receives the other actors’ recorded future actions, A⁻ⁱ=A⁻ⁱ_(t, t+Δ]. Task J tests prediction given the joint action A=(Aⁱ,A⁻ⁱ). For a fixed Δ, the two conditional distributions satisfy

    P(O_t+Δ|Hₜ,Aⁱ)= ∑_A⁻ⁱP(A⁻ⁱ|Hₜ,Aⁱ) P(O_t+Δ|Hₜ,A).

    		(3)

    The first factor describes how the other actors may act, and the second describes the world’s response to the joint action. The gap between the tasks shows how much knowing the other actors’ actions improves prediction.

    4 Event World Benchmarks

    To evaluate how well LLMs predict future observations and support agent decisions, we build two complementary benchmarks from multi-actor event logs (Table 1). Both support prediction of recorded outcomes. Diplomacy additionally provides a rules engine for checking actions never taken and evaluating agents. Polymarket has no such engine, but it tests prediction in a real market where many traders act at any moment.

    Diplomacy.

    Diplomacy is a board game in which seven players move armies and fleets on a map of Europe to capture supply centers. In each round, called a phase, all players write their orders in secret, and the orders are carried out together. Units move and fight in movement phases, beaten units withdraw in retreat phases, and players add or remove units in adjustment phases. The players’ intentions, the hidden part Xₜ, can evolve on their own. Given the current board and all players’ orders, the rules determine the next board Oₜ₊₁.

    Polymarket.

    Polymarket is a market for betting on future events, where a share’s price, between 0 and 1, reads as the chance that the event happens. Traders buy and sell at any moment, and each trade is filled by the waiting offers in the order book, which our trade logs do not show. These offers and the traders’ beliefs, the hidden part Xₜ, may change between recorded trades as news arrives. The same trade can therefore move the price by different amounts, so the price stays uncertain even when every trader’s orders are known.

    Benchmark Construction.

    We turn the raw records into event world benchmarks in two steps. First, we prepare and verify the records. For Diplomacy, we replay the 33,279 games without negotiation from webDiplomacy [(Paquette et al., 2019)] with the rules engine and keep the 99.7% that it reproduces exactly, so the engine can be trusted for any orders. For Polymarket, we take the on-chain trade records [(Wang et al., 2026)], keep the 4,176 markets traded for at least 30 days with at least 5,000 trades, and merge their trades into 79M orders by trader. Second, we turn each event log, produced by all actors together, into samples from one agent’s view. At each decision point t, we choose the agent, rebuild the history Hₜ known at t, and split the actions in (t,t+Δ] into the agent’s Aⁱ and the other actors’ A⁻ⁱ. Task S receives Aⁱ, Task J also A⁻ⁱ, and both predict the same recorded O_t+Δ. The change from Oₜ to O_t+Δ is a transition. In Diplomacy, we select two players at each phase and construct a separate sample from each player’s perspective. In Polymarket, decision points are the moments when a trader places a large order, with this trader as the agent, plus random moments without an agent action. More details about benchmark construction are in Appendix B. This yields 940k transitions from seven-player Diplomacy games and 1.02M one-hour transitions from Polymarket. We split the data by game or market event, with statistics and details in Appendix B.3.

    5 Experimental Setup

    We summarize the world model training and evaluation setup and defer full implementation details to Appendix D. Unless otherwise specified, all experiments follow the default settings below.

    Data.

    The training and test sets contain 849k and 39k transitions in Diplomacy, and 687k and 88k in Polymarket. We fine-tune on 20k samples per world, split evenly between Tasks J and S. To limit evaluation costs, we compare all models on shared test subsets of 1,000 transitions in Diplomacy and 1,333 in Polymarket, unless stated otherwise.

    Input and Output.

    Each decision point is written as text with the current observation Oₜ, optionally the previous K transitions of the log as history (K=0 unless stated otherwise), and the agent’s action, plus the other actors’ actions in Task J. LLMs output only their prediction of the next observation. In Diplomacy, LLMs predict the next board. In Polymarket, LLMs predict future buy and sell prices, the mid-price change, and its uncertainty. Prompts are in Appendix D.1.

    Models.

    We prompt two closed models, GPT-6-Luna and GPT-6-Sol, and fine-tune Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B [(Yang et al., 2025)] (Appendix D.2). Prompting tests whether pretrained LLMs can predict future observations, while fine-tuning tests whether event logs improve their predictions.

    Baselines.

    In Diplomacy, we keep the board unchanged, or apply the given orders literally as if every order succeeded (in Task S only the agent’s own orders). In Polymarket we report a no-change forecast and LightGBM [(Ke et al., 2017)], a gradient-boosted tree model on hand-crafted features of all 687k training points (Appendix D.3).

    Metrics.

    In Diplomacy, exact match (EM) counts a prediction as correct only if the whole next board is right. Since a single wrong unit fails the whole board, F1 also scores units one by one, matching each predicted unit (its player, type, and location) against the true board. In Polymarket, accuracy (Acc) checks whether the model predicts the right direction, that is, whether the mid-price falls, does not change, or rises. The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) [(Gneiting and Raftery, 2007)] evaluates the price-change distribution constructed from the model’s outputs (Appendix D.4). We label Diplomacy movement phases and Polymarket hours with at least two orders from other traders as high-interaction, and the rest as low-interaction.

    6 Can LLMs Be Event World Models?

    We evaluate LLMs with four questions (Figure 2). Q1 tests prediction given every actor’s action, while Q2 provides only the agent’s action. Their performance gap shows how unknown actions affect prediction. Q3 tests predictions over multiple steps and for actions never taken, and Q4 tests whether LLMs as event world models help an agent act. We compare both input conditions in Q3 and Q4 to examine how this gap affects simulation and agent decisions.

    6.1 Can LLMs Learn the World’s Dynamics Given Every Actor’s Action?

    Given the event log and joint action (Task J), we evaluate predictions of the next board in Diplomacy and the price changes in Polymarket against the recorded outcomes.

    LLMs learn the world’s dynamics from the log, building on pretraining. As shown in Table 2, even Qwen3-1.7B, fine-tuned on 20k transitions, reaches 59.7% EM in Diplomacy, well above the best zero-shot prompted LLM. In Polymarket it reaches 66.1% Acc, close to LightGBM, which is trained on all 687k transitions. The log alone is not enough either. As shown in Table 13, the same Qwen3-1.7B architecture trained from random initialization on the same 20k transitions reaches only 32.0% EM in Diplomacy.

    Data matters more than model size. As shown in Figure 3, Task J EM in Diplomacy and Acc in Polymarket rise steadily as the number of training transitions grows. However, larger models improve performance much less than more data does.

    Fine-tuned LLMs learn how much the world changes as time passes. An LLM that has learned this should know that the longer the horizon Δ, the more likely the world has changed. Figure 4a tests this in Polymarket, where the horizon can vary. It compares each model’s predicted probability that the price does not change with the observed frequency, the share of test windows in which the price did not change. The Qwen3-1.7B, which saw all three horizons in fine-tuning, matches the observed frequency at each of them. Prompted LLMs overestimate it and the gap grows with the horizon.

    What fine-tuned LLMs learn transfers to unseen settings of the same world. If the models learned the dynamics rather than the training games and markets, they should stay robust when the setting changes. On two-player Diplomacy games, the fine-tuned LLMs keep a clear margin over applying the orders literally. On markets that open after the training period, they keep or improve their Acc, while LightGBM falls behind them (Appendix E.5).

    6.2 Can LLMs Learn the World’s Dynamics Given Only the Agent’s Own Action?

    An agent does not know the others’ actions in advance. Without them (Task S), an LLM also has to anticipate the other actors.

    Not knowing the other actors’ actions hurts most when their actions, rather than the agent’s, determine the next observation. Without their actions, the fine-tuned Qwen3-8B falls from 65.1% to 20.8% EM in Diplomacy (Table 2). On high-interaction transitions no model beats applying the agent’s own orders and assuming the others do nothing. By contrast, in Polymarket the drop is smaller, because the agent’s own large order may drive the price. As shown in Figure 4b, knowing the other traders’ orders raises Qwen3-1.7B’s Acc substantially when the agent is idle, but barely when its large order drives the price. In Diplomacy retreat phases, the gain roughly doubles when the agent is idle. In adjustment phases, the gain is large either way, because the other players issue most of the orders whether the agent acts or is idle.

    The gap remains with history, more data, and larger models. As shown in Figure 5, history raises Task S a little for Qwen3-1.7B in both worlds and more for GPT-6-Sol in Diplomacy, while GPT-6-Luna gets worse. Asking models to also predict the other actors’ behavior improves the fine-tuned models’ Task S scores only slightly, from 20.8% to 22.9% EM in Diplomacy for Qwen3-8B and from 59.9% to 60.4% Acc in Polymarket for Qwen3-1.7B (Table 17). The gains are larger for GPT-6-Sol, from 7.5% to 11.9% in Diplomacy and from 48.5% to 52.6% in Polymarket. As shown in Figure 3 and Table 12, more data improves Polymarket Task S overall. In Diplomacy, Task S improves mainly on low-interaction transitions. Larger models help little in either world. For the fine-tuned LLMs and GPT-6-Sol, Task S with history also remains below Task J in both worlds.

    6.3 Can LLMs Simulate Situations Not in the Event Log?

    An agent uses a world model to try out its options before acting. This requires predictions in two situations not in the event log: the observations several steps ahead, where the model builds on its own predictions rather than on recorded observations (a long-horizon rollout), and the outcome of an action the agent never took. A rollout can be checked against later observations in the log, but logs alone cannot establish the effect of an action never taken [(Oberst and Sontag, 2019)]. We use the Diplomacy engine to check predictions for alternative orders. In Polymarket, Appendix G.3 compares predicted responses to modified orders with average price responses in the logs.

    LLMs’ errors accumulate during a rollout, especially when the other actors’ actions are not given. After a five-step rollout in Diplomacy, most models have EM≈0, so we report F1. As shown in Table 3, when fed their own predictions in Task J, the prompted LLMs lose much more F1 than the fine-tuned LLMs. Fine-tuning therefore reduces error accumulation. However, in Task S every model loses much of its F1 as it also has to anticipate the other actors’ actions. In Polymarket, the rollout recursively predicts prices while reading trading activity from the log each hour. The fine-tuned LLMs’ direct 24-hour forecasts are more accurate than their rollouts even with these activity updates.

    Without the other actors’ actions, LLMs misjudge the effect of an action never taken. Given those actions, the fine-tuned LLMs misjudge it far less. An LLM that has learned the world’s dynamics should still predict the next observation accurately when the agent’s action is changed. However, where the new orders do not change the next board, the fine-tuned LLMs still predict a change in more than half of the cases in Task S (spurious, Table 4). Giving the other players’ recorded orders should then remove much of the error from imagining their orders wrongly, or differently for the agent’s original and new orders. It sharply raises the fine-tuned LLMs’ F1 and sharply lowers their spurious rate. The prompted GPT-6 models, in contrast, do not improve, and they predict a change in most of the cases where there is none. The log teaches how the world responds to a fixed joint action. When the model has to imagine the others, its prediction for an action never taken therefore mixes the effect of that action with the effect of wrong or inconsistent imagined orders.

    6.4 Can LLMs as Event World Models Help an Agent Act?

    So far we have evaluated LLMs as world models on their own. We further ask whether LLMs can serve an agent and help it perform better. Answering this requires an engine that executes the agent’s actions, so we use Diplomacy. The agent plays against six other actors controlled by DipNet [(Paquette et al., 2019)], a deterministic policy trained to imitate human players. The agent succeeds if it ends 10 phases with at least its initial number of supply centers.

    Without the other actors’ actions, plans look more successful inside an LLM than they turn out to be in the engine. An LLM can serve an agent as a simulator in which the agent tries out its plans before acting. If an LLM captured how the opponents play, plans made inside it would work as well in the engine. The agent plays each game in the engine and inside the LLM, and its orders from inside the LLM are replayed in the engine. As shown in Figure 6b, in Task S the agent succeeds more often inside the fine-tuned LLMs and GPT-6-Sol than in the engine. However, replayed in the engine, these plans succeed far less often than plans made in the engine. Even in Task J, replayed plans succeed less often (Figure 6a).

    Choosing among candidate actions with an LLM helps mainly when the joint action is known. At every movement phase, the agent samples B candidate actions, the LLM predicts the board after each, and the agent chooses the best one. As shown in Figure 7a, in Task J the agent gains more supply centers as more candidates are offered. With B=10 candidates, Qwen3-1.7B trained on 320k transitions nearly matches the engine. However, in Task S the agent gains almost nothing with the same LLM. The LLM’s predicted gain grows with more candidates while the realized gain does not, so it overrates its pick (Figure 7b).

    Imagined games can replace part of the real games, but not all of them. We train a Qwen3-1.7B policy by behavior cloning on the agent’s orders in successful games, played in the engine or inside the 320k LLM given only the agent’s orders. As shown in Table 5, 1k imagined games train a policy nearly as good as 1k real games. Adding 1k imagined games to 1k real ones also helps nearly as much as 1k more real games. However, 2k imagined games train a weaker policy than 2k real games, so more imagined games add less than more real ones (Appendix H).

    Starting the policy from a world model helps, and more so from a better one. Recent work [(Zhang et al., 2025)] suggests that exposing a model to environment dynamics before policy learning gives it a useful inductive bias. A world model can thus also serve as the starting point of the agent’s policy. As shown in Table 5, a policy cloned from 1k real games does better when initialized from the 20k world model, and better still from the 320k one.

    7 Conclusion

    We define event worlds and introduce two complementary benchmarks, Diplomacy and Polymarket. Our evaluation covers prediction, simulation beyond the log, and usefulness to agents. Fine-tuned LLMs learn world responses given all actors’ actions, but struggle when only the agent’s action is known. More data and larger models do not close this gap. In Diplomacy, this limitation also affects predictions for alternative actions and agent decisions. These findings highlight modeling other actors’ unknown actions as a central direction for improving event world models.

    Limitations

    Our study has two main limitations. First, it covers only Diplomacy and Polymarket, and the models receive observations prepared from event logs. Broader domains and evaluation directly from raw event streams are needed to assess how well the findings generalize. Second, we verify the outcomes of alternative actions and evaluate agents only in Diplomacy, using its rules engine. The agent experiments use fixed opponent policies, so their findings may not extend to interactions with humans or opponents that learn over time. The Polymarket intervention analysis relies on associations in observed trades and does not establish causal effects.

    Potential Risks

    Our experiments show that LLMs can overestimate plan success when other actors’ actions are unknown. Relying on these predictions without further checks could lead to poor decisions, especially if the models are applied to financial or medical settings. Applications should be evaluated using only information available before acting and should make prediction uncertainty clear.
